Annie Besant's Esoteric Christianity, in its second edition of 1905, looks for the deep truths she believed lay beneath the surface of Christian teaching. Published by the Theosophical Publishing Society in London and Benares, it opens with Clement of Alexandria on mysteries before the mysteries.

Besant argues that popular zeal spread Christian teachings so widely that their inner meaning was vulgarized and lost. The chapters trace that hidden wisdom through symbols, sacraments, and the lives of great teachers, offering a Theosophist reading of the faith for readers open to its mysteries.
26948-modern-women-and-what-is-said-of-t:
Modern Women and What Is Said of Them, published in New York in 1868 with an introduction by Mrs. Lucia Gilbert Calhoun, reprints a series of articles from London's Saturday Review. The essays on woman had already been widely reprinted and hotly discussed by readers of both sexes.

The volume leaves its authorship open, noting that the names guessed in public probably had nothing to do with the papers. What it preserves is the debate itself: able, sharp Victorian writing on women's place, answered and argued over in the journals of two countries.
26950-humorous-ghost-stories:
Edited by Dorothy Scarborough, a Columbia lecturer, this 1921 anthology collects ghost stories meant to amuse rather than frighten. Its centerpiece is Oscar Wilde's Canterville Ghost, in which an American family refuses to be scared by the ghost of an English manor.

Other tales come from Gelett Burgess, Ellis Parker Butler, and Frank R. Stockton, in which ghosts are outwitted, debated, or treated as a nuisance rather than a terror. Scarborough's introduction frames the joke at the heart of each piece, making the book a light entry point to the supernatural tale.
26993-the-copper-princess-a-story-of-lak:
Kirk Munroe's 1898 boys' adventure The Copper Princess is set among the mines of Lake Superior, with Harper and Brothers illustrations by W. A. Rogers. Tom Trefethen gets a startling introduction, Peveril ties Blacky's record, and a varsity stroke meets adverse fortune.

Later chapters bring Darrell's Folly, a battle with smugglers, and a sea fight on the lake. Then comes the first news of the Copper Princess herself, glimpsed as a girlish figure on a cliff face. Mike Connell comes to the rescue in one chapter, and Peveril is taken for a ghost in another. Munroe mixes mining life, chases, and rescues in the brisk style of his Mates series.
26995-montezuma-s-castle-and-other-weird:
Charles B. Cory's Montezuma's Castle and Other Weird Tales, published in New York in 1899, collects strange stories by the author of Dr. Wandermann and Hunting and Fishing in Florida. The title tale and its companions trade in ghosts, odd bargains, and voices from beyond.

One story lets a dead man talk back, threatening to mark squares on the living with chalk and play hop-scotch on him, and warning that the living too must die sometime. Cory writes his weird tales with a sportsman's plain voice, letting the uncanny arrive without ceremony.
27000-what-the-moon-saw-and-other-tales:
Hans C. Andersen's What the Moon Saw and Other Tales, translated by H. W. Dulcken and published by Routledge in 1866, serves as a sequel to the 1864 Stories and Tales. Eighty illustrations by A. W. Bayes, engraved by the Dalziel brothers, picture tales such as Waldemar Daa and his daughters.

The preface explains the mix: children's tales sit beside graver stories with deeper meaning, meant for children of a larger growth. Readers get Andersen's fancy and instruction together, in the simple form that made his tales travel the world. The two volumes together formed the most complete collection of Andersen's tales published in Britain.
27025-old-familiar-faces:
Theodore Watts-Dunton's Old Familiar Faces, published in 1916, gathers recollections of friends that he had contributed to The Athenæum. Watts-Dunton, slow to write and slower to publish, had meant to collect them for years before his death.

The chapters recall George Borrow, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Christina Rossetti, Dr. Gordon Hake, and Lord de Tabley, among others. Visitors to his house at The Pines, at the foot of Putney Hill, knew his keen interest in life and letters, and these portraits preserve it at first hand.
27050-de-canibus-britannicis-of-englishe:
De Canibus Britannicis, Of Englishe Dogges, pairs John Caius's Latin treatise on British dogs with Abraham Fleming's English translation, both from the 1912 Cambridge edition of Caius's complete works. Caius wrote as a letter to the naturalist Gesner, sorting the dogs of Britain by kind and use.

The volume adds a combined text, giving Latin and English in small alternating segments, with the great table of the original broken into five smaller dialls in translation. For readers of natural history, it is the classic survey of Tudor dogs: hunters, herders, and house dogs of the realm.
27056-louis-xiv-makers-of-history-series:
John S. C. Abbott's Louis XIV, in the Makers of History series from Harper and Brothers, tells the Sun King's life for young readers. The chapters run from birth and childhood and the boy-king through matrimonial projects, the marriage of the king, and festivities of the court.

Later chapters cover death in the palace, the war in Holland, Madame de Maintenon, and the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. The book closes with intrigues, wars, and the last days of Louis XIV, with engravings of Blois, Fontainebleau, and the palaces of his reign.
27065-a-manual-or-an-easy-method-of-mana:
John M. Weeks of Salisbury, Vermont, offers an easy method of managing bees in this 1837 second edition, promising the most profitable manner for the owner. His plain, concise rules aim above all at one enemy: the European moth, which had crossed to America and wrecked whole districts.

Weeks argues that bee culture, the keeping of Apis Mellifica, had been too long neglected because the moth's depredations drove keepers away. His infallible rules to prevent destruction by the moth, tested by experience, tell any careful owner how to keep a colony strong, housed, and paying.
27085-rootabaga-stories:
Carl Sandburg's Rootabaga Stories, published by Harcourt, Brace in 1922 with illustrations by Maud and Miska Petersham, invents a prairie fairyland for children. The stories tell how the Zigzag Railroad was found and how the village of Cream Puffs blew away and was brought back. Five rusty rats help in finding a new village.

Other tales follow the Potato Face Blind Man, the pigs with bibs on, and a gold buckskin whincher that turns hats, mittens, and shoes to popcorn. Sandburg's Rootabaga country, with its villages of Liver-and-Onions and Cream Puffs, remains a classic of American nonsense for the young.
27090-great-pirate-stories:
Great Pirate Stories, edited by Joseph Lewis French and first printed in November 1922, packs two volumes into one. Its contents open with The Piccaroon from Michael Scott's Tom Cringle's Log and the capture of Panama in 1671 from John Esquemeling's Buccaneers of America.

James Fenimore Cooper supplies the Malay proas, Samuel Purchas the fight of the Exchange of Bristol with Algiers pirates, and Daniel Defoe the daughter of the Great Mogul. Barbarossa, king of the corsairs, closes the roll, with his motto to Charles V: king of the land, but I am king of the sea.
27137-the-scholfield-wool-carding-machin:
Grace L. Rogers's The Scholfield Wool-Carding Machines, Smithsonian paper 1, tells how carding came to America. First among textile inventions came the flying shuttle, then spinning devices, and lastly machines to card raw fibers for spinning and weaving.

John and Arthur Scholfield arrived in the United States in 1793 with knowledge of building a successful wool-carding machine, and Morse recommended them to wealthy men of Newburyport. An original machine, built between 1803 and 1814, anchors the paper, which traces the Newburyport Woolen Manufactory and a new industry. Rogers served as curator of textiles at the National Museum. The machine on show bore catalogue number T11100.
27143-the-cavern-of-the-shining-ones:
Hal K. Wells's science-fiction story The Cavern of the Shining Ones follows Don Foster on Layroh's expedition through the Mojave desert. Layroh hires husky down-and-outers for a plan made ages past, and his tent, pitched apart on a rise, hums with scientific mystery at night.

Foster wakes from a nightmare of a giant blue-bottle fly to a real droning buzz from Layroh's tent, after a week crossing a thirty-mile stretch of desert. The cavern's wonders wait below: boxlike crystal cells with gelatinous bodies, pear-shaped and glowing with pale, ever-changing opalescence.
27149-italian-harpsichord-building-in-th:
John D. Shortridge's Italian Harpsichord-Building in the 16th and 17th Centuries, Smithsonian paper 15 of 1970, studies instruments from the Hugo Worch Collection in the United States National Museum. Harpsichord making flourished in Italy through both centuries, yet the Italian instruments stayed simpler than North European ones.

They stayed simpler, without a second manual or the usual array of stops, and mid-sixteenth-century examples can hardly be told from those made around 1700. Shortridge describes typical examples in detail, with illustrations, and explains puzzling variations in keyboard ranges and vibrating string lengths. Shortridge served as associate curator of cultural history at the National Museum. The paper runs from page 93 to page 107 of Bulletin 225.
2715-the-real-thing-and-other-tales:
Henry James gathers tales in this 1893 Macmillan volume, issued for circulation in India and the British Colonies. The title story studies artists, models, and the difference between the real thing and its imitation, a theme James knew from life.

Other tales follow writers, painters, and society folk caught between art and commerce, truth and pose. James writes with his late subtlety, in sentences that turn like conversations. The book rewards readers who like fiction about fiction, and about the price of being genuine. James's artists and models debate what truth in art requires.
27164-seven-and-nine-years-among-the-cam:
Seven and Nine Years Among the Camanches and Apaches, an autobiography published at Jersey City in 1874, tells Eastman's years as a captive. The chapters run from the capture and a strange adventure through the Indian town, the torture, and Wa-ko-met-kla, to a new vocation and the mystery bag.

Eastman, pariah of the little community, performed menial tasks under suspicion and ill-treatment, while Mrs. Eastman's story runs through many chapters. Buffalo dances and hunts, a grizzly treeing, and a war party fill a narrative of endurance among the Comanche and Apache.
27182-more-peers-verses:
H. Belloc's More Peers, with pictures by B. T. B., published by Duckworth, continues his satire of the peerage in verse. Lord Roehampton strains a vocal chord shouting at an election, and Lord Henry Chase wins a libel case against the Daily Howl, giving his small damages to a hospital.

Other peers follow: Calvin of Peebles, Heygate of Bayswater, the Earl of Epsom, Lord Finchley, Ali-Baba of Salonika, Lord Hippo, Uncle Tom of Maarfontein, and Lucky, Earl and then Duke of Bradford. Belloc's rhymes are sharp, funny, and merciless to rank.
27189-bethink-yourselves:
Leo Tolstoy's Bethink Yourselves, published by Ginn in 1904 for the International Union, was reprinted from the London Times. It opens with a cry: again war, again sufferings necessary to nobody, again fraud and brutalization. Buddhists, whose law forbids killing even animals, face Christians professing brotherhood and love, yet acting as wild beasts on land and sea.

Tolstoy, translated by V. Tchertkoff, asks how men separated by thousands of miles seek each other out to kill, torture, and mutilate. The tract pleads with readers to wake from the dreadful reality of war and remember the law they profess.
27190-pussy-and-doggy-tales:
E. Nesbit's Pussy and Doggy Tales, published by Dent in 1899 with illustrations by L. Kemp-Welch, divides its animal stories in two. Pussy tales include Too Clever by Half, The White Persian, A Powerful Friend, The Selfish Pussy, Meddlesome Pussy, and Nine Lives.

Doggy tales follow with Tinker, Rats, The Tables Turned, A Noble Dog, The Dyer's Dog, and The Vain Setter. A kitten argues with Dolly over whether it was born white, showing its claws when imagination fails, in Nesbit's funny, unsentimental voice for children who know cats and dogs.
2721-eric-brighteyes:
H. Rider Haggard sets this saga in Iceland, opening with Asmund the priest finding Groa the witch, and Eric telling his love to Gudruda in snow on Coldback. Asmund bids Eric to his Yule feast, Eric comes down Golden Falls, and Eric wins the sword Whitefire.

Betrothals, feuds, and a fight with Skallagrim the Baresark on Mosfell follow, in the manner of the old sagas Haggard loved. The prose is archaic and bold, full of snow, blood, and oath keeping. The novel stands as Haggard's most Norse romance, and a tribute to the saga age.
27248-the-raid-on-the-termites:
Paul Ernst's The Raid on the Termites, a complete novelette, shrinks two men to ant size and sends them, armed with splinters of steel, into a termitary. The mound squats a yard high and three and a half across in a grassy grove, like an enormous inverted soup plate.

Dennis Braymer saws with delicate care into the hard cement near the rounded top, seeing inside a dark world like Dante's second Inferno, peopled by blind and terrible demons. Denny bounds free and drives his spear home again and again, in a pulp adventure of scale, courage, and horror.
27259-a-soldier-in-the-philippines:
N. N. Freeman's A Soldier in the Philippines, published in 1901, gives the Spanish-American War from a private's point of view. Needom Freeman, in the regular army during 1898 to 1900, was born at Barrettsville, Dawson County, Georgia, on September 25, 1874.

Freeman notes that officers' accounts dominate war writing, while a private's ideas, lacking the prestige of office, receive little credit. His memoir runs from farm work and village school to Philippine fighting, where foes under a white flag scheme seized hidden rifles to kill officers, until soldiers fired regardless of the flag.
27265-the-wagnerian-romances:
Gertrude Hall's The Wagnerian Romances, published by John Lane in 1907 and dedicated to John Sanburn Phillips, retells Wagner's operas in prose. Parsifal opens the book, followed by the Ring of the Nibelung: The Rhine-Gold, The Valkyrie, Siegfried, and The Twilight of the Gods.

The Master-Singers of Nuremberg, Tristan and Isolde, Lohengrin, Tannhäuser, and The Flying Dutchman complete the set. Hall recounts Titurel's keeping of the chalice and spear, the temple of Monsalvat above Gothic Spain, and the Norns spinning by Brünnhilde's sleep as the gods' end approaches.
27284-the-talking-horse-and-other-tales:
F. Anstey, author of Vice Versa, published this set of humorous tales in a second edition in London in 1892. The title story opens on a wet July afternoon on the train to Sandown Park. There the narrator meets a mild, horsey-dressed man who turns out to have a most unusual horse to talk about.

Other tales in the volume include a good little girl, a greedy dog named Don, a matter of taste, and a canine Ishmael, each told with the same dry comic touch. Animals, children, and grown-ups swap roles and get their comeuppance in turn. Readers looking for light Victorian fantasy with a sharp edge will find the stories still easy to enjoy.
27297-path-flower-and-other-verses:
Olive T. Dargan's Path Flower and Other Verses was published in 1914 by Dent in London and Scribner's in New York. It gathers lyrics from Path Flower and The Piper to To a Hermit Thrush, Thanksgiving, and The Road. La Dame Revolution, The Rebel, and These Latter Days sit beside Abnegation, The Little Tree, and The Game.

A ballad, a dirge, a poem to Moina, and verses at the grave of Heine and to a lost comrade follow. To Sleep addresses sleep as a lover taking the weary light into dusk arms, in Dargan's measured, musical verse of nature, memory, and quiet grief.
27312-nero-makers-of-history-series:
Jacob Abbott wrote this life of the Roman emperor Nero as part of his Makers of History series, in a Harper edition that carries an 1881 copyright on an 1853 original. Abbott promises in his preface to follow the ancient accounts exactly, adding no incident, however small, and putting no words in a speaker's mouth without express authority from the sources.

The narrative follows Nero's life and actions as they have come down from ancient times, told in clear prose for general readers. Readers should expect a story drawn from old histories rather than a modern critical study. As an entry point to Rome's most notorious emperor, it remains readable and direct.
27374-a-young-man-in-a-hurry-and-other-s:
Robert W. Chambers, author of The King in Yellow and Cardigan, published this illustrated set of short stories with Harper and Brothers in New York and London in October 1904. The title story takes its motto from Labiche, in French: I am a young man in a hurry, but modest.

That young man bursts from the offices of the Florida and Key West Railway Company at ten minutes before five, suitcase in one hand and umbrella in the other, and speeds away. Other stories in the set include A Pilgrim, The Shining Band, The Fire-Warden, The Market-Hunter, and Marlitt's Shoes. Chambers writes light, romantic tales with a deft, amused touch.
2741-the-borgias-celebrated-crimes:
April 8, 1492, in a Vatican bedroom, opens this Celebrated Crimes history of the Borgias. The prologue opens on April 8, 1492, in a bedroom of the Vatican, as Rodrigo Borgia moves toward the papacy that will make his family infamous.

Pope Alexander VI, his son Cesare, and his daughter Lucrezia preside over murder, simony, and splendor in Renaissance Rome. Gusto turns chronicle into dark romance, and the Vatican scenes glitter with menace. The book remains the classic popular history of a family whose name became a byword for corruption. Dumas spares neither pope nor prince in his telling.
27411-the-house-with-the-mezzanine-and-o:
Anton Tchekoff's stories appear here in English translated by S. S. Koteliansky and Gilbert Cannan, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in August 1917. The volume gathers seven stories, headed by The House with the Mezzanine, a painter's story, and including Typhus, Gooseberries, In Exile, The Lady with the Toy Dog, Goussiev, and My Life.

The title story opens seven years back, with the painter idle on a landowner's estate. He sleeps in a pillared hall where the chimney moans even in calm weather and the house rocks in a storm. Tchekoff's quiet observation of Russian country life, its talk, and its wasted afternoons runs through the whole set. It is a fine introduction to his short fiction.
2742-cenci-celebrated-crimes:
Dated 1598, this entry in Dumas's Celebrated Crimes turns to the Cenci family of Rome, whose name became a byword for a father's tyranny. A visitor to Rome who seeks shade under the tall pines of the Villa Pamphili will descend toward the Janiculum by a charming road, and there the tale begins.

Beatrice Cenci, her tyrant father, and a murder born of abuse drive one of history's most famous trials. Romantic fire turns records into drama here, and the trial scenes carry the horror. The story remains a harrowing classic of crime, family horror, and justice in Renaissance Rome.
2743-massacres-of-the-south-1551-1815-ce:
Nearly three centuries of religious killing in southern France fill this Celebrated Crimes volume, spanning 1551 to 1815. The reader whose memory reaches back to the Restoration will recall a France still bleeding from religious war.

Catholics and Protestants slaughtered each other across the Midi for nearly three centuries, in towns like Nimes and Avignon. Partisan fire chronicles mob murder, reprisal, and royal indifference across the Midi. The book stands as a grim history of sectarian hatred, and of its long French shadow. Dumas counts the cost in villages, churches, and broken families.
2744-mary-stuart-celebrated-crimes:
Some royal names are predestined to misfortune, Dumas warns at the start of this Celebrated Crimes volume on Mary Stuart, dated 1587. Dumas begins with that warning, and in France the name Henry carries poison, while Mary's own name carries tragedy.

From her French girlhood to her English prison and scaffold, Mary moves through plots, lovers, and rival queens. Sympathy for the doomed queen and fire for her enemies mark the telling. The book offers a romantic history of a life that still divides readers, four centuries on. Dumas writes her fall as high tragedy, not cold chronicle.
27449-border-ghost-stories:
Howard Pease, author of Tales of Northumbria and The Lord Wardens of the Marches, published these Border ghost stories in London with Erskine Macdonald in 1919. Pease inscribed them to the memory of Sir Walter Scott, tutelary genius of the borderland, and signed his dedication from Otterburn Tower in Northumberland in April 1919.

The tales belong to the country between England and Scotland, where old castles, battlefields, and border law give ghosts a natural home. Pease draws on Scott himself, citing Demonology and Witchcraft and the Woodstock tale of Funny Joe. Readers who like their ghosts with history attached will find the border a fitting haunt.
2745-karl-ludwig-sand-celebrated-crimes:
A German student with a dagger opens this Celebrated Crimes portrait of Karl Ludwig Sand, murderer of Kotzebue in 1819. Sand, a young German student fired by nationalist dreams, murdered the writer August von Kotzebue in 1819, believing him a traitor to Germany.

Idealistic youth gives way to assassin, trial, and scaffold, and the telling holds both sympathy and horror. The murder shocked Europe and brought repression down on German universities. The book remains a classic portrait of political fanaticism in a young man. His scaffold speech made him a martyr to German students.
27458-aeschylus-prometheus-bound-and-the:
Theodore Alois Buckley translated these two tragedies of Aeschylus literally, with critical and illustrative notes, in a Philadelphia edition from David McKay in 1897, with an introduction by Edward Brooks Jr. Prometheus Bound gives the Titan chained for defying Zeus, and The Seven Against Thebes gives the assault of seven champions on the city.

Brooks introduces Aeschylus, born at Eleusis in 525 B.C., son of Euphorion, who first appeared as a tragic writer in 499 B.C., won a prize in 484, and fought at Marathon in 490 and Salamis in 480. The curious tale of his death at Gela in 456, when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head, closes the sketch. The volume suits readers new to Greek tragedy.
2746-urbain-grandier-celebrated-crimes:
Loudun in November 1631 opens this Celebrated Crimes account of Urbain Grandier, a priest accused of sorcery. On Sunday, November 26, 1631, great excitement seized Loudun, and a priest stood accused of sorcery, demonic possession, and a pact with the devil.

Grandier's trial, with nuns, exorcists, and Cardinal Richelieu's agents, became a byword for judicial murder. Indignation drives the narrative, turning documents into a story of power crushing a man. The book remains a classic account of witch panic and political revenge. Loudun's devils and judges share the blame in Dumas's telling. The nuns' possessions and the exorcists' theater made the trial a spectacle.
27464-a-scientist-rises:
D. W. Hall wrote this short science-fiction tale, which opens on a summer day. The sky over New York is unflecked by clouds and the city lies like a vast oven under pouring heat. In Washington Square, children splash in the fountain while mothers, tramps, and out-of-works lounge listlessly on the hot benches.

Then a man walks out of a house on the north side of the square with a calm, steady stride, and onlookers gaze in surprise. He is a giant, at least eleven feet in height, well-formed and in perfect proportion, and he steps over the railing onto the grass. Hall's epigraph calls the giant's face that of a god, and the tale that follows turns on what such a being means.
2747-nisida-celebrated-crimes:
Naples in 1825, the city of the see Naples and die proverb, sets this Dumas crime tale of Nisida. Readers tempted by the proverb to see Naples and die are advised to land at the mole or at Mergellina on a fine summer day. The tale begins in that enchanted city.

Nisida, a beautiful Neapolitan woman, becomes the center of love, jealousy, and murder in a city of sun and shadow. Southern color and romantic passion fill a city of sun and shadow. The story offers a vivid Neapolitan crime tale, where beauty and violence walk side by side.
27477-astronomical-instruments-and-acces:
Wm. Gaertner and Company of Chicago, at 5345 to 5349 Lake Avenue, issued this trade catalog, Catalog A, in 1908, for astronomical instruments and accessories. The notice warns that this catalog supersedes former editions, that prices are net without packing, and that orders should give catalog number and shipping instructions.

Most instruments were constructed to order, though smaller telescopes with accessories, chronographs, and simpler measuring machines were usually kept in stock. Everything was of Gaertner's own manufacture except astronomical regulator clocks, listed for customer convenience, and every piece was tested, inspected, and guaranteed as represented. Buyers could read it with ease and pick the tool they needed for their own star work.
2748-derues-celebrated-crimes:
A September afternoon in 1751 at Chartres opens this Dumas true crime tale, as schoolboys burst from their school like partridges. One September afternoon in 1751, toward half past five, some twenty small boys burst from a religious school at Chartres, chattering like a covey of partridges.

From that innocent scene grows a tale of a poisoner, a swindler, and a murderer whose pious face hid cold calculation. Schoolboy tricks lead, step by step, to the scaffold, and the horror grows with each crime. The book stands as a classic of true crime, and a study of evil in respectable dress.
2749-la-constantin-celebrated-crimes:
Dumas warns readers not to search the records before this 1660 tale begins, for La Constantin keeps her own counsel. Before beginning, Dumas warns readers not to bother searching contemporary records, for the tale that follows keeps its own counsel about names and places.

A woman known as La Constantin moves through a world of gallantry, betrayal, and murder in the France of Louis XIV. Romantic mystery lets legend fill gaps where documents fail. The story charms as a tale of passion and crime, half history and half invention. The tale keeps its mystery to the final page.
2750-joan-of-naples-celebrated-crimes:
Naples asleep on January 15, 1343, opens this Celebrated Crimes life of Joan, queen from 1343 to 1382. In the night of January 15, 1343, while Naples lay wrapped in peaceful sleep, a queen's reign began in murder and storm.

Joan, beautiful, passionate, and ruthless, ruled Naples through husbands, lovers, and wars, until her own violent end. Romantic sweep turns chronicle into tragedy, and Joan's reign reads like a play. The book offers a vivid portrait of a medieval queen who defied popes, kings, and custom. Naples, Avignon, and Rome all play parts in her stormy reign.
27519-the-settlement-of-wage-disputes:
Herbert Feis, associate professor of economics at the University of Kansas, published this study with the Macmillan Company in New York in October 1921. Feis asks how wage disputes can be settled on principles rather than expedients, so that industrial peace lasts.

Past experience, he argues, furnishes much guidance, yet the principles actually used in settlements have usually resulted from compromise, with reason and economic analysis secondary. Later chapters work through the present industrial situation, the principles of wages, wages and price movements, and the standard wage. The book is a sober, early attempt at a science of wage settlement.
2752-martin-guerre-celebrated-crimes:
Why should two faces not match, Dumas wonders at the opening of this Celebrated Crimes tale of Martin Guerre. We marvel at the likeness of strangers, Dumas begins, yet it is the difference that should surprise us, for why should two faces not match.

A man vanishes from his village, another takes his place, wife, and life, and only a trial can tell true husband from impostor. Wonder and legal suspense carry one of history's strangest cases to its verdict. The book remains the classic telling of an identity stolen and unmasked.
27521-the-watchers-of-the-plains-a-tale-:
Ridgwell Cullum published this tale of the western prairies with A. L. Burt in New York in March 1909, from a George W. Jacobs copyright, with a frontispiece by J. C. Leyendecker. Cullum dedicates it affectionately to B. W. M., his good friend and counselor.

Chapters follow a letter, an alarm in Beacon Crossing, Rosebud, a birthday gift, and an Indian pow-wow. They go on to Seth washing a handkerchief, the adventures of Red Riding Hood, and the devotion of Wanaha. Warnings follow, with the movements of Little Black Fox, and Seth playing a strong hand. The watchers of the title keep eyes on a dark horizon. It is a lively prairie romance of Seth and his neighbors.
27523-masterpieces-of-mystery-in-four-vo:
Joseph Lewis French edited this volume of detective stories in the Masterpieces of Mystery set, published by Doubleday, Page at Garden City, New York, in 1922. French thanks a long list of helpers, from Professor Brander Matthews of Columbia to Anna Katherine Green Rohlfs and Arthur Reeve, creator of Craig Kennedy.

The contents open with Poe's Purloined Letter, Reeve's Black Hand, and Wilkie Collins's Biter Bit. Anna Katherine Green's Missing: Page Thirteen follows. The anthology gathers classic detection in one place. Mystery readers get founding tales of the form, chosen by an editor who knew the field.
2753-ali-pacha-celebrated-crimes:
Audacious enterprises and strange turns of fortune mark the early nineteenth century, and Ali Pacha's career fits the age, in this Celebrated Crimes volume. The early nineteenth century, Dumas begins, was a time of audacious enterprises and strange turns of fortune, and Ali's career fits the age.

Ali Pasha of Janina rose from banditry to rule Albania as a near independent prince, defying sultans and courting Europe. His fall, siege, and murder close a life of cunning and cruelty. Epic sweep turns an Ottoman strongman into a romantic tyrant. Janina's lion ruled by terror, tribute, and cunning diplomacy.
2754-the-countess-of-saint-geran-celebra:
Horsemen riding into an Auvergne village at midday near the end of 1639 open this Dumas tale of the Countess de Saint Geran. Toward midday, a troop of horsemen rode into a little village at the northern edge of Auvergne, from a direction no one expected.

A stolen child, a substituted heir, and a countess fighting for her son drive a tale of aristocratic crime. Romantic indignation turns a lawsuit into a melodrama of stolen childhood. The book stands as a classic of family conspiracy, and of a mother's long fight for truth.
2755-murat-celebrated-crimes:
Waterloo decided Europe's destiny on June 18, 1815, while a beggar walked the road from Toulon to Marseilles in this Dumas tale. On June 18, 1815, as Europe's destiny was decided at Waterloo, a man dressed like a beggar followed the road from Toulon to Marseilles.

The beggar was Joachim Murat, once King of Naples and Napoleon's dashing cavalry chief, now a fugitive. His flight through Corsica to Pizzo, and his execution there, close a career of glory and folly. Sympathy follows a brave, reckless king who outlived his star. His white plumes and brave charges made him a legend first.
2756-marquise-brinvillier-celebrated-cri:
A crowd on the Pont Neuf on a fine autumn evening near the end of 1665 opens this Celebrated Crimes portrait of the Marquise de Brinvilliers. Toward the end of 1665, on a fine autumn evening, a crowd gathered on the Pont Neuf where it turns down to the rue Dauphine.

The marquise, a poisoner of husbands and kin, moved through Paris society with beauty and piety as her mask. Her crimes, her trial, and her scaffold end unfold with fascinated horror. The book remains a classic of true crime, and a portrait of evil in high places.
2757-vaninka-celebrated-crimes:
Four o'clock sounding from St. Peter and St. Paul above the ramparts opens this Dumas tale of Vaninka, set near the end of Paul I's reign. Toward the end of Paul I's reign, as four o'clock sounded from the church of St. Peter and St. Paul above the ramparts, a St. Petersburg drama began.

Vaninka, a Russian woman of fierce pride, pursues vengeance through love and murder in the court of a mad emperor. Northern color and romantic intensity carry a court where passion meets despotism. The story offers a rare Dumas excursion into Russia, where passion and despotism meet. St. Petersburg's winter cold matches the tale's chill heart.
2758-marquise-de-ganges-celebrated-crime:
A plain carriage with no arms painted on it stops one evening near the close of 1657, opening this Dumas tale of the Marquise de Ganges. Toward the close of that year, a carriage bearing no painted arms stopped one evening before a house in the rue Hautefeuille.

The marquise, a young widow of beauty and fortune, fell victim to her husband's family and their greed. Romantic horror turns a famous murder into a tale of innocence destroyed. The story remains a classic of French true crime, and of aristocratic cruelty.
27589-coronation-anecdotes:
Giles Gossip, Esquire, gathered these select and interesting fragments of English coronation ceremonies, printed for Robert Jennings in the Poultry, London, in 1823. Its epigraph, from Pope, bids readers recall the fancied scene and see coronations rise on every green.

The advertisement argues that a coronation gives an intelligent eye much to ponder. It sums up the genius of the monarchy and miniatures the leading events of English annals. Connected with the first establishment of Christianity in the island, it keeps alive some of Britain's earliest notions of public liberty. The ceremonies, Gossip says, exhibit the character of each part of the political body.
27639-new-vegetarian-dishes:
Mrs. Bowdich wrote this vegetarian cookery book, published by George Bell and Sons in London and New York in 1892, with a preface by Ernest Bell of the London Vegetarian Society.

Bell complains that most vegetarian books are mere compilations with the meat dishes left out, with porridge and a few beans and peas added, and too many puddings and sweets. What is required, he says, is a book that provides something to take the place of meat, nourishing and palatable at once. Bowdich's dishes aim to meet that need, giving vegetarians real fare rather than leftovers.
2771-the-island-pharisees:
John Galsworthy wrote this novel of a young Englishman, Shelton, born to go a journey like every man. At first he sits in the dust with chubby hands reaching at nothing, then he toddles onto the high road of life, where society waits to shape him.

Shelton's engagement, his travels, and his quarrels with convention expose the pharisaism of island England, polite, smug, and cruel. Galsworthy writes with irony and pity for a hero learning to see. The book stands as an early satire of English respectability, and a portrait of conscience waking.
27722-masterpieces-of-mystery-in-four-vo:
Edited by Joseph Lewis French and published in 1922, this volume collects nine ghost stories by writers including Algernon Blackwood, M. R. James, Guy de Maupassant, and Robert Louis Stevenson. It was the ghost-story volume of a four-volume anthology of mystery writing.

The tales range from Blackwood's tale of a London lodger who hears too much through thin walls to Pliny the Younger's ancient letter about a haunted house. Together they show how the ghost story changed across centuries while keeping its core device: an ordinary person meeting something that should not be there.
27764-dramatic-reader-for-lower-grades:
Florence Holbrook wrote this dramatic reader for lower grades, published in 1911 by the American Book Company. Its little plays turn well-known stories into dialogue for children who enjoy pretending to live with favorite characters in forest, palace, or fairyland.

Contents include Little Red Riding-Hood, Goldilocks, Cinderella, The Pied Piper, Hänsel and Gretel, Robin Hood, and William Tell. Holbrook urges children to speak in each character's voice, arguing that putting oneself in another's place trains imagination, kindness, and sympathy. Later plays include Cornelia and Her Jewels, The Days of the Week, The Gingerbread Man, and The Good Fairy.
27779-solomon-crow-s-christmas-pockets-a:
Ruth McEnery Stuart published this 1897 collection with Harper and Brothers, headed by the title tale of Solomon Crow's Christmas pockets. Other stories include The Two Tims, The Freys' Christmas Party, Little Mother Quackalina, Old Easter, and Duke's Christmas.

Stuart writes in Southern dialect and local color, with Christmas, family, and church life at the center. The frontispiece shows Solomon Crow at work on bad tempers, and the book preserves a popular late nineteenth-century voice telling stories of Black and white Southern households. Stuart dedicated the book to her niece, little Miss Lea Callaway, and Harper priced similar volumes at one dollar and fifty cents.
27784-tales-of-the-malayan-coast-from-pe:
Rounsevelle Wildman, American consul general at Hong Kong, collected these tales of the Malayan coast in 1899, dedicating the book to Admiral George Dewey. Henry Sandham supplied the illustrations.

Stories range from a boy's adventure with a tiger to pirates, a crocodile hunt, a pig hunt on Mount Ophir, and a visit to the court of Johore. Wildman writes as a traveler and official on the edge of empire, and the tales preserve the color, danger, and humor of the region at century's end. Dewey replied from the flagship Olympia at Manila that he was flattered by the dedication request.
27810-chips-from-a-german-workshop-volum:
F. Max Müller's Chips from a German Workshop, volume five, gathers miscellaneous later essays published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1881. The contents include essays on freedom, the philosophy of mythology, false analogies in comparative theology, spelling, and Sanskrit texts found in Japan.

The opening essay, a presidential address at Birmingham in 1879, engages John Stuart Mill's Essay on Liberty and defends individual freedom against society's encroachments. The volume shows Müller, the great Oxford philologist, ranging from language to religion and politics. Müller quotes Mill's rule that society may punish only acts prejudicial to the interests of others.
27813-merry-garden-and-other-stories:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch published Merry-Garden and Other Stories in 1907, collecting tales set largely in Cornwall. The title story opens beside a winding creek of the Lynher River, near Saltash, where a roofless building stands backed by cherry orchards.

Other stories include The Bend of the Road, Hi-Spy-Hi, His Excellency's Prize-Fight, The Black Joke, and Where the Treasure Is. Quiller-Couch writes with affection for Cornish customs, such as anointing apple trees with cider at Christmas, and for characters caught between old ways and new. The title story recalls Aunt Barbree Furnace, her maid Susannah, and the boy Nandy anointing apple stems with cider.
2783-the-trampling-of-the-lilies:
Rafael Sabatini sets this romance in revolutionary France, opening under the old rule with a secretary, lords of life and death, and the word of Bellecour. Disciples of Rousseau gather as the old order cracks.

Under the new rule, sheep turn wolves, a citizen commissioner rules, and La Boulaye discharges a debt, with invalids at Boisvert caught between. Sabatini writes with his usual sweep about revolution's promises and terrors. The novel offers a vivid tale of France trampling its own lilies. Sabatini's lilies fall beneath the Revolution's marching feet. The lilies never rise again.
27850-the-young-alaskans-in-the-rockies:
Emerson Hough published The Young Alaskans in the Rockies with Harper and Brothers in 1913, illustrated, following Rob, John, and Jesse from camp into the mountains. The boys travel westward, cross the Athabasca, and push through high altitudes toward Rainbow Lake and the pass.

Later chapters follow white goats, the Fraser River, the great mountain Mount Robson, Leo the grizzly-hunter, and the Columbia rapids to the end of the trail. Hough writes outdoor adventure with a naturalist's eye, and the book is a favorite of the Young Alaskans series. The frontispiece shows a trapper's shack beside a mountain lake, green and mirror-like, ringed by great walls.
27868-the-glow-worm-and-other-beetles:
J. Henri Fabre's The Glow-Worm and Other Beetles, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and published in New York by Dodd, Mead in 1924, is the second volume on beetles. The title essay was written specially for English translation near the close of Fabre's life.

Chapters cover sitares and their larvae, oil-beetles, hypermetamorphosis, the capricorn, dung-beetles of the pampas, insect coloring, burying-beetles, and the simulation of death. Fabre's patient observation and vivid prose made him the classic popular entomologist, and this volume shows his method at its best.
2791-essays-and-tales:
Joseph Addison wrote these essays and tales, gathered in the 1888 Cassell edition, with an introduction on his life and art. Public credit, household superstitions, opera lions, and women and wives open a set that ranges from finance to fashion.

The Italian opera, lampoons, and true and false humour follow, with Sa Ga Yean Qua Rash Tow's impressions of London. Addison writes with the easy politeness that made the Spectator famous. The volume offers a fine sample of Augustan essay writing, urbane, witty, and humane. Addison's Spectator manner made the essay a daily companion.
27934-it-and-other-stories:
Gouverneur Morris published It and Other Stories with Charles Scribner's Sons in March 1912, dedicated to Elsie with verses calling them bread-and-butter stories. The contents include It, Two Business Women, The Trap, Sapphira, The Bride's Dead, Holding Hands, and The Claws of the Tiger.

The title story lands its narrator on Prana Beach, cut off by an orchid-haunted morass, where canoemen refuse to land him dry for fear their canoe will shrivel like hide in fire. Morris writes witty, worldly short fiction of love, business, and adventure, with the polish of a popular magazine author.
27971-a-lover-s-litanies:
Eric Mackay published A Lover's Litanies in London with Field and Tuer at the Leadenhall Press in 1888, and in New York with Scribner and Welford. The book holds ten litanies, from Virgo Dulcis and Vox Amoris to Stella Matutina, Lilium inter Spinas, and Gloria in Excelsis.

Each litany is a sequence of short verses addressed to a beloved, blending devotion and desire in the language of prayer. Mackay, author of Love Letters of a Violinist, writes late Victorian love poetry at its most musical and ardent, and the volume shows the era's taste for sacred imagery in secular love.
28028-scottish-football-reminiscences-an:
D. D. Bone published Scottish Football Reminiscences and Sketches in Glasgow in 1890 with John Menzies and Company, with Hay Nisbet and Company and an Edinburgh edition. The volume's front and back matter carry Glasgow advertisements for badges, hats, corn plasters, and billiard rooms, giving the book a local, period flavor.

Bone's reminiscences and sketches recall Scottish football's early days, its clubs, players, and matches, before the modern professional game took shape. The book is a rare contemporary record of Scottish sport, written by an enthusiast close to the grounds and the men who played.
28038-watch-and-wait-or-the-young-fugiti:
Oliver Optic published Watch and Wait, or the Young Fugitives, in Boston with Lee and Shepard in 1868, after an 1864 copyright, as the third of six Woodville stories. The preface says the book was not written for the anti-slavery cause, but for stirring adventure, though it may kindle sympathy for the oppressed.

Optic hopes readers will love gentle Lily, respect Dan's manly independence, and smile at Cyd's oddities, and that the story will increase love of liberty and hatred of tyranny. The tale of young fugitives belongs to the boys' adventure fiction of the Civil War era.
28070-a-man-of-two-countries:
Alice Harriman published A Man of Two Countries with the Alice Harriman Company in New York and Seattle in 1910, with chapter headings by C. M. Dowling. The book is set before cowboys and irrigation, when Indians, traders, trappers, wolfers, whiskey smugglers, missionaries, and Mounted Police crossed the boundary of the Whoop Up Country.

Harriman writes types rather than individuals, weaving friendships and enmities through two books, The River and The Prairie, with a thread of love's gold. The novel preserves the Montana and Alberta border country as it passed from frontier chaos toward statehood and province.
28094-mediaeval-tales:
Mediaeval Tales, with an introduction by Henry Morley, gathers four old sources of romance in one volume. First comes Turpin's History of Charles the Great and Orlando, a chronicle before 1122 that claims a friend of Charlemagne as author. Next are Spanish ballads on Charlemagne, translated by John Gibson Lockhart in 1823.

The third part draws stories from the Gesta Romanorum, and the fourth gives the first Faust tale in English, the source of Marlowe's play. Morley's notes link these tales to Ariosto and later romance. The book offers a broad, readable path into medieval story telling.
28160-the-pioneer-light-passenger-locomo:
Paper 42 of Smithsonian Bulletin 240, issued in Washington in 1966, studies the Pioneer light passenger locomotive of 1851. The paper, from the Museum of History and Technology, traces an early American engine built for light, fast passenger service. Side notes on Alba F. Smith and Seth Wilmarth, moved to the end in this e-book, give builder detail.

Readers learn how the engine was built, how it ran, and why its design mattered in the growth of rail travel. Drawings and notes from the museum's records support the account. The paper suits rail historians and readers who want a close, factual look at one early locomotive.
28190-a-chapter-of-adventures:
G. A. Henty wrote A Chapter of Adventures as a boys' tale of sea, war, and escape. The story opens in a fishing village, where a boy is caught by the tide, runs from Harwich, and survives a wreck and rescue. Later chapters take him aboard the Wild Wave to Alexandria, through a riot, prison, and bombardment in Egypt.

Henty, born near Cambridge in 1832, served as a war correspondent in Crimea, Italy, Abyssinia, and France before writing for boys. His heroes learn courage, loyalty, and quick thinking under fire. The book offers brisk, old-fashioned adventure in the author's well-known style.
28192-mr-turtle-s-flying-adventure-hollo:
Albert Bigelow Paine's Mr. Turtle's Flying Adventure, published in October 1917, is a Hollow Tree story for children. Mr. Turtle, who lives in a stone house on the Wide Blue Water and fishes for a living, welcomes the Hollow Tree people and Jack Rabbit for a day out. J. M. Conde drew the pictures.

The title tale has Mr. Turtle tell of his childhood and an old fable, while other stories cover a deep-woods elopement, a ride in Mr. Man's car, and how Mr. Possum's tail became bare. Paine's animals talk like friendly neighbours. The book suits reading aloud to young children.
28193-mr-rabbit-s-wedding-hollow-tree-st:
Albert Bigelow Paine's Mr. Rabbit's Wedding, published in October 1917, is a Hollow Tree story for children. A little lady, fresh from her first reader, climbs into the Story Teller's lap by the fire and hears of Jack Rabbit's school days, Cousin Redfield and the molasses, and Mr. Bear's spring call. J. M. Conde drew the pictures.

The title tale follows Mr. Rabbit to his wedding, with animal neighbours, jokes, and gentle morals along the way. Paine's animals talk like kindly country folk, and each story ends with warmth. The book suits reading aloud to young children who love animal tales.
28199-louis-philippe-makers-of-history-s:
John S. C. Abbott wrote Louis Philippe in 1904 for the Makers of History series, first entered in 1871. Abbott calls Louis Philippe's life one of the most changeful in history, from the storms of 1789, which sent his father to the guillotine and his family to prison and exile. His wanderings took him among Laplanders and American Indians. Engravings illustrate the volume.

Chapters follow the king through revolution, exile, and a reign that ended in 1848, with nearly two thousand miles by boat with his brothers. Abbott writes for young readers, in a lively, moral style. The book offers a readable life of France's citizen king.
28204-how-mr-rabbit-lost-his-tail-hollow:
Albert Bigelow Paine's How Mr. Rabbit Lost His Tail, a Hollow Tree story, tells how the Hollow Tree animals lost their tails and how Mr. Dog played Santa Claus. The book, copyright 1901 and 1910, includes a map of the Hollow Tree and Deep Woods country, where the top is south, and paths, bridges, and Mr. Turtle's house are marked. J. M. Conde drew the pictures.

Stories cover Mr. Dog at the circus, Mr. Coon as a little boy, and the rabbits' loss, told by the Story Teller to the Little Lady. Paine's animals act like kind, funny neighbours. The book suits young children who love animal tales read aloud.
28251-a-preliminary-study-of-the-emotion:
Sanford Bell, fellow in Clark University, wrote A Preliminary Study of the Emotion of Love Between the Sexes as an early scientific paper on love. Bell notes that no writer had yet treated love from a genetic, or developmental, standpoint, and that most psychology books said little on the subject. He quotes Ribot and Havelock Ellis on the gap.

Bell gathers cases and observations to trace how love grows, changes, and varies between people. His tone is careful and academic, aiming to move the topic from novels to science. The paper offers a frank, early look at the psychology of love before modern sex research.
28255-shelters-shacks-and-shanties:
D. C. Beard wrote Shelters, Shacks, and Shanties, New York, 1916, copyright 1914, as a boys' handbook for building in the woods. Beard, with his own pictures, teaches half-cave shelters, fallen-tree shelters, Adirondack lean-tos, bark teepees, beaver-mat huts, and sod houses. He dedicates the book to Daniel Bartlett Beard, for love of the outdoors.

Later chapters cover tree-top houses, caches, axes, log splitting, notching, and Navajo hogans. Beard stresses safety, care for trees, and simple tools. The book suits scouts, campers, and readers who enjoy making shelter with their own hands.
28263-soap-bubble-stories:
Fanny Barry wrote Soap-Bubble Stories in 1892 as a children's book for Vera, Elsie, Oskar, and eight other young readers. The frame tale opens at twilight, as children tired of blowing bubbles gather round a fire, watching snow and bare trees outside. A watcher in shadow whips up froth in a fairy basin and blows bubbles of her own, less bright than the children's, but full of stories.

Each bubble holds a tale, told in the glow of blazing logs, with elfin shadows in the corners. James Pott and Company published the book in New York. Barry, author of The Fox Family, writes with gentle fancy for bedtime reading.
28282-egyptian-literature-comprising-egy:
Egyptian Literature, edited by Epiphanius Wilson, New York and London, 1901, gathers Egyptian tales, hymns, litanies, invocations, the Book of the Dead, and cuneiform writings. Wilson's special introduction leads to hymns to the setting sun, to Osiris, and to Ra, with chapters on giving a mouth, a heart, and memory to Osiris. The Co-operative Publication Society published the volume.

Later chapters beat back crocodiles and serpents, drive away Apshait, and claim dominion over air, water, and elements. The book offers English readers a broad, early survey of ancient Egyptian religion. It serves as a useful door into texts once known only to scholars.
28306-the-christmas-fairy-and-other-stor:
The Christmas Fairy and Other Stories, London and New York, printed in Bavaria in 1878, gathers three holiday tales for children. John Strange Winter's title story follows boys at Miss Ware's school, dreaming of home, parties, pantomimes, and gifts from grannies, uncles, and aunts. Shivers, one boy, meets a tall, handsome lady who takes him in her arms.

Mrs. Molesworth adds Not Quite True, and Frances E. Crompton adds In the Chimney Corner. Ernest Nister published the picture book, with Ernest Nister and E. P. Dutton as houses. The volume offers old-fashioned Christmas warmth, with pictures throughout.
28307-a-christmas-accident-and-other-sto:
Annie Eliot Trumbull wrote A Christmas Accident and Other Stories, New York, 1900, copyright 1897, as a collection of New England tales. The title story first appeared in the Hartford Courant, After the Deluge in the Atlantic Monthly, and other tales in the Home Maker, Outlook, New England Magazine, and McClure's. A. S. Barnes and Company published the volume.

Contents include a memoir of Mary Twining, a postlude, a daily morning chronicle, hearts unfortified, and her neighbour's landmark. Trumbull, author of White Birches, writes with quiet humour and care for character. The book offers a charming shelf of turn-of-the-century short stories.
28308-the-children-s-book-of-christmas-s:
Asa Don Dickinson and Ada M. Skinner edited The Children's Book of Christmas Stories, Garden City, 1913, as a holiday anthology. Dickens opens with Christmas at Fezziwig's Warehouse, from A Christmas Carol, and Andersen follows with The Fir-Tree. Stars mark tales for younger children, daggers for older ones, in the contents list.

Other stories include Mary E. Wilkins Freeman's masquerade, Susan Coolidge's Toinette and the Elves, and tales of chimes, birds, and wooden shoes. A German legend of the Christ-child and a voyage of a wee red cap add variety. The book remains a rich shelf of Christmas reading for families.
28351-dick-and-his-cat-and-other-tales:
Edith Carrington adapted Dick and His Cat and Other Tales, London, 1895, for the Animal Life Readers, edited by Carrington and Ernest Bell. The book, published for the Humanitarian League, aims to teach children gentleness and humane treatment of animals, as the school code of 1894 to 1895 urged. Pictures by F. M. Cooper and Harrison Weir fill the volume.

Tales include Dick and his cat, Trusty, Out in the Cold, a fly's story, and Betty and Snowdrop. Permission to reprint two tales came from the R.S.P.C.C. Carrington argues that kindness to animals is a first step to kindness to people. The book suits teachers of humane reading.
28377-lessons-of-the-war-with-spain-and-:
Alfred T. Mahan, a captain in the United States Navy, collected his magazine essays on the war with Spain in Lessons of the War with Spain and Other Articles. The main series, first printed in McClure's Magazine from December 1898 to April 1899, studies how the war was fought at sea.

Mahan weighs the strategic value of Puerto Rico, the blockade of Cuba, the movements of Admirals Sampson and Cervera, coast defence, cruisers, and the size of battleships. Further essays cover the peace conference, America's new dependencies, and common fallacies about naval subjects. The book remains a classic of naval thought by the author of The Influence of Sea Power upon History.
28381-ben-the-luggage-boy-or-among-the-w:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s Ben, the Luggage Boy, the fifth book in his Ragged Dick series, tells the story of a boy making his way on the streets of New York. Alger states in his preface, dated April 5, 1876, that Ben himself gave him the main facts nearly two years earlier.

Ben runs away from home and earns a living carrying luggage around the wharves and railway stations, among bootblacks, newsboys, and other street boys. One chapter recalls a room under a wharf that newspaper readers of the day would have known. Alger presents Ben's rise as a tale of honesty, hard work, and good habits rewarded.
28415-history-plays-for-the-grammar-grad:
Mary Ella Lyng wrote History Plays for the Grammar Grades, copyright 1922, as short plays for school children. Lyng, dedicating the book to Miss Cora Gallagher, principal of McKinley School, covers Columbus, John Smith and Pocahontas, Raleigh, Penn, Drake, Pilgrims, Washington, Clark, Jackson, Fremont, Webster, Clay, and Calhoun. Later plays treat Lincoln, Grant and Lee, and women of history.

The Columbus play opens in Genoa, where a boy fond of sea stories dreams of a westward route to India, then pleads his plan at the Spanish court. Lyng writes in simple dialogue for classroom performance. The book offers teachers ready plays for American history lessons.
2843-little-travels-and-roadside-sketche:
William Makepeace Thackeray, writing as Titmarsh, records short journeys in Little Travels and Roadside Sketches, starting from Richmond in Surrey toward Brussels. He leaves the Rose Cottage Hotel, which he prefers a thousand times to the Star and Garter, where a sneering waiter and a ten-shilling bottle of claret await the lone traveler. Ghent, Bruges, and Waterloo follow on the road.

Thackeray's sketches blend guidebook detail with jokes about fellow travelers, innkeepers, and national pride. He teases Belgians for brawling over politics while France, England, and Prussia spare them the trouble of thinking. The book charms as travel writing by a novelist, observant, funny, and fond of the small scenes beside the road.
28447-a-treatise-of-schemes-and-tropes:
Richard Sherry's Treatise of Schemes and Tropes, first printed in 1550, is a Renaissance handbook of rhetoric gathered from the best grammarians and orators. This facsimile edition, published by Scholars' Facsimiles and Reprints in 1961 from a Bodleian Library copy, pairs Sherry's text with his translation of Erasmus's Education of Children.

Sherry explains elocution, evidence and plainness, the three kinds of style, scheme and figure, and figures of sentence, in the spelling of his own day. His preface warns that the strange title may puzzle English ears. The book is a valuable source for students of Tudor English, rhetoric, and the teaching of good authors.
28502-the-busted-ex-texan-and-other-stor:
W. H. H. Murray's The Busted Ex-Texan and Other Stories, published by De Wolfe, Fiske and Company of Boston in 1890, opens at a camp in the foothills. The party sleeps in a grove of lofty firs beside a rivulet, with hammocks swung for the ladies and blankets and rifles marking each man's place. Laughter, talk, and song fill the camp before the title tale begins.

The title story gives the volume its comic voice, a busted ex-Texan telling his tale by the fire. Two more stories follow: how Deacon Tubman and Parson Whitney celebrated New Year's, and The Leaf of Red Rose. Readers get frontier humor, camp talk, and short tales from the American West.
28510-rambles-in-the-islands-of-corsica-:
Rambles in the Islands of Corsica and Sardinia, published by Longman, Brown, Green, Longmans, and Roberts in 1858, records a walking and riding tour of both islands. The traveler lands at Bastia, hires mules, and sets out through mountain villages and evergreen thickets. Corsican shepherds, the vendetta, and bandit life fill the early chapters.

Later chapters treat Corsican agriculture, Greek and Roman colonies, and the memoirs of King Theodore de Neuhoff. Nelson's exploit at San Fiorenzo, the siege of Bastia, and the Paoli family at Corte add history to the road. Readers get travel, antiquities, and island politics in one Victorian volume.
2852-the-hound-of-the-baskervilles:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Hound of the Baskervilles as another adventure of Sherlock Holmes, crediting a West-Country legend told to him by his friend Robinson. Sir Henry Baskerville comes to a hall shadowed by a family curse, and Dr. Watson reports from the moor while Holmes works from London. Chapters move from the curse and the problem to Baskerville Hall, the Stapletons of Merripit House, and a light upon the moor.

Watson's diary and reports carry the dread, as footsteps, strange neighbors, and the man on the tor build toward a rational answer. The novel's fog, mire, and hound made it the most famous Holmes tale after the detective's supposed death. It still works as both a ghost story and a detective puzzle.
28537-soldier-stories:
Rudyard Kipling's Soldier Stories, published by the Macmillan Company in 1896, collects tales of British soldiers in India. The opening scene stands at the main gate of Fort Amara on a stifling June night, where Mulvaney speaks to the guard. Kipling's soldiers talk in barrack dialect, telling stories of fighting, drink, and comradeship.

Contents include With the Main Guard, The Drums of the Fore and Aft, The Man Who Was, and The Courting of Dinah Shadd. The Incarnation of Krishna Mulvaney, The Taking of Lungtungpen, and The Madness of Private Ortheris follow. Readers get Kipling's India at its most vivid, in the voices of the ranks.
28562-wild-life-on-the-rockies:
Enos A. Mills's Wild Life on the Rockies, published by Houghton Mifflin in March 1909 with photographs, is dedicated to John Muir. Mills begins as Colorado snow observer, a post he calls strange and unmatched. Under irrigation engineer L. G. Carpenter, he worked three winters as a government experiment officer, traversing the upper slopes and the crest of the continent alone.

Essays follow a thousand-year pine, the beaver and his works, wilds without firearms, and climbing Long's Peak. Midget the return horse, Faithful Scotch, birds, lodge-pole pine, forests, and bears besieging camp complete the book. Readers get Rocky Mountain nature from a man who wintered in it.
28580-an-ohio-woman-in-the-philippines:
Emily Bronson Conger's An Ohio Woman in the Philippines, published with illustrations by the Press of Richard H. Leighton of Akron in 1904, follows a mother traveling alone. Conger dedicates the book to her husband Arthur Latham Conger, whose love and approval she calls her incentive and reward. She sails out of the Golden Gate hoping to do something useful for her boy and other boys.

Her index runs from Honolulu and Japan through Shanghai and Hong Kong to Manila, Iloilo, and Jaro. Wooings and weddings, markets, agriculture, church festivals, osteopathy, the McKinley campaign, Governor Taft at Jaro, and a shipwreck follow. Readers get a personal account of island life at the century's turn.
28594-the-peanut-plant-its-cultivation-a:
B. W. Jones of Virginia wrote The Peanut Plant, published by the Orange Judd Company of New York in 1902, for beginners. Jones promises that any intelligent person who has farmed can raise good peanut crops by following his directions, even without ever seeing the growing plant. Minor points he leaves to the farmer's own discovery.

Chapters describe the plant, whose native country remains unascertained and which has never been found truly wild. Planting, cultivation, harvesting, and marketing follow, with soil, seed, fertilizers, moles, implements, cold, drought, picking machines, and prices. Uses close the book: oil, roasted nuts, candy, coffee, chocolate, bread, soap, stock food, and hay.
2862-the-twins-of-table-mountain-and-oth:
Bret Harte's Twins of Table Mountain and Other Stories opens on a vast stony plateau above the California country. A river roars far below, and winds spend their force before the summit. The title story follows twins raised in that high isolation. The volume adds An Heiress of Red Dog, The Great Deadwood Mystery, A Legend of Sammtstadt, and Views from a German Spion.

Harte's California runs through the whole book, from ferry mansion houses and sleepy barkeepers to mining camps and river towns. The tales mix rough humor with sentiment, and the mountain setting gives the twins' story its stark mood. Readers who enjoy Harte's gold-country sketches will find the same voice here, broadened across several kinds of tale.
28633-paul-jones:
Hutchins Hapgood's Paul Jones, number 12 in the Riverside Biographical Series, was published by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in 1901. John Paul, known as Paul Jones, was born in July 1747, son of a peasant near Arbigland in Kirkcudbright, on the Solway Firth. His father lived by fishing and gardening, and his mother Jeanne Macduff was a Highlander's daughter.

The sea called him early: at twelve he handled a fishing boat like a veteran, and a Whitehaven merchant watched him ride a squall into harbor. Chapters follow the Providence and the Alfred, the Ranger, the fight with the Serapis, Paris society, and Russian service. Readers get a compact life of a restless seeker after distinction.
28636-the-grey-woman-and-other-tales:
Mrs. Gaskell's The Grey Woman and Other Tales, in an illustrated London edition of 1865 from Smith, Elder and Company, gathers eight stories. The title tale leads, followed by Curious If True, Six Weeks at Heppenheim, Libbie Marsh's Three Eras, and Christmas Storms and Sunshine. Hand and Heart, Bessy's Troubles at Home, and Disappearances complete the volume.

The Grey Woman opens at a mill by the Neckar, on the flat Mannheim side of Heidelberg, where coffee drinking is almost national in Germany. The miller Scherer, a grand, prosperous man, serves coffee, kuchen, and cinnamon cake in willow arbours, whistling a plaintive air. His family held the mill since old Palatinate days, losing two mills to French burnings. Readers get Gaskell's German setting and English sympathy.
28657-a-winter-amid-the-ice-and-other-th:
Jules Verne's A Winter Amid the Ice and Other Thrilling Stories, published by the World Publishing House of New York in 1877, gathers five tales with sixty illustrations. Doctor Ox's Experiment leads, set in Quiquendone, a town absent from even the best maps. Burgomaster Van Tricasse and Counsellor Niklausse consult Doctor Ox, a physiologist and audacious experimentalist.

Master Zacharius, A Drama in the Air, and the title tale follow, with Jean Cornbutte's Arctic project, a house of snow, burial alive, and white bears. An ascent of Mont Blanc closes the volume. Readers get Verne at his most playful and most chilling, in short form.
28667-genghis-khan-makers-of-history-ser:
Jacob Abbott's Genghis Khan, in the Makers of History series, was published by Harper and Brothers in 1901. Abbott opens by noting that khan is a title, not a name, meaning chieftain or king among the peoples of Central Asia. Genghis Khan stands as the greatest of these princes, and one of history's most renowned conquerors.

Abbott warns that fully reliable facts from so distant a time no longer survive, and answers only for honest compilation from the best sources at hand. Chapters move from pastoral life in Asia and the Monguls through Temujin in exile, the death of Vang Khan, and the empire's establishment. Conquests in China, the fall of Bokhara, and grand celebrations follow.
28680-the-young-surveyor-or-jack-on-the-:
J. T. Trowbridge wrote this 1875 boys' novel about Jack, a young surveyor on the prairies. The story follows Jack and his friend Vinnie through deer hunts, a journey to Chicago, a new home, and a long-running quarrel over section corners and boundary fences. Chapters with names like Old Wiggett's Section Corner, The Battle of the Boundary Fence, and Peakslow in a Tight Place set the shape of the plot.

Surveying gives the book its spine: measuring land, settling claims, and defending a line against rivals. Around that work, Trowbridge adds humor, danger, and prairie travel in the style of his Jack Hazard books. Young readers get a lively picture of frontier boyhood, where a boy's skill with instruments and his nerve both get tested.
28722-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems for children, published here in an illustrated edition by J. B. Lippincott with pictures in color by Maria L. Kirk. The book is dedicated to Alison Cunningham, the nurse who watched over Stevenson through long nights and led him through uneven land. Its verses speak in a child's voice about gardens, shadows, rain, ships, and bedtime.

A Child's Garden of Verses has stayed in print since the 1880s because its poems treat childhood seriously, without talking down. Stevenson writes of play, fear, and wonder as a child feels them, in short musical lines that read well aloud. Families still use it as a first poetry book, and this edition pairs the familiar text with bright early twentieth-century pictures.
28726-the-boy-scouts-book-of-stories:
Franklin K. Mathiews, chief scout librarian of the Boy Scouts of America, edited this 1920 story collection for boys. Mathiews explains that he kept meeting stories written for grown-ups that were also perfect for boys in their early teens, and with authors' permission he gathered them here. The book covers scout stories, school stories, sea and wild west tales, detective and mystery stories, and a good number of humorous ones.

Walt Louderback's pictures and Arthur D. Scott's decorations dress a volume meant to widen a boy's reading beyond books written only for boys. The collection shows what the Boy Scouts thought good reading was in 1920: adventure, humor, and character, without preaching. Young readers still find here a varied shelf of short fiction chosen by a librarian who knew boys well.
2873-the-prehistoric-world-or-vanished-r:
E. A. Allen wrote The Prehistoric World, or Vanished Races, as a popular survey of early humanity, reviewed chapter by chapter by leading scholars of the day. The reviewers included Peabody Museum curator F. W. Putnam, Smithsonian curator Charles Rau, Michigan geologist Alexander Winchell, and Bureau of Ethnology scholar Cyrus Thomas. Their names signal a book meant to carry current science to general readers.

Allen compares ancient races with living peoples, arguing that widely scattered groups such as the Turanian or Mongoloid peoples follow patterns seen in geology. The prose moves from stone tools to migrations across Asia and northern Europe. The book now reads as a period piece of anthropology, valuable for how the nineteenth century imagined deep human history.
28748-the-sandman-his-sea-stories:
William J. Hopkins wrote this 1908 book of sea stories told by the Sandman, with forty pictures by Diantha W. Horne. The stories have plain, inviting titles. They include the September-gale story, the fire story, the porpoise story, and the seaweed story. The flying-fish story, the log-book story, the shark story, and the Christmas story follow. Later tales bring a stowaway, an albatross, a derelict, a lighthouse, a privateer, and a race.

Hopkins, who also wrote the Sandman's farm and ship stories, tells each tale as a bedtime yarn for children, with sailors, storms, and strange catches. The book belongs to a series that made the Sandman a familiar storyteller to American children. Young readers get gentle sea adventure, told in a warm voice and meant to be read aloud before sleep.
28757-divided-skates:
Evelyn Raymond wrote this 1900 children's story, published by Thomas Y. Crowell in New York as part of the Sunshine Library. Divided Skates stands beside other Sunshine titles like Aunt Hannah and Seth, The Blind Brother, and Jessica's First Prayer, all short moral tales for young readers. Raymond also wrote Monica and Mixed Pickles, and her books were steady sellers for family shelves.

The story itself, like its companion volumes, teaches kindness and fair dealing through a child's small crisis over shared skates. Raymond writes plainly and warmly, without talking down to her readers. The book offers a period example of the improving children's tale: short, clear, and built around one lesson a child can carry home.
28764-getting-acquainted-with-the-trees:
J. Horace McFarland wrote this tree book, first published by the Outlook Company in 1904 and reissued by Macmillan in 1914, with photographs by the author. Its chapters treat maples, the growth of the oak, pines, apples, willows and poplars, the elm and the tulip tree, and nut-bearing trees. An index and a list of botanical names close the volume.

McFarland writes for walkers and gardeners, not botanists, showing how to know trees by flower, leaf, fruit, and winter shape. His own photographs show silver maple flowers, young red maple leaves, and a lone pine on the Indian River. Readers get a friendly field companion, meant to turn a walk among trees into acquaintance with old friends.
288-the-certain-hour-dizain-des-poe-tes:
James Branch Cabell gathers ten portraits of poets at their certain hour in this 1916 volume. The Certain Hour, subtitled Dizain des Poètes, takes its epigraph from criticism's limits: it can only note the impression a work made at a moment. Cabell dedicates the book to Robert Gamble Cabell.

Each tale shows a poet meeting love, death, or chance, with Cabell's ironic, musical prose. The framing verse insists that love, God-born, outlasts hourly change. Copyright pages trace the stories through magazines from 1909 to 1915. The volume introduces Cabell's Poictesme world to new readers.
2884-the-mason-bees:
Jean Henri Fabre gathered his essays on mason bees in this volume, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos from the Souvenirs entomologiques. The book covers the Chalicodomae, the mason bees proper, and adds essays on Fabre's cats and on red ants, both bearing on the bees' sense of direction. A separate volume treats the Osmiae, also mason bees by habit, under the title Bramble-bees and Others.

Fabre tests popular stories with patient experiment, asking how far a cat deserves its fame for finding home across tiles and haylofts. He distrusts casual observers and children's natural histories, preferring trials he can repeat. The essays remain a model of close insect observation, written with a naturalist's curiosity and a storyteller's ease.
28846-little-jack-rabbit-s-adventures:
David Cory wrote this 1921 children's book about Little Jack Rabbit, first in a long series of animal tales. The short chapters follow Jack through a railroad, his first train, a narrow escape, school, a spelling mistake, stolen eggs, a dam, a bonfire, and a sugar-coated carrot. H. S. Barbour's pictures show Jack hiding behind his mother's skirt and meeting his woodland neighbors.

Cory wrote for very young readers, using short sentences, talking animals, and small lessons about obedience and kindness. The book belongs to a series that also followed Jack with Danny Fox, the Squirrel Brothers, and Chippy Chipmunk. It offers gentle, old-fashioned animal fun, the kind of bedtime reading that American children of the 1920s knew well.
28862-the-time-of-roses:
Mrs. L. T. Meade wrote this novel about Bertha, Florence, Maurice Trevor, and Mrs. Aylmer, opening with a homecoming in the time of roses. The long chapter list follows Bertha's quandary, a tempting offer, a blunt question, an essay that arouses criticism, a telegram, and a proposal, through Mrs. Aylmer's will to a denouement and a world smiling again. The little mummy, a small scheming figure, threads through the plot.

Meade, a prolific writer of girls' and family stories, mixes romance with domestic strategy: wills, essays, and social maneuvering decide as much as love does. The novel's pleasures are those of a well-plotted Victorian family tale, with misunderstandings, secrets, and a satisfying close. Readers who enjoy period domestic fiction will find it an absorbing example of Meade's busy, popular style.
2892-irish-fairy-tales:
James Stephens retold Irish legend in Irish Fairy Tales, gathering stories of Finn, Tuan mac Cairill, Bran, Becfola, and Mongan. The book opens with Finnian, abbot of Moville, hurrying south and east on hearing that people in his province still honor gods he does not approve. The abbot learns of a powerful gentleman who keeps neither saint's day nor Sunday, and the old tales unfold from that clash.

Stephens writes the Fenian cycle with humor and poetry, letting heroes, enchanted caves, and frenzied kings share the stage. A later passage lists torments for a miscreant so ingenious that listeners' blood runs chill. The collection remains a favorite doorway into Irish myth, told in prose that feels both ancient and newly made.
28931-in-the-musgrave-ranges:
Jim Bushman, pseudonym of Conrad H. Sayce, wrote this 1922 Australian adventure, In the Musgrave Ranges, published by Blackie and Son. The story opens at Hergott Springs, a cattle-trucking depot of central Australia, where a shabby mixed train stops at the end of a long hot day. Men of the desert wait under a veranda: tall, thin, weather-beaten Australians and dignified Afghans in white turbans.

Chapters follow a tornado, camels, wild cattle, riding tests, smoke signals, and stealthy foes, through thirst, a sandstorm, and a rescue, to Sidcotinga station and the outpost of death. Bushman writes of mustering, branded cattle, and revenge in the desert. Readers get a sturdy boys' adventure of the Australian outback, full of heat, horses, and hard men.
28932-eskimo-folk-tales:
Knud Rasmussen collected these Eskimo folk tales, edited and rendered into English by W. Worster, with pictures by native Eskimo artists. Published in London and Copenhagen in 1921, the book gathers stories from Greenland and the Arctic. They include two friends who set out on a journey around the world, the coming of men long ago, and Nukúnguasik, who escaped from the Tupilak.

Later tales bring a woman with a bear as foster son, a man who ate his wives, the raven and the goose, the great bear, and the man who became a star. Rasmussen, who lived among Inuit people, preserves their humor, dread, and wonder in plain English. Readers get a firsthand treasury of Arctic storytelling, illustrated by the people whose tales they are.
28979-child-life-in-japan-and-japanese-c:
Mrs. M. Chaplin Ayrton wrote Child-Life in Japan and Japanese Child Stories, edited by William Elliot Griffis and published by D. C. Heath in Boston in 1909. Griffis, who helped bring the American public school system to Japan, met Ayrton in Tokyo a quarter century earlier. She was a graduate of Edinburgh University, with degrees in letters and sciences, and had studied medicine in Paris.

Ayrton married Professor William Edward Ayrton, the electrical engineer then at Japan's Imperial College of Engineering. She studied the Japanese people and their country with keen interest, touring famous places with Griffis's sister. The book, with pictures drawn and engraved by Japanese artists, gives English readers a warm, observant account of Japanese childhood.
28982-ghetto-comedies:
Israel Zangwill wrote this collection of comedies set in the Jewish East End of London, published with advertisements for new six-shilling novels beside it. Zangwill, already famous for Children of the Ghetto, turns here to humor, showing ghetto life through comic plots and dialect speech. The transcriber notes preserve the book's Yiddish and other dialects, with inconsistent spelling kept as printed.
