The comedies find laughter in courtship, family quarrels, and the clash between old customs and new London ways. Zangwill writes with affection for his people and a sharp eye for their talk. Readers get a lively, humane set of stories from a writer who made the ghetto known to English readers, comic where his earlier work was tragic, but no less observant.
29008-the-elm-tree-tales:
F. Irene Burge Smith wrote this 1856 book, The Elm Tree Tales, published by Mason Brothers in New York. The preface asks the reader to travel to a sylvan nook far from the city. There an old stone cottage peeps from thick foliage, past a maple avenue, an ancient mill, and a rustic bridge, to a giant elm spreading broad branches. Books and work lie on the turf, flowers peep from the green, and fair faces greet the visitor.

Smith opens with verses contrasting rural shades with the dark cellars of the crowded town, where poverty hides its tattered forms. The tales that follow gather a happy circle under the elm. Readers get a mid-nineteenth-century book of rural stories, gentle and moral, written for families who liked their fiction set in green places.
29029-a-nest-of-spies:
Pierre Souvestre and Marcel Allain wrote this 1917 detective novel, A Nest of Spies, in their Fantômas series, published by Brentano's in New York. The chapters open with sudden death and document number six, then move to Baron Naarboveck's house, a cordial reception, and the second bureau. Later chapters bring Juve's stratagem, the hooded cloak of Fantômas, and the traitor's apprenticeship.

The plot runs through an Elysée ball, the stronghold of the enemy, and a caravan drama, ending with a council of war and an ambassador. Souvestre and Allain mix spy intrigue with the master criminal's tricks, in the sensational French style. Readers get a fast, melodramatic thriller from the age of Fantômas, full of disguises, arrests, and narrow escapes.
29093-old-man-curry-race-track-stories:
Charles E. Van Loan published this collection of race track stories in 1917, in a memorial edition with an introduction by L. B. Yates. Its hero, Old Man Curry, is a veteran of the turf, and each story follows a race, a wager, or a scheme at the track. Titles include Levelling with Elisha, Playing Even for Obadiah, and By a Hair.

Van Loan writes from inside racing life: trainers, jockeys, owners, and the gamblers who live by a horse's stride. The stories mix humor with the hard arithmetic of odds. Readers get a set of sporting tales from the golden age of American horse racing, affectionate toward its rogues and sharp about its risks.
2910-the-little-dream-an-allegory-in-six:
John Galsworthy's The Little Dream is an allegory in six scenes about a mountain girl named Seelchen and a climber named Lamond. The dream characters include mountains as horns, flowers as the edelweiss, alpenrose, and gentian, and voices such as cowbells, mountain air, and a far view of Italy. Things in books, moth children, dancing youths, and forms of workers and their work also appear.

Seelchen asks Lamond whether she will be safe, and he answers by asking whether she is safe in her mountains. The Town then enters in dance, with girls in white satin and rags paired with youths in velvet and poverty. The play uses dream logic to weigh country innocence against city life, and it rewards readers who enjoy symbolic theatre.
2918-the-first-and-the-last-a-drama-in-t:
John Galsworthy's short drama The First and the Last uses only three characters and three scenes to stage a moral crisis. Keith Darrant, a King's Counsel, sits in his dark-curtained study on a November evening, lamplight falling on a Turkey carpet, books, and a blue-and-gold coffee service. His brother Larry and a woman named Wanda draw him into a secret that tests law against loyalty.

Thirty hours pass between the first two scenes, and two months between the second and third. Wanda begs Keith not to take Larry from her, kissing his hand and recoiling when he draws it away. The play's tension lies in what a respectable lawyer will do for family, and it ends as a compact study of conscience under pressure.
2919-the-little-man-a-farcical-morality-:
John Galsworthy's farcical morality The Little Man plays out at an Austrian railway station, where travelers of several nations wait on a departure platform. An Englishman, an Englishwoman, an American, a German, and a Dutch boy sit at buffet tables served by a pale young waiter. A woman of lowly station sits beside two large bundles, with her baby swathed in a black shawl on one of them.

The little man of the title charms the company by tending the baby, which sucks his finger while the American wonders whether he has created babies in his leisure moments. National pride, kindness, and absurdity collide in three scenes. The play works as a small moral fable about how strangers judge one another in transit.
29245-a-breath-of-prairie-and-other-stor:
Will Lillibridge published this story collection in Chicago in 1911 with A. C. McClurg and Company, illustrated in color by J. N. Marchand. Lillibridge, author of Ben Blair and The Dominant Dollar, writes prairie fiction, and the title story leads thirteen pieces. A tribute notes that novelists put their own traits into their heroes, and friends saw William Otis Lillibridge clearly in his.

Other stories include The Dominant Impulse, The Stuff of Heroes, Arcadia in Avernus, Journey's End, A Prairie Idyl, and A Frontier Romance of Jumel Mansion. Readers get a western story collection, warm toward its plains people and varied in mood, from heroism to humor to the touch human.
2928-time-and-life-mr-darwin-s-origin-of:
Thomas Henry Huxley's Time and Life takes Darwin's Origin of Species as its subject and opens with the earth's thin accessible crust, hardly ten miles thick. That film holds beds of stone, the consolidated muds and sands of former seas and lakes, laid one upon another so that deeper layers are older. Geologists group those strata into formations, and formations into primary, secondary, and tertiary assemblages.

Huxley then asks what it means that some animal types persist with little change across vast stretches of time while the world's population as a whole changes greatly. The bearing of that fact on the history of life becomes the lecture's question. The essay remains a fine popular statement of deep time and the fossil record.
29286-noble-deeds-of-the-world-s-heroine:
Henry Charles Moore published this collection of heroines' deeds in London in 1903 with the Religious Tract Society, illustrated in color. Moore groups brave deeds by kind: rescue, mission field, and war-time. Rescue stories include Alice Ayres and the Union Street fire, Grace Bussell and the wreck of the Georgette, and Mary Rogers and the wreck of the Stella.

Mission stories follow Jane Chalmers alone among cannibals, Anna Hinderer in the Yoruba country, and Olivia Ogren escaping the Boxers. War-time heroines include Mary Seacole, the soldiers' friend, Laura Secord of Canada, Lady Bankes at Corfe Castle, and Lady Sale in Afghan captivity. Readers get an Edwardian celebration of women's courage, earnest and vivid, across fire, sea, mission, and war.
29287-aino-folk-tales:
Basil Hall Chamberlain collected these Aino folk tales, privately printed for the Folk-Lore Society in 1888, with an introduction by Edward B. Tylor. The Aino, now called the Ainu, are the Indigenous people of northern Japan, and Chamberlain, a scholar of Japan, gathered their stories at a time when their culture was under pressure.

The volume presents the tales with the society's scholarly apparatus, including its officers and council, from the Earl of Strafford as president to Andrew Lang among the vice-presidents. Readers get a pioneering English collection of Ainu oral literature, valuable for its stories and for its place in the early history of folklore study.
29311-irish-fairy-tales:
Edmund Leamy wrote these Irish fairy tales, published in Dublin in 1906 by M. H. Gill and Son, pictured by S. W. Fazain. The preface calls Leamy among Ireland's brightest and most poetic spirits of the last half century. It calls him among the most patriotic Irishmen of his generation. He loved his country, its people, its traditions, its hills, lakes, raths, and mounds.

Contents include Princess Finola and the Dwarf, The House in the Lake, The Little White Cat, and The Golden Spears. The Fairy Tree of Dooros, The Enchanted Cave, and The Huntsman's Son follow, with notes at the end. Readers get a classic collection of Irish wonder tales, told with poetry and patriotism, and illustrated for young and old alike.
29329-sandwiches:
Mrs. S. T. Rorer, author of the Philadelphia Cook Book and Bread and Bread-Making, published this sandwich book in Philadelphia, in a revised and enlarged edition copyrighted in 1894 and 1912. Rorer, a leading American cooking teacher, treats the sandwich as a subject worthy of a whole book, not a footnote.

Contents run from keeping sandwiches and making bread, including German potato bread and nut bread, to anchovy, anchovy and egg, cold beef, and caviar sandwiches. Later sections cover sweet sandwiches and scented sandwiches, with additional recipes. Readers get a compact Victorian cookbook on a single food, practical for lunches and useful as a record of what Americans ate between bread.
29346-tales-of-fishes:
Zane Grey, president of the Long Key Fishing Club, published this fishing book in 1919 with Harper and Brothers, illustrated from photographs by the author. Grey, the western novelist, writes here as an angler, and his chapters record fights with great fish in warm waters. The book appeared in June 1919.

Chapters include Byme-by-Tarpon, The Island of the Dead, and The Royal Purple Game of the Sea. Two fights with swordfish, sailfish, Gulf Stream fishing, and bonefish follow, with some rare fish, the gladiator of the sea, and seven marlin swordfish in one day. Big tuna and Avalon the Beautiful close the book. Readers get a sportsman's tales of the sea, vivid and boastful in the best fishing tradition.
29360-the-bad-family-other-stories:
Mrs. Fenwick's 1898 book, third in the Dumpy Books for Children chosen by E. V. Lucas, gathers short tales of children who misbehave with great verve. Master Henry heads the set: a boy proud of his skill as a boxer, his black eyes, and his bloody noses. The tales were made for young readers, with short scenes and plain morals tucked inside the fun.

Each story lets a bad child run wild for a page or two, then shows the cost in scrapes, scoldings, or shame. The humor is broad and old-style, but the point stays clear: pride and rough play lead to trouble. Parents and children today can read it as a lively sample of Edwardian tales meant to amuse while they warn.
29363-henry-esmond-the-english-humourist:
William Makepeace Thackeray's works fill this Oxford University Press volume, edited with an introduction by George Saintsbury and fifteen illustrations. The volume gathers three major works: The History of Henry Esmond, Esq., The English Humourists, and The Four Georges. Together they show Thackeray as novelist, critic, and historian.

Henry Esmond, a colonel in Queen Anne's service, writes his own history from Castlewood, Virginia, through the Esmond family, plots for James II, and the world of early eighteenth-century England. The English Humourists lectures and The Four Georges histories add criticism and royal portraiture. Readers get a substantial Thackeray omnibus, useful for reading the novelist alongside his own view of English letters and kings.
29389-raiders-of-the-universes:
Donald Wandrei wrote this story of a dark star's conquest in the thirty-fourth century. The great astronomer Phobar stands, childlike, before the metallic invaders of a ravished solar system. Phobar discovered the dark star while sweeping the heavens with a newly invented multi-powered Sussendorf comet-hunter, catching a new star of great brilliance beside Hercules.

Through the rest of the night, Phobar set aside all plans and watched the one star. Mercia's nullifier, a device based on four-dimensional geometry, let observers see events that light would take hundreds of years to carry. Readers get a cosmic invasion tale, vast in scale, about a star that conquers and the astronomer who first saw it coming.
294-the-captain-of-the-polestar-and-othe:
A medical student keeps a journal aboard a whaler locked in Arctic ice. Arthur Conan Doyle's Captain of the Polestar and Other Tales opens at latitude 81 degrees 40 minutes north, amid enormous ice fields. The captain's strange visions haunt the crew.

Other tales follow: J. Habakuk Jephson's statement, the Great Keinplatz Experiment, and the Ring of Thoth. Doyle thanks Cornhill, Temple Bar, and other magazines for first printing them. The collection mixes horror, science, and adventure. It shows Doyle before Sherlock Holmes took over. Doyle's Arctic horror shows the imagination that built Holmes.
2942-two-penniless-princesses:
Charlotte Yonge wrote Two Penniless Princesses as a historical romance of fifteenth-century Scotland and England. The story opens at Dunbar Castle, standing on steep rocks above the North Sea, where battlements served as the only recreation ground for ladies in disturbed times. Lady Margaret walks the walls looking over a sea purpled by cloud shadows, with sails fleeting before the wind.

The princesses of the title move through courts, churches, and palaces, including a quiet unveiling before a noontide meal in a tapestry-hung room called Paradise. Yonge follows their fortunes without fortune, relying on rank, kinship, and conduct. The novel appeals to readers who enjoy Yonge's gentle historical fiction and its attention to medieval manners.
29485-faro-nell-and-her-friends-wolfvill:
Alfred Henry Lewis's 1913 book of Wolfville stories centers on Faro Nell, a frontier woman. She rides a calico pony as the Goddess of Liberty, firing her pistol with the rest on the Fourth of July. Set in the cattle town of Wolfville and its rival Red Dog, the tales follow Dead Shot Baker and Old Man Enright's uncle. Cynthiana, Old Monte the official drunkard, and a mocking bird won in a wager join them. Pictures by W. Herbert Dunton and J. N. Marchand add color.

Lewis writes in the tall-tale voice of the old West: rough, funny, and fond of its rogues. Each story stands alone, yet the town and its folk grow familiar across the book. Readers who love western humor and frontier yarns will find a lively, old-style collection with a heroine who steals every scene she enters.
29486-a-forest-hearth-a-romance-of-india:
Charles Major, author of Dorothy Vernon of Haddon Hall and When Knighthood Was in Flower, set this 1903 romance in Indiana in the thirties, printed by Macmillan of New York and London. A picture shows a small gold watch bearing the name Rita engraved on its case, a clue to the tale's heart. Major opens with a hard truth: an unbending sense of right can disturb a household more than any other virtue. Those ruled by it are often as disagreeable as they are good.

The forest hearth of the title shelters love, duty, and frontier struggle in the young state. Major writes with local color and warm romance. Readers of historical fiction will find a sturdy, old-style tale of Indiana pioneers, their hearths, and their hearts.
29531-silhouettes:
Arthur Symons's Silhouettes, second edition revised and enlarged, printed in London in 1896 by Leonard Smithers, gathers short poems and prose sketches of Paris, Dieppe, and London. Its preface speaks a word on behalf of patchouli. Its contents move from after sunset and rain on the downs to masks and faces, pastel, her eyes, and an angel of Perugino. Nocturnes, fetes galantes, and city nights stand beside them.

Symons writes in the Decadent mode: brief, scented, and keen on mood, color, and the fleeting hour. Each piece is a small impression, caught before it fades. Readers of fin-de-siecle verse will find a classic of the 1890s, polished, sensuous, and deliberately slight, in the best sense of that word.
29596-funny-big-socks-being-the-fifth-bo:
Funny Big Socks, the fifth book of the Sock Stories by Aunt Fanny's Daughter, was printed in New York in 1863 by Leavitt and Allen. It is dedicated to a genial good man and profound philosopher, the Rev. Dr. S. I. Prime. Its contents run from storm stories and the cabbages through the gold stone to the philosopher, with a picture of Dr. Mumbudget's door-plate.

Its narrator sighs that he writes books about goodness and beauty, yet nobody buys them, since readers care nothing for such things. If only he could tell a tale, he wishes, something with a stir. Young readers and collectors of Victorian children's books will find a charming, moral volume in a beloved series.
29609-six-letters-from-the-colonies:
R. C. Seaton's Six Letters from the Colonies was printed for private circulation at Hull in 1886 by Wildridge and Company. It records eleven months away from England, from November 1884 to October 1885. The first three letters were reprinted, with slight changes, from a Hull paper. The last three were written after Seaton's return, and he drops the fiction of writing them from Australia.

Seaton warns his own readers that a traveler of so short a stay is hardly justified in firm opinions about fresh countries. Yet he writes with candor about the voyage, the colonies, and the steamers and sailing ships he met. Readers of Victorian travel letters will find a modest, honest account of Australia seen by a brief, observant visitor.
29657-mixed-faces:
Roy Norton's 1921 novel, printed by Grosset and Dunlap of New York, opens with a puzzle of nature: why did the learned judge and astute politician Hon. J. Woodworth-Granger, and Mr. James Gollop, a traveling drummer for a chocolate house, look so alike? Woodworth-Granger never spoke until he had formed a complete sentence and edited it, while Gollop wandered the roads selling sweets.

Outwardly the two could pass for specimen twins and win the blue ribbon, yet inwardly their traits differed as much as any two men's. Norton builds a comedy of doubles, swapped lives, and mistaken identity. Readers of light American fiction will enjoy a witty tale of faces that match and fortunes that do not.
29672-cossack-fairy-tales-and-folk-tales:
R. Nisbet Bain chose, edited, and rendered these tales from Cossack lore, with pictures by Noel L. Nisbet, in a London volume dated MCMXVI. The tales run from forest tsars and wind spirits to foxes, cats, and the iron wolf, and from sly peasants to tsars, angels, and saints. Each story is short, plain, and built for telling aloud, with a trick, a test, or a hard bargain at its heart.

Among them are the tale of Ivan and the daughter of the sun, the serpent wife, the magic egg, and Ivan the Fool with Saint Peter's fife. Bain keeps the Cossack flavor while making the English clear and brisk. The book serves both as fireside reading and as a first door into the folk tales of the steppe lands.
29701-the-mother-s-manual-of-children-s-:
Charles West, founder of the Hospital for Sick Children, wrote this manual for mothers, printed in New York in 1885. He states his aim plainly in the advertisement. He wants to give, in small compass and without technical detail, an account of the diseases of infancy and childhood. The book should help a mother grasp their nature and symptoms, and spare her needless fear about how they will end.

West warns that the book is not a nursery handbook and not a guide to treating illness without a doctor. Its use is to help a mother wisely second the doctor in his work for a cure. Written during a stay at Nice, it is short, clear, and kind, and it still reads as a sane voice for anxious parents.
29704-masterpieces-of-mystery-in-four-vo:
Joseph Lewis French edited this volume of riddle stories, printed in Garden City in 1922 with a 1920 copyright. It is one of four volumes of masterpieces of mystery, and its nine tales turn on a puzzle, a hidden thing, or a strange room. Cleveland Moffett opens with The Mysterious Card, and an unnamed author follows with The Great Valdez Sapphire.

Edgar Allan Poe gives The Oblong Box, Nathaniel Hawthorne The Birth-Mark, and Wilkie Collins A Terribly Strange Bed. Villiers de l'Isle Adam, Florence Marryat, William Archer, and Fitz-James O'Brien close the set. Each tale leaves the reader to guess the riddle before the end. The book is a fine shelf of classic short mystery writing.
29705-interference-and-other-football-st:
Harold M. Sherman's 1932 book of football stories, printed by the Goldsmith Publishing Company of Chicago, gathers Interference, A Case of Nerves, The Bright Token, Butter Fingers, and For the Glory of the Coach. Its title story opens as Mack Carver, substitute back on Grinnell's varsity squad, steps into Coach Edward's office, carrying one hundred and eighty-seven pounds with athletic swagger and a scowl.

Mack and a rival have battled for two years on the gridiron, and now their cracking good teams face each other. Sherman writes schoolboy sport with earnestness and pep. Young readers and fans of sports fiction will find a lively, old-style collection of gridiron tales.
29797-the-prison-chaplaincy-and-its-expe:
Rev. Hosea Quinby, once chaplain of the New Hampshire State Prison, printed this record in Concord in 1873. It comes in two parts, and the first covers work under the reformatory system. Quinby tells of his first meeting for worship, the Sabbath school, the warden, prison order, and the daily round of a chaplain's duty. He also gives a plain account of the prison and how it was run.

Later entries treat prayer meetings, prison funerals, a new chapel, and efforts for single men, including Pike, the Hampton murderer. A mother's plea for her son and a warden's work for a young man show the human side of the job. The book is a first-hand record of faith at work inside prison walls.
29813-the-big-nightcap-letters-being-the:
Aunt Fanny, the pen name of Fanny Barrow, printed this fifth book of her series in New York in 1861. Her preface states her favorite theory in plain words. By blending light-hearted tales with sober ones, a teacher can show children the goodness and beauty found in a truly Christian life. She recalls skipping the grave parts of her own childhood story books, and she trusts that child nature has not changed.

Every tale in the book tries to stir in its young readers a wish to act well, to live well, and to ask their Father in Heaven for help in prayer. The book mixes light tales with sober lessons, so the moral never sits alone. A sixth book, a full fairy story, is promised at the end. The volume is a kind sample of mid-century books for children.
29839-the-house-in-the-water-a-book-of-a:
Charles G. D. Roberts wrote this book of animal stories, with a 1907 copyright and a first impression in May 1908. Charles Livingston Bull and Frank Vining Smith drew and decorated it. The title story follows life at a beaver house in the water, where a dam, a crest, and a foraging fish-hawk set the scene. Otters, beavers, and other wild folk move through its pages.

Nine more stories follow: The White-slashed Bull, When the Blueberries Are Ripe, The Glutton of the Great Snow, and The Return of the Moose among them. A fight at the wallow, a truce of the wild done, and Sonny and the Kid close the set. Roberts writes with close knowledge of beast ways, in the style of his Kindred of the Wild.
29865-highacres:
Jane D. Abbott published Highacres in Philadelphia and London in 1920, with J. B. Lippincott Company. Her dedication answers her young readers, who asked for a school story with a heroine who has a mother and a father. They were tired of poor orphans, they said, and Abbott grants them one small step-father by way of apology. Harriet Roosevelt Richards drew the pictures.

Jerry, the heroine, travels from Kettle Mountain and Sunnyside, by the road to Cobble, to the Westleys and the school at Highacres. A secret door, a debate, a party, disgrace, and the Lincoln award follow. The third violinist, the family councils, and poor Isobel add to the school tale. Abbott writes warmly for girls who like school, friends, and fair play.
29894-a-romance-of-the-west-indies:
Eugene Sue wrote this romance of the West Indies, translated from the French by Marian Longfellow and printed in 1898 by F. Tennyson Neely in London and New York. Longfellow dedicates it to the memory of Wilkie Collins, author and artist, who first drew her attention to the work and suggested its translation into English. Four parts and an epilogue make up thirty-seven chapters.

The tale opens in May 1690, when the three-masted schooner Unicorn sails from Rochelle for Martinique. A passenger, a female Blue Beard, a priest's house, a cavern, and the Devil's Cliff follow. A buccaneer, Master Rend-Your-Soul, a marriage, and an envoy from France lead to storm, betrayal, and a viceroy of Ireland and Scotland. Arrest, a martyr, a frigate, judgment, and a chase close, with an abbey and a reunion.
299-tales-from-two-hemispheres:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boysen's tales cross between Norway and America, as he himself did. Tales from Two Hemispheres, published in 1877, opens with a young Norseman, Halfdan Bjerk, landing at Castle Garden on June 2. A gruff officer demands name, birthplace, and money.

Later tales follow an outcast, a good-for-nothing, a scientific vagabond, and Truls the nameless. Asathor's vengeance closes the set with Norse myth. Boysen writes immigrant life with humor and sympathy. The collection introduced Norwegian America to English readers. Boysen later became a Columbia professor and a bridge between literatures.
2990-never-again-a-protest-and-a-warning:
Edward Carpenter wrote Never Again! as a protest and warning to the peoples of Europe after the First World War. Carpenter asks which path Europe will follow, and whether the barbarities of war have become more abhorrent to common humanity. His question is addressed to peoples, not merely governments, who must ponder and decide the future.

The pamphlet recalls bodies of men in the trenches of northern France and on the eastern front, where war happened a hundred times over in mud and slaughter. Carpenter argues that the peoples themselves, not their rulers alone, must refuse another war. The tract remains a short, earnest statement of postwar pacifism from a veteran socialist voice.
29952-the-american-mind-the-e-t-earl-lec:
Bliss Perry gave The American Mind as the E. T. Earl Lectures, printed in Boston and New York in 1912 by Houghton Mifflin Company. Perry dedicates the book to Walter Morris Hart. Six lectures make up the volume: Race, Nation, and Book; The American Mind; American Idealism; Romance and Reaction; Humor and Satire; and Individualism and Fellowship. Perry was already known for books on Whittier, Whitman, and prose fiction.

He opens as a student in a foreign university, attacking a six-volume German history of the English drama with youthful complacency. He lost courage long before the author reached Elizabeth, but he recalls the opening chapter on the physical geography of Great Britain. Taine's theory of place, period, and environment ruled that triumphant hour, and Perry weighs chalk cliffs, midland fatness, rainy climate, and a proud, tenacious folk as makers of a national mind.
2997-time-s-laughingstocks-and-other-ver:
Thomas Hardy's Time's Laughingstocks and Other Verses gathers poems first published in 1909, in the Macmillan edition reprinted through 1928. Hardy thanks editors and proprietors of periodicals where certain poems first appeared, and the collection shows his lyric voice turning on irony, memory, and lost love. The poems are short, plain, and musical.

One poem, dated Weymouth 1869, finds four footprints on sand where two lovers stood heart to heart and hand to hand the evening before. The morning sun has baked them dry, and the woman confesses she married another a week ago, showing her ring. The book rewards readers who enjoy Hardy's verse at its most compressed and bleakly tender.
30082-westward-with-the-prince-of-wales:
W. Douglas Newton wrote Westward with the Prince of Wales, printed in New York and London in 1920 by D. Appleton and Company. Newton served as authorized correspondent in America with His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales. A transcriber's note frames the book as a British journalist's account of the cross-Canada tour by train in 1919 of Edward, then Prince of Wales.

Chapter one opens in Newfoundland. St. John's greeted the Prince before any other city of the Western continent, and it also gave him an affectionate, if inexplicable, nickname. A seaman leaning over the side of the Dauntless smiled at a vivid little Newfoundland flapper wearing a sunset-colored jumper. She wore a New York cut skirt, white stockings, and white canvas boots, and rode a gas launch. You bet, she said, he's a dandy boy. He's a plush.
30092-lords-of-the-housetops-thirteen-ca:
Carl Van Vechten collected Lords of the Housetops, thirteen cat tales, printed in New York in 1921 by Alfred A. Knopf, with a preface by Van Vechten. Van Vechten dedicates the stories to amuse Avery Hopwood. Thirteen tales follow, from Mary E. Wilkins Freeman's The Cat to Charles Dudley Warner's Calvin.

Guy Wetmore Carryl gives Zut, Algernon Blackwood a psychical invasion, and Honore de Balzac the afflictions of an English cat, translated from the French by Van Vechten. Booth Tarkington gives Gipsy, G. H. Powell the blue dryad, and Mark Twain Dick Baker's cat. Edgar Allan Poe's black cat, Thomas A. Janvier's Madame Jolicoeur's cat, W. H. Hudson's friendly rat, William Livingston Alden's Monty's friend, and Peggy Bacon's queen's cat complete a cat anthology. The Cat opens in falling snow, fur stiffly pointed, crouched for the death-spring.
30109-the-russian-garland-being-russian-:
Robert Steele edits a garland of Russian folk tales translated from a collection of Moscow chap-books, with pictures by de Rosciszewski. Lyubim Tsarevich meets the winged wolf, a self-playing harp sounds its wonder, and the seven brothers Simeon ply their trades. Ivan, the peasant's son, seeks the golden mountain, while Iliya of Murom faces the robber Nightingale and Bova Korolevich courts Princess Drushnevna.

Later tales add a mild man and his cantankerous wife, a duck with golden eggs, Bulat the brave companion, Emelyan the fool, and the judgment of Shemyaka. Philpot published the London volume, and its frontispiece shows a horse rearing higher than the waving forest. Readers get old Russian wonder tales in plain English, full of heroes, beasts, and clever fools.
30120-the-happy-prince-and-other-tales:
Oscar Wilde gathers five literary fairy tales, with pictures by Charles Robinson, in a volume first published by David Nutt in May 1888. The Happy Prince leads, followed by The Nightingale and the Rose, The Selfish Giant, The Devoted Friend, and The Remarkable Rocket. Twelve full-colour plates enrich the book, and most pages carry a line drawing in the margin or around the text, as the transcriber notes.

Brentano's issued the New York volume, later reset by Duckworth, and the cover reads And Other Stories while interior pages read And Other Tales. Wilde's tales blend beauty, wit, and sorrow, with statues, birds, giants, friends, and fireworks as moral actors. Readers new to Wilde will find here the short, polished stories that made his name beyond the stage.
30121-the-art-of-confectionary-shewing-t:
Edward Lambert, confectioner in Pall-Mall, wrote The Art of Confectionary, printed in London in 1761 for T. Payne in Castle-Street, at one shilling. The book shews the various methods of preserving all sorts of fruits, dry and liquid. Oranges, lemons, citrons, golden pippins, wardens, apricots green, almonds, gooseberries, cherries, currants, plumbs, raspberries, peaches, walnuts, nectarines, figs, and grapes follow. Flowers and herbs follow, as violets, angelica, and orange-flowers.

 The ground-work of the confectioner's art, he says, depends on knowing how to clarify and boil sugars, and he sets the degrees down distinctly so later terms are easily understood. Through the whole treatise he sticks to these denominations of boiling: clarifying, smooth, blown, feather'd, cracked, and carmel. To clarify sugar, break the white of one egg into the preserving pan with four quarts of water.
30129-old-french-fairy-tales:
The Comtesse de Ségur gathers five French fairy tales for young readers, with pictures by Virginia Frances Sterrett in the 1920 Penn volume. Blondine wakes in a magic wood and must learn repentance after wrong choices. Good Little Henry tends his sick mother and earns the plant of life, while Princess Rosette faces a court festival full of pride and peril. A little grey mouse and the bear-prince Ourson close the set with trials, sacrifice, and reward.

Each tale moves by clear moral tests: kindness is repaid, greed and spite are punished, and a brave act at the right hour undoes a spell. Talking beasts, wicked fairies, and enchanted woods fill the stories. The lessons stay plain and close to home, so the book reads as a gentle first shelf of French wonder tales, not a dark or tangled one.
30147-opportunities:
Susan Warner continues her series with Opportunities, a sequel to What She Could and the second of four novels. The London volume, dated 1871 in Roman numerals, opens the morning after the Sunday when Matilda was baptized. Girls come down to make breakfast as usual, with Maria in a cloudy, captious humour Matilda cannot grasp. The kitchen runs hot, butter softens, milk turns, and bread dries out.

Matilda notes the bread was baked days before, while Maria blames Aunt Candy for wanting bread dry and hates running to the cellar for butter fifty times an hour. Small household friction carries the chapter, in Warner's plain domestic manner. Readers of What She Could will find the same sisters, the same home duties, and a new set of chances to use them well.
30181-fungi-their-nature-and-uses:
M. C. Cooke explains fungi, their nature, influences, and uses, in volume 15 of the International Scientific Series, published by Appleton in New York in 1875. The Reverend M. J. Berkeley edited the book, after first planning to write it himself and then yielding to engagements and uncertain health. Cooke opens with the broad marks by which a casual observer tells animal, plant, and stone apart, then turns to the fungal world itself.

Fourteen chapters cover nature, structure, classification, uses, notable phenomena, spores and their spread, germination and growth, sexual reproduction, polymorphism, influences and effects, habitats, cultivation, distribution, and collection and preservation. Figures show agarics growing, a common mushroom in section, and spores of many genera. The book suits readers who want Victorian fungal science in clear, systematic form.
30202-flowers-of-freethought-first-serie:
G. W. Foote gathers short freethought pieces in a first series published in London in 1893, with titles that show its combative humor. Old Nick, Fire, Sky Pilots, Devil Dodgers, and Fighting Spooks sit beside Damned Sinners, Where Is Hell, and two pieces on Spurgeon and hell. Later items treat Shelley's atheism, the gospel of freethought, ridicule, Christianity and common sense, and who killed Christ.

Foote's preface salutes Heinrich Heine as a soldier in the army of human liberation, a leader whose sword flashed for freedom. Other pieces ask whether Jesus ascended, test St. Paul's veracity, and weigh Jesus and Paul on women, plus notes on Hugo, Whitman, and Tennyson. The book suits readers who want Victorian secularist satire, sharp, brief, and openly irreverent.
30203-flowers-of-freethought-second-seri:
G. W. Foote gathers a second series of freethought flowers, published in London by B. Forder in 1884, in the same sharp, satirical manner as the first. Luscious piety, the Jewish Sabbath, and Professor Stokes on immortality open the set, with Paul Bert, Bradlaugh's ghost, Christ and brotherhood, the sons of God, and Melchizedek following. Infidel homes, rain doctors, and pious puerilities sit beside questions on whether atheists are cruel or wicked.

Later pieces treat Christian charity, religion and money, clotted bosh, Bacon on atheism, and Christianity and slavery, with Christ up to date and secularism against Christianity. Martin Luther, happy in hell, the act of God, Keir Hardie on Christ, and blessed be ye poor widen the attack. Converted infidels, Mrs. Booth's ghost, Talmage on the Bible, and Jesus at the Derby close a combative Victorian collection.
30207-men-women-and-gods-and-other-lectu:
Helen H. Gardener lectures on men, women, and gods in a Truth Seeker volume from New York, in a twelfth edition under an 1885 copyright, with an introduction by Robert G. Ingersoll. Gardener dedicates the book to Eva Ingersoll, brave and happy wife of America's greatest orator. In her home, Gardener says, superstition and fear never entered, while human equality and freedom found their highest illustration. Time, she adds, deepened youthful love into a worship diviner than angels offer.

Lectures treat accident insurance, chiefly women, why women support the church, what it teaches, and the fruit of the tree of knowledge. Knowledge not a crime, vicarious atonement, fear, creeds, self-control, geographical religion, revelation, and evidence of faith follow, with the church's money box, historical facts against theological fictions, civilization, and women as persons. Gardener argues for reason, equality, and free thought throughout.
30208-the-ghosts-and-other-lectures:
Robert G. Ingersoll gathers his best-known lectures in a New York volume published by C. P. Farrell in 1892, entered in 1878. The title lecture opens with a famous claim. The idea of immortality was born not of any book, creed, or religion, but of human affection. It ebbs and flows with hope and fear as long as love meets death. Ghosts, liberty, and the past rise before the reader like a dream, in Ingersoll's rolling oratorical style.

Other lectures treat the liberty of man, woman, and child, the Declaration of Independence in 1776, farming in Illinois, and a Cincinnati speech. A Grant banquet address and tributes to Alexander Clark and Ebon C. Ingersoll close the set. Ingersoll says orthodox malice had mangled his texts, so he published them whole, in simple justice to himself.
30209-bible-romances-first-series:
G. W. Foote retells Bible stories as romances in a first series whose contents run from the creation story to Lot's wife. Noah's flood, Eve and the apple, the Bible devil, and the ten plagues with Jonah and the whale follow. The wandering Jews, the tower of Babel, Balaam's ass, God's thieves in Canaan, and Cain and Abel complete the list. Foote opens on Genesis, noting the common teaching that God made the universe in five days, man on the sixth, and rested on the seventh.

Every student knows that account false, Foote says, every scientist rejects it, and even most clergy disbelieve it, yet they do not disabuse the popular mind. The doctrine of the Fall, he argues, hangs on the Genesis creation tale, so discrediting one threatens the other. The series suits readers who want Victorian freethought applied, story by story, to the Bible itself.
30239-the-babe-in-the-bulrushes:
Amy Steedman retells the finding of Moses for young readers, in a Nelson volume from New York, with pictures including the baby Moses in the bulrushes. Many long years have passed since Joseph's brothers and their families settled in Egypt, and their people now form a great nation in numbers. Egyptians still rule over them as servants, and new Pharaohs, hating foreigners, treat the Israelites harshly as too many strong slaves to leave unchecked.

Work runs from morning till night, with beatings for slow work. Then a worse order spreads sorrow through Goshen: every baby boy born must be thrown into the river, while girl babies may live as future slaves. Near the great Nile, a woman holds her tiny baby, beautiful, strong, and fair, while tears run down her cheeks. Steedman tells a hard Bible story in simple, tender prose for children.
30245-phemie-frost-s-experiences:
Mrs. Ann S. Stephens, author of Fashion and Famine and The Rejected Wife, gives Phemie Frost's experiences in a Carleton volume from New York in 1874, with Low of London. Stephens dedicates the book to Frank Leslie, one of her best-tried and most valued friends, calling it the light amusement of her leisure hours, from the St. Cloud Hotel in March 1874. Her preface poem sends thistle down to the wind, lightly and wildly, a silvery mist trembling on the air.

Like wide thorny leaves whose mother root threw up a crown of rich purple bejewelled with dew, those feathery nothings, sparsely barbed with seeds, must struggle for life among brambles and weeds. Chapters open with leaving home, and Phemie's story follows in the same light, episodic manner. Readers of Stephens will find a cheerful, old-fashioned tale of a young woman out in the world.
30246-under-the-maples:
John Burroughs gathers nature essays under the maples in a Houghton Mifflin volume from 1921, his last book. A portrait made at Pasadena Glen on March 23, 1921, six days before his death, fronts the volume, which he dedicates to Clara Barrus of Riverby on the Hudson. Chapters treat falling leaves, the pleasures of a naturalist, the flight of birds, bird intimacies, a midsummer idyl, and near views of wild life.

Later pieces recall Roosevelt at Pine Knot, a strenuous holiday, and genial skies, with lawn birds, silken chambers, a desert note, and sea dogs. A sheaf of nature notes closes the book, touching nature's wireless, Maeterlinck on the bee, the robin, and the weasel. Burroughs writes as an old friend of fields and woods, keen eyed and plain spoken to the end.
30292-how-to-tie-flies:
E. C. Gregg teaches fly tying in a Barnes volume from New York in 1940, with drawings and photographs by the author. An introduction leads to tools, hooks, and materials, from the fly tier's vise, hackle pliers, and scissors to quill bodies, herl bodies, hackles, tails, cheeks or shoulders, ribbing, wings, and tying silk. Bucktail streamers, wet flies, dry flies, and nymphs with their construction follow in turn.

A table of standard dressings lists flies for the tier to copy, though the transcriber notes it holds 319 dressings, not the 334 its title claims. Paragraphs sometimes span pages split by full-page pictures, and a library listing moved to the end for continuity. Gregg writes for anglers who want to tie their own flies, in plain, practical steps from first thread to finished fly.
30320-trail-tales:
James David Gillilan tells Trail Tales, published by the Abingdon Press in New York and Cincinnati in 1915. It is dedicated to his mother and wife, and to the preachers of the Utah Mission and Idaho Annual Conference. A preface and God's minister open, with the western trail, the long trail, the desert, sagebrush, and the iron trail. Indians of the trail follow, with Pocatello the chief.

The babyless mother, Mary Muskrat, Bad Ben, a three-cornered sermon, three years after, Chief Joseph and his lost Wallowa, and the white man's book carry that section. Lights and sidelights, the stagecoach, and among the hills follow, with the mother deer, the shepherd, and the feathered drummer. Mormondom, the trail of the Mormon, some Mormon beliefs, Weber Tom, Ute polygamist, and polygamy of to-day follow. Great Salt Lake, Argonaut Sam's tale, the wraith of the blizzard, and the great northwest follow.
30321-the-adductor-muscles-of-the-jaw-in:
Richard C. Fox reconstructs jaw muscles in some primitive reptiles. His University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper, volume 12, number 15, pages 657 to 680, with eleven figures, is dated May 18, 1964. Information on bone changes in reptile groups that gave rise to mammals survives in the fossil record, Fox notes, but the muscles themselves are lost forever. A reasonably accurate picture of muscle form and placement can still be inferred from scars and marks on fossil bones.

Study of those marks, which delimit where muscles began and ended on skeletons, joins study of living genera to build the reconstruction. Fox warns plainly that such a rebuild stays largely speculative, especially where fossil groups are concerned. The paper suits readers of vertebrate paleontology who want jaw mechanics traced from reptiles toward mammals, with method and limits stated together.
30335-the-wilderness-fugitives:
Edward S. Ellis tells The Wilderness Fugitives, illustrated, published by the John C. Winston Company in Philadelphia, Chicago, and Toronto, under a copyright of 1893 by the Price-McGill Company. Ellis, author of the Deerfoot, Log Cabin, and Boy Pioneer series, opens alone and together. Soft and low, eavesdropping, the course of true love, a light ahead, the fragments of the feast, and the report of a gun follow. Mr. Isaac Perkins, border bravery, and on the river follow.

An unfavorable omen, forced backward, a new peril, diamond cut diamond, a task, and Iroquois against Iroquois carry the tale. At last, the shore, the Mohawk objects, and the way home follow. A discovery, a fugitive, doubt and perplexity, a guide, the hiding-place, and proceedings follow. What does it all mean, up and doing, a check, a fate, the Mohawk explains, the tree, and captive and captors close the book.
30358-a-history-of-horncastle-from-the-e:
James Conway Walter writes an illustrated history of Horncastle from its earliest period to the present time, published in Horncastle in 1908. Born within a mile of the town, he spent many years on research in many directions. The front matter shows the seal of Simon de Islip, vicar in 1349 and later Archbishop of Canterbury.

Walter traces the town through its market place, memorials, parishes, and local families, using records and local knowledge rather than a broad national survey. His preface stresses patient, local labor. The book serves as a town chronicle for readers who want Horncastle's own past told street by street and generation by generation.
30374-futurist-stories:
Margery Verner Reed tells Futurist Stories, published by Mitchell Kennerley in New York in 1919. Moonbeams, The Dream Muff, Rose Petals in a Field, Incalculable, A Neapolitan Street Song, In Algiers, Candles, and Igor fill the first half. Two Had Lived, The Fifth Symphony, The Mad Artist, Old Scores, The Last Ashes, Nancy Turner, The Pawn Shop Keeper, Something Provincial, and Conflict follow. That Night His Sorrow Was Lifted closes the volume.

Moonbeams, dedicated to V. Z. R., opens on a glorious winter night, with snow shining under a magical moon and trees glistening in branches, almost as light as day, enchanting rather than bleak. Into the woods walks the Spirit of Art, sad that he never reproduced such splendor, and promising to do better tomorrow. The Spirit of History follows, hands soiled with blood and dark crimes, asking why history could not be as white as the snow.
30396-books-and-authors-curious-facts-an:
This Edinburgh collection gathers curious facts and characteristic sketches about books and authors, printed by Murray and Gibb for William P. Nimmo. Contents include an anecdote on Wycherley's wooing and a note on finding the manuscript diary of John Evelyn, with a front illustration of that discovery.

Anecdotes, illustrative sketches, and memorabilia fill the volume. One tale turns on a long versus short vowel in Latin, and a letter shows Beaumont letting his thoughts wander to Jonson. The book suits readers who love literary gossip, odd facts, and brief portraits. It offers browsing pleasure rather than a single argument, chapter by chapter.
304-rio-grande-s-last-race-and-other-ver:
A. B. Paterson's Rio Grande runs his last race in the title poem, as told by Macpherson. Rio Grande's Last Race and Other Verses, from the original 1902 Sydney edition, gathers verses printed from London to Bloemfontein to Sydney. War poems, drought poems, and horse poems share the book.

Contents list Mulga Bill's Bicycle, the Pearl Diver, Saltbush Bill's gamecock, and Hay and Hell and Booligal. Paterson's galloping lines suit cattle, railways, and surveyors. The collection followed his Man from Snowy River fame. It keeps Paterson's bush voice at full stride.
30400-all-the-way-to-fairyland-fairy-sto:
Evelyn Sharp offers fairy stories for young readers longing for a full trip to Fairyland. John Lane published the book in 1898, with eight colored illustrations by Mrs. Percy Dearmer. Dedicated to Geoffrey, Christopher, Tristan, Iseult, Margaret, Boy, and Everard, the book opens with a princess floating on a soft white cloud.

Contents include the country called Nonamia and why the Wymps cried. They add the story of Honey and Sunny, the little princess and the poet, the wonderful toymaker, the professor of practical jokes, and the doll that came straight from Fairyland. Sharp writes with gentle wit and wonder, making each tale a small journey into a kind, strange world.
30410-christology-of-the-old-testament-a:
Hengstenberg's Christology of the Old Testament, volume one, appears in Clark's Foreign Theological Library, second series, volume one, published in Edinburgh by T. & T. Clark, 38 George Street, with London and Dublin publishers. The e-text rests on images from the 1868 edition, with unclear or missing punctuation corrected by reference to the 1854 edition. Latin diphthong oe appears as oe in brackets, superscripts carry a caret, as in 2^a, and Greek words are transliterated directly.

Greek eta becomes ê and omega ô. Diacritic marks are omitted except the initial hard breathing mark, shown as h before the initial vowel. Hebrew words, mainly without vowel and pronunciation points, follow a fixed table, from Alef as a and Bet as b through Shin as w and Tav as t. The volume gives a learned nineteenth-century reading of the Old Testament as pointing toward Christ, in a form built for close study rather than casual reading.
3044-desperate-remedies:
Thomas Hardy's first novel, Desperate Remedies, unfolds through chapters titled by time, from the events of thirty years down to the events of three hours. The structure itself tells the story, as a long past compresses into a fortnight, eight days, one day, twelve hours, and eighteen days of crisis. Hardy later called the book a sensation novel, and its machinery of secrets, wills, and disguises shows it.

A scene of organ music in a small room, loud and soft, simple and complicated, weird and grand, moves a listener out of proportion to the notes themselves. Light and sound strive outside while the music swells within. The novel appeals to readers who enjoy Hardy before Wessex hardened into tragedy, with melodrama handled by a master.
30466-wild-oranges:
Joseph Hergesheimer sets Wild Oranges in a still bay, where John Woolfolk brings a ketch to anchor among cypress limbs, bare roots, and gathering shadows. First printed in 1918 inside Gold and Iron, then reprinted twice and issued separately in March 1922, the novel was also illustrated with scenes from King Vidor's Goldwyn photoplay.

Woolfolk calls to a white-clad figure in the bow to let go the anchor, and the quiet water mirrors a yellow western sky. Hergesheimer builds mood from light, stillness, and the murmur of waves on far bars, letting place shape the tale. The novel pairs a coastal setting with a tense human story, told in rich, visual prose.
3049-a-group-of-noble-dames:
Thomas Hardy collected A Group of Noble Dames, first in 1891, in the 1920 Macmillan edition with a map of Wessex. The dames include the first Countess of Wessex, Barbara of the House of Grebe, and the Marchioness of Stonehenge. Lady Mottifont, Squire Petrick's lady, the Lady Icenway, Anna Lady Baxby, the Lady Penelope, the Duchess of Hamptonshire, and the Honourable Laura complete the company. Milton's line about ladies whose bright eyes rain influence serves as epigraph. The tales are told by a club of antiquaries.

Barbara's story turns on a frightened woman creeping from a room while her husband sits down to a supper he cannot eat, his worst surmises confirmed. Barbara sinks on her bed and buries her face in the coverlet. The collection shows Hardy's gift for scandalous history told with sympathy.
3052-complete-works-of-plutarch-volume-3:
Plutarch's Complete Works, volume three, gathers his essays and miscellanies, translated in this edition by several hands. Philosophical essays ask whether one can live pleasurably by Epicurus, whether a philosopher should converse with great men, and whether the Stoics speak greater improbabilities than the poets. Symposiacs, common conceptions against the Stoics, the eating of flesh, and fate follow. Literary essays take up the life and poetry of Homer.

Table talk ranges from why air cools water to why stones and iron resist air's passage where bronze and earthen vessels let it through. Plutarch's curiosity runs through every page. The volume suits readers who want the Greek moralist in his essayistic mood, conversational and wide-ranging.
30547-the-thirteen-little-black-pigs-and:
Mrs. Molesworth writes The Thirteen Little Black Pigs and Other Stories, illustrated by W. J. Morgan and published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Contents open with the title tale, then add Right Hand and Left, A Shilling of Halfpence, A Friend in Need, and Pansy's Pansy.

Later stories include Pet's Half-Crown, A Catapult Story, and A Very Long Lane, or Lost in the Mist. The title tale opens with a house on rising ground, its nursery at the top except for attics above, with a good view from two large windows. Molesworth writes gentle, imaginative tales for children, full of home, play, and small wonders.
3056-wessex-tales:
Thomas Hardy collected Wessex Tales with a preface apologizing for presenting two consecutive stories of hangmen in so small a book. Hardy explains that tales of executions formed a large part of local tradition near county towns. As a boy he knew a man who applied for the hangman's office and sank into incurable melancholy at failing to get it. The contents include An Imaginative Woman, The Three Strangers, The Withered Arm, Fellow-Townsmen, Interlopers at the Knap, and The Distracted Preacher.

The Withered Arm follows Gertrude to a lonely cottage by a deep slow river under prison cliffs, seeking the Casterbridge hangman. The stream waters Stickleford and Holmstoke meads lower down, though Gertrude does not know it. The tales show Hardy's Wessex at its darkest, where folklore and fate meet.
30577-told-in-the-coffee-house-turkish-t:
Cyrus Adler and Allan Ramsay collect and translate Told in the Coffee House, Turkish tales published in New York and London in 1898 by Macmillan. Contents open with How the Hodja Saved Allah, Better is the Folly of Woman than the Wisdom of Man, and The Hanoum and the Unjust Cadi.

Later tales add what happened to Hadji, a merchant of the Bezestan, how the junkman traveled to find treasure in his own yard, and how Chapkin Halid became chief detective. Cobbler Ahmet as chief astrologer, the wise son of Ali Pasha, the merciful khan, and King Kara-Kush follow. Adler and Ramsay present Turkish folk wit in clear, readable English.
3058-a-changed-man-and-other-tales:
Thomas Hardy collected A Changed Man and Other Tales in 1920, reprinting a dozen minor novels from periodicals at various dates. The contents include A Changed Man, The Waiting Supper, Alicia's Diary, The Grave by the Handpost, Enter a Dragoon, A Tryst at an Ancient Earthwork, and Master John Horseleigh, Knight. Hardy reprints them to make them accessible in the complete series from his publishers.

A passage from one tale has a listener hidden at the back of an upper landing, hearing a lighter step than her father's cross the hall into a drawing room. Caroline's sweet face in a black gown, weeping, touches her lover deeply. The collection shows Hardy's short fiction at its most varied, from Wessex romance to historical irony.
30608-christology-of-the-old-testament-a:
Christology of the Old Testament and a Commentary on the Messianic Predictions draws on the 1861 edition held by Harvard and digitized in 2006. It corrects unclear punctuation by reference to the 1856 edition. Transcriber notes explain Latin, Greek, and Hebrew forms in plain terms.

Latin oe appears as oe in brackets, and Greek words are transliterated into English equivalents. Eta appears as e with a circumflex and omega as o with a circumflex, with most diacritics omitted except an initial hard breathing shown as h. Hebrew words appear mainly without vowel and pronunciation points, with Alef as a, Bet as b, and Gimel as g. The work offers a scholarly, text-critical study of messianic passages.
307-three-elephant-power-and-other-stori:
Banjo Paterson's chauffeur Alfred taps a speed indicator and tells of Henery and an elephant. Three Elephant Power and Other Stories, in the 1917 edition, gathers Paterson's journal tales with one piece by Knott Gold. The Oracle, the Cast-Iron Canvasser, and the Merino Sheep follow.

Stories cover bullocks, dogs, steeplechase riders, and a cat sitting in judgment. Paterson's Australian voice is dry, fast, and fond of rogues. Done for the Double, by Knott Gold, closes the book. The collection suits readers who love Paterson's verse in prose form. Paterson's prose tales are less known than his ballads, but just as lively.
3070-the-hound-of-the-baskervilles:
This edition of Arthur Conan Doyle's Hound of the Baskervilles presents the novel in fifteen chapters. They run from Holmes and the curse through Sir Henry Baskerville, Baskerville Hall, the Stapletons, Watson's reports, the man on the tor, death on the moor, fixing the nets, and a retrospection. Holmes sends Watson to Devon while he works the case from afar. Suspicion gathers around Barrymore, the pale-faced, handsome, black-bearded man who first found Sir Charles's body, with only his word for the circumstances of the death.

Watson wonders whether Barrymore was the man seen in a cab in Regent Street. The novel's moor, fog, and hound carry the terror until reason closes the net, and the tale remains Doyle's finest long Holmes story.
30731-industrial-conspiracies:
Clarence S. Darrow, noted lawyer, philosopher, author, and humanitarian, delivers Industrial Conspiracies as a lecture in the Heilig Theatre, Portland, Oregon, on 10 September 1912, stenographically reported and published by permission at ten cents. Darrow opens with a credo: the earth is moving, the universe is working, and all laws of creation work toward justice.

Creation moves toward a better humanity, a higher ideal, and a time when men will be brothers the world over, he declares. Darrow applies that faith to industrial life, arguing against conspiracies of wealth and power that block justice. The short lecture serves as a populist, humanitarian statement from one of America's most famous trial lawyers.
30830-weeds-by-the-wall-verses:
Madison Cawein wrote this 1901 book of verses, published by John P. Morton in Louisville, with an epigraph attributed to Emerson that calls the speaker God in nature and a weed by the wall. Cawein dedicates the volume to Dr. Henry A. Cottell. Most of the poems had first appeared in periodicals such as the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's Magazine, Lippincott's, and the Saturday Evening Post.

Contents run from A Wild Iris, The Path by the Creek, and The Road Home through A Twilight Moth, Along the Stream, The Cricket, Voices, and The Grasshopper. They end with The Tree Toad, The Screech-Owl, and The Chipmunk. Cawein writes of small wild things with a Kentucky eye, in musical, old-fashioned verse. Readers who love nature poetry will find a gentle, observant book, rooted in creek, field, and garden wall.
30927-jack-of-no-trades:
Charles Cottrell wrote this science fiction story, printed in Amazing Stories in August 1960. Its headnote lays out the method: first the investigators discovered the Willy Maloon category, then they discovered Willy himself, then they data-researched and postulated a theory. Every step went smoothly right up to proving the theory. The narrator follows Willy Maloon, who guns a runabout past cruising speed to reach a little asteroid.

At such times Willy shows undue impatience, and the narrator follows at a distance, homing in on the same rock to find out what he is up to. Archie Crosby, the scoundrel, has lent Willy a homer unit out of supply, on Willy's word that it replaces a defective one in the cache. Willy then works on the unit, a radio transmitter, tuning it to a frequency on the far high side of the cache band.
30957-adequate-preparation-for-the-teach:
J. Daley McDonald wrote this study of adequate preparation for the teacher of biological sciences in secondary schools. It was submitted to the School of Education of the University of California in partial fulfillment of the minor requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy on November 15, 1921. Its contents map a whole program of teacher preparation, from subject matter to method to practice.

Early sections cover retarding factors in improvement, qualifications in subject matter, the scope of biology, its values and relations, adaptation of the course to community conditions, and freedom from textbook slavery. They cover materials and laboratory equipment. Later sections treat the historical setting, the spirit of research, qualifications in method, the problem method, accuracy and logical thinking, and practice teaching. It is a detailed early study of how biology teachers should be trained.
30958-jack-winters-campmates:
Mark Overton wrote this boys' camp story for M. A. Donohue in Chicago and New York, with a 1919 copyright held by the New York Book Company. Its twenty chapters run from a great streak of luck and Jack and his mates in camp through a first night under canvas, looking around, Toby's adventure, and signs of more trouble. They continue with prospecting for pictures and a night alarm.

Later chapters bring a rascally thief, fisherman's luck, a man with a pickax, Jack lifting the lid, storm-bound days, prospectors, and inside the enemy's lines, closing out of the woods. The book opens with Toby calling at Jack's door, where the latch-string is always out to chums, and Steve picked up on the way across. It is a wholesome camp adventure, full of woods, water, and boys working together.
30970-miss-cayley-s-adventures:
Grant Allen wrote this book of adventures, published by Grant Richards in London in 1899, with pictures by Gordon Browne, printed in April and reprinted in July 1899. Its heroine is Miss Cayley, and its chapters are a string of adventures, each named for the person or place at its center. An illustration shows her all agog to teach the higher mathematics.

Early adventures include The Cantankerous Old Lady, The Supercilious Attaché, The Inquisitive American, The Amateur Commission Agent, and The Impromptu Mountaineer. Later ones bring The Urbane Old Gentleman, The Unobtrusive Oasis, and The Pea-Green Patrician, with more to follow. It is a bright, episodic novel of a resourceful young woman making her way through the world, adventure by adventure.
30987-porto-rico-its-history-products-an:
A. D. Hall, author of books on Cuba and the Philippines, wrote this 1898 account of Porto Rico, published by Street and Smith in New York. Hall opens by saying the island, also called Puerto Rico, has lately become of first importance. By then the United States had effectively taken hold of the island, which would soon add another star to its flag. His twelve chapters run from the aborigines and the struggles of the past to topography, climate, population, and towns.

Later chapters cover resources, manners and customs, the dawn of freedom, naval lessons taught by the war, what the army achieved, and how the Porto Ricans received the Americans. They close with the American claim and what possession will mean. It is a period guide to the island's history, products, and possibilities, written from a frankly American point of view in the year of its transfer.
31019-four-ghost-stories:
Mrs. Molesworth, author of Carrots and Hathercourt Rectory, wrote this collection of four ghost stories. It was published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1888 and dedicated to her nieces Lilian and Georgina Molesworth on December 5, 1887. Its four stories are Lady Farquhar's Old Lady, Witnessed by Two, Unexplained, and The Story of the Rippling Train. The first is headed A True Ghost Story.

Its narrator says she herself has never seen a ghost, and is by no means sure she wishes ever to do so. Her friend's experience has been less limited. Living at extreme ends of the country, the two meet seldom. During a visit the talk falls on supernatural visitations, and the narrator recalls that her friend Margaret has seen a ghost herself. It is a quiet, Victorian collection of ghost tales, told as remembered testimony rather than sensation.
31082-the-mermaid-of-druid-lake-and-othe:
Charles Weathers Bump's 1906 Baltimore collection holds twelve stories, several reprinted with the aid of the Baltimore News. The title tale begins on a hot June night, when a sleepless Edwin Horton leaves his Bolton Avenue home at dawn for a stroll in Druid Hill Park. There he finds a young woman seated alone by the lake inside its high iron railing.

Other stories take up a goddess of truth, a daughter of Cuba Libre, a two-party telephone line, and the night Patti sang. They also bring a pink ghost in Franklin Square, a vanished mummy, and a Mount Vernon telephone number. Light, local, and gently comic, the volume preserves Baltimore storytelling of the early 1900s at its most charming.
31103-a-christmas-greeting-a-series-of-s:
Hans Christian Andersen's Christmas Greeting, published in New York by James Miller, gathers thirteen stories dedicated to Charles Dickens, whom Andersen addresses from his quiet Danish home after a visit to England. The tales include The Old House, The Drop of Water, The Happy Family, and The Story of a Mother. They also include The False Collar, The Shadow, The Old Street-Lamp, and The Dream of Little Tuk.

The set closes with The Naughty Boy, The Two Neighboring Families, The Darning Needle, The Little Match-Girl, and The Red Shoes, with a final address to young readers. Illustrated and warmly told, the collection shows Andersen at his most tender and most unsettling, turning everyday objects into moral fables for Christmas reading.
31115-an-account-of-our-arresting-experi:
Conway Evans's privately printed 1914 memoir was issued by the Merrymount Press in Boston in just one hundred copies. It tells how three American women travelers were caught by the outbreak of war. Evans, Lyra Nickerson, and Katherine Schermerhorn reached Berlin on July 29, 1914, after a tour through Germany, meaning to sail from Hamburg on the Viktoria Luise for a northern cruise.

A lost box from Dresden, a concert, a motor trip to Potsdam, and talk of war crowd the first days, before arrest turns holiday into alarm. Dedicated to her two plucky little fellow prisoners, the little book is a vivid, personal snapshot of summer travel collapsing into the Great War.
31122-the-mystery-of-witch-face-mountain:
Charles Egbert Craddock's 1895 collection holds three stories, led by the title tale of a mountain face that appears only in certain light. On bright moonlit nights or in storm lightning, a huge, stern profile shows on a bare sandy slope. Climbers who cross the stream and climb to the spot find only bare ground, gullies, and scattered rock.

The other two stories, Taking the Blue Ribbon at the County Fair and The Casting Vote, round out a volume of mountain life, local pride, and hard choices. Craddock's mountain writing is known for its close landscape detail and its sympathy for isolated folk, and this collection shows both gifts in compact form.
31124-a-diary-without-dates:
Enid Bagnold's diary, first printed in London in January 1918 with a second impression the next month, records wartime life inside an institution during the Great War. Its sections move from outside the glass doors to inside them, and then to the boys, the wounded young soldiers at the center of the writer's days.

Bagnold writes in short, sharp entries about discipline, routine, and the strange freedom of belonging to a large organization rather than a small circle of friends. The book's lack of dates suits its mood: days blur into one another. What stays is the voice of a young woman watching war at close quarters, with humor, impatience, and care.
31160-free-joe-and-other-georgian-sketch:
Joel Chandler Harris's 1887 collection, published by P. F. Collier in New York, holds five Georgian sketches: Free Joe, Little Compton, Aunt Fountain's Prisoner, Trouble on Lost Mountain, and Azalia. The title sketch follows Free Joe, a free Black man in the village of Hillsborough in 1850, whom white villagers watch with suspicion as a drifting man without an owner.

Harris, best known for Uncle Remus, writes in the local-color manner of his day, mixing humor, dialect, and pathos as he pictures a slave society's fear of the free. The sketches remain widely read both as Georgia storytelling and as evidence of how white Southern writers framed Black life after Reconstruction.
31161-german-problems-and-personalities:
Charles Sarolea's 1917 volume, published by Chatto and Windus in London, collects wartime essays on Germany by a writer who had warned of war years before it came. Early chapters revisit his forecasts of 1906 and 1912 and turn to the Hohenzollern curse and a war triumvirate of Nietzsche, Treitschke, and Bernhardi. They add further studies of Frederick the Great and the worship of Goethe.

Later pieces examine Mecklenburg's Junkers, the German race heresy, the tragic isolation of Germany, Russia and Germany, Prince von Bülow as peacemaker, and the coming revolution, closing with a road to peace. Passionate and partisan, the book is a vivid record of how one Allied observer explained Germany to wartime Britain.
31167-the-old-willow-tree-and-other-stor:
Carl Ewald's nature stories, translated by A. Teixeira de Mattos and published in London in 1921, gather nine tales named for trees and plants. The old willow-tree leads, followed by the mistletoe, the lilac-bush, the beech and the oak, the weeds, the anemones, and the wood and the heath. Somewhere in the wood and the cousins follow, with drawings by Helen M. Jacobs and G. E. Lee.

The translator's dedication notes that most of the stories were new to Britain, and the volume belongs to the Royal Road Library of children's books. Gentle and observant, Ewald's tales give young readers the woods as a living community, full of small dramas among roots, branches, and leaves.
31185-chapters-in-the-history-of-the-ins:
Daniel Hack Tuke's 1882 history, published by Kegan Paul, Trench in London, traces the treatment of the insane in the British Isles from superstition toward reform. Chapters take up early medical and superstitious treatment, Bethlem Hospital and St. Luke's, eighteenth-century asylums and the founding of the York Retreat, pictured in the frontispiece, and the course of lunacy legislation.

Later chapters follow reform at Lincoln and Hanwell, criminal lunatics at Broadmoor, chancery lunatics, idiots and imbeciles, and the separate stories of Scotland and Ireland, closing with the progress of psychological medicine. Tuke, former visiting physician to the York Retreat, writes as both historian and reformer, and the book remains a standard early history of its subject.
31186-what-shall-we-do-now-five-hundred-:
Dorothy Canfield and others' 1907 book, published by Frederick A. Stokes in New York, answers its title question with five hundred games and pastimes for children. Its illustrations run from a Pueblo settlement frontispiece through outdoor games for girls and boys, playing alone, and country play. They go on to the house that glue built, a Dutch house, an Esquimau sled, Indian costumes, pets, and reading.

Inside, young readers find knots from bowline to dogshank, hop-scotch, prisoner's base, bean-bag boards, daisy chains, cardboard doll furniture, and drawing tricks, with text figures to guide each game. Practical and generous, the book remains a treasury of play from the days before radio and screen.
31189-the-monster-and-other-stories:
Stephen Crane's 1899 collection, published by Harper and Brothers, holds three stories led by The Monster. It opens with little Jim playing at being engine number 36 between Syracuse and Rochester, fourteen minutes behind time. Then a wheel of his cart crushes a peony and his father, the doctor mowing the lawn, turns to look.

The Blue Hotel and His New Mittens complete the volume, with illustrations captioned from the text, from Henry Johnson's shouted name to a pair of very wet mittens. Crane's irony, color, and eye for small humiliations run through all three tales, making the book a fine short entry to his fiction beyond The Red Badge of Courage.
31191-a-letter-to-the-hon-samuel-a-eliot:
Written under the name Hancock and published in Boston in 1851, this letter answers Representative Samuel A. Eliot's published apology for voting for the Fugitive Slave Bill. Hancock charges that Eliot voted precisely as those who procured his nomination intended. He then found his name a byword and reproach in Massachusetts, declined to face the voters, and rashly appealed to the public through a newspaper with reasons for his vote.

The letter mocks the transcendental logic of Eliot's defense, with its talk of New England's climate, soil, and scenery. It argues that a vote to catch and enslave free-created men cannot be dressed as obedience to God's law. Sharp and learned, it is a classic of abolitionist pamphleteering.
31203-medica-sacra-or-a-commentary-on-th:
Richard Mead's Medica Sacra, translated from the Latin under the author's eye by Thomas Stack and printed in London in 1755, reads the Bible as a casebook. Fifteen chapters take up, in turn, the disease of Job, leprosy, the diseases of Saul, Joram, and Hezekiah, the disease of old age, and Nebuchadnezzar's affliction. They go on to palsy, demoniacs, lunatics, the woman with an issue of blood, a rigid spine, the bloody sweat of Christ, and the diseases of Judas and Herod.

Mead, physician to the king and fellow of the Royal Society, brings eighteenth-century medicine to ancient texts, asking what modern doctors would call these famous sufferings. The book remains a landmark where scripture commentary and medical history meet.
31209-indian-fairy-tales:
Maive Stokes's Indian Fairy Tales, published in London by Ellis and White in 1880 with notes by her mother Mary Stokes and an introduction by W. R. S. Ralston, collects thirty tales told in Hindustani. Calcutta and Simla supply the settings for the opening twenty-five, narrated by the ayahs Dunkní and Múniyá together with Karím, who served as khidmatgar. Múniyá alone recounted the closing five to Stokes's mother.

At first the servants would tell their stories only to the child Stokes, who would not laugh at them, though the ayahs later retold almost all of them for the press. With help on botany, spelling of native names, and an index from family and friends, the book preserves Indian household storytelling in faithful English dress.
31270-the-writings-of-thomas-paine-compl:
This volume of The Writings of Thomas Paine, collected and edited by Moncure Daniel Conway, gathers The American Crisis, the series of pamphlets that carried American morale through the Revolutionary War. Crisis numbers one through thirteen run here, with a supernumerary Crisis. They run from addresses to Lord Howe and the people of England to the final essay on the peace and its probable advantages.

Conway's preface untangles an old publishing blunder, in which an early London publisher printed a borrowed essay as Paine's first Crisis and left confusion in its wake. The volume lets readers follow Paine's war rhetoric in order, from crisis to crisis, as Americans first read it.
31296-the-ethnology-of-the-british-colon:
R. G. Latham's 1851 volume, published by John Van Voorst in London, surveys the peoples of the British colonies and dependencies as ethnology then understood them. Early chapters cover Europe's dependencies, from Heligoland and the Frisians through Gibraltar, Malta, the Ionian Islands, and the Channel Islands. They then cover Africa, from the Gambia and Sierra Leone through the Gold Coast, the Cape, Mauritius, and Black Americans.

The Asian chapters run wider still, from Aden and Hong Kong through the Tenasserim provinces, Assam's many tribes, and the Tamil, Telugu, Kanara, and Malayalam languages. Dated in its language and categories, the book remains a substantial Victorian attempt to map the empire's peoples.
3134-backlog-studies:
Warner builds these fireside studies around a fading New England custom. The backlog once burned on the hearth while the family gathered round it. That hearth has gone out, he laments, and the family's center with it. Age earns less respect, and old rites like toast and cider have faded. Roasting apples and mince pies at ten at night belong to a world slipping away.

Each study starts at the fireside and turns to manners, morals, and change. The book is no manual for winter evenings. It is a quiet protest against hurry and new ways, in the plain, companionable style that made Warner a favorite fireside author.
31349-satan-and-the-comrades:
Ralph Bennitt's story, printed in Fantastic Universe in September 1956 as a sequel to Satan on Holiday, brings Nick, the Prince of Darkness, home from a year's holiday as a college boy. Slowing from fifth dimension to fourth above the wastes of Chaos, he finds the broad highway Sin and Death built eons ago repaired by his chief engineer Mulciber. The court wag Belial advertises at new roadhouses along the way.

Unsure whether just the right improvements have been made in Hell, Lucifer applies a dash of sulfur with Satanic skill. The magazine's headnote promises chuckles as he holds a mirror up to human nature at its most Luciferian. Mordant and jovial at once, the yarn is a craftsman's comic fantasy of Hell modernized.
31351-a-record-of-study-in-aboriginal-am:
Daniel G. Brinton's 1898 volume, printed for private distribution at Media, Pennsylvania, surveys forty years of his own work in American linguistics, the study of native speech. Suggested by his late friend James Constantine Pilling, whose bibliographies of American aboriginal languages faced the difficulty of cataloguing writings scattered across journals, proceedings, and volumes, the survey groups Brinton's articles geographically. It adds notes on their aims and conclusions.

Early entries include his 1885 papers on Humboldt's philosophic grammar of American languages and on polysynthesis and incorporation, word-building habits of these tongues, and his 1894 characteristics of American languages. For students of Native American languages, the book is an author's own map to a lifetime of scholarship.
31381-the-squire-s-daughter-being-the-fi:
Archibald Marshall's The Squire's Daughter, the first book in the Chronicles of the Clintons, was published by Dodd, Mead and Company, first in October 1912 and in this edition in 1920. Its chapters open with a court ball, move to the Bay of Biscay, introduce the Clintons of Kencote, young and old, and take up the question of marriage. The novel follows an English country family through social life, travel, and the choices of its younger members.
