Marshall writes the chronicle novel with ease, letting family history unfold through conversation and event. The squire's daughter stands at the center of a world where class, money, and affection shape every decision. Readers of Edwardian country-house fiction will find a warm, well-observed opening to a longer family saga.
31386-mad-shepherds-and-other-human-stud:
L. P. Jacks's 1910 volume, published by Henry Holt in New York with a frontispiece by L. Leslie Brooke and dedicated to Sir Robert Ball, collects studies of eccentrics and ordinary people. The Mad Shepherds sequence follows Shoemaker Hankin, Snarley Bob on the stars, Snarleychology theoretical and experimental, two miracles, Shepherd Toller of Clun Downs, Snarley Bob's invisible companion, and Snarley Bob's death.

Other human studies include Farmer Perryman's tall hat, a gravedigger scene, an attempt to act the Good Samaritan, and Macbeth and Banquo on the blasted heath. Opening with a meditation on how dread of mortality embases the soul, the book treats its odd, vivid characters with philosophy and humor, finding the universal in the local.
31399-banked-fires:
E. W. Savi's novel Banked Fires, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1919, takes its epigraph from Proverbs, chapter thirty-one, verse ten, asking who can find a virtuous woman, for her price is far above rubies. Savi, author of The Daughter-in-Law and Sinners All, opens in Bengal. An autumn evening draws to a close beside government tents, with smoke veiling the sheltering trees and harvested fields lying flat in the dusk. The first chapter is called "The Lonely Encampment."

From that Anglo-Indian opening, the novel follows its characters through passion held in check, the banked fires of the title. Savi writes of love, duty, and reputation in a colonial world. Readers of Edwardian popular fiction will find a romantic novel of restraint and feeling, set against the heat and stillness of India.
31410-the-boy-slaves:
Captain Mayne Reid's adventure novel The Boy Slaves, in a new edition with a memoir by R. H. Stoddard, follows young captives in a harsh foreign land. Its opening chapter, "The Land of the Slave," paints a burning African landscape of lions, elephants, camels, and panthers. The long contents list runs through pursuits, Moorish justice, escapes, and a final conclusion across more than eighty chapters.

Reid wrote for young readers. The book moves at the pace of a serial: danger, capture, flight, and return, with the boys forced to use wits and courage to survive. The novel also preserves the attitudes of its era toward Africa and slavery, which modern readers will read with care. As adventure, it is one of Reid's most sustained juvenile tales.
31420-la-sorcie-re-the-witch-of-the-midd:
J. Michelet's La Sorcière, translated into English as The Witch of the Middle Ages by L. J. Trotter in the only authorized English translation, was published in London in 1863, the year given on the title page as MDCCCLXIII. Trotter's preface praises Michelet's trenchant humor, scornful eloquence, and epigrammatic dash, and says he has tried to recast those qualities in worthy English. The book's chapters run from the death of the gods to temptations, possession, the covenant, and the sabbath.

Michelet argues that the witch was a figure of rebellion and healing in a despairing age, with the devil appearing as physician and prince of nature. Readers will find a passionate, poetic history rather than a dry survey. It remains influential for its bold reading of witchcraft as protest, and for the vivid, partisan voice that carries it.
31426-eagles-of-the-sky-or-with-jack-ral:
Ambrose Newcomb's Eagles of the Sky, or With Jack Ralston Along the Air Lanes, is a boys' aviation adventure. It was published by the Goldsmith Publishing Company of Chicago, with copyright in 1930. Jack Ralston, its hero, takes to the air lanes in a Curtiss-Robin plane. Chapter titles promise a night owl on the wing, a dance of fireflies, a battle royal, and a tear-bomb attack. The story moves from getting ready for business to one aerial scrape after another.

Newcomb, author of The Sky Detectives, writes for young readers who followed aviation as the great new adventure of the age. The appeal is speed, machines, and daring, with Jack at the controls. Readers looking for period boys' fiction will find the technology of early flight treated as romance, and the hero's courage tested in the sky rather than on the ground.
31431-old-time-stories:
Old-Time Stories, told by Master Charles Perrault and translated from the French by A. E. Johnson, with illustrations by W. Heath Robinson, was first published in 1921 by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York. A prefatory note explains that of the eleven tales in the volume, the first eight are from the master hand of Charles Perrault. The remaining tales complete a collection of classic fairy stories in a handsome English dress.

Perrault's tales, among them the best-known stories of the European tradition, appear here with Robinson's distinctive illustrations. The volume suits both children and adults who love fairy tales in their classic form. Its value lies in the pairing: Perrault's clear, elegant storytelling and Robinson's witty, detailed pictures, which have made this edition a favorite among collectors.
3152-the-junior-classics-volume-1-fairy-:
William Patten selected and arranged this first volume of The Junior Classics. Charles W Eliot, president emeritus of Harvard, wrote the introduction, and William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. The whole set was planned in ten volumes and about five thousand pages, sorting tales, stories, and poems for young readers, both ancient and modern.

This volume holds fairy and wonder tales. Its purpose is to put good stories within a child's reach in a graded order. Parents and teachers get a trusted shelf in one book, and children get tales chosen for fancy and moral sense rather than mere novelty. The set became a standard home library for a generation of American families.
31578-room-number-3-and-other-detective-:
Anna Katharine Green's Room Number 3 and Other Detective Stories, published by the A. L. Burt Company of New York by arrangement with Dodd, Mead and Company, gathers Green's detective tales. Green, author of The Mystery of the Hasty Arrow, The Golden Slipper, and That Affair Next Door, was America's first great woman detective novelist. Copyright in 1912 by Green, with earlier copyrights by the Crowell Publishing Company and Abbott and Briggs, the volume appeared as Masterpieces of Mystery in another form.

The title story and its companions show Green's method: careful plotting, domestic settings, and detection by reason rather than violence. Her detectives, often amateurs or young lawyers, unravel mysteries from small, telling details. Readers of detective fiction will find a foundational American collection, where the modern mystery story was taking shape.
3167-wessex-poems-and-other-verses:
Thomas Hardy gathers his Wessex poems in this 1919 Macmillan volume, joining them with Poems of the Past and the Present. Wessex Poems first appeared in 1898, with a new edition in 1903 and pocket editions after. Poems of the Past and the Present followed in 1901, dated 1902, with a second edition in 1903.

The verses return to the country Hardy made his own: farms, churchyards, lanes, and the folk who worked them. Love, loss, and the ironies of time run through them, in the plain speech of his novels turned to meter. Readers who know Tess or The Mayor of Casterbridge will hear the same voice here, sadder and shorter, and no less sure.
31680-generals-help-themselves:
M. C. Pease's story opens with an admiral, affectionately known as the Old Man, telling his aide that his plea for P-boats has failed. From the President on down, everyone dwells on nothing but the Combine's overrunning of Venus. They answer that the Venusians too relied on P-boats, and were crushed by Combine dreadnoughts in a single battle.

The aide protests that the Venusians fought their small, light, fast P-ships idiotically, slugging it out with dreadnoughts instead of using Plan K. The Old Man has staked his whole reputation on Plan K and a balanced space fleet, against the fleets of the Combine of Jupiterian Satellite States. With no one to help him, the general must help himself.
31697-the-shepherd-of-salisbury-plain-an:
Hannah More's 1859 New York collection gathers tales for the common people, headed by The Shepherd of Salisbury Plain. Its contents also include The Two Shoemakers, The History of Tom White the Post Boy. They also include The Sunday School, the sequel The History of Hester Wilmot, and stories of Betty Brown, Black Giles the Poacher, and other humble folk.

The title tale follows a poor shepherd and his visitor Mr. Johnson, who studies how a man of such piety spends his Sunday at home with his family. Readers get moral stories of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, written to instruct as much as to entertain.
31703-mid-pleasures-and-palaces:
James McKimmey Jr.'s story Mid Pleasures and Palaces, illustrated by Philip Parsons, opens with William Kirk on a remote and set-apart planet, where nothing had made him think he might find human life. Just beyond a thorn bush like a bursting rose, he sees eyes, a nose, and yellow hair that are definitely human. Kirk stands motionless, three miles from the rocket and from Leo, waiting inside it.

Kirk feels like a man in a gully watching a boulder teeter above him, ready to crush his life out, with only brain and voice for defense. Leo had warned him on landing that this kind of planet could be the end of twelve years. McKimmey's tale turns a first contact into a test of nerve.
3172-fenimore-cooper-s-literary-offences:
Mark Twain opens by quoting praise for Cooper, then sets out to demolish it. Professor Lounsbury had called The Pathfinder and The Deerslayer pure works of art, standing at the head of Cooper's novels as finished wholes. Twain grants that other Cooper books hold parts as perfect and scenes as thrilling, but denies that any matches those two as a whole.

The essay then lists Cooper's offences against his craft: broken rules of dialogue, impossible woodcraft, and characters who say and do what no living person would. Twain's famous count of eighteen rules violated in one passage still circulates. The piece endures as comic criticism: a great humorist teaching, by negative example, how fiction ought to be built.
31763-irish-fairy-tales:
W. B. Yeats's Irish Fairy Tales, edited with an introduction by Yeats and illustrated by Jack B. Yeats, was published in London by T. Fisher Unwin in 1892. Yeats's opening verses, dated London, January 1892, send his gathered words out on untiring wings to sing to a sad heart in the night, beyond waters storm darkened or starry bright.

The collection groups tales of land and water fairies, opening with The Fairies' Dancing-Place and The Rival Kempers. Readers get a founding book of the Irish literary revival, gathering folk tales with a poet's care for their strangeness, humor, and melancholy.
31785-for-john-s-sake-and-other-stories:
Annie Frances Perram's collection For John's Sake and Other Stories, published in London by the Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School Union, is a temperance book through and through. Its preface warns that readers may think its scenes impossible, but assures them that its darkest pictures are minutely faithful to life and its saddest incidents occurred under the writer's own observation.

The title story follows Ruth, afraid for herself, through John's brother, hopes and fears, and a happy ending. Other tales cover moderate drinking and its results, a committee's decision, and how a husband was lost and found. Readers get earnest Victorian moral stories, written to show the snares and perils outside total abstinence.
31798-games:
Katherine MacLean's short story Games, printed in Galaxy in March 1953, opens with a boy named Ronny playing by himself, which means he is two tribes of Indians having a war. He fires an imaginary rifle, then decides it is a time before white people sold Indians guns, and changes the rifle into a bow.

Ronny mimics the sound of an arrow striking flesh, folds down onto the grass in defeat and death, and climbs to his feet to be another man. All the while, his mother offers chocolate milk from the kitchen. Readers get a science-fiction story about a child who cannot tell where a daydream ends and impossibility begins, told with humor and tenderness.
3184-alonzo-fitz-and-other-stories:
Mark Twain gathers a mixed set of stories and speeches in this volume. The loves of Alonzo Fitz Clarence and Rosannah Ethelton lead the contents, beside a piece on the decay of the art of lying and one on magnanimous incident literature. Punch, brothers, punch, the great revolution in Pitcairn, and the canvasser's tale follow, with an encounter with an interviewer.

Paris notes, a legend of Sagenfeld in Germany, and speeches on the babies and on the weather round out the book. A piece concerning the American language closes the range. Together they show Twain's short form at its liveliest: romance mocked, liars praised, and a public speech turned into a comic set piece, all in the space of a few pages each.
3186-the-mysterious-stranger-and-other-s:
Mark Twain wrote The Mysterious Stranger in 1898 and never finished it. Editors of his collected works completed the story before publication. The note to this edition admits the join is unclear. No one can say exactly where Twain left off and the editors began. The tale opens in Austria in the winter of 1590, far away in time and place from Twain's America.

A fable, a piece on the deceitful turkey, and the McWilliamses and the burglar alarm share the volume. The stranger at the center tests faith and fate with cold logic. The book's unfinished state suits its theme: a story about a world that may itself be a dream, left open at the end.
31871-the-voice-of-science-in-nineteenth:
Robert Emmons Rogers's Voice of Science in Nineteenth-Century Literature, published by the Atlantic Monthly Press in 1921 with an introduction by Henry Greenleaf Pearson, is an anthology of representative prose and verse. Rogers, assistant professor of English at Massachusetts Institute of Technology, selected and arranged the volume for classes in composition and current literature.

Its contents include Matthew Arnold on the function of criticism, Michael Foster on the growth of science. They also include Thomas Huxley on the history of nature and the physical basis of life, John Tyndall on scientific materialism, and poems by Arnold, Clough, Swinburne, and Browning. Readers get a school anthology in which literature is read for what it says about a century transformed by science.
3188-mark-twain-s-speeches:
Mark Twain gathers his after-dinner and platform speeches in this volume. The contents run from Plymouth Rock and the Pilgrims and compliments and degrees to books, authors, and hats. The horrors of the German language, German for the Hungarians, and a new German word show his war with German grammar. The weather and the babies supply his most famous set pieces.

Unconscious plagiarism, educating theatre-goers, poets as policemen, and the dress of civilized woman fill the later pages. The speeches show Twain the performer: a joke timed for a hall, an insult polished for a banquet, a compliment that bites. Read aloud, they still play. The book is the best record of how America heard its humorist when he stood up to speak.
31884-a-guest-at-the-ludlow-and-other-st:
Edgar Wilson Nye's A Guest at the Ludlow and Other Stories was published in 1897 by the Bowen-Merrill Company with illustrations by Louis Braunhold. Nye readied it a few months before he died, and it reached print through an agreement with Mrs. Edgar Wilson Nye. Nye, known as Bill Nye, was one of America's best-loved humorists.

Its twenty-one pieces include Old Polka Dot's Daughter, A Great Cerebrator, Hints for the Household, A Journey Westward, A Prophet and a Piute, and My Matrimonial Bureau. Readers get a posthumous collection of Nye's gentle, wry humor, from the Ludlow asylum, reached by a five-cent elevated fare, to the American West.
31896-idyllic-monologues-old-and-new-wor:
Madison Cawein's 1898 collection Idyllic Monologues, old and new world verses, published at Louisville by John P. Morton and Company and dedicated to R. E. Lee Gibson, is almost entirely new, except for three or four poems from earlier volumes ten years before, carefully rewritten until they hardly resemble the originals except in subject.

Its contents include The Brothers, Geraldine, The Moated Manse, The Forester, My Lady of Verne, An Old Tale Re-told, The Water Witch, At Nineveh, and How They Brought Aid to Bryan's Station. Readers get a Kentucky poet's dramatic lyrics, in which single speakers tell stories of love, history, and legend.
31913-undertones:
Madison Cawein's 1896 poetry book Undertones, third in the Oaten Stop series and published at Boston by Copeland and Day, is inscribed to the pathetic memory of the poet Henry Timrod. Its opening verses lament long days and three times long nights, weary hours as a heavy chain upon Earth's dear delights, and a soul climbing its Calvary.

Contents include The Dreamer, Quiet, Unqualified, Unencouraged Aspiration, The Wood, Wood Notes, Success, Song, The Old Spring, Hills of the West, Flowers, and Second Sight. Readers get a melancholy, musical collection from a Kentucky poet of nature, loss, and quiet hope.
3192-the-curious-republic-of-gondour-and:
Mark Twain gathers whimsical sketches here, most of them written for The Galaxy from May 1870 to April 1871. The rest appeared in The Buffalo Express. The curious republic of Gondour leads the set, beside a memory, an introduction to Memoranda, and a piece about smells. A couple of sad experiences, Dan Murphy, and a tournament in the year 1870 follow.

A curious relic for sale, a reminiscence of the back settlements, and a royal compliment round out the humor. Gondour itself is Twain's joke republic, where sense and nonsense trade places. The sketches show the young Twain finding his satirical range: short, sharp, and willing to aim at anything, from a smell to a system of government.
31940-artists-past-and-present-random-st:
Elisabeth Luther Cary's Artists Past and Present, a volume of random studies illustrated and published in New York, gathers art criticism on painters past and present. Cary, author of studies of William Blake and of James McNeill Whistler, opens her passages on a panel by Carlo Crivelli. Sham jewels in the Virgin's crown and in saints' rings fail to destroy the dignity of the execution.

Later passages compare two renderings of a Pietà. One is a grave altarpiece in which two infant angels support Christ's body with pensive sorrow. The other is a more passionate version in which child angels grieve in agony. Readers get Edwardian art writing, attentive to color, gesture, and feeling, that treats old masters as living presences rather than museum names.
32007-the-spiritualists-and-the-detectiv:
Allan Pinkerton's Spiritualists and Detectives, volume five of his detective stories, follows the tangled affairs of Lilly Nettleton of Kalamazoo, a wild heart and a burning brain. Its chapters introduce a circuit-rider, the Reverend Mr. Bland, a compact where golden maple leaves fall, and a scared young woman stealing away from home.

Later chapters follow Lilly in Detroit, a funeral sermon preached by Bland, a dainty cottage holding more than neighbors knew, and Dick Hosford, a returned Forty-Niner, beginning a despairing search. Readers get a Victorian detective melodrama in which spiritualism, seduction, and detection cross, told by America's most famous detective.
32018-jaw-musculature-of-the-mourning-an:
Robert L. Merz's 1963 paper for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History studies the jaw musculature of the mourning and white-winged doves. Investigators have long held that the two genera are closely kin: Zenaida covers the white-winged and Zenaida doves, while Zenaidura covers the mourning, eared, and Socorro doves.

Merz reports investigations of dove jaw muscles, hoping that together with other studies, the relationships of the two genera can be established more firmly. Readers get a detailed anatomical paper, with twenty-two figures, for ornithologists tracing how dove genera are related through the muscles that move their jaws.
32031-a-raw-recruit-s-war-experiences:
Ansel D. Nickerson's 1888 memoir A Raw Recruit's War Experiences, printed in Providence for private distribution only, was first read before the Rhode Island Soldiers and Sailors Society on October 19, 1886. Nickerson, late private of Company B, Eleventh Rhode Island Volunteers, dedicates it to his wife, whose patriotic spirit prompted him to offer his services to his country.

Its first chapter opens in the winter before the firing upon Sumter. Young men gathered evenings at the village grocery to hear older people debate the nation's affairs and the probabilities of war between North and South. Readers get a modest, first-hand account of a recruit's service, from village debates to camp and campaign.
32036-the-unprotected-species:
Melvin Sturgis's short story, printed in Fantastic Universe in September 1956, strands a surveying party on a chill, terrifying planet. Its camp has barely been secured when four members of the surveying section bring in a wounded man. Gallifa, the senior biologist, is loading a halftrack when the stretcher is set in the shade of his truck. Bradshaw, one of his own team, is beaten and bloody, with a deep gash above his face.

The mystery deepens from that injury: something on the planet is driving crew members toward homicidal madness, while small, furtive natives watch from the cold landscape. Gallifa, who had congratulated himself on the ease of operations, must face a threat he cannot yet name. Readers get a tense planet story, where the danger is less a monster in the open than a force that turns a crew against itself.
32102-barclay-of-the-guides:
Herbert Strang's Barclay of the Guides, published in London by Humphrey Milford of Oxford University Press, carries a 1908 United States copyright and a 1924 British reprint. Its contents trace a boys' adventure on India's northwest frontier, through the Guides, a corps whose name gives the book its title. Chapters run from The Raid and The Making of a Pathan through Sky-high and The Return of Sherdil to Reprisals and In the Nets.

Later chapters introduce Jan Larrens, a competition wallah, a fakir, and the Delhi Road, with the Missy Sahib, a bluff, and lathi-wallahs and a camel along the way. Within the gates, the coming of Bakht Khan, the doctor's divan, and the spoilers spoiled lead toward wolf and jackal, master and servant, and a final fight. Readers get a stirring frontier tale of India, told for boys in the imperial adventure manner.
32117-eleven-possible-cases:
Eleven Possible Cases, published by Cassell and Company in London, Paris, and Melbourne in 1891, gathers eleven short stories by eleven writers. Its contents list reads like a roll call of late Victorian storytellers: Franklin Fyles, Frank R. Stockton, Joaquin Miller, Q., Maurice Thompson, Ingersoll Lockwood, Edgar Fawcett, Brainard Gardner Smith, Kirke Munroe, Nym Crinkle, and Anna Katherine Green.

Their stories range widely. Fyles offers The Only Girl at Overlook, Stockton A Thing That Glistened, Miller A Lion and a Lioness, Thompson The Mystic Krewe, and Lockwood Strange Adventures of a Million Dollars. Green's Shall He Marry Her closes the book. The opening story introduces the only girl at Overlook, whom local men always address as Miss Warriner, though two names are used for her. Readers get eleven possible cases, each a complete tale.
32155-the-love-letters-of-henry-viii-to-:
The Love Letters of Henry VIII to Anne Boleyn, with notes, published in Boston and London by John W. Luce and Company in 1906 and printed at the Merrymount Press, gathers the king's letters to his future queen. Its table of contents runs from Letter First through Letter Eighteenth, with one letter from Anne Boleyn to Wolsey, a postscript by Henry, and notes at the end. The letters are numbered in roman figures from i to xlv.

Letter First opens with Henry turning over in his mind the contents of Anne's last letters. He puts himself in great agony, unsure how to read them, or whether they speak against him. Readers get the Tudor courtship in the king's own words, with an editor's notes to guide them. The collection shows Henry as suitor rather than monarch, anxious, ardent, and uncertain of Anne's meaning.
32157-priests-women-and-families:
J. Michelet's Priests, Women, and Families, translated from the eighth edition of Le Pretre, la Femme, et la Famille, was published in London in 1874 by the Protestant Evangelical Mission. Its subject is the power of priests, and especially Jesuits, over women and the family. Michelet wrote to the translator that the work could not fail to interest the people of England, among whom the Jesuits were then madly pursuing their work of conversion.

The editor's preface recalls 1845, when Jesuit intrigues were thought chimerical even by many forced to join the crusade. One bishop, directed by Dr. Wiseman to use a litany for the conversion of England, replied that prayer might as well seek to make a black man white. Ordered to Rome, he spent six months in detention, which quieted his opposition. Readers get a polemical French work in English dress, aimed at clerical influence in the home.
32167-the-ballad-of-st-barbara-and-other:
Gilbert Keith Chesterton's verse collection, published in London by Cecil Palmer in a first edition of 1922, takes its title from The Ballad of St. Barbara and other verses. Chesterton dedicated the book to F. C. in memoriam, Palestine, 1919. Its opening verses remember a lost moment outside time and space. Travellers pass the portal of a disastrous, divine place, where life was slain and truth slandered on a hill holier than Rome.

The same verses recall a mystic, many-gated city, Herodian stones waiting two thousand years to be a throne, and a road climbing past rocks and hollows toward a towering dream. Bodies wandered far abroad that evening, the poem says, while souls came home. Readers get Chesterton's characteristic mix: vivid, paradoxical verse on faith, place, and memory, with Palestine and St. Barbara at its centre.
32176-witch-stories:
E. Lynn Linton's Witch Stories, published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1861, collects witch tales from historical sources. Linton, author of Azeth the Egyptian and Amymone, fronts the book with a text from Exodus: thou shalt not suffer a witch to live. The collection offers old stories of witchcraft, gathered and retold for Victorian readers curious about a darker past.

Linton's preface is candid about its limits. She does not claim to have exhausted the subject or made a complete summary, having been denied entry to certain private libraries that hold many concealed riches. She worked instead with authorities found in the British Museum and other public libraries open to her. Readers get a source-based miscellany of witch lore, honest about what it could and could not reach.
32198-cleek-of-scotland-yard-detective-s:
T. P. Hanshew's Cleek of Scotland Yard, published in New York by W. R. Caldwell and Company, gathers detective stories about Cleek, already known from Cleek the Master Detective and Cleek's Government Cases. Copyrights run from 1912 to 1914, with Doubleday, Page and Company. A frontispiece shows Cleek with Ailsa, the woman at the centre of his private life, and the book's thirty-eight chapters follow a London case.

Headlines inside the book announce a reign of terror in London, an appalling atrocity in Clarges Street, and a shocking dynamite outrage. Cleek, the master detective of Scotland Yard, works through that terror while his romance with Ailsa runs beside the case. Readers get an Edwardian detective novel in the popular manner: sensation, deduction, and a hero whose only kingdom, as the frontispiece puts it, lies in a dear woman's arms.
32217-czechoslovak-fairy-tales:
Parker Fillmore's Czechoslovak Fairy Tales, retold with illustrations and decorations by Jan Matulka, was published in New York by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1919. It brings Czech, Slovakian, and Moravian tales to American children. Fillmore dedicates the book to Miss Marjorie Rahlson, and an illustration shows Zloboha in Dobrunka's clothes. His note explains the method plainly, and honestly.

This rendering, Fillmore writes, is not a literal or scholarly translation. He retold the stories in a way he hoped would please American children. He tried hard to keep the flavour of the originals, but took the liberty of a short cut here, an elaboration there, wherever those made the English clearer and more interesting. Readers get retold Slav fairy tales, flavoured but not literal, for young readers.
32220-a-captive-of-the-roman-eagles:
Felix Dahn's historical romance, published in Germany as Bissula and translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, appeared in Chicago with A. C. McClurg and Company on September 13, 1902. Safford, translator of Aspasia and Cleopatra, presents Dahn in her preface as one of the most distinguished novelists of his day in Germany, likely to be equally appreciated by Americans. Like Georg Ebers, Dahn based his historical novels on earnest study.

The preface explains that Dahn chose above all the age of German-Roman clashes, and of rival peoples fighting for mastery in lands now German, Swiss, and French. He describes the life of those far-off times with vivid colours and dramatic power. Readers get a German historical romance of Rome and the northern peoples, told with a scholar's groundwork and a novelist's colour.
3226-records-of-journeys-to-venice-and-t:
Albrecht Dürer records his journeys to Venice and the Low Countries in this memoir, first in a series of his works. The great German artist of the Renaissance kept a diary of travel, trade, and talk as he moved between courts and workshops. Money, pictures, and patrons fill the entries, alongside weather, roads, and the people he met.

The book matters because Dürer himself wrote it, not a later biographer. Readers see a working artist abroad: selling prints, seeking commissions, and measuring the art of Italy against his own. For students of the Renaissance, the diary is a firsthand window onto how art traveled in 1520, in the hand of one of its masters.
32335-the-old-soldier-s-story-poems-and-:
James Whitcomb Riley's The Old Soldier's Story, poems and prose sketches, was published in Indianapolis by the Bobbs-Merrill Company, with copyrights in 1913, 1914, and 1915, and dedicated to George Thompson. Its dialect is kept as in the original, and its contents run from the title poem through Somep'n Common-Like, Monsieur Le Secretaire, A Phantom, In the Corridor, and Louella Wainie.

Later pieces include The Text, William Brown, Why, and The Touch of Loving Hands. They continue with A Test, A Song for Christmas, Sun and Rain, With Her Face, My Night, and The Hour Before the Dawn. Good-By, Old Year, False and True, A Ballad from April, Brudder Sims, Deformed, Faith, and The Lost Thrill follow. At Dusk, Another Ride from Ghent to Aix, and In the Heart of June close the set. Readers get the Hoosier poet in poems and sketches, dialect and sentiment side by side.
32376-notes-on-stable-management-in-indi:
J. A. Nunn's handbook, in a second edition revised and enlarged in 1897, gives practical advice on keeping horses in India and the colonies. Nunn, a veterinary captain in the Army Veterinary Department and former principal of Lahore Veterinary College, wrote first for Anglo-Indians in India. This edition adds a glossary of common Hindustani words for readers newly arrived in the East.

The notes aim at the newcomer setting up a stable for the first time, covering daily care, feeding, and management in a hot climate. Plain, direct guidance replaces theory, with attention to local terms, staff, and routines a fresh arrival would need at once. The book remains a clear window on colonial horse-keeping and veterinary practice at the end of the nineteenth century.
3242-the-doctor-a-tale-of-the-rockies:
Ralph Connor sets this Rocky Mountain tale around a young doctor and a manse family. The old stone mill opens the chapters, followed by the daughter of the manse and the raising. A dance and a new teacher lead to the young doctor himself, with a good cheer department and Ben's gang close behind. Love's tangled ways and Iola's choice shape the middle of the book.

Later chapters weigh a heretic rejected, a man who looks on a woman, and the challenge of death. Connor, a minister writing of frontier Canada, gives his doctor work that tests both skill and faith. Medicine, mining camps, and moral choice meet where help is scarce and neighbors matter most.
32455-christmas-eve-and-christmas-day-te:
Edward E. Hale's collection, published in Boston in 1873 with illustrations by F. O. C. Darley, gathers ten Christmas stories, some previously published. Its contents include They Saw a Great Light, Christmas Waits in Boston, Alice's Christmas-Tree, and Daily Bread. Hale adds a short essay on the first Christmas of Italy's king in Rome, and notes that the first story in the book had never before been published.

Hale stresses that Laura's night duty alone on her island was not drawn from imagination alone. It retells what a brave New England woman actually did because duty lay close at hand. The stories mix faith, charity, and home life, making the volume a warm, old-fashioned Christmas book for family reading.
32469-here-lies:
H. W. Guernsey's tale, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, opens with two old boys hoarding words on a wooded hill. Chauncey knocks the dottle from his corncob and asks Old Shep, without emotion, whether he will ever finish his blasted stick. Shep, lips tight, flicks pine with a scalpel-pointed knife, working a chain whose links, satin-finished like ivory, already number four hundred and seventy-two.

Chauncey then stalks to a woodpile, cleaves a fat log with one effortless axe stroke, and hikes indoors wagging his jaw. Their log-built house, a model of careful carpentry, stands on St. Paul's Hill near town. Guernsey's sidenote frames the story as an ironic tale of a practical communist who teaches his friend when to take him seriously, a lesson that gives the title its sting.
32488-just-so-stories:
Rudyard Kipling's Just So Stories, in a 1912 Doubleday Page edition with pictures by Joseph M. Gleeson, tells how animals got their marks and habits. Separate copyrights show the tales' magazine origins. How the Whale Got His Tiny Throat and How the Camel Got His Hump date from 1897. How the Rhinoceros Got His Wrinkly Skin, The Elephant's Child, and The Beginning of the Armadillos date from around 1900. Later tales include How the Leopard Got His Spots and How the First Letter Was Written.

Kipling writes for children in a playful, rhythmic voice, with animals, jokes, and just-so explanations that invite reading aloud. The transcriber notes that spelling quirks were kept, since it is hard to tell Kipling being clever from printer's creativity. The volume remains a classic of children's literature, full of wit, wonder, and memorable beasts.
3251-the-man-that-corrupted-hadleyburg-a:
Mark Twain leads this collection with the story that gives it its name. The man that corrupted Hadleyburg exposes a town proud of its honesty, undone by a sack of gold and nineteen letters. My first lie, and how I got out of it, and the Esquimaux maiden's romance follow, with Christian Science and the book of Mrs Eddy.

Is he living or is he dead, my début as a literary person, and at the appetite-cure share the set. Concerning the Jews, from the London Times of 1904, about play-acting, and travelling with a reformer round it out. Diplomatic pay and clothes close the book. Together the pieces show late Twain at his most searching: funny, skeptical, and unwilling to flatter his age.
32517-black-forest-village-stories:
Berthold Auerbach's Black Forest Village Stories, translated by Charles Goepp and published in New York in 1869, opens with The Gawk, a portrait of a village youth. The narrator sees him now, yellow hair cropped short except a long tail at the neck like a plough-horse's, broad face, great blue goggle eyes, and a mouth never shut. They met one morning in a hollow where new houses stand, when the youth cut the narrator a willow twig for a whistle.

On Sundays the youth wore a fur cap trimmed with gold tasselling, while weekdays meant a shirt, red suspenders, and black-dyed linen pantaloons. Auerbach, with facsimiles of original German woodcuts, writes village life with warmth and humour, from a distance of thousands of miles. The stories suit readers who enjoy regional fiction, German country manners, and character sketches drawn from memory.
32523-mrs-turner-s-cautionary-stories:
Mrs. Turner's Cautionary Stories, published in London in 1897 as part of the Dumpy Books for Children selected by E. V. Lucas, offers short moral tales for young readers. A first section, Bad Boys and Good, includes the window-breaker, a gunpowder plot, Peter imitating the clown, Ben's heavy punishment, and the chimney-sweeper. The fighting wicket-keeper, the good scholar, his fights, and the death of his foe follow, with thoughtless brothers and light punishments.

A second section, Good Girls and Bad, includes Rebecca's afterthought, a hint to Mary Anne, how to write a letter, news for papa, and Maria's charity. The neglected Turk, pride and priggishness, and how to look when speaking continue the pattern. Each tale pairs a fault or virtue with a clear, often comic consequence, in the cautionary manner Victorian children knew well.
32543-the-white-chief-of-the-caffres:
A. W. Drayson's White Chief of the Caffres starts with a Delhi childhood: the narrator's father was a major in service to the old East India Company. An only son, he lost his mother shortly after birth and lived at Delhi until ten, attended by an ayah and taught to ride by one of his father's syces. He learned Hindustani before English and felt at home among black people, as he puts it in the language of his time.

His father, Major Peterson, had a bachelor brother in England, a rich East Indian merchant and the narrator's godfather, after whom he was named Julius. Just before Julius turned ten, a letter from that uncle changed his life and led to the adventures of the tale. Drayson, a major general, writes a Victorian adventure of empire, travel, and African chiefdoms.
3255-moments-of-vision-and-miscellaneous:
Thomas Hardy published Moments of Vision in 1917, and this Macmillan volume reprints it with miscellaneous verses. The 1919 edition, with pocket editions following, opens on moments of vision itself and the voice of things. Hardy, past seventy, looks back at a life of writing and at a world at war, in poems of memory and foreboding.

The verses are short, grave, and musical, full of ghosts, lost houses, and the irony of time. Hardy trusts plain speech and a strict stanza to carry feeling that prose would blunt. Readers who know his novels will hear the same mind here, older and sparer: a poet watching the past return unbidden, and finding in it both comfort and rebuke.
32571-hans-andersen-s-fairy-tales-first-:
Hans Andersen's Fairy Tales, first series, edited by J. H. Stickney and illustrated by Edna F. Hart, gathers twenty tales with notes. The Fir Tree opens the book, where a little fir, unhappy despite sun, air, and passing children, longs to grow tall like the pines and firs around it.

Later tales include Little Tuk, The Ugly Duckling, Little Ida's Flowers, The Steadfast Tin Soldier, Little Thumbelina, The Little Match Girl, Ole-Luk-Oie the dream god, and The Snow Queen. Stickney's edition presents Andersen's stories for young readers, with pictures and notes to carry them from tale to tale.
32572-hans-andersen-s-fairy-tales-second:
Hans Andersen's Fairy Tales, Second Series, edited by J. H. Stickney and illustrated by Edna F. Hart, was published in Boston, New York, Chicago, and London in 1915. Contents open with The Flax, The Daisy, The Pea Blossom, and The Storks, followed by The Wild Swans, The Last Dream of the Old Oak, and The Portuguese Duck. The Snow Man, The Farmyard Cock and the Weathercock, and The Red Shoes follow.

Later tales include The Little Mermaid, Buckwheat, The Pen and the Inkstand, The Teapot, and Soup from a Sausage Skewer. Later tales include What the Goodman Does Is Always Right, The Old Street Lamp, and The Shepherdess and the Chimney Sweep. The Swineherd and The Flying Trunk appear, with The Real Princess, The Emperor's New Clothes, and Great Claus and Little Claus. Notes close a handsome school edition of Andersen.
32575-the-head-girl-at-the-gables:
Angela Brazil's The Head Girl at the Gables, illustrated by Balliol Salmon, opens ten days before the autumn term at The Gables. Miss Kingsley, rested after the summer holiday, plans a fresh year's work at her desk. Miss Janet jots suggestions on the back of an envelope in a rocking-chair.

Chapters follow a momentous decision, the first day of term, new brooms, a question of discipline, the sea-nymphs' grotto, Kilmeny, a sinister incident, Rosemary's secret, and Smugglers' Cove. Brazil writes for schoolgirls about leadership, loyalty, and trouble, as the head girl learns to carry authority among her friends.
32578-religious-perplexities:
L. P. Jacks's Religious Perplexities, published in London in 1922, grew from two lectures given at the invitation of the Hibbert Trustees in Manchester, Liverpool, Leeds, and Birmingham in March and April 1922. Jacks, principal and doctor of divinity, literature, and laws, revised the spoken word for print, adding a wholly new first section as a short introduction the lecture time had not allowed. Contents cover the source of perplexity, religious perplexity in general, and perplexity in the Christian religion.

The first and greatest perplexity, Jacks argues, springs from existence as individual souls: why are we here at all? If we knew our purpose, we might hold a key to God, freedom, duty, and immortality, but without it we grope. The book offers plain, thoughtful discussion for readers facing doubt without despair, in the author's motto: perplexed, yet not unto despair.
32591-henry-horn-s-x-ray-eye-glasses:
Dwight V. Swain tells of Henry Horn, an inventor whose glasses work on the X-ray principle and let the wearer see through walls and fences. Henry first sells peeks at a nudist camp next door, to the fury of his partner, Professor Paulsen.

The joke turns grave when Major Coggleston of Army Intelligence, guarding a nearby explosives plant, hunts Axis agents bent on sabotage. A red-headed buyer of Henry's glasses points the hunt toward the camp, and the inventor's toy becomes a tool in a wartime spy chase.
3260-a-short-history-of-wales:
Owen Edwards writes this short history of Wales, first published in 1906 and reprinted through 1922. The contents open with what Wales is made of and what it is like. Wandering nations follow, with Iberians and Celts, then Rome and the Roman conquest. The chapters proceed in order through the princes, the Tudors, and the making of modern Wales.

Edwards wrote for general readers and for schools, in clear, short chapters. His aim is a national story told from inside, not a footnote to English history. The book served Welsh classrooms for a generation. It still offers a compact, readable path through Welsh history, from the earliest peoples to the industrial age.
32713-women-of-the-romance-countries-ill:
John R. Effinger traces the history of women in the Romance countries, in volume six of the Woman in All Ages series, published by George Barrie and Sons. The opening part treats Italian women, beginning in the eleventh century, when the First Crusade stirred religious fervor yet left women in a low and uncertain place.

Effinger shows feudal law treating wives almost as property, husbands holding a legal right to punish them, and scholars debating whether women even possessed souls. Against that background he sets figures of force and feeling, from the Countess Matilda of Tuscany to Beatrice Cenci, whose portrait, sad and patient, closes a study of bondage, beauty, and endurance.
32728-the-english-in-the-west-indies-or-:
James Anthony Froude records a voyage through the British West Indies, published by Longmans in 1888. He sailed to learn the state of the colonies at first hand, and he relates what he saw and heard, with his own broad judgments on policy.

Chapters weigh union or separation, self-rule, and a proposed West Indian federation, then visit Barbados, St. Vincent, Grenada, Tobago, and Trinidad. Froude notes sugar, coolie labor, and the Darien canal scheme, and he closes by urging a fortified coaling station at St. Lucia. The book is a Victorian traveler's view, not a neutral history.
32748-mate-in-two-moves:
Winston Marks tells of Dr. Sylvester Murt, a thirty-eight-year-old pathologist at High Dawn Hospital, and his assistant Dr. Phyllis Sutton. In 1961 an epidemic sweeps the world, and its first signs look like pantie raids, classroom romances, and a surge of marriages at school and college level.

Murt names the cause Murt's Virus, a plague that loves its victims to death, and he and Sutton test a drug called sulfa-tetradine. The cure calms desire into cool, friendly ease, with strange costs: Murt forgets his own wedding night, and the marriage is annulled next day. The tale is a sharp, comic warning.
32772-rewards-and-fairies:
Rudyard Kipling gathers stories told to Dan and Una, a brother and sister in the English countryside, by Puck, the last survivor in England of the people mortals call fairies. Each tale is paired with a poem, and the book opens with a charm of English earth and flowers meant to restore a failing sight.

Stories range from Cold Iron and Gloriana to King Henry VII and the shipwrights, the Marklake witches, the knife and the naked chalk, Brother Square-Toes, the conversion of St. Wilfrid, and the tree of justice. Through smiths, sailors, saints, and smugglers, Kipling links the children's own fields and downs to the long history of England.
3278-cambridge-pieces:
Samuel Butler gathers Cambridge pieces in this 1914 volume, edited by R A Streatfeild. On English composition and other matters leads the contents, with our tour following. A translation from an unpublished work of Herodotus and the shield of Achilles, with variations, show Butler the classicist at play. A prospectus of the Great Split Society adds his satire.

The pieces come from Butler's university world and after, mixing scholarship with mischief. Composition, travel, and ancient poetry share a volume with schemes for splitting society itself. A joke and an argument are often the same thing in Butler's hands, and Cambridge gives him both.
32786-legends-of-florence-collected-from:
Charles Godfrey Leland, known as Hans Breitmann, collects legends of Florence from the people and retells them, in this first series published in London by David Nutt in 1895. Many tales were obtained for him and written out by Maddalena.

Legends explain streets, palaces, and statues: the three horns of Messer Guicciardini, the pills of the Medici, and the lanterns of the Strozzi palace. Goblins haunt the Via del Corno and the Bargello, the bronze boar stands in the Mercato Nuovo, and the fairy of Giotto's campanile watches the tower. Dante and Michelangelo appear as ghosts, Orpheus seeks Eurydice, and a wizard-blooded boy cheats a devil who asks for ever more work.
32787-du-rer-artist-biographies:
M. F. Sweetser writes this life of Albrecht Dürer for the Artist-Biographies series, published in Boston by Houghton, Osgood and Company in 1879. The series promised reliable, compact lives of famous artists at fifty cents a volume. Its volumes appeared at the rate of one or two each month.

Chapters follow Dürer from 1471 through his work in Nuremberg, his Venetian letters, and his Lowland journals. Sweetser describes his paintings, engravings, and carvings, and his quaint literary works. He also defends Dürer's wife Agnes against old slanders, drawing on Thausing, Scott, Colvin, and Heaton.
3279-canterbury-pieces:
Samuel Butler gathers early pieces in this 1914 volume, edited by R A Streatfeild. Darwin on the origin of species leads the contents, with a dialogue and a piece on barrel-organs. Letters from February, March, April, and June 1863 follow, from the years of Butler's New Zealand life and his first grappling with Darwin's ideas.

The pieces show Butler before Erewhon made him famous: sharp, curious, and unafraid to argue with giants. Darwin's theory, music machines, and colonial letters sit side by side, all in his clear, ironic prose. Butler young is the book's reward: a sharp mind testing its powers on Darwin and finding its voice in the test.
32800-the-romance-of-natural-history-sec:
Philip Henry Gosse, Fellow of the Royal Society, continues his romance of natural history in this second series, published in London by James Nisbet and Company in 1861. The book treats wonders of nature as stories, with evidence weighed and fancies tested.

The first chapter, on the extinct, ranges from the dinothere of Germany and the sivathere of India to the mammoth, the mastodon, and the great sloths of South America. Gosse weighs the Irish elk, the dodo, the giant eggs of Madagascar, and the Notornis of New Zealand. He asks whether man lived beside the tertiary fauna, and whether worked flints prove it. A later chapter turns to serpent-charming.
32811-holiday-house-a-series-of-tales:
Catherine Sinclair offers a series of tales from Holiday House, published in New York by Robert Carter in 1839 and dedicated to Lady Diana Boyle. Her preface protests an education that manufactures young minds like webs of linen, stuffing memory like a cricket-ball with facts and ready-made opinions.

Sinclair wants art and nature to go hand in hand, on a foundation of Christian faith and sound morality, pruning weeds while cherishing blossoms that spring spontaneously. Harry and Laura, uncle David, and Major Graham people the tales. A dying Mrs. Mackay begs a place for her boy Evan, fond of geraniums, and Major Graham makes him under-gardener. The children learn that naming an absent person may summon him at once.
32858-the-cruise-of-the-elena-or-yachtin:
J. Ewing-Ritchie tells of a cruise aboard the yacht Elena in the autumn of 1876, published in London by James Clarke and Company in 1877. The volume is dedicated to John Anderson of Glen Tower, owner of the Elena.

Ritchie accepted the invitation just as London summer heat nearly gave him up, and he left Fleet Street for the Western Islands of Scotland. Nine chapters run from Greenock and Ardrossan through Oban, Glencoe, Mull, Portree, and Stornoway to Kintyre and back. He admires the Clyde panorama, Loch Linnhe, and Stornoway's shops and weekly library, and retells the Lismore tale of MacLean of Duart.
32877-my-dark-companions-and-their-stran:
Henry M. Stanley gathers stories told around African camp fires, beginning in 1875, when Sabadu, a page of King Mtesa, astonished listeners with the tale of the Blameless Priest. The nightly circle was free to all, and accomplished narrators were suitably rewarded.

Stanley calls himself only a translator, rendering the tales as directly and truly as he can. He begins with the Creation of Man, told by Matageza of the Basoko in December 1883. Other tales tell how a man forced his shoulders through the moon, leaving the dark spots parents now cite to children. Still others tell how an elephant council swore hatred of the sons of man who murdered kin by lance, spear, snare, and trap.
32921-old-hendrik-s-tales:
Captain Arthur Owen Vaughan's Old Hendrik's Tales gathers animal stories told on a South African farm beside the Vaal River. The first tale explains why the old baboon has a kink in his tail. It begins on a hot day when the koppies simmer blue and brown. An old kitchen worker settles to sleep in the shade of a mimosa, only to be woken by three children who climb aboard him for a ride. The frame gives each tale a warm, spoken feel.

Hendrik's stories draw on the creatures of the veldt and on the lore of the people who lived among them, told with humor and a storyteller's timing. Vaughan lets the tales carry their own morals without preaching. The collection suits readers who enjoy animal fables and a vanished farm world, told as if heard after dinner on a hot afternoon.
32954-the-black-arrow-a-tale-of-the-two-:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Black Arrow, a tale of the two roses, appears here in a Scribner edition illustrated by N. C. Wyeth, with a dedication to his critic on the hearth. Stevenson notes that this is the one book of his that his critic never read and never will, a joke that opens a story written years earlier for a young audience. The tale is set in the Wars of the Roses, when rival houses fought for England's crown.

A young hero, a band of outlaws, and a mysterious arrow that marks its victims drive a plot of ambush, loyalty, and revenge in the English countryside. Wyeth's pictures give the adventure a bold, romantic color. It remains one of Stevenson's most readable romances, less famous than Treasure Island but just as swift, and a good first step into historical fiction for younger readers.
33064-the-blind-man-s-eyes:
William MacHarg and Edwin Balmer's Blind Man's Eyes, copyrighted in 1916, is a mystery built around a blind financier and the eyes that serve him. Its chapters run from a financier dies and an express held for a personage through Miss Dorne meeting Eaton and a truce. They go on to a hand in the aisle, suspicion fastening on Eaton, and questions. Later chapters bring the blind man's eyes and an ally in the house, before a fight in the study and a pursuit.

The frontispiece shows a lover's promise, until I come to you as you have never known me yet. The novel mixes romance with detection as Eaton fights to clear himself. MacHarg and Balmer keep the plot moving through trains, houses, and dark rooms. It is a brisk, period thriller for readers who enjoy a mystery with a strong central device.
3309-manners-and-monuments-of-prehistori:
The Marquis de Nadaillac surveys prehistoric peoples in this illustrated volume, translated by Nancy Bell. One hundred and thirteen illustrations accompany the text, opening with the fossil man of Mentone. Nadaillac, correspondent of the Institute and author of works on prehistoric America and the first men, writes for general readers curious about the deep past.

Manners and monuments share the inquiry: how early humans lived, buried their dead, and raised the stones that outlasted them. Bell, author of histories of art and the early earth, carries the French into clear English. The story it tells has since been rewritten by radiocarbon and DNA, which makes this readable version a period piece in its own right.
33123-a-transient-guest-and-other-episod:
Edgar Saltus's Transient Guest, and Other Episodes, gathers four stories: A Transient Guest, The Grand Duke's Rubies, A Maid of Modern Athens, and Fausta. It was published in Chicago, New York, and San Francisco in 1889. The title story opens aboard the Koenig Wilhelm of the Dutch East India service, leaving Batavia under a torpidly blue sky. A suffocats indigo that seems so near a traveler fancies he could touch it with a stick, while stars at night stab it through and leave it bluer still.

Saltus writes with the polished, decadent style that made his name, setting tales of wealth, beauty, and disillusion in ships, harbors, and foreign cities. The episodes are short, ornamental, and sharp, each turning on a guest who passes through a life and leaves it changed. The collection suits readers who enjoy late nineteenth-century literary fiction at its most elegant and world-weary.
33127-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume five, gathers the entries running from Capefigue to Carneades. Its articles include Jean-Baptiste Raymond Capefigue, Arthur Capel, Edward Capell, Martianus Minneus Felix Capella, Cape May, Capernaum, Cape Town, Cape Verde Islands, John Capgrave, and James Thomas Brudenell Cardigan. The list goes on to carbon bisulphide, carbonic acid, the carboniferous system, carborundum, Cardiff, cardinal virtues, capital punishment, and carding. Transcriber's notes record a correction to capillary action.

The slice mixes biography, geography, chemistry, and history in the confident voice of early twentieth-century reference writing. Readers get the facts and judgments educated readers of the day were expected to trust, from a Crimean cavalry commander to a chemical compound. As a reference text it is dated, but as a record of how knowledge was ordered, it remains a useful window on the period.
33153-american-world-policies:
Walter E. Weyl's American World Policies, published by Macmillan in February 1917, examines America's place among nations on the eve of American entry into the First World War. Weyl, author of The New Democracy, divides the book into an idealistic past and a second part on the root of imperialism. The idealistic past runs from America among the nations through the skeleton of war, peace without effort, an unripe imperialism, and facing outward. The second part runs from the integration of the world through imperialism and war to industrial invasion.

Later chapters treat the revolt against imperialism and the appeal of imperialism, asking why a republic founded against empire might be drawn toward it. Weyl writes as a progressive critic, hopeful for democracy but wary of power. The book remains a analysis of American foreign policy at a turning point, when idealism, trade, and war were pulling the country .
33160-christian-hymns-of-the-first-three:
Ruth Ellis Messenger's Christian Hymns of the First Three Centuries surveys the earliest Christian song. It was published as paper nine of the Hymn Society of America in 1942 and edited by Carl F. Price. The society's series had already covered John Bunyan's hymns, the religious value of hymns, praise of the Virgin in early Latin hymns, and the old French psalter. Messenger's paper carries that work back to the church's first centuries, when hymns were still being formed.

Messenger traces how early Christians sang their faith, in Greek and Latin, in psalms, canticles, and new hymns that shaped worship for centuries after. Her paper is short and scholarly, written for hymn lovers and church musicians who wanted roots, not only repertory. For students of early Christianity and of hymnody, it remains a clear, compact guide to a period when Christian song was young and its forms were still being found.
33196-five-minutes-stories:
Mrs. Molesworth's collection offers short tales meant to be read in about five minutes each, ideal for bedtime or a quiet pause. The contents run from Abdallah the Unhappy and Fifine and her cat to the Long Ladder, the Bad Fairy, the Goblin Face, and a lost brooch. Each story is brief, clear, and built round one small wonder or kind turn.

Published in a twelfth thousand printing, the book shows Molesworth's gift for writing to children without talking down to them. Animals, fairies, and everyday children share the stage, and most tales end with a gentle moral earned by the plot. For young readers and for adults reading aloud, it is a handy volume of short, pleasing stories.
33197-do-derlein-s-hand-book-of-latin-sy:
Döderlein's Hand-Book of Latin Synonymes is a reference work for readers of Latin who need to tell near words apart. Its entries distinguish verbs, nouns, and adjectives that English translations flatten into one word, showing how Roman writers chose among them for shade, force, and propriety. The text uses italics, small capitals, and spaced type to mark emphasis, and Greek words appear transliterated between marks in this version, with the oe ligature shown as two letters.

Cross-references guide readers from one entry to another, and transcriber's notes flag errors and additions, so the handbook can be used with confidence. For students of Latin prose, the book remains a practical tool. It teaches not only what a word means, but when a Roman would use it and when he would choose its neighbor instead. That fine judgment is the heart of good Latin style.
33233-tahara-among-african-tribes:
Harold M. Sherman's adventure tale, copyrighted in 1933, follows Tahara among African tribes, through eyes of dread, kings of two tribes, Arab raiders, and battles that rage across jungle trails. Its fifteen chapters move from a plot woven by Cimbula to war canoes, a stampede, jungle dancers, and a rescue, ending with Tahara ready for new adventures. Sherman writes for young readers who love a fast, exotic tale.

The book's appeal lies in its pace and its vivid scenes of tribal life, war, and wilderness, told in plain, stirring prose. Its hero faces danger with courage and quick wit, and each chapter ends with a fresh peril. For fans of old-fashioned boys' adventure, Tahara offers a brisk journey into a world of chiefs, warriors, and jungle trails.
33358-great-singers-on-the-art-of-singin:
James Francis Cooke's volume gathers educational conferences with foremost singers on the art of singing, in personal study talks with the most renowned opera, concert, and oratorio singers of the time. Copyrighted in 1921, it opens with the technic of operatic production and asks what the American girl should know about an operatic career. Cooke planned the talks especially for voice students.

The book's value lies in its first-hand advice, as great singers speak of breath, tone, and stage craft in their own words. Its tone is practical and encouraging, suited to students and teachers alike. For lovers of vocal music, Great Singers offers a rare chance to learn from masters, in talks that still ring true for singers today.
33368-tales-of-the-toys-told-by-themselv:
Frances Freeling Broderip's Tales of the Toys, Told by Themselves, published in London in 1869, lets toys speak for themselves. Broderip, author of My Grandmother's Budget, opens with a hurrah for a trip to Sandbay, and her tales follow dolls, soldiers, and playthings through their small adventures. Tom Hood's illustrations add to the fun.

The book's charm lies in its gentle, fanciful voice, as toys tell of holidays, mishaps, and home life in their own words. Its tone is warm and old-fashioned, suited to young readers and to adults who remember childhood. For lovers of Victorian children's books, it is a delightful volume, where the nursery comes alive.
33373-kyphosis-and-other-variations-in-s:
Hobart M. Smith's paper on kyphosis and other variations in soft-shelled turtles, published in July 1947, studies shell deformities in these river turtles. Issued as volume one, number six of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History publications, from pages 117 to 124, the paper notes how soft-shells vary in form. Kyphosis, a humped back, is among the variations found.

The paper suits readers of herpetology, offering a short, technical survey of variation in one turtle group. Its tone is precise and factual, with specimens and notes to back its findings. For turtle researchers, it is a useful, if narrow, source on how shells can bend and differ in nature.
33379-dietetics-for-nurses:
Fairfax T. Proudfit's Dietetics for Nurses, in a second edition completely revised in 1923, teaches nurses how food affects health and healing. Proudfit, a dietitian at Memphis hospitals, sets out foodstuffs, sugars, and diets for varied conditions, with tables and diagrams to guide practice. The book was first published in 1918 and reset for its second edition.

The volume suits nursing students and historians of medicine, offering a clear, practical course in diet as the profession then knew it. Its tone is systematic and helpful, with chapters on conditions affected by diet. For readers of nursing history, it is a solid, early text, showing how dietetics grew into a science of care.
33380-love-s-usuries:
Louis Creswicke's Love's Usuries gathers stories of love's costs and gains, several reprinted from Black and White and The Gentlewoman. Creswicke, author of Magnetism and Mystery, opens by asking whether happiness is courted in vain, a question his tales then test in varied lives. His stories move through courtship, regret, and the bargains lovers strike with fate.

The collection's appeal lies in its bittersweet tone, where love pays interest in joy and sorrow alike. Creswicke writes with a light, journalistic touch, suited to magazine readers of his day. For fans of Victorian short fiction, Love's Usuries offers a set of tales that are easy to dip into, each turning on one sharp twist of the heart.
33429-the-philosophy-of-the-weather-and-:
T. B. Butler's Philosophy of the Weather, and a Guide to Its Changes, published in New York in 1856, seeks the rules behind rain, wind, and fair skies. Butler, writing before modern forecasting, sets out a philosophy of weather, with signs by which readers might guess coming change. His book belongs to an age when farmers, sailors, and travelers watched the sky with care.

The volume's charm lies in its earnest, pre-scientific effort to make weather readable, blending observation with theory. Its tone is plain and instructive, suited to general readers. For students of meteorology history, it is a revealing source on how the nineteenth century tried to turn sky-watching into a science.
33494-the-library-and-society-reprints-o:
Arthur E. Bostwick's Library and Society, published in 1920 and issued in January 1921, reprints papers and addresses on the free public library in America. Edited by Bostwick for the Classics of American Librarianship, it opens with the historical evolution of the library and its true function in the community, then takes up general community relations. Its notes guide readers through a formative age of librarianship.

The volume suits librarians, historians, and all who care about public reading, offering the arguments that built the modern library. Its tone is scholarly yet practical, aimed at workers in the field. For students of library history, it is a key source on how libraries learned to serve whole towns, not just scholars.
33511-tales-of-passed-times:
Charles Perrault's Tales of Passed Times, told by Master Charles Perrault with twelve illustrations by Charles Robinson, gathers the fairy tales that made Perrault famous. Published in London in 1900 in the Temple Classics for Young People, the book notes that we owe to Perrault our acquaintance with most good old-fashioned fairy tales. Its tales have charmed children for centuries.

The volume's charm lies in its clear, classic retellings, from sleeping beauties to cinder girls, with Robinson's pictures to guide the eye. Its tone is gentle and timeless, suited to reading aloud. For young readers and for adults who love fairy lore, Tales of Passed Times offers the old tales in a handsome, faithful form.
33515-misread-passages-of-scriptures:
J. Baldwin Brown's Misread Passages of Scripture, published in New York in 1869, gathers sermons. Their texts are often read amiss. Brown, author of The Divine Life in Man, notes that his sermons form part of a series he planned but could not complete through ill health. He sends them forth in imperfect form at his publishers' wish. His topics aim to correct common misreadings.

The book's value lies in its plain, pastoral correction, as Brown takes a text, shows how it is misread, and sets it right. Its tone is earnest and learned, suited to preachers and lay readers alike. For Bible students, it remains a thoughtful, old-fashioned guide to reading scripture with care.
33520-wondrous-love-and-other-gospel-add:
D. L. Moody's Wondrous Love and Other Gospel Addresses gathers sermons delivered during Moody and Sankey's first campaign in England. Moody, author of Prevailing Prayer and Sovereign Grace, preaches of a seeking Saviour and a wondrous love that pursues sinners. The volume, in the World-Wide Library, was published by Pickering and Inglis in London, Glasgow, and Edinburgh.

The addresses suit readers of evangelical preaching, offering short, plain sermons meant to win hearts. Their tone is earnest and direct, with stories and appeals that made Moody famous. For students of revival history, Wondrous Love remains a vivid record of a campaign that stirred England, in the voice of its greatest preacher.
33532-the-camp-fire-girls-behind-the-lin:
Margaret Vandercook's Camp Fire Girls Behind the Lines, copyrighted in 1918, follows the Camp Fire Girls. They serve in wartime. Its chapters move from El Camino Real and the land of romance to a call to service, the camp, and abalone shells. A sentry ordering Dan to stop his car appears in its frontispiece. Vandercook, author of the Ranch Girls and Red Cross Girls series, writes for girls who want to help.

The tale's charm lies in its patriotic, wholesome adventure, as girls learn service, courage, and friendship behind the lines. Its tone is warm and encouraging, suited to young readers. For fans of girls' series books, Behind the Lines offers a lively, wartime story of girls doing their part.
33538-a-bed-of-roses:
W. L. George's novel opens aboard a ship leaving Bombay, where lascar stokers watch the shore recede. A woman named Victoria Fulton lies awake in her berth, turning over a life she describes in terms of bondage and narrow choice. The epigraph, borrowed from Shaw's Mrs. Warren's Profession, warns that the work at the novel's center is no bed of roses, whatever pious talk may claim.

From that shipboard start, the story follows Victoria and her companion Molly through the world of women who must earn a living on terms set by others. George writes with sympathy and social criticism about money, reputation, and the limited work open to women. The novel suits readers interested in Edwardian fiction of social protest and the economics of respectability.
33542-the-new-gulliver-and-other-stories:
Barry Pain offers a set of witty, unsettling tales headed by a new Gulliver adventure. Lemuel Gulliver Jr., whose opening manuscript pages were damaged by fire, survives a shipwreck and a sea fog. He swims ashore and explores a flat, bleak island of sand, coarse grass, and stunted shrubs, where a column of smoke rises as if from inside the earth. Pain plays the Swiftian voyage for both comedy and strangeness.

Further stories include a London garden, a tale called Zero, a time when the narrator was king, a satyr, a choice, a piano tuner, and pearls before swine. Pain's voice is urbane and ironic, turning everyday settings toward the fantastic. Readers who enjoy short fiction with a twist will find the collection clever, compact, and faintly macabre.
33583-l-arrabiata-and-other-tales:
Paul Heyse, translated from the German by Mary Wilson, offers a set of tales headed by L'Arrabiata, set among the fishermen of Sorrento beneath Vesuvius. The title story opens at dawn over the bay, with boats drawn ashore, nets hauled in, and families at work along the marina, before turning to a passionate local romance. Heyse writes with close attention to coastal labor and custom.

The remaining tales include Count Ernest's Home, Blind, Walter's Little Mother, and a group gathered around the Dead Lake, with stories of doom, a fortnight's stay, Beatrice, and beginnings and endings. Together they show Heyse's range in short fiction: Italian color, domestic feeling, and fateful turns of fortune, in an authorized 1867 edition.
33587-six-thousand-country-churches:
Charles Otis Gill and Gifford Pinchot examine the state of rural churches in Ohio in this 1919 study. The authors explain how their facts were gathered, map the churches of the state, and summarize what they found: many small, weak congregations, thin attendance, short ministerial terms, and divided effort.

Later chapters look at where church efficiency runs lowest, study the church across eighteen counties, and propose a policy and program. Remedies include better support and training for ministers, resident pastors, rearranged circuits, and cooperation between congregations, including federated and community churches. The book is a landmark survey for readers interested in rural religion and social reform.
33608-bride-roses:
W. D. Howells writes a single-scene play, Bride Roses, published in 1900 with copyrights from 1893 and 1900. The scene is a florist's shop on a freezing day, where a lady enters with her muff to her face. The scene greets the florist, Mr. Eichenlaub, urging him to wrap his flowers in plenty of cotton lest they freeze stiff. Inside, the shop feels tropical, with a refrigerator keeping roses from sunstroke, while icebergs pattern the windows.

Dialogue between the lady and the florist, with a young man sent out on deliveries, carries the whole piece. These include small talk, a card slipped into a bouquet, and the social comedy of a wedding errand. Howells's realism shines in dialect, detail, and manners. The short play suits readers who enjoy his quiet, observant comedy of American middle-class life.
33662-a-republic-without-a-president-and:
Herbert D. Ward imagines an unprecedented calamity in the title story of this 1891 collection. On the morning of June 8, 1893, crowds gather before newspaper bulletins in New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, San Francisco, and Boston. They read that the president and his wife have been spirited away from the White House, with two servants found gagged and no trace of the couple. Business halts, stocks fall sharply within half an hour, and the country stands aghast.

Ward plays the disappearance as both mystery and political speculation, with some suspecting a colossal hoax by a defeated party. Further stories in the volume extend his interest in strange, high-concept premises. Readers of early American speculative fiction will enjoy the story's brisk journalism, its national panic, and its cool, unsettling what-if.
33665-the-preliminaries-and-other-storie:
Cornelia A. P. Comer writes three stories of courtship, family, and inheritance in this 1912 Houghton Mifflin volume. The title story follows young Oliver Pickersgill, in love with Peter Lannithorne's daughter Ruth, while Peter serves a six-year term in the penitentiary for embezzlement. Ollie believes a man ought to marry the girl he loves and let prejudices hang, but negotiations for Ruth's hand prove more complicated than winning her consent.

The Long Inheritance and Clarissa's Own Child complete the set, exploring how money, reputation, and family obligation shape women's choices. Comer writes with clear-eyed sympathy for heroines caught between love and respectability. Readers who enjoy early twentieth-century American stories of manners will find her plots thoughtful, humane, and quietly surprising.
33678-reasonableness-of-catholic-ceremon:
The Reverend John J. Burke explains and defends Catholic ceremonies and practices in this 1909 Benziger volume, published with imprimatur (church license) from the Archbishop of New York. Opening with Numbers on keeping the Passover according to all its ceremonies, Burke argues that ceremonies are necessary to divine worship. He also treats vestments used by the priest at Mass and the ceremonies of the Mass itself.

Further chapters cover vespers and benediction, devotion to the Blessed Sacrament, Holy Communion, confirmation, honoring the Virgin, confession, indulgences, the last sacraments, praying for the dead and to the saints, and crucifixes. Further chapters also cover relics, images, sacramentals (blessed items) from holy water and candles to rosary and Stations, feasts, infant baptism, marriage, respect for superiors, and celibacy. The book offers a systematic (step-by-step), accessible apology (defense) for Catholic practice.
33707-yiddish-tales:
Helena Frank translated this 1912 collection of Yiddish tales for the Jewish Publication Society of America, gathering stories from the leading Yiddish writers of the day. Contents include Reuben Asher Braudes, Jehalel, Isaac Löb Peretz, Mordecai Spektor, Sholom-Aleichem, and Eliezer David Rosenthal. They also include Isaiah Lerner, Judah Steinberg, David Frischmann, Micha Joseph Berdyczewski, David Pinski, Abraham Raisin, Hirsh David Naumberg, Shalom Asch, and others, with a glossary and notes.

The tales range from a woman's wrath and a treasure to an original strike. The tales also range from a gloomy wedding, poverty, a clock, a teacher, a Passover guest, Sabbath and Yom Kippur, military service, and a scholar's mother. Frank's translations open a window onto East European Jewish life: its humor, piety, hardship, and family feeling. The collection remains a landmark introduction to Yiddish literature in English.
33786-readings-from-latin-verse-with-not:
Curtis C. Bushnell, a professor of classics at Syracuse University, prepared this 1908 school book of Latin verse. He chose passages for their literary merit and for the range of authors they put before students early in a college course. Notes follow the verse, and a list of reference works stands behind them.

The selections open with Ennius and move through Roman poets whose lines students once met in class. Bushnell aimed to widen the usual reading list beyond a few set authors. The book still serves a reader who wants Latin poetry with help close at hand, in short, well-chosen pieces.
33789-barbarossa-and-other-tales:
Paul Heyse's tales appeared in Leipzig in 1874, translated from the German by L. C. S. The set takes its name from Barbarossa, the opening tale, and adds five more: stories of an embroideress, a lost son, a fair Kate, and two lovers named Geoffroy and Garcinde. Heyse sets them in Italy and Germany alike.

The opening tale finds its narrator alone in a ruined mountain nest above Rome, hungry for quiet after city life. Later tales turn on love, craft, and family bonds tested by distance. Together they show Heyse's gift for short, polished stories with a strong sense of place.
33813-rodman-the-keeper-southern-sketche:
Constance Fenimore Woolson gathers Southern sketches in this Harper volume, written during a residence in the South embracing the greater part of six years. Woolson records real impressions, though she doubts any writing can give the inward charm of a beautiful land she loves and leaves with regret. Two sketches appeared in the Atlantic Monthly, four in Appletons' Journal, and one each in Scribner's Monthly, the Galaxy, Lippincott's Monthly, and Harper's Magazine.

Contents include Rodman the Keeper, Sister St. Luke, Miss Elisabetha, Old Gardiston, The South Devil, In the Cotton Country, Felipa, Bro., King David, and Up in the Blue Ridge. The title sketch opens with a keeper of the dead, guarding heroes' graves by the Potomac, the Cumberland, and the Shenandoah. Woolson writes with sympathy for a defeated, changing South, and her sketches remain classics of American regional literature.
33824-mr-punch-s-after-dinner-stories:
J. A. Hammerton edited this volume of Mr. Punch's After-Dinner Stories for the Punch Library of Humour. The series runs to twenty-five volumes designed to give the cream of national humor from Punch's beginning in 1841 to the present day.
