The book gathers jokes meant for telling after dinner, with 155 illustrations by John Leech, Charles Keene, George du Maurier, Phil May, L. Raven-Hill, and J. Bernard Partridge. F. H. Townsend, Reginald Cleaver, Lewis Baumer, and others also contributed illustrations.

The opening essay notes that all good stories are really for telling, and that post-prandial wit has its own pleasures: short, pointed, and sociable. Cartoons and anecdotes on progress, physique, and armor set the tone. Readers who enjoy Victorian and Edwardian cartoon humor will find a well-chosen anthology, complete in itself, from the magazine that defined British comic art.
33843-the-natives:
Katherine MacLean wrote this short science tale, first printed in Science Fiction Stories in 1953. An old one and a youngster of a strange people follow a dark, fast-moving thing that sucks heat and takes in light. The elder warns the child not to get too close, lest he take in too much and grow overcharged.

MacLean tells the tale from the aliens' side, so human readers must guess what the moving thing really is. The story turns on youth, teaching, and the danger of a power not yet understood. It is a clever twist on first contact, told in a few pages with warmth and wit.
33873-dolly-s-college-experiences:
Mabel Cronise Jones wrote this college tale, published in Boston in 1909 with the Roman date MDCCCCIX on its title page. Dolly, a new freshman at Westover, sits on her bed and looks around forlornly, far from home and known by no one. Old girls chatter outside her door, but no one takes notice of her yet.

Chapters follow Dolly through classes, walks with Beth, music, and introductions to new friends. Jones writes warmly for girls about to leave home. The book remains a sweet, early portrait of women's college life in America.
33899-optical-projection-part-1-the-proj:
Lewis Wright wrote this manual on the magic lantern, and Russell S. Wright rewrote it for a fifth edition in 1920. Part one covers the projection of lantern slides for shows and for scientific display. It explains lamps, light sources, lenses, screens, and the handling of the lantern itself.

Chapters move from oil lamps and gas burners through acetylene, limelight, and electric light to the optical system and the lantern body. Diagrams show each part in place. The manual gives a clear, hands-on account of a tool that once lit lecture halls, classrooms, and public shows.
33904-a-briefe-discription-of-new-englan:
Samuel Maverick wrote this brief account of New England in 1660, from a manuscript later found in the British Museum by Henry F. Waters and printed at Boston in 1885. Maverick describes the several towns of New England and the government then in place, in the spelling of his own age. A note on Greenwich leaves a missing distance blank.

The account argues that most inhabitants were shut out of rights they ought to enjoy, and it weighs their regard for the Church of England and for the king's power over them. The tract gives a rare, early voice from inside the colony, frank about its quarrels.
33916-the-dead-lake-and-other-tales:
Paul Heyse's tales appeared at Leipzig in 1870, translated from the German by Mary Wilson. The title tale spends a fortnight at a dead lake in the Alps, where a storm, an inn, and a restless household set a somber mood. Two more tales follow: Doomed Beatrice, and a tale of a beginning and an end.

Heyse writes with the polish of a practiced storyteller, letting landscape press on his people. Love, fate, and guilt run through the set, and each tale closes with a sharp turn. The book offers a compact sample of the short fiction that made Heyse a leading German voice of his day.
33921-cacao-culture-in-the-philippines:
William S. Lyon, in charge of seed and plant introduction, wrote this 1902 bulletin for planters in the Philippines. Issued as Farmer's Bulletin Number 2 by the Bureau of Agriculture at Manila, it gives practical advice on growing cacao. Lyon notes that Philippine cacao already won buyers at a premium over common Java grades, despite poor curing.

Chapters cover climate, site, soil, drainage, planting, pruning, harvest, pests, and the cost of a plantation. Lyon points to Mindanao and Negros, where the plant grew with striking vigor even under neglect. The bulletin still reads as a clear, hands-on guide for a tropical crop.
33923-special-method-in-primary-reading-:
Charles A. McMurry, director of practice at the Northern Illinois State Normal School, wrote this 1903 teacher's manual, reprinted in 1905. He argues that telling and reading stories to young children, before they can read alone, is a key step in learning. The book gives reasons for oral work, then sets out stories for first, second, and third grades.

Later chapters cover reading through games and side exercises, a method for primary reading, and a list of books for the early grades. McMurry writes for teachers in plain, practical terms. The manual still shows how story-first teaching was meant to turn listening into reading skill.
33931-popular-tales:
Andrew Lang edited this set of Charles Perrault's tales, first issued by the Clarendon Press at Oxford in 1888 and reprinted by Arno Press in 1977. Perrault, who lived from 1628 to 1703, wrote the classic French fairy tales that later readers know in many forms. Lang worked from the original editions and added an introduction.

The tales in the set are the stories of old France retold for English readers, with their morals and marvels intact. Lang's care for the source texts makes the book more than a nursery retelling. It serves readers who want Perrault as he first appeared, in a scholarly yet readable form.
33935-food-habits-of-the-thrushes-of-the:
F. E. L. Beal, assistant biologist for the Bureau of Biological Survey, wrote this 1915 bulletin on what thrushes eat. Thrushes, robins, bluebirds, and Townsend's solitaire form a small group of retiring birds noted as singers. Beal treats each kind in turn: wood thrush, veery, gray-cheeked, hermit, and others.

The bulletin sets out food by season and kind, drawn from stomach records and field notes. Farmers and bird lovers learn which insects, fruits, and seeds each thrush takes. It remains a solid early study of bird diet, useful to anyone who watches thrushes in garden or wood.
33942-beatrice-boville-and-other-stories:
Ouida, author of Strathmore and Chandos, published this third series of stories in Philadelphia in 1905. The title tale follows Beatrice Boville through pride, a first shadow, and a fall, as a narrator who once played rival in all innocence watches her fate. Other tales include a line in the Daily, holly wreaths, silver chimes, and slander.

Ouida writes of rank, love, and reputation with high color and sharp feeling. Her heroines pay dearly for pride or for the talk of others. The set gives a late sample of a once-famous novelist of society life, still readable for its drama and its polish.
33947-the-nerve-of-foley-and-other-railr:
Frank H. Spearman wrote this set of railroad stories, published in New York and London in 1900 by Harper and Brothers, with pictures. The title tale opens amid winter rumors that engineers will strike, while men of the operating department sleep with an ear alert, like soldiers. Andrew Cameron, one of the best men on a locomotive, is also one of the hardest.

Other tales follow Second Seventy-Seven, the Kid Engineer, Soda-water Sal, the McWilliams Special, a million-dollar freight train, and Siclone Clark. Spearman writes from inside railroad life, with engines, orders, and danger. The book remains a classic of American railroad fiction.
33955-remodeled-farmhouses:
Mary H. Northend wrote this book on remodeled farmhouses, published in Boston in 1915 by Little, Brown, with many pictures. Northend, author of books on colonial homes and historic homes of New England, visits house after house: Iristhorpe, Limovady, the Kittredge house, the Curtis house, Green Meadows, Nawn Farm, and Boulder Farm.

Each chapter shows how an old farmhouse gained new rooms, porches, and gardens without losing its character. Pictures of fronts, porches, dining rooms, and living rooms aid the text. The book serves readers who love old houses made fit for new life.
33956-true-politeness-a-hand-book-of-eti:
An American lady wrote this handbook of etiquette, entered for copyright in 1847 and published in New York by Leavitt and Allen. It lays down rules for introductions, salutations, dress, conversation, visits, and receiving visits. Later chapters cover ball-room parties, music, the dinner table, courtship, servants, letters, and funerals.

The rules are firm and detailed: the lesser is presented to the greater, and a lady takes precedence over a gentleman. The book shows how a mid-century American woman was expected to move through society. It remains a clear window on the manners of its age.
33970-the-raid-of-the-guerilla-and-other:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this set of mountain stories, published at Philadelphia and London in 1912, with pictures by W. Herbert Dunton and Remington Schuyler. The title tale opens at Tanglefoot Cove, where judgment day seems at hand as a noted guerilla with a reckless troop means to raid the cove.

Other tales ask who crosses Storm Mountain, tell of Una of the hill country, a lost guidon, Wolf's Head, an unquiet ghost, a Chilhowee lily, and a Christmas miracle. Craddock writes of Tennessee mountains with local color and feeling. The book offers a strong sample of her mountain fiction.
33974-candy-making-revolutionized-confec:
Mary Elizabeth Hall wrote this book on candy made from vegetables, published in New York in December 1912 with pictures. Hall opens with help for the novice, the candy-maker's table, the thermometer, steam, crystallization, chocolate coating, and sugar. A second section turns to decorative candies from potato paste and potato fondant.

Green leaves, violets, daisies, calla lilies, red apples, roses, pea-pods, and grapes all take shape from potato work, with potato caramels to follow. Hall writes for home candy-makers who want pure candy. The book offers a curious, practical piece of kitchen invention.
33976-jane-stewardess-of-the-air-lines:
Ruthe S. Wheeler wrote this girls' aviation tale, published in Chicago in 1934. Jane Cameron is one of seventeen senior nurses graduating from Good Samaritan Hospital at University City, held back half an hour by a surgery emergency on the third floor. Graduation night opens a story of opportunity, westward flight, and crash landing.

Chapters follow Jane's first call, an unexpected delay, a black plane, a flight through fog, a crash in flames, and a promotion. Wheeler writes briskly for girls who dreamed of the air lines. The book offers a lively early tale of a stewardess at work.
3404-april-hopes:
William Dean Howells opens this 1887 novel at Harvard, where Elbridge Mavering watches Class Day crowds from the floor of the gymnasium. Pretty girls in varied dress promenade with young men, and Mavering, older than the students around him, looks for one face in particular. The scene sets up a story of courtship, money, and manners among well off Boston families.

As the novel moves on, Mavering must learn what his hopes are actually worth. Howells follows his suit through drawing rooms, country visits, and family talk, testing charm against character. The book rewards readers who like social novels where the drama sits in conversation, conscience, and the small choices that shape a marriage.
34046-whispering-wires:
Henry Leverage wrote this mystery novel, adapted from his Saturday Evening Post story and published in New York in 1918. A rich Fifth Avenue mansion, with turret and tower and gates from Hyderabad, stands at the center of a tale of guilt and guile. A whispering voice, a magpie, a man in olive-drab, and a murder set the plot moving.

Chapters follow first clews, Harry Nichols, a spot of black, tangled wires, a woman's call, and a closing net, until a silent prisoner speaks and a voice sounds on the wire. Leverage writes in the brisk manner of the popular mystery. The book remains a lively period thriller.
34089-the-celestial-omnibus-and-other-st:
E. M. Forster published this set of stories in London in 1912, dedicated to the memory of the Independent Review. The stories first appeared in the Albany Review, the English Review, the Independent Review, the Pall Mall Magazine, and Putnam's Magazine. Contents run from The Story of a Panic and The Other Side of the Hedge to The Celestial Omnibus, Other Kingdom, and The Road from Colonus.

The opening tale begins in chestnut woods above Ravello, where Eustace, a boy of fourteen, stays with his aunts, the Miss Robinsons, and Mr. Sandbach, a former curate turned tutor. Forster writes with wit and wonder. The book shows his early gift for the uncanny in ordinary life.
34102-a-divided-heart-and-other-stories:
Paul Heyse's tales reach English readers in this 1894 volume translated by Constance Stewart Copeland, who also wrote the opening life of Heyse. Born at Berlin in 1830, Heyse rose to fame with a calm, fortunate career quite unlike the hard youth of most authors.

The book holds three pieces: A Divided Heart, Minka, and Rothenburg on the Tauber, a portrait of an old German town. Copeland's preface praises Heyse's poise and high ideals, and the stories show his gift for quiet feeling, clear scenes, and lives caught between duty and desire. Copeland's introduction also sketches Heyse's father, a scholar of words who kept a warm and bookish house.
34177-the-idyl-of-twin-fires:
Walter Prichard Eaton wrote this idyl of country life, illustrated by Thomas Fogarty and published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with copyright in 1914 and 1915 by Doubleday, Page. Chapters run from buying a farm on sight and watching money go as a farmer comes. New joy in an old orchard, pumping up a ghost, and being humbled by a drag scraper follow.

Later chapters seat Thoreau in the chimney nook, climb a hill together, welcome the Pilligs, bake a first lemon pie, build a pool, and praise country winter and spring in the garden. Eaton writes with humor and warmth. The book offers a gentle tale of a farm and its fires.
34220-two-royal-foes:
Eva Madden's 1907 novel Two Royal Foes sets a girl named Bettina at Jena in the days of Napoleon's wars against Prussia. The mighty foe of the title is Napoleon, and the second royal figure is the Queen of Prussia, praised in the book as the mother of her people.

Thirty chapters follow Bettina from Jena to Memel and Tilsit, through flight, trouble, and the entry into Berlin, as war breaks a kingdom and tests a family. Madden tells the great clash through small eyes, keeping court and camp close to a child's home and heart.
34238-rural-rides:
William Cobbett's Rural Rides gathers his horseback tours across southern England, from London into Hampshire, Surrey, Sussex, Berkshire, and beyond. Each ride names its road town by town, from Newbury and Marlborough to Lewes, Brighton, and St. Albans.

Cobbett writes as he goes, on farming, wages, labourers, and the state of the land, with praise for good tillage and sharp words for what he saw as waste and wrong. The book remains a sharp, first-hand portrait of English country life between town and field. Cobbett's contents run from London rides to a Norfolk and Suffolk journal, widening the tour.
343-fables:
Robert Louis Stevenson lets his Treasure Island puppets step out for a pipe after chapter thirty-two. Fables, from the 1901 Longmans edition, opens with Long John Silver and Captain Smollett debating duty and character. Silver protests he is only a character in a sea story.

Smollett replies that he does not really exist either, which seems to settle matters. Later fables turn the same trick on morals, art, and human nature. Stevenson writes with wit about fiction's double life. The short book delights readers who love Treasure Island. Stevenson's fables show his playful side beyond adventure tales.
3452-tea-leaves:
This short book from the New York tea merchants Francis Leggett and Company treats tea as a trade good and a daily pleasure. It explains where tea grows, how leaves are picked and prepared, and how different kinds reach the cup. The firm writes as sellers who know their stock, and the book mixes practical advice with the romance of far off gardens.

Readers learn how to judge leaf, judge a brew, and store tea so it keeps its scent. The book also reflects an age when grocers taught customers about imports face to face. It suits tea lovers and social historians alike, offering a small, clear guide to a drink that once linked China, India, and the American table.
346-the-troll-garden-and-selected-storie:
Willa Cather gathers early tales of the Nebraska plains and the art world in this volume. The first half holds prairie stories of Norwegians, Bohemians, and lone dreamers on hard land. The second half, The Troll Garden, turns to artists, singers, and small-town folk who chase art in Boston and New York.

Paul's Case, the best known tale here, follows a restless boy who steals to taste city luxury for a few bright days. Other stories weigh the price of art, the pull of home, and the ache of exile. Cather's prose is spare and sure, and these tales mark the start of her mature voice.
3472-merton-of-the-movies:
Harry Leon Wilson writes a comic novel about a small town young man who dreams of becoming a serious film actor. Merton Gill leaves home for California, sure that the screen needs his noble talent, and he walks into a studio world of directors, cameramen, and actors who see him very differently. Chapter titles such as Western Stuff, The Watcher at the Gate, and Alias Harold Parmalee trace his education.

The joke, and the warmth, lies in Merton's blind spot. He aims at tragedy and finds fame as a comedian, winning laughs precisely when he tries hardest to be grand. Wilson satirizes early Hollywood without cruelty, and the novel suits readers who enjoy show business comedy and a hero who succeeds by accident.
34860-east-of-suez-a-play-in-seven-scene:
W. Somerset Maugham wrote this play in seven scenes, printed in 1922. The scene of the work is Peking, as the first leaf states. The folk of the play are named in a list: Daisy, George Conway, and Henry Anderson lead it. Harold Knox, Lee Tai Cheng, Sylvia Knox, and a nurse named Amah Wu fill out the cast. The first scene is a street in Peking.

The next scene is set on a small porch on a high floor of the house of the British American Tobacco Company. The title of the play points east of the Suez road, to the far ports where men of the West live and trade among the folk of China. A list of the author's past works stands at the front of the book.
3488-great-catherine-whom-glory-still-ad:
George Bernard Shaw writes a comic play about Catherine the Great of Russia, with a title borrowed from Byron. Shaw's apology warns readers not to expect the Catherine of diplomacy, campaigns, and letters to Voltaire. His Catherine belongs instead to the lighter pages of history, where gallantry, court intrigue, and sham cities built by scenic artists for a royal visit take center stage.

The play follows an English captain caught in Catherine's court, where flattery and favor rule and a ruler's whim can change a life. Shaw turns the empress into a witty, willful figure and the court into a theater. Readers who like Shaw's historical farces will enjoy the comedy, while those seeking a serious life of Catherine should look elsewhere.
3492-homespun-tales:
Kate Douglas Wiggin gathers stories set in a small Maine village in this collection, called Homespun Tales. Wiggin explains that the tales belong together because they share one background: an imaginary village, any village a reader chooses, within or near York County, Maine. Two of the stories first appeared as gift books with wide margins and decorative borders.

The village holds a meeting house and a Dorcas Society whose members once scrubbed the pews during a season of generous bankruptcy. Wiggin writes about neighbors, church suppers, and small kindnesses with warmth and humor. The book suits readers who enjoy gentle New England fiction, where character matters more than plot.
352-buttered-side-down-stories:
Twelve short tales by Edna Ferber make up this 1912 set, first framed by a foreword that teases old fairy-tale endings. The stories stop short of happy-ever-after and end, as Ferber puts it, with life simply going on. Their people are actors, shop girls, small-town folk, and hopeful strivers.

Scenes shift from New York streets to home towns, stage doors, and kitchens, where pride, love, and work collide in small ways. A heroine may win a part yet lose her ease, or a man may come home changed by years away. The charm lies in Ferber's sharp eye for how plain hopes bend, but do not break.
3550-la-mere-bauche-from-tales-of-all-co:
Anthony Trollope writes a short story set in the Eastern Pyrenees, drawn from his Tales from All Countries. The valley holding the baths of Vernet is little known to English travelers, who rarely push beyond Luchon, though Trollope calls Luchon the loveliest spot in those mountains. Under the stern peak of Canigou lie the hot baths, in a close, secluded valley.

The tale follows visitors to Vernet and the household of La Mere Bauche, with Trollope's usual care for manners, money, and marriage. He writes as a traveler who knows the place, noting hotels, passes, and local life. The story suits readers who enjoy Trollope in short form and a glimpse of French spa life in the nineteenth century.
35681-psycho-phone-messages:
Psycho-Phone Messages is a book of messages said to be spoken by the dead, recorded by Francis Grierson. The title page lists the speakers and their themes. General U. S. Grant speaks on fit preparation in America. Thomas Jefferson speaks on the future of American democracy. Benjamin Disraeli speaks on English and Irish affairs, and Prince Bismarck on the indemnities.

John Marshall is listed on the psychology of the Supreme Court, and Alexander Hamilton on the forces that go before revolution. Abraham Lincoln speaks on the future of Mexico, and Robert Ingersoll on our great women. Henry Ward Beecher is listed on the new Puritanism, and Benjamin Wade of Ohio on President Harding. General B. H. Grierson speaks on Japan, Mexico, and California. The book is a record of claimed spirit speech on public themes.
3601-the-captives:
Hugh Walpole writes a novel that opens with the sudden death of the Reverend Charles Cardinal, rector of St Dreots in South Glebeshire, as he bends toward a drawer of his washstand. Walpole dedicates the book to Arnold Bennett and prefaces it with a reflection on the invisible world, suggesting that God himself may draw strength from human fidelity.

The story follows the rector's family after this loss, as faith, grief, and unseen forces press on ordinary lives. Walpole, known for his Lake District and London novels, writes here about spiritual hunger and the search for meaning after death. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth century novels where religion is felt as mystery rather than argued as doctrine.
3613-miscellaneous-pieces:
John Bunyan's short works are gathered in this volume, transcribed from the 1845 edition of the Works of the Puritan Divines. Contents include Of the Trinity and a Christian, Of the Law and a Christian, Bunyan's Last Sermon, and Bunyan's Dying Sayings. The opening piece advises a young or shaken Christian how to carry the weighty doctrine of the Trinity, or plurality of persons in the Godhead.

Bunyan writes in plain, earnest prose for ordinary believers facing doubt, law, and death. His last sermon and dying sayings give the book a farewell tone, as the author of Pilgrim's Progress speaks one final time to his flock. The volume suits readers interested in Puritan devotion beyond Bunyan's famous allegory.
3615-john-bull-on-the-guadalquivir-from-:
Anthony Trollope writes a short story about an Englishman whose marriage connects him with the south of Spain. The narrator insists he is an Englishman living in England. His wife would not be pleased to be called anything but an Englishwoman, yet his tale requires him to describe Spanish trade and family life. The Pomfret and Daguilar families have long traded together, and their alliance shapes the plot.

Set on the Guadalquivir river, the story follows an English visitor, a Spanish household, and a young woman courted across national lines. Trollope writes with his usual humor about money, marriage, and national character. The tale suits readers who enjoy Trollope in short form, with Spain as a bright change from his usual English counties.
36712-the-best-psychic-stories:
The Best Psychic Stories is a set of tales of the unseen, edited by Joseph Lewis French. French was the editor of Great Ghost Stories and Masterpieces of Mystery. An opening essay by Dorothy Scarborough, a lecturer in English at Columbia and author of a work on the supernatural in English letters, stands at its front. The book came out in New York in 1920 from Boni and Liveright.

The contents open with a preface by French and the opening essay. When the World Was Young, by Jack London, stands first among the tales. The Return, by Algernon Blackwood, stands next. The Second Gener— breaks the list in the part shown. The book is a chosen set of tales of ghosts and strange powers, made by a known maker of such sets.
368-acres-of-diamonds-our-every-day-oppo:
Russell Conwell, founder of Temple University, gives his famed lecture on finding wealth close to home in this volume. The core talk tells of a man who sold his farm to seek diamonds abroad, while diamonds lay in his own fields. Around it sits a life sketch by Robert Shackleton, tracing Conwell from Lexington to pulpit and lecture hall.

Conwell argues that chance lies in one's own town, trade, and neighbors, not in far lands. He backs the point with tales of small sums, hard work, and gifts that built a school. The book reads as both a speech and a brief life, and it kept its pull for crowds across the United States.
36820-visits-and-sketches-at-home-and-ab:
Visits and Sketches at Home and Abroad is a work in three volumes by Mrs. Jameson. The third volume, in a second edition, came out in London in 1835 from Saunders and Otley. The full title adds tales and miscellanies now first gathered. Mrs. Jameson was the author of works on the traits of women and on famed female sovereigns.

The contents of the third volume open with a sketch of Mrs. Siddons, then a sketch of Fanny Kemble. Tales follow: The False One, Halloran the Pedlar, and The Indian Mother. A piece called Much Coin, Much Care ends the list as shown. The volume is a mix of life sketches of stage women and short tales, from a writer known for her books on women and art.
37024-the-express-companies-of-the-unite:
The Express Companies of the United States is a study of a public utility by Bert Benedict. It was put out in New York in 1919 by the Intercollegiate Socialist Society, at ten cents a copy. A foreword by that body presents the work to the public. It calls the pamphlet a careful study of its theme by Mr. Bertram Benedict.

The foreword holds the theme to be a weighty one, and the time well chosen. The nation was then at work, it says, to frame its course on the future control of the express trade and of kindred services. The study thus bears on a live public question of its day: who should own and run the firms that carry goods and parcels for the country at large. The pamphlet is a short work of public affairs.
3725-famous-men-of-the-middle-ages:
John Haaren and Poland wrote this school history to teach the Middle Ages through lives rather than dates. The preface argues that a child grasps history best when a single person stands at the center of each scene, like a mountain peak in a landscape. Short chapters therefore follow kings, warriors, saints, and scholars one by one, each with a clear tale and a plain moral.

Harun al-Rashid of Baghdad stands as one example, a caliph who prized poets and scholars and whose court helped pass algebra and the numerals we still use into western Europe. Other chapters range from Rome's fall to the dawn of modern states. Teachers and young readers still use the book as a first map of the medieval world, short on jargon and rich in human incident.
374-fantastic-fables:
Ambrose Bierce packs short, biting fables into this 1899 volume, each with a sting in its tail. Kings, priests, politicians, poets, and fools act out small moral plays, then meet a twist that mocks their pride. Titles name the game: the moral principle, the crimson candle, the ingenious patriot, and the poet's doom.

Bierce writes in terse, polished prose, with a satirist's cold eye for cant and power. No party or creed escapes his lash. The book reads as a sharp tonic for readers who like fables with teeth, where virtue seldom wins and folly pays its own price.
3752-voyager-s-tales:
This volume draws its tales from the great collections of Richard Hakluyt, the Elizabethan clergyman who spent his life gathering accounts of voyages. The introduction follows Hakluyt from Westminster School to Christ Church, Oxford, where maps, globes, and sailors' stories fixed his passion for a wider knowledge of the globe. His first book of 1582 on voyages toward America set the pattern for the vast work that followed.

The tales themselves range across seas and ports, with ships from Tripoli meeting at Zante amid drums, trumpets, and cannon fire. Readers meet merchants, mariners, and adventurers in their own words, often rough and direct. The book suits anyone who wants the age of discovery told by those who sailed it, rather than by later historians alone.
3753-peacock-pie-a-book-of-rhymes:
Walter de la Mare wrote these rhymes for children, grouping them under headings that map a child's world. Up and Down opens the book with horsemen and huntsmen, Boys and Girls follows with windows and lost shoes, and Three Queer Tales add berries, thieves, and a castle. Later groups visit places and people, beasts, witches and fairies, earth and air, and close with songs.

The poems mix nonsense, eeriness, and tenderness in short stanzas, with an old soldier begging a crust at a door and a sailor wasting away far from home. De la Mare keeps his language simple and musical, so the verses read aloud well. Parents and young readers will find a book to dip into at bedtime, one rhyme at a time, without any need to read straight through.
3757-the-white-bees:
Henry van Dyke gathers lyric and patriotic verse in this collection, crowned by its title poem. The White Bees retells the legend of Aristaeus, the shepherd whom Apollo made keeper of golden bees, with honey, music, and orchard light woven through the stanzas. Around it stand songs for America, a New Year's Eve sequence, and praise poems for poets from Milton and Wordsworth to Keats, Shelley, Browning, and Longfellow.

Later lyrics turn personal and wistful, with a hermit thrush, a firefly city, a window at twilight, and a ride through the Alps. Van Dyke writes in clear, musical lines that favor warmth over puzzle. Readers who like verse that can be read aloud will find a book of gentle craft, American feeling, and old legends made new.
3805-the-vultures:
Henry Seton Merriman sets this novel among English travelers and a Polish family living on a volcano. Joseph Mangles, a dry and dyspeptic Englishman, opens the book smoking on an Atlantic deck, grumbling at fine weather because it brings women on deck. His path crosses Cartoner, a younger Englishman, and the Bukatys, who have lived with unsettled times since childhood, when they watched the streets from a nursery window in April 1861.

The Bukatys know what it means to live gayly on the edge of revolt, with fathers in the streets and empires overhead. Merriman writes with cool irony and a sharp eye for national pride. Readers who like political romance will find a tale of spies, families, and a Poland that refuses to lie still.
3806-a-modern-cinderella-or-the-little-o:
Louisa May Alcott gathers four stories for girls in this volume, led by the title tale of a modern Cinderella. Among green New England hills stands an old many gabled house, where sisters Nan and Di pass a summer morning with books, brooks, and birches. A little old shoe, lost and found, sets the romance moving, with a prince in modern dress and a heroine who earns her happy ending by kindness rather than by magic.

Debby's Debut, Brothers, and Nelly's Hospital follow, with Aunt Pen murmuring that propinquity works wonders as a young guest dresses for a hop. Alcott writes with warmth and humor throughout. Readers who know Little Women will find the same blend of home life, moral sense, and high spirits in shorter compass.
3807-the-different-forms-of-flowers-on-p:
Charles Darwin devoted this botanical volume to a puzzle of flowers, why many plants bear two or three different forms of blossom. The cowslip and its kin lead the inquiry, with long styled and short styled forms that prove fertile only when crossed in the right way. Hybrid oxlips, flax with twisted pistils, and the purple loosestrife, with three forms of stamens matched to three pistils, supply the evidence.

Tables of pollen grain diameters, counts of seeds, and careful notes on legitimate and illegitimate unions fill the chapters. Darwin dedicates the book to Asa Gray and argues from experiment rather than from theory alone. Readers with patience for close science will find a classic of plant study, showing how small floral differences drive the whole business of crossing and seeding.
3810-the-man-eaters-of-tsavo-and-other-e:
Lieutenant Colonel J H Patterson wrote this plain account of two years building a railway through British East Africa. The famous chapters tell how two man eating lions stalked the Tsavo camps, killing workers night after night while Patterson hunted them. He insists he toned the facts down rather than up, and writes for readers who may doubt what they read.

Other chapters follow hippos, lions, and camp life, with one long watch ending as a great hippo hides behind a tree, tooting and splashing for hours. Patterson's prose is direct and unadorned, with the railway itself as a second hero. Readers who like true adventure will find a tense and vivid book, and a window on East Africa before the railway changed it.
3815-rolling-stones:
O Henry's posthumous collection gathers stories, sketches, and fragments left at his death, with an introduction to frame them. The contents run from The Dream and A Ruler of Men to The Atavism of John Tom Little Bear, The Marionettes, The Marquis and Miss Sally, and A Fog in Santone. A German concert hall scene, with palms, marble tables, and soft shod waiters bringing beer, shows O Henry's eye for place even in an unfinished piece.

The book also holds an unfinished Christmas story, an apology, and a snapshot at the president, mixed with tales of sharp twists and tender endings. The quality varies, as in any posthumous gathering, but the voice stays unmistakable. Readers who want O Henry beyond the famous hits will find a miscellany worth browsing, story by story.
382-edinburgh-picturesque-notes:
Robert Louis Stevenson sketches his home city in this short travel book, first framed as picturesque notes. He opens with Edinburgh on its three hills above the Firth of Forth, a grand site cursed by wind, rain, and sea fog. Old Town closes, New Town streets, bridges, and views fill the chapters that follow.

Stevenson writes as a native who loves the city yet mocks its weather and its grim airs. He notes scholars, rogues, and ghosts of old Scotland in the same breath. The book gives a vivid walk through a city of stone, mist, and sharp contrasts, seen by one of its most fond and frank sons.
3837-hospital-sketches:
Louisa May Alcott drew these sketches from her own months as a Civil War nurse, first printed in the Boston Commonwealth and then enlarged in book form. Chapters follow her from obtaining supplies and a forward movement to a day, a night, and off duty hours in a Union hospital. The publisher gave five cents of every copy to orphans made fatherless or homeless by the war, a fact the advertisement states with pride.

The sketches mix humor with horror, as a delirious patient flourishes a mug and an old boot for canteen and knapsack, declaiming in a toga while an attendant sleeps off whiskey. Alcott names no names, quoting Sairy Gamp for her warrant. Readers who know Little Women will find the same warm voice here, turned to wounds, laughter, and death in the wards.
385-the-redheaded-outfield-and-other-bas:
Zane Grey gathers eleven baseball tales in this volume, most set in the minor leagues of his day. The title story follows Delaney's red-haired outfield trio: Gilbat, Clammer, and Ray, each gifted, each a headache for his manager. Other tales track a country pitcher called the Rube through pennants, marriage, and defeat.

Grey writes the game in vivid, slangy detail, from circus catches to clubhouse rows. Managers, knockers, and old pros fill the dugouts. The stories capture early baseball as work, show, and gamble, and they still charm fans who love the game's rougher, smaller-town past.
4016-prince-eugene-and-his-times:
L. Muhlbach's historical romance follows Prince Eugene of Savoy, the soldier prince whose honor and affections suffer a mortal wound. For a day he stays alone in his room, longing for the privilege of grieving without witnesses, while his servant Conrad keeps vigil outside.

Through the long night Conrad hears his master's slow, measured step, pacing out grief that no medicine can cure. Muhlbach builds the tale from court intrigue, war, and love, in the full manner of nineteenth-century romance. Readers who enjoy long historical novels will find a warm, old-fashioned life of a famous general.
4018-japanese-fairy-tales:
Yei Theodora Ozaki's collection retells old Japanese tales for English readers, with princesses, stepmothers, and moral lessons at their heart. A dying mother tells her daughter Hase-Hime to honor her father and his second wife, to obey her superiors, and to be kind to those below her.

Hase-Hime listens in respect and promises to do all she is told, in the manner of a model heroine. Other tales in the book follow the same pattern of duty, kindness, and reward. The collection suits young readers and anyone curious about Japan's story tradition, told in clear, gentle prose.
4030-travellers-stories:
A mother's travel stories for her sons Frank and Harry open on a stormy evening, as the boys beg for tales of her five years in Europe. Seated on the old sofa, she recalls cities, coaches, and the small mishaps of travel.

One tale leaves mother and sons in the middle of a street, their noddy driver poring over a directory in a bright shop to find Dr. Nichol's house. The stories mix sights, manners, and mild comedy, told in a warm, fireside voice. Young readers will enjoy a book that turns a mother's journeys into lessons in curiosity and good humor.
40312-the-intoxicated-ghost-and-other-st:
The Intoxicated Ghost and Other Stories is a set of short tales by Arlo Bates. It came out in Boston and New York in 1908 from Houghton, Mifflin and Company. The contents list nine tales. The title tale stands first, then A Problem in Portraiture, The Knitters in the Sun, and A Comedy in Crape. A Meeting of the Psychical Club and Tim Calligan's Grave-Money stand in the list as well.

The title tale opens with a portrait of Irene Gaspic. It was not her beauty that made her out of the common run, the tale says, though she was of great charm. Nor was it her wit, her skill, or her wealth, though she had a full share of all those gifts. Other girls were fair and rich as well, the first page notes, as it sets up its lead figure.
4066-wild-apples:
Henry David Thoreau's essay on wild apples celebrates the orchard tree and the old custom of wassailing it. Villagers throw cider about the roots, lay toast on the branches, and circle a good bearer to drink a toast three times.

Here's to thee, old apple tree, they sing, wishing hats full, caps full, bushels and sacks full of fruit. Thoreau uses the rite to praise wild flavor over tame orchard crops, and to link farming with poetry. Readers who love Thoreau's Concord walks will enjoy this short, fragrant essay on apples and autumn.
4077-the-mariner-of-st-malo-a-chronicle-:
Stephen Leacock's chronicle of Jacques Cartier follows the Mariner of St. Malo into the Gulf of St. Lawrence. On June 25, Cartier turned west from Newfoundland into what looked like open sea, then sighted land again near the Magdalen Islands.

Two abrupt rocks rose side by side, one pierced by surf into a passage that caught Cartier's eye. Leacock tells the voyages with the clarity of the Chronicles of Canada series, mixing navigation, first meetings, and French claims. Readers who like exploration history will enjoy a brisk, vivid life of Cartier.
4097-alice-of-old-vincennes:
Maurice Thompson's novel Alice of Old Vincennes sets a frontier romance in the Illinois country during the American Revolution. Father Gibault, a simple missionary of great worldly knowledge and force, brings the wave of revolution to Vincennes.

Colonel George Rogers Clark makes Gibault's acquaintance at Kaskaskia, and great movements reach even the quietest nooks like tides of the sea. Alice, the heroine, stands amid French settlers, soldiers, and shifting flags. Readers who enjoy historical romance of the old Northwest will find a spirited tale of love and loyalty on the frontier.
410-hell-fer-sartain-and-other-stories:
John Fox Jr. sets nine tales in the Kentucky mountains in this volume, told in rich mountain speech. The title story opens at a wild Christmas dance on Hell-fer-Sartain Creek, where two rivals fight over Nance Osborn. Later tales follow courtship on Cutshin, a trick of trade, a preacher on Kingdom Come, and a baby left in strange hands.

Fox writes feuds, loves, and church meetings with humor and a keen ear for dialect. His folk are proud, quick to fight, and slow to forgive. The book keeps a lost mountain world alive in story, where kin ties rule and a word carelessly said can start a war.
4221-shearing-in-the-riverina-new-south-:
Rolf Boldrewood's account of shearing in the Riverina follows a shed day from first bell to last count. At six o'clock the bell ends work, and each man's sheep are counted in his presence and noted with scrupulous care.

The record is written out in full and hung for public inspection in the shed next day, a ceremony of fairness in a hard trade. Master, men, manager, and laborers then part to separate lodgings, avoiding each other's company after the day. Readers who like Australian bush life will find a vivid, exact picture of shearing.
4233-jeanne-of-the-marshes:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this romance around a princess who has withdrawn to a quiet life, only to be disturbed by the arrival of Major Forrest on urgent business. From that opening interview the story widens into a tale of rank, secrecy, and danger, set partly in the flat marsh country that gives the book its title.

Oppenheim, known for thrillers of diplomacy and high society, keeps the focus on the heroine's choices as old ties and new threats close in on her. Readers looking for an early twentieth-century popular romance, with a proud heroine and a plot driven by visits, letters, and revelations, will find it here.
4238-on-the-economy-of-machinery-and-man:
Charles Babbage's On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures, a founding text of industrial economics, asks how work, machines, and skill combine to make goods cheaply. A chapter on forces too great for human power notes the skill and apparatus needed for many men to exert full force at one point.

With hundreds or thousands at work, difficulties multiply, and no overseer can easily tell whether each man exerts his whole strength. Babbage turns that puzzle into principles of division of labor and machine design. Readers who like economics with a mechanical mind will find a classic still sharp today.
4253-dramatic-romances:
Robert Browning's Dramatic Romances collects some of his finest short poems, edited with introduction and notes by Charlotte Porter and Helen A. Clarke from the 1898 Crowell edition. The contents include The Patriot, My Last Duchess, Count Gismond, The Boy and the Angel, The Glove, The Last Ride Together, and The Pied Piper of Hamelin.

Other poems range from Porphyria's Lover and Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came to A Grammarian's Funeral and The Heretic's Tragedy. Each poem gives its speaker a voice and a moment of crisis, and the collection is a good entry point for readers new to Browning's dramatic monologues.
42677-fires-book-1-the-stone-and-other-t:
Wilfrid Wilson Gibson wrote these tales, printed at London in 1912 as the first book of Fires. A verse at the front is a gift to George Clausen. The man who speaks sits snug in his chair and stirs the fire to flame. Wild shapes of dream come with the flare: streams of gold wood, isles of dreams, towns of dusk in flame, and caves of bright stone.

The dreams turn at the close of the verse. The man shuts his eyes to heat and light, and sees in the dark a shape that crouches in the drip. It is the man who hews the coal that feeds his fire, with stark, damp arms. That turn sets the tone of the tales. The Stone, The Wife, and The Machine stand at the head of the list of parts.
4281-helen-s-babies:
John Habberton wrote this comic novel around Harry Burton. He is a twenty-eight-year-old bachelor salesman of white goods. His married sister Helen asks him to look after her two small children, Budge and Toddie, for a fortnight. Helen and her husband want to visit friends who have not invited the children.

The babies are therefore left with their uncle. Harry's account of those ten days made the book a popular success. It records the children's innocent, crafty, angelic, and impish ways. The comedy comes from a bachelor learning how little he knows about feeding, scolding, and amusing two lively boys.
4283-brazilian-sketches:
Rev. T. B. Ray, educational secretary of the Foreign Mission Board of the Southern Baptist Convention, wrote these sketches after traveling in Brazil with his wife. His chapters cover the country itself and Rio de Janeiro. They cover a visit to a country church, two presidents, and saint worship. They cover penance and priest, and the gospel withheld and then triumphant.

Later sketches tell of Jose Barretto, Captain Egydio, and Felicidade. They tell of persecution, of the Bible as a missionary factor, and of the mettle of native Christians. Ray writes as a missionary observer, interested in both the land and the people. The book gives a mission-board view of Brazil in the early twentieth century.
429-the-magic-egg-and-other-stories:
Frank Stockton gathers twelve witty tales in this volume, opening with the title story of a magic egg shown at a private theatre. A traveler back from the East displays wonders to friends at the Unicorn Club, and each tale that follows turns on a trick, a bargain, or a surprise. A widow's cruise, a piece of red calico, and a Christmas wreck add their own twists.

Stockton writes in smooth, urbane prose, with a fondness for neat reversals. His folk are polite, clever, and often outwitted by their own schemes. The book charms as light, well-made entertainment, where humor and a gentle moral walk hand in hand.
4324-fifty-famous-fables:
Lida Brown McMurry collected fifty famous fables for young readers, retelling them in plain language for school and home. The tales come from Aesop and the wider fable tradition, where animals speak and act out human faults: foxes flatter, wolves threaten, and ants plan ahead while grasshoppers sing.

Each fable is short enough to read aloud, and each carries a moral stated or implied. McMurry's book was made for teachers as well as children, with stories chosen for clarity and for talk afterward. It remains a handy first fable book, where the lessons are simple and the animals do the teaching.
4355-david-crockett-his-life-and-adventu:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this life of David Crockett for the American Pioneers and Patriots series. His preface admits Crockett was not a model man, but a representative one, of a large class whose modes of life most citizens know as little as the customs of the Comanche. Crockett's wild life, Abbott argues, deserves a patriot's study.

The book follows Crockett from frontier youth through hunting, soldiering, and Congress to the Alamo, in Abbott's popular style. It stresses character over legend, while keeping the tall tales that made Crockett famous. Readers get a nineteenth-century biography, admiring but frank, of a man whose name every American then knew.
43551-the-white-horses:
The White Horses is a novel by Halliwell Sutcliffe, the author of Ricroft of Withers and The Open Road. It came out in London, Melbourne, and Toronto in 1916 from Ward, Lock and Company. The book is given to the memory of the author's sister. A front picture shows Old Squire Metcalf, who broke into a roar of laughter as he went out to meet a guest.

The chapter heads mark the tale as a story of the English civil war age. Who Rides for the King? stands first, then Skipton-in-Craven and Some Men of Fairfax's. The Lady of Ripley, How Michael Came to York, and A Halt at Knaresborough stand in the list. How They Sought Rupert, The Loyal City, and The Riding In carry it on. A Stanley for the King and The Scots at Micklegate stand later in the list.
4357-american-fairy-tales:
L. Frank Baum, author of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, wrote these American fairy tales for children. The contents include The Box of Robbers, The Glass Dog, The Queen of Quok, The Girl Who Owned a Bear, The Enchanted Types, and The Laughing Hippopotamus. Later tales bring the Magic Bon Bons, the Capture of Father Time, and the King of the Polar Bears.

The first tale leaves Martha alone one afternoon, while her family scatters to a card party, a drive, and the office. Baum sets his wonders in American homes and streets, rather than in a far kingdom. The stories are gentle, funny, and inventive, and they show Baum's gift for making magic feel close to home.
4358-the-sea-fairies:
L. Frank Baum wrote this undersea fantasy for children, with pictures by John R. Neill. He begins by noting that two-thirds of the earth's surface is water, and that land folk have always wondered who inhabits it. Odd beings sometimes rise from the seas, and stranger ones may live unseen in the depths.

In Baum's story the sea folk speak and behave much like land folk, and the mermaids resemble fairies children already know. Trot and Cap'n Bill visit their kingdom, meeting its rulers and wonders. The book is fanciful throughout, but Baum insists its sea people are real within the tale, and young readers will take them as such.
4387-present-at-a-hanging-and-other-ghos:
Ambrose Bierce gathered these ghost stories from his 1918 collection Can Such Things Be, in a selection titled Present at a Hanging. The contents divide into the ways of ghosts, soldier-folk, and haunted houses, with tales such as A Cold Greeting, A Wireless Message, An Arrest, and A Man with Two Lives. Later stories bring the Isle of Pines and the Spook House.

Bierce's ghosts are terse, ironic, and often military, reflecting his Civil War service. A hanging watched, a message from nowhere, and a field that cannot be crossed give the book its chills. The stories suit readers who like short, sharp supernatural tales, where the horror lies in a plain fact quietly stated.
4399-a-few-figs-from-thistles:
Edna St. Vincent Millay wrote these poems and sonnets under the title A Few Figs from Thistles, thanking the editors of Ainslie's, The Dial, Pearson's, Reedy's Mirror, and Vanity Fair for reprinting several pieces. This edition adds poems not in earlier ones, and it opens with the famous First Fig, whose candle burns at both ends.

The Second Fig builds a shining palace upon sand, while Recuerdo recalls a night spent going back and forth on a ferry, tired and merry. Millay's voice is bright, defiant, and lyrical, with sonnets of love and independence. The collection made her a voice of her generation, witty about freedom and frank about desire.
45-anne-of-green-gables:
An orphan girl arrives by mistake at a Prince Edward Island farm. Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables wanted a boy to help Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert. Instead they get Anne Shirley, talkative, dreamy, and quick to blush.

Anne charms the island with mishaps at school, tea parties, and puffed sleeves. Diana Barry becomes her bosom friend; Gilbert Blythe becomes her rival. Matthew's quiet love steadies her temper. The book launched a beloved series about growing up with imagination. Sequels, stage shows, and screen versions spread Anne's island world far beyond Canada.
4518-madame-de-treymes:
Edith Wharton sets this short novel in Paris, where an American, John Durham, waits in a hotel doorway looking out toward the Tuileries gardens. He has come back to France with a personal stake in the city, and he soon meets Madame de Malrive, a woman caught between an American past and a French marriage. Around them stand old families, strict customs, and the glitter of a capital planned for pleasure.

Durham learns how hard it is for an outsider to move inside French family life, where divorce, honour, and duty carry a weight he did not expect. Wharton contrasts brisk American frankness with Parisian reserve and tact. Readers get a compact drama about love, social rules, and the cost of crossing from one world into another.
4519-the-descent-of-man-and-other-storie:
Edith Wharton gathers ten stories in this volume. It opens with The Descent of Man, in which Professor Linyard returns from a Maine holiday changed by an idea he picked up on his travels. The book then moves through The Other Two, Expiation, and The Lady's Maid's Bell. It goes on to The Mission of Jane, The Reckoning, The Letter, The Dilettante, The Quicksand, and A Venetian Night's Entertainment. Each story turns on a social choice made in polite company.

Wharton is sharp on marriage, money, reputation, and the small lies people tell to keep their place. Her characters often learn, too late, what a single decision has cost them. Readers get a polished set of early Wharton tales, witty and unsparing, showing the New York and European worlds she knew best, and the moral traps hidden inside good manners.
4533-the-hermit-and-the-wild-woman-and-o:
Edith Wharton gathers seven stories in this 1908 volume, opening with the title tale of a hermit living in a cave in a hill hollow. Below him runs a stream through oaks and alders. Across the valley stands a walled town that once flew a Guelf standard, and later fell to steel-clad men-at-arms. The hermit, once a town lad, now watches war, faith, and wildness from his lonely height.

The other stories, The Last Asset, In Trust, The Pretext, The Verdict, The Pot-Boiler, and The Best Man, return to Wharton's usual ground of money, marriage, art, and reputation. Together they show how private choices harden into public fates. Readers get a varied Wharton collection. A medieval opening gives way to modern social drama, and every tale turns on what a character will pay to keep, or lose, their good name.
45348-french-dishes-for-american-tables:
Pierre Caron wrote this book of French fare for the tables of America, printed in 1886. He had been chef of the sweet course at Delmonico's. Mrs. Frederic Sherman put his work in English dress. A few words at the front state the aim of the book. It is to put in front of the crowd a count of fine bills of fare, in a form so clear and brief that their make is in the reach of all.

That is a need long felt, the words go on. The books of worth on the art of the cook that have come out are in the main in French. Those in English, for all their bits of worth, in the main swarm with the terms of the trade. Such terms fret and maze the new hand.
4539-back-to-god-s-country-and-other-sto:
James Oliver Curwood gathers nine northern stories in this volume. The title tale, Back to God's Country, opens the set. Other stories include The Yellow-Back, The Fiddling Man, and L'ange. They go on to The Case of Beauvais, The Other Man's Wife, The Strength of Men, The Match, and The Honor of Her People. Bucky Severn, His First Penitent, Peter God, and The Mouse close the set. The first tale begins on the Fraser River in British Columbia, when Shan Tung, a Chinese gold collector from Vancouver, sets out with Tao, a Great Dane.

Curwood's north is a place of gold trails and old grudges, where a fuse lit in one winter can explode forty years later. Heroes and villains meet in snow, river, and camp, and loyalty is tested by greed and love. Readers get a set of Canadian wilderness tales, full of animals, outlaws, and rough justice.
4542-checkmates-for-three-pieces:
Checkmates for Three Pieces is a working file for chess players, not a book of prose. It lists board positions in FEN notation, the short code that records where each piece stands, whose move it is, and the state of play. The positions cover endings with only three pieces on the board, such as a king with a queen or a rook against a lone king, in many different squares and corners.

Players can set each position on a board and work out the winning moves, or feed the lines into a chess program for study. Because the file gives positions rather than explanations, it suits readers who already know basic checkmate patterns and want practice material. It is a reference set for drill and testing, best used beside a board or an engine, not read as a story.
4549-artemis-to-actaeon-and-other-verses:
Edith Wharton published this poetry volume in New York in 1909, opening with the title poem, Artemis to Actaeon. In that poem the goddess speaks to the hunter who could not look on her and live. He had seen her in cloud, wave, and bough, and in shapes that lurk between lid and eyeball in the dark. Part one goes on to Life, Vesalius in Zante, Margaret of Cortona, and A Torchbearer, mixing myth, history, and travel.

Part two, called The Mortal Lease, gathers Experience, Grief, Chartres, Two Backgrounds, The Tomb of Ilaria Giunigi, The One Grief, and The Eumenides. Part three adds Orpheus, an autumn sunset, moonrise, All Souls, All Saints, and other lyrics. Readers get Wharton as a poet: formal, learned, and moving, with classical myth used to speak about love, loss, and the limits of mortal sight.
456-the-door-in-the-wall-and-other-stori:
H. G. Wells gathers eight tales of wonder and dread in this volume, opening with the title story. Lionel Wallace tells a friend of a green door in a London wall that led, in childhood, to a garden of delight. Each time he passes it in adult life, duty pulls him on, until one last chance decides his fate.

Other tales send a star toward Earth, dream an Armageddon, and blind a whole country to sight. Wells writes with clear, probing prose, mixing science with moral fable. The book shows his short fiction at its most haunting, where a single marvel tests a whole life.
4560-verses:
Susan Coolidge, best known for her children's stories, gathers her poems in this volume, opening with a dedication to two friends whose youth grew under peaceful suns and gracious dew. The opening poem praises friends who held beauty and ease as a trust. They scattered brightness on harder roads, so that roses, in the old saint's tale, turned to bread for hungry and weary souls. That note of kind, useful goodness runs through the book.

Coolidge writes in clear, musical verse about friendship, home, nature, faith, and the duties of a good life, without showy difficulty. Her poems suit reading aloud and quiet reflection, and they carry the same warmth readers know from her prose. This volume offers a gentle nineteenth-century poetry collection, modest in manner but sure in feeling, for readers who like verse that comforts and steadies rather than puzzles.
4584-mont-saint-michel-and-chartres:
Henry Adams wrote Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres as a private, jealously guarded book before it reached a wider public, and this edition carries an introduction by Ralph Adams Cram. Adams takes two great French monuments, the island abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel and the cathedral of Chartres, and uses them to open up the whole medieval world. Theology, philosophy, politics, art, and daily life all meet in his reading of stone, glass, and song.

At Chartres, Adams lingers on the great windows, where colour breaks from darkness into pools of sapphire and rose, and where the rose window hangs like a constellation. The book treats the cathedral as a living statement of faith, not a museum piece. Readers get a rich, personal work of cultural history, best read slowly, by an American writer trying to feel what the Middle Ages believed and built.
4591-after-a-shadow-and-other-stories:
T. S. Arthur published After a Shadow, and Other Stories in 1868, gathering seventeen short tales. The contents run from After a Shadow, In the Way of Temptation, and Andy Lovell, through A Mystery Explained, What Can I Do?, On Guard, and A Visit with the Doctor, to Hadn't Time for Trouble, A Good Name, Little Lizzie, and Alice and the Pigeon. Later pieces include Dressed for a Party, Coffee vs. Brandy, Amy's Question, An Angel in Disguise, Which Was Most the Lady?, and Other People's Eyes.

The title story opens on a bright June morning, with Mrs. Mayflower calling to her little boy Arty from a window, in excitement at his new performance. Arthur's tales mix domestic comedy, temptation, and moral warning. Readers get a varied Victorian storybook for family reading, where small choices, a party dress, a cup of coffee, or a guarded tongue, carry a clear moral weight.
4595-heart-histories-and-life-pictures:
T. S. Arthur published Heart-Histories and Life-Pictures in 1853, opening with an introduction on how seldom we think of other people's inner lives. We are so given up to our own ends, hopes, joys, fears, and disappointments, he says, that we rarely consider the bright and sombre life-pictures other eyes look upon. Yet every heart has its history, and dreamy eyes, sober faces, and subdued, mournful tones on daily paths testify how sad many of those histories are.

Remembering this, Arthur argues, awakens a kinder feeling toward others, and draws our minds away from too exclusive thoughts of self. Whatever awakens sympathy and interest in humanity is both a personal benefit and a common good. The sketches that follow aim to create that sympathy, story by story. Readers get a gentle Victorian collection about compassion, written to make ordinary encounters feel less lonely and less judged.
4714-mr-achilles:
Jennette Lee published Mr. Achilles in 1912, opening with Achilles Alexandrakis arranging fruit on his stall in front of his little shop on Clark Street, Chicago. On a clear, breezy October morning, cool but not cold enough to endanger his fruit, he builds oranges into a yellow pyramid, grouping figs, dates, melons, pears, grapes, and pineapples around them. That happy moment, arranging fruit with dark, slender fingers, is the best of his day.

Already Alcibiades and Yaxis have left with pushcarts, north and south, calling antiphonally in clear, high voices that fade as they go. They will not return until night. From that shop grows a story of Greek immigrants, work, friendship, and American city life. Readers get a warm, humane novel about a fruit seller and his neighbours, told with care for small daily joys.
4739-fly-leaves:
C. S. Calverley, author of Verses and Translations, published Fly Leaves at Cambridge in 1884, in a tenth thousand printing from Deighton, Bell and Company, with George Bell and Sons in London. Its contents run from Morning and Evening, through Shelter and In the Gloaming, to The Palace, Peace, and The Arab. Lines on hearing the organ, Changed, First Love, and Wanderers follow, with Sad Memories, Companions, and a Ballad.

Later poems include Precious Stones, Disaster, Contentment, and The Schoolmaster, with Arcades Ambo, Waiting, Play, and Love. Thoughts at a railway station, On the Brink, Forever, Under the Trees, and Motherhood lead to Mystery, Flight, On the Beach, and Lovers, and a Reflection. The Cock and the Bull and an Examination Paper close the set. Morning opens with white-horsed Day chasing Night's mares away, as Phoebus opens dawn's gates. Readers get witty, musical Victorian light verse, polished and playful.
4758-late-lyrics-and-earlier-with-many-o:
Thomas Hardy published Late Lyrics and Earlier, with Many Other Verses, at London in 1922, with Macmillan. In his apology, roughly half the poems date from recent months, and the remainder are older pieces set aside in manuscript while earlier books went to press. Those earlier books already offered readers enough pages at once, especially amid wartime distraction.

The oldest pieces here, he explains, were simply missed when earlier collections were assembled. Their freshness, now beyond recovery, seemed to offset their rawness and to warrant printing them. A few poems are dated, while other dates cannot be found. Launching such a volume in neo-Georgian days, by a writer who began in mid-Victorian times, called for a few words. Readers get late Hardy lyrics, with older pieces rescued beside them.
4765-loyalties:
John Galsworthy wrote Loyalties as a play in the fifth series of his plays. Charles Winsor, owner of Meldon Court near Newmarket, and his wife Lady Adela head the cast, with Ferdinand de Levis, young, rich, and new. Treisure, Winsor's butler, General Canynge, a racing oracle, and Margaret Orme follow, with Captain Ronald Dandy, retired, and his wife Mabel.

Inspector Dede, Robert, Winsor's footman, and a constable attend, with Augustus Bobbing and Lord St Erth. A footman of the club and Major Colford, a brother officer of Dancy's, appear. Edward Graviter, a solicitor, a young clerk of Twisden and Graviter's, Gilman, a large grocer, and Jacob Twisden, senior partner, complete the cast. Set among racing people, country houses, and clubs, the play tests what loyalty means when friendship, honour, and prejudice collide. Readers get a sharp Galsworthy drama of society judging one of its own.
4783-riley-farm-rhymes:
James Whitcomb Riley wrote Riley Farm-Rhymes, inscribed to the good old-fashioned people. Its opening poem finds deadening and thicket boiling full of June, from cricket rattle to yellow-hammer tune. The catbird in the bottom and the sap-sucker on the snag seem able only to brag. Music fills the twitter of bluebird and jay, a sassy critter's pecking all day, the flicker, the thrush, and a chipmunk's snicker in the brush.

Music sends the speaker back in a sweeter-than-sleep dream, to a stream splitting the meadow where dandelions grew, where he stands knee-deep, redder than sunset down the road. Contents include Brook Song, The Canary at the Farm, A Clover, and The Country Pathway, with How John Quit the Farm, June, and Mylo Jones's Wife. Old-fashioned farm life, in Riley's dialect, runs through the book. Readers get musical farm rhymes.
487-songs-of-travel-and-other-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers late verse in this volume, sent home for print months before his death in Samoa. Written mostly after he left England in 1887, the poems range from the vagabond's road song to youth and love, highland places, and winter lanes. An editor's note explains their tangled titles and order.

Stevenson meant them to join Underwoods as a third book. Their tone mixes wanderlust, longing, and a traveler's farewell. Lines on the open road and the fading light rank among his most quoted. The volume gives readers his last songs, brief, musical, and full of restless hope.
4901-the-only-true-mother-goose-melodies:
This essay traces Mother Goose in nineteenth-century Boston, asking which rhymes the city's old families actually grew up with. It discusses Whitmore's paper on the subject, Isaiah Thomas's 1785 edition reproduced in facsimile, and the French tales of Perrault's Mother Goose tradition behind them.

The author writes for readers who loved the rhymes as children and now want their history straight: which books carried them, and how a Boston line kept them alive. The record names no author for this work. The piece works as literary history for nursery-rhyme lovers, separating the true old Boston Mother Goose from later imitations.
4902-chess-history-and-reminiscences:
H. E. Bird's history of chess traces the game from its disputed origins to its growing popularity in his own day. Indian traditions, Persian and Arab courts, and early European mentions all get their turn, with figures from Chosroes and Harun to Charlemagne, Offa, and Alcuin appearing in the story.

Bird also gathers praise and censure of the game, including Pope's lines, and follows chess through India, China, Egypt, Greece, Rome, Scandinavia, and Spain. Reminiscences of players and play sit alongside the history. Readers who play chess, or who simply like games with long pasts, get both a chronicle and a memoir of the board.
4921-young-canada-s-nursery-rhymes:
Young Canada's nursery rhymes gather the old favorites Canadian children learned by heart. The crooked man and his crooked cat and mouse lead the set. Curly locks will not wash dishes. The little old man quarrels over money. Bow-wow-wow's dog barks through another rhyme.

Multiplication is vexation, and the Rule of Three puzzles the schoolroom singer, just as in the English originals. The collection frames them for young Canadian readers. No author or editor is named in the record. Parents and teachers get a simple, singable treasury, useful for reading aloud and for sharing rhymes that crossed the Atlantic intact.
4932-a-knight-of-the-white-cross-a-tale-:
G. A. Henty's Knight of the White Cross opens in June 1470 at the royal chateau of Amboise. A stately lady watches from a window. A knight talks with a lady at a tambour frame. A lad of seventeen strokes a hawk at another window. A boy of nine studies pages at a table. The lady turns impatiently to ask what will come of it all.

The tale follows the Knights of St. John to the siege of Rhodes, where the White Cross stands against the Ottoman advance. Henty builds the siege from character and incident, with young heroes learning war. Readers get a historical adventure of chivalry and defense, told in Henty's brisk, instructive style.
4938-u-s-presidential-inaugural-addresse:
This collection gathers the inaugural addresses of American presidents from the early republic onward, in chronological order. Washington's successors speak in turn. Madison speaks in 1813. Monroe speaks in 1817 and 1821. John Quincy Adams speaks in 1825. Jackson, Van Buren, Harrison, Polk, Taylor, and Pierce follow.

Each address states a new administration's principles, fears, and promises at the moment of taking office. Read together, they trace how the presidency described itself as the country grew. Students of American politics get a primary-source survey, useful for comparing how different eras framed the same office.
4960-on-picket-duty-and-other-tales:
Louisa May Alcott's On Picket Duty and Other Tales opens on a Civil War night. A great tree draped in gray moss stands scarred by lightning. It looks like a venerable warrior whose campaign is nearly done. Beneath it stands a guard of four. Campfires twinkle on a distant plain. A road strewn with the relics of a rout winds behind them.

A sluggish river glides toward jungle on one side. A Southern swamp breathes malaria on the other. The men on duty are friends as well as comrades. Alcott's tales mix camp humor, homesickness, and courage. Readers get war stories told from the picket line, where waiting and watching mattered as much as fighting.
4970-there-are-crimes-and-crimes:
August Strindberg's There Are Crimes and Crimes is a drama of guilt and judgment, published together with a companion piece called A Mystery under the common title In a Higher Court. The introduction places it after Strindberg's confessional works Inferno and Legends and the dream-play Toward Damascus, all finished between 1897 and 1898.

Behind those works lay a mental crisis in Paris, where Strindberg sought gold by transmutation while his spirit traveled through seven hells seeking heaven. The play itself weighs crime against conscience in a higher court than any earthly one. Readers get Strindberg at his most searching, turning personal crisis into drama.
5008-katherine-s-sheaves:
Katherine's Sheaves begins at four in the afternoon on the first day of Hilton Seminary's midwinter term, at a well-regarded school in a handsome old town in western New York. In a roomy recreation room, cheerful girls assemble noisily, like magpies, swapping holiday greetings, talking over their studies, classes, and roommates, and chatting about incoming teachers and pupils.

A tall, kindly woman of around thirty-five steps into the doorway, her pleasant face bright with amused delight at the lively scene. Katherine, the heroine, gathers her sheaves of friendship, study, and duty through the term. The catalog entry is anonymous. Readers get a girls' school story of the older kind, warm and orderly.
5010-state-of-the-union-addresses:
George Washington's State of the Union addresses gather the first president's annual messages, from the new government's earliest sessions onward. One message congratulates Congress on North Carolina's accession to the Constitution, on rising national credit and respectability, and on goodwill toward the Union, with concord, peace, and plenty blessing the country.

Later messages address finance, defense, Indian relations, and the whiskey troubles, always in Washington's measured style. The set shows a president inventing the office as he filled it. Students get the founding presidency in its own words, formal, cautious, and deeply concerned with union itself.
5011-state-of-the-union-addresses:
John Adams's State of the Union addresses gather the second president's annual messages to Congress, from his first message in November 1797 through the end of his term. The opening message deals with sickness in Philadelphia, where the legislature's meeting place itself became a question, and with the public expense and inconvenience of moving Congress.

Later messages carry Adams through quasi-war with France, naval buildup, and the partisan storms of the 1790s. Read together, they show a president defending a young republic's neutrality and institutions. Students get a primary source for the Federalist era, in Adams's own formal and anxious voice.
5012-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Thomas Jefferson's annual messages gather the third president's reports to Congress, written after years of war in Europe. Jefferson says with joy that the wars afflicting sister nations have at last ended. The links of peace and trade are opening again among them.

America's own peace, kept through a perilous season, draws his special thanks. Later messages cover the Louisiana Purchase, the Lewis and Clark expedition, and the road toward embargo. Jefferson's prose is spare and republican throughout. Readers get the early republic's growth and its foreign-policy caution, from the president who embodied both.
5013-state-of-the-union-addresses:
James Madison's State of the Union addresses collect the fourth president's annual messages, written through the long crisis with Britain and France. One message reports a deal with a leading belligerent nation. Then deep concern follows. Britain refuses to honor its minister's act. It pursues a harder policy toward the United States.

War, embargo, and the defense of a republic against the world's great powers run through the set. Madison's messages move from diplomacy to war and back to peace, always in the language of constitutional duty. Readers get the War of 1812 era from the desk of the president who asked Congress to declare it.
5014-state-of-the-union-addresses:
James Monroe's State of the Union addresses gather the fifth president's annual messages from the Era of Good Feelings. Monroe celebrates abundant harvests, extensive and profitable commerce, public credit at an extraordinary elevation, and defense preparations advancing under a well-digested system.

A free government founded on the people's interest and affections, he argues, has gained strength through experience. Later messages proclaim the Monroe Doctrine, address Florida, and manage a growing nation. Readers get the 1820s in the voice of a president who presided over prosperity and laid down the doctrine that would bear his name.
5016-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Andrew Jackson's State of the Union addresses gather the seventh president's annual messages, beginning with his first address to a federal legislature of twenty-four sovereign states and twelve million happy people. Jackson presents a view of national affairs and proposes measures he judges necessary to promote the Union's objects, with unfeigned satisfaction at the trust placed in him.

Later messages defend the Bank veto, Indian removal, and the spoils system, and report on nullification and foreign affairs. The set shows Jacksonian democracy in full voice: popular, combative, and jealous of concentrated power. Students get the 1830s from the general who remade the presidency.
5017-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Martin Van Buren's State of the Union addresses collect the eighth president's annual messages, delivered as the young republic weathered financial panic and frontier conflict. Van Buren, Jackson's successor, defends the independent treasury, reports on the nation's finances, and addresses relations with Britain, Mexico, and Native nations.

The messages show a careful party manager turned president, arguing for hard money and limited government while the economy shuddered. Read in sequence, they trace a single-term presidency shaped by the Panic of 1837. Students get a primary source for Jacksonian democracy's second act, in Van Buren's precise and lawyerly prose.
5018-state-of-the-union-addresses:
John Tyler's State of the Union addresses gather the tenth president's annual messages, delivered after he succeeded William Henry Harrison in 1841. Tyler rejoices in general prosperity, civil and religious liberty, and unexampled means of education, knowledge, and improvement, with peace in American borders and plenty in American homes.

Disease visited a few portions of the land, he notes, yet the people's health was generally preserved. Later messages address Texas annexation, the tariff, and the veto fights that left him a president without a party. Readers get a primary record of the 1840s, from a president who governed alone and changed the map anyway.
5019-state-of-the-union-addresses:
James Polk's State of the Union addresses collect the eleventh president's annual messages, written during a presidency of territorial expansion. Polk reports on Texas annexation, the Oregon question, and the war with Mexico, along with tariffs, the independent treasury, and the growth of a continental republic.

The messages are businesslike and confident, setting out administration policy as accomplished fact. Read together, they show how a one-term president pursued a clear program and left the map changed. Students get a primary record of Manifest Destiny from the president who most deliberately carried it out.
5020-state-of-the-union-addresses:
