Frank Harris gathers Elder Conklin and other stories, published by Macmillan in New York and London in 1894. The contents list the title tale, The Sheriff and His Partner, A Modern Idyll, Eatin Crow, and The Best Man in Garotte, with Gulmore the Boss. Elder Conklin opens as the elder leaves the supper table and his daughter walks out with the new schoolmaster onto the stoop, or verandah, running round the frame house.

The day was warm, but evening chill betokened the near approach of Indian summer. The house stood on the crest of a prairie roll. The pair leaned on the railing looking over a small peach orchard to Cottonwood Creek, two hundred yards away at the bluff's foot, fringed by the trees that named it. Harris writes prairie life with sharp, unsentimental eyes.
7182-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's great collection gathers the voyages, traffics, and discoveries of English seamen, keeping the spelling of his sixteenth-century original while expanding old manuscript short forms for modern eyes. The editor's notes explain that footnotes follow later spelling, while Hakluyt's own sidenotes stay his, marking the line between the old text and new help.

Readers meet a vast store of sea tales, trading ventures, and coastal claims, told in the voices of captains, merchants, and chroniclers. Hakluyt built the book as a record of English enterprise abroad, and its bulk still shows how wide that enterprise ran. This text preserves both the journeys and the manner of their first telling.
7187-seven-english-cities:
William Dean Howells walks through seven English cities in this illustrated book of travel and comment, opening with a view of Monk Bar. Howells was already known for books on Rome, English towns, and London, and here he turns the same easy eye on streets, buildings, and local life in a set of linked sketches.

The charm lies in observation rather than in guidebook fact: a gate, a market, a quiet lane, and the talk that rises around them. Howells writes as a friendly visitor, noting what pleases him and what puzzles him without pretending to master each place. The result reads like good company on a slow tour, full of small scenes that stay in mind.
71883-the-high-ones:
Poul Anderson wrote this tale of the stars, first printed in a journal of such tales in June 1958. A note at the head sums the plight of the crew. A revolt has given the Whites charge of the starship. But that means they can never go back to an Earth ruled by the Reds. The tale opens with Eben Holbrook at a port of glass. He sees a world of green and blue and white cloud, across many cold stars.

The sight gives him a sense of home, and brings tears to his eyes. The ship is three units of the void and fifty-eight years from Earth. The wait drags, and the nerves of the crew are worn thin by strife. No man knows if the star Tau Ceti has a world where men can walk free.
7212-memories-of-canada-and-scotland-spe:
The Marquis of Lorne gathers speeches and verses on Canada and Scotland in this volume, dedicated with respect and affection to the members of the Royal Society of Canada. Verses on Canadian subjects lead the way: a Canadian national hymn, river rhymes, a robin, legends of the St John river, Mohawk guides, prairie roses, Cree fairies, and the Qu'Appelle valley.

Speeches follow the poems, joining public voice to private verse, and the whole book moves between two northern lands the author knew well. Lorne writes as a statesman with a poet's ear, praising lakes, rivers, and peoples in measured lines. The collection preserves a late Victorian view of Canada from inside its public life.
7255-cambridge-sketches:
Frank Preston Stearns sketches Cambridge men he knew without ever seeking them out. His preface owns a regret: he never introduced himself to distinguished persons or sought their notice, and only later wished he had seized chances his youth let pass. Knowing these men, he writes, gave him a more elevated idea of human nature than he might otherwise have held.

Charles Sumner faces the volume, and the sketches that follow mix memory with portraiture, letting talk and habit reveal character. Stearns writes as a neighbour rather than a biographer, fond and frank by turns. The book preserves a Cambridge of friends, teachers, and talk before fame fixed them in print.
7306-autobiographic-sketches:
Thomas De Quincey's Autobiographic Sketches gathers selections, grave and gay, from writings published and unpublished, chosen for an American edition he was revising in 1853. His letter from Lasswade that January explains his plan: to revise and considerably alter, for republication in England, such of his writings as it seemed proper deliberately to avow.

De Quincey stresses that he does not disown anything he published, only that some pieces served a transient occasion and need not stand unchanged. The sketches that follow mix memory, confession, and wit in his famous winding prose. Readers meet a master of the personal essay sorting his own past for a new public.
7366-three-comedies:
Björnstjerne Björnson was Norway's leading writer and a public voice in its national life, and these three plays show him turning from peasant tales to the stage. The volume opens with The Newly-Married Couple, follows with Leonarda, first performed in 1879, and closes with A Gauntlet, written in 1883. An introduction traces Björnson's life from a remote parsonage in the north to literary fame.

The plays take up marriage, reputation, and the rules society sets for women and men. Leonarda and A Gauntlet stirred sharp controversy in Norway, since they pressed social and religious questions that audiences were not used to hearing on stage. Read together, the three comedies show a dramatist using domestic life to argue about freedom, duty, and the cost of defying convention.
7368-lifted-masks-stories:
Susan Glaspell, a playwright and novelist of the American Midwest, writes here about people caught between who they seem and who they are. The stories often place Americans abroad, as in the Paris scene where a young woman's clothes, bought in France, still cannot hide that she is American. Manners, money, and marriage all act as masks her characters wear.

The title points to the moment each story builds toward: a mask lifted, a pretense dropped, a truth spoken at last. Glaspell's people are plain speakers in elegant rooms, and their small rebellions carry real weight. Readers who know her plays will find the same interest in women's inner lives, told here in compact, quietly dramatic fiction.
7399-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
This last volume reaches back to Holmes's oldest portfolio, to verses first printed in The Collegian in 1830 and in illustrated annuals of his youth. The Meeting of the Dryads, The Toadstool, The Spectre Pig, and The Ballad of the Oysterman show a student poet trying on masks: classical fancy, comic parody, and Yankee humor in turn. A poem called The Poet's Lot already wonders what a life in verse will cost.

The charm of the book is its earliness. These are the experiments of a young man who did not yet know he would become Boston's beloved doctor-poet. One of the poems, the preface hints, won kind words from Thackeray. Read after the later volumes, the collection shows where Holmes began: playful, curious, and already fond of the odd corners of New England life.
7437-a-peep-behind-the-scenes:
Mrs. O. F. Walton, author of Christie's Old Organ, looks behind the fairground in this moral tale for young readers. The show people, who seem gay and carefree from the front of the booth, live hard lives in their caravans, grumbling at the weather and counting their takings. The story follows Rosalie, a girl of the little theatre, through the day after the fair and the actress's story.

Later chapters bring a circus procession, a doctor's visit, a family secret, and a lone lamb lost and found, as Rosalie learns what lies behind the painted scenes. Walton writes plainly and kindly, with a Victorian evangelical's eye for suffering and hope. The book's charm is its backstage view: the fair as work, home, and hardship, not only as a holiday show.
7438-friends-in-council-first-series:
Sir Arthur Helps was a Victorian civil servant who wrote his way into literature, and Friends in Council, first published in 1847, was the book that made him known. Born at Streatham in 1813, educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge, Helps served as private secretary to the Chancellor of the Exchequer before turning to letters. The book takes the form its title promises.

Friends meet in council and talk through the questions of life: conduct, work, friendship, and the duties of ordinary people. The dialogue form lets Helps argue with himself, giving each side a fair voice. Later series followed, but this first one sets the pattern: thoughtful, good-tempered conversation as a way of thinking, written for readers who enjoy ideas at leisure.
7439-english-fairy-tales:
Who says that English folk have no fairy tales of their own? Joseph Jacobs opens his collection with that challenge, and answers it with a selection from some 140 tales of which he found traces in England. He admits the oddity in his title: few of these stories actually speak of fairies, just as few in Grimm speak of them. The name covers a wider kind of folk tale.

Jacobs invites the child reader in with a playful key and door, then tells the tales plainly, in the voice of the storyteller. Giants, clever youngest sons, talking beasts, and tricksters all appear, in stories that had lived by word of mouth long before they were printed. The collection stands as the classic English counterpart to Grimm, and the source of many tales children still know.
7466-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations is the great Elizabethan collection of English voyages, traffics, and discoveries, and this volume is one part of it. The edition retains the spelling of Hakluyt's sixteenth-century original, expanding only old manuscript abbreviations, so readers meet the accounts in something close to their first form. Editor's footnotes in modern spelling guide the way.

This volume opens amid grim eastern history: Tartar chieftains and their followers destroying whole provinces without respect for condition, fortune, sex, or age. From such accounts the collection builds its picture of a world opening to English ships and traders. For readers of travel history, Hakluyt remains the first source, vast, vivid, and unmistakably of its age.
7471-the-man-with-two-left-feet-and-othe:
P. G. Wodehouse's 1917 collection takes its title from a story about a man who cannot dance, but its pleasures run wider. The contents include Bill the Bloodhound, about Henry Pifield Rice, a detective whose trade is not quite what it seems; Extricating Young Gussie; Wilton's Holiday; and two parts of The Mixer. Crowned Heads at Geisenheimer's and The Romance of an Ugly Policeman add restaurant and street comedy.

Dogs, chorus girls, policemen, and young men in scrapes fill these stories, all told in Wodehouse's bright, effortless voice. The book shows him between his school stories and his mature Jeeves and Blandings work, already master of the comic short story. Readers who want Wodehouse in small, perfect doses will find this collection ideal.
7476-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
This volume of Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations opens with its author's own preface, a defense of recording English deeds at sea. Hakluyt notes how nations love to blaze abroad their pedigrees, painting ancestors' arms on their walls, while poets trace obscure heroes back to the gods themselves. Against fable, he sets the undoubted truth of voyages, traffics, and discoveries, gathered from sailors and merchants.

Like its companion volume, this edition retains Hakluyt's sixteenth-century spelling, expanding only manuscript abbreviations, with editor's footnotes in modern spelling. The collection as a whole remains the foundation of English travel literature. This volume's preface is the place to start for readers who want to know why Hakluyt gathered his vast library of voyages at all.
7505-half-past-seven-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson wrote these stories for half-past seven, the bedtime hour, and the Toyman tells them. That is what the Toyman used to say, the book promises. If you ever go to the White House with the Green Blinds by the Side of the Road, the Toyman will say it still, whatever the weather. Dorothy Hope Smith's color illustrations picture the tales.

The contents run from The Little Lost Fox and The Big Bobsled to The Jolly Roger. Then come The Blue Croaker, the Bright Agate, and the Little Gray Mig, and the old woman who lived on the canal. Anderson dedicates the book to Sarah Davis Anderson, the youngsters' Aunt Sally. The stories are gentle, funny, and just strange enough for bedtime, told for children who are not quite ready to sleep.
7506-the-huge-hunter-or-the-steam-man-of:
Edward S. Ellis wrote one of America's first science-fiction adventures in this dime novel of the prairies. A colossal figure strides across the plains, looking like some Titan taking giant steps, with a black volume of smoke issuing from its mouth or the top of its head. At a distance no one can scrutinize the phenomenon closely, and terror spreads before it.

The terror is the Steam Man, a giant machine built by a genius. It travels with a trapper and an artisan up the Yellowstone, among miners and Indians, on buffalo hunts and against a grizzly bear. Chapters promise the steam man as hunter, in wolf ravine, and in an appalling danger. Ellis's huge hunter is the ancestor of the robot tale, a wonder of steam and iron loose on the frontier.
7515-the-glory-of-the-trenches:
Coningsby Dawson, author of Carry On: Letters in Wartime, wrote this interpretation of the trenches from his own service as a Canadian officer. His father, W. J. Dawson, introduces the volume. The epigraph gives its thesis: the glory is all in the souls of the men, nothing external. Dawson had been wounded, removed to a base hospital and then to a military hospital in London, where amputation of his right arm was gravely feared but happily avoided.

As soon as he could use his hand, he was asked to write for Canada about its forces. The book opens with letters from home carried by runners through battle smoke, up Death Valley spouting flame, and down roads no one uses by day. Dawson writes for those at home, to show what the trenches meant to the men who held them. It is a soldier's book, earnest and unsentimental.
7516-crucial-instances:
Edith Wharton's Crucial Instances gathers seven stories in which a single moment decides a life. The contents run from The Duchess at Prayer and The Angel at the Grave through The Recovery, a dialogue called Copy, and on to The Rembrandt, The Moving Finger, and The Confessional. Italy, art, and old houses provide much of the scenery.

The opening story asks the reader to question the shuttered front of an old Italian house, a motionless mask behind which buzz the secrets of the confessional. Other houses declare the lives they shelter, Wharton writes, but the old palace in its narrow street is as impenetrable as death. Each tale turns on such a masked moment, when character shows itself and cannot be hidden again.
7518-more-jataka-tales:
Ellen C. Babbitt retold the Jataka tales, the Buddhist birth stories, for children, and this second volume answers the cry for more. The first collection, published ten years earlier, had won readers young and old, and Felix Adler had confessed himself captivated by the charm of the tales. Babbitt dedicates this companion volume to Rudyard Kipling, in the name of all children who troop to his call.

The stories come from a Guild of Jataka Translators under Professor E. B. Cowell of Cambridge, and Babbitt turns their scholarship into simple, lively tales. Animals talk, kings learn, and kindness wins, in stories first invented to please and instruct cousins far away in the East. Here East meets West, as the foreword says, in a book meant to be read aloud.
7519-the-nomad-of-the-nine-lives:
A. Frances Friebe tells this story through a cat. Her nephew Tom finds his uncle in a brown study before a comfortable fire. He asks why the uncle does not write the story of his life. The uncle, who has spent hours relating his thrilling adventures, finally grants the request. The book that follows hopes to interest people as well as cats, and Clara R. Atwood's illustrations picture its hero.

The hero is the Nomad, a cat of nine lives, whose wanderings carry him through streets, seashores, and homes. Friebe dedicates the book to the Reverend Francis H. Howley, president of the S.P.C.A., and its spirit is humane throughout: June, the preface notes, is when people abandon dogs and cats as they move to the seashore. It is an animal story with a conscience, told by the animal himself.
7541-quotes-and-images-from-celebrated-c:
Alexandre Dumas père, famous for romantic novels, also wrote histories of famous crimes, and this volume gathers quotations and images from that series. Dumas, the notes remind us, was a novelist who knew his history. He was meticulous in research in his early works, and these books are histories that place most romantic novels in the shade. They cover many centuries and many lands.

The contents list reads like a rogue's gallery of Europe. There are the Borgias, the Cenci, and the Massacres of the South. There are Mary Stuart, Karl-Ludwig Sand, and Urbain Grandier. There are Nisida, Derues, La Constantin, and Joan of Naples. The Man in the Iron Mask appears as an essay, not the novel, beside Martin Guerre, Ali Pacha, and Murat. The Renaissance popes, the notes say, are especially intriguing.
756-arizona-sketches:
Joseph A. Munk wrote these sketches of Arizona when it was still a rough frontier of desert, mines, and small towns. He describes the land, its climate, its people, and its ways, from prospectors and ranchers to Native peoples and new settlers. His eye is that of a visitor who stayed long enough to learn the country.

Munk mixes travel notes with local history and anecdote, praising the clear air and wide skies while noting the hardships of desert life. The sketches give a vivid picture of Arizona at the turn of the century, before dams and cities remade it. Readers who love the old Southwest will find here a plain, first-hand portrait.
760-enoch-soames-a-memory-of-the-eightee:
Max Beerbohm wrote this tale as a mock memoir of Enoch Soames, a would-be poet of the 1890s who fades into obscurity. Soames, a pale young man in a waterproof cape, haunts London cafés and dreams of fame, while the narrator watches with amused pity. A deal with the devil lets Soames glimpse his future fame, or lack of it.

Beerbohm mixes real figures of the decade with invention, and the joke turns tender as Soames learns his fate. The tale is a small masterpiece of irony, poking fun at artistic vanity while mourning lost youth. It remains one of the most quoted stories about the nineties, and about the cruelty of literary fame.
764-hans-brinker-or-the-silver-skates:
Mary Mapes Dodge wrote this tale of Holland, where canals freeze in winter and every child skates. Hans Brinker, a poor boy, hopes to win the silver skates offered in a great race on the ice. His father lies ill from a fall, and the family scrapes by with little money and much pride.

Dodge mixes the race with lessons on Dutch life: dikes, windmills, markets, and the customs of town and farm. Hans and his sister Gretel face hardship with pluck, and the race becomes a test of heart as much as speed. The book, aimed at young readers, has long served as a friendly guide to Holland and to honest effort.
774-essays-and-lectures:
Oscar Wilde gathered essays and lectures that show his wit at full stretch before his plays made him famous. He writes on art, dress, the English Renaissance, and the value of beauty, arguing that art needs no excuse beyond itself. The lectures, given on tour, carry his gospel of aestheticism to new audiences.

Wilde's prose sparkles with paradox and epigram, turning each topic into a performance. Beneath the glitter lies a serious claim: that beauty and form matter as much as morals or facts. The volume gives readers the young Wilde as critic and prophet, and it helps explain why his later plays still dazzle.
775-when-the-sleeper-wakes:
Herbert George Wells wrote this tale of Graham, a man who falls into a trance in 1897 and wakes more than two hundred years later. He finds a London of moving roads, vast halls, and a Council that has grown rich on his sleeping wealth. A leader named Ostrog seeks to use him as a figurehead for revolt.

Graham must choose between the Council and the people, and his choice leads to war in the streets of the future city. Wells uses the sleeper to judge his own age and the age to come, on wealth, power, and the crowd. The novel is a founding work of dystopian fiction, and it still grips as a tale of a man out of time.
7763-the-law-breakers-and-other-stories:
Robert Grant's The Law-Breakers and Other Stories opens with George Colfax, a passive reformer. He reads the Nation, hates the spoils system, votes for the best men, and gives a dollar a year to civil-service reform. He talks well about public decay, yet does little beyond talk.

Other tales in the volume include Against His Judgment, St George and the Dragon, and The Romance of a Soul. An Exchange of Courtesies, Across the Way, and A Surrender follow. Together they satirize genteel Boston morals, where right views cost little and real action costs much more.
7769-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques, and Discoveries of the English Nation gathers the great age of English sea travel, edited here by Edmund Goldsmid. This edition keeps the spelling of Hakluyt's sixteenth-century original, while expanding old manuscript shortenings for modern readers.

Footnotes follow nineteenth-century spelling, sidenotes stay Hakluyt's own, and two kinds of notes guide the reader through dense old texts. Sailors, merchants, and explorers fill its pages, from first Atlantic ventures to far eastern trade, making it a first source for how England learned the wider world by ship.
7780-notes-to-shakespeare-volume-01-come:
Samuel Johnson's Notes to Shakespeare, volume one on the comedies, appears here in the Augustan Reprint Society edition, edited with an introduction by Arthur Sherbo. General editors from Michigan, California, and London universities frame a text that returns to Johnson's famous critical work.

Johnson's preface to Shakespeare, the general introduction notes, ranks among the great essays of the eighteenth century, yet students often forget it is, precisely, a preface. This volume collects his notes on the comedies, where his plain sense, learning, and sharp judgment meet the plays line by line.
78-tarzan-of-the-apes:
A lord's infant son grows up among apes after his parents die on an African shore. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Tarzan of the Apes traces the boy from a jungle cabin to lord of his tribe. Books left in the cabin teach him to read before he can speak with men.

Tarzan battles apes, lions, and a village of black warriors, then meets Jane Porter and her party. He learns his true name and rank, yet hesitates between two worlds. The novel's final choice leaves him apart from Jane. Burroughs launched a century of Tarzan tales with this book.
7802-seven-o-clock-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson's Seven O'Clock Stories, told first to Jean and Malcolm, offers twenty nights of bedtime tales. Early nights bring three happy children, their playmates, noisy folks, the toyman, a willow whistle, and Mr Scarecrow. Then comes the prettiest fairy story in the world.

Later nights add Mother Hen and Robber Hawk, Duckie the stepchild, and a tall enemy. A sleigh and tiny reindeer, Jack Frost and the Man in the Moon, a circus, a jolly clown, and lions of the north wind follow. Pictures show a fat old man on a hill with pipe and sack, ready for story time.
7813-madame-de-mauves:
Henry James's Madame de Mauves opens on the terrace at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, where Paris lies spread in dusky vastness, domed and fortified, girdled by the silver Seine. Behind the viewer stands a stately park, then a forest of turfy avenues where one may forget the boulevards half an hour away.

One mid-spring afternoon a young man, fond of rural things yet drawn to the city's hive, watches Paris with wistful curiosity, feeling that to miss it is to miss a thrilling chapter. His winter there proved fruitless, yet the view still pulls him. The tale that follows tests honor, love, and restraint.
7838-fifty-one-tales:
Lord Dunsany's Fifty-One Tales, published in 1915, gathers brief fantasies. They run from The Assignation and Charon through The Death of Pan, The Sphinx at Giza, and The Hen, to Wind and Fog and The Raft-Builders. Death meets Odysseus and an orange, a flower prays, and time trades with a tradesman.

Later tales bring a giant poppy, a man with golden earrings, and King Karna-Vootra's dream. A mistaken identity and the true history of the hare and tortoise follow. Short, polished, and strange, the book shows Dunsany's gift for turning myth, jest, and melancholy into tales a few pages long.
7865-jackanapes-daddy-darwin-s-dovecot-a:
Juliana Horatio Ewing's Jackanapes, Daddy Darwin's Dovecot, and Other Stories, pictured by Randolph Caldecott, opens with Byron on battle's stern array, where rider and horse lie in one red burial. The title tale follows a gallant boy soldier, Jackanapes, from village green to battlefield, loved for pluck and heart.

Two donkeys and geese, a dovecot, and other short tales follow, in Ewing's warm, moral style for young readers. Through humor, pathos, and country life, the collection praises courage, kindness, and duty, and remains a classic of Victorian children's writing, tender without preaching, and still readable today.
7894-the-fallen-leaves:
Wilkie Collins's The Fallen Leaves, dated Gloucester Place, July 1, 1879, opens with the author refusing prefatory pleading. Readers who followed its serial run at home and abroad, he says, already grasp its design and its delicate treatment. He leaves the book to speak on its own merits.

A prologue traces remote causes shaping a young man's life. A stranger household's misfortune, falling while he still wore his first jacket, steers his happiness years later. Through love, shame, and social judgment, Collins follows fallen leaves of society with sympathy and firm moral sight.
7900-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques, and Discoveries of the English Nation, in this second hosted copy, again keeps sixteenth-century spelling while expanding old shortenings. A transcriber's note explains macrons, Latin endings, and the old y-for-th spellings, so modern eyes can follow the text.

Footnotes use nineteenth-century spelling, Hakluyt's own sidenotes stay marked, and marginal notes sit at their points except in verse. Sailors, merchants, and explorers crowd its pages, making this a core source for England's first age of ocean travel and trade, in a faithful, readable reprint.
7927-the-celibates:
Honore de Balzac's The Celibates, the longest single-titled section of the Comedie Humaine after Lost Illusions, joins three tales whose only firm bond is bachelors and old maids as heroes. Its introduction admits the union is weak, and judges Pierrette, the opening tale, below its companions.

Written for the young Countess Anna de Hanska, Pierrette carries a studied, artificial air, the introduction says, unlike the freer later tales. Linked loosely to the Arcis series with The Tenebreuse Affaire, the volume shows Balzac turning single lives into a panorama of French society.
79384-recluses:
Raymond S. Spears wrote this tale of a dog, as its first leaf states. The dog is of a kind bound by long years of habit and drill in the ways of man. Yet she thrills to the call of the wild, which no drill can still. A cut at the front shows a man named Danvers as he smashes the big hand of a man who breaks in. The tale opens with the breed of the dog.

A vast count of breeds was used to breed the ugliness out of the wolves of the Black Forest, to make them tame guards of sheep. That work could not fail to rub out some of the wolf in them as well. Their shape, looks, and frame stayed the same, but their minds grew soft and kind. At the end of that line stands Queen.
7949-the-historical-nights-entertainment:
Rafael Sabatini collected this second volume of historical tales from The Premier Magazine, dedicating it in London in June 1919 to its editor, David Whitelaw. Each story takes one dramatic night or episode from history: the absolution of Afonso Henriques, first king of Portugal; the False Demetrius. Pretended son of Ivan the Terrible; and an episode of the Inquisition in Seville called The Hermosa Fembra. Further tales follow the same pattern.

Sabatini's gift is to find the human turning point inside a famous event and tell it as a short, tense story. The volume reads quickly, story by story, and needs no knowledge of the first series. For readers who like history with a plot, it is an entertaining way to meet figures and crises that textbooks usually flatten.
7955-historical-miniatures:
August Strindberg's Historical Miniatures, translated by Claud Field, offers short visions from the whole sweep of human history. Julian the Apostate and Peter the Hermit appear alongside Attila and Luther, Alcibiades and Eginhard. While the scenes range from the empires of the Pharaohs and the Czars to the Athens of Socrates and a Merry England. Critic Maximilian Harden praised it in 1907 as a book the public should read.

Strindberg writes as philosopher and poet rather than historian, letting each episode stand as a vivid scene. The miniatures are brief, so the book can be read in sittings, each one a different age. It suits readers who want history as imagination: famous lives and turning points, lit up by one of Scandinavia's most restless minds.
79701-too-many-heroes:
Too Many Heroes is a western tale by Ray Humphreys. The scene at the start is the office of Sheriff Joe Cook of Monte Vista. The sheriff is in a foul mood and calls out his deputy, Shorty McKay, for being gone all morning. A bold robbery the day before has set the town on edge. A lone masked bandit had robbed the Second National Bank and got away with three thousand dollars in cash.

Shorty gives a soft answer: he has been in the public library. The sheriff sneers at the thought of a book as a help in the hunt for a bank robber. Shorty is a deputy who, as the sheriff puts it, is of little help in a hard hour. The tale opens as a clash of tempers in the law office, with a manhunt still to come.
8007-the-bible-king-james-version-book-7:
Judges tells of Israel between Joshua and the kings, when the people fell into a repeated cycle: they turned from God, suffered under oppressors, cried out, and were rescued by a judge. Deborah leads an army, Gideon tests God with a fleece and routs Midian with a handful of men. Jephthah makes a tragic vow, and Samson, strong and reckless, brings down a Philistine temple on himself. The book ends in anarchy, with everyone doing what was right in his own eyes.

The stories are rough, vivid, and morally unsettling, which is why they endure. Judges refuses to tidy its heroes, showing deliverers who are flawed and a nation drifting. In the King James Version, its battles, songs, and betrayals read like a dark chronicle of freedom without leadership, and a warning about what follows when a people forgets.
8013-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
Adam, Seth, Enosh: First Chronicles begins with a genealogy that runs from the first man through Noah, Abraham, and Israel's tribes. After the long lists, the narrative turns to David, his wars, his preparations for the temple, and his organisation of priests, singers, and gatekeepers. The book ends with David's death and Solomon ready to build.

The chronicler writes history as a family record, tracing how worship was ordered and why it mattered. Readers who push past the names find a portrait of David as temple planner rather than warrior king. In the King James Version, the genealogies carry a quiet claim: the returned exiles belonged to a story that began at creation itself.
8014-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
Second Chronicles retells Israel's history from Solomon to the exile, with its eye on the temple, the priests, and worship. Solomon builds the temple in Jerusalem, and the book follows Judah's kings through reform and apostasy, measuring each reign by faithfulness to God's house. Where Kings spreads its view across both kingdoms, Chronicles concentrates on Judah, and it ends with Cyrus of Persia allowing the exiles to return and rebuild.

The result is a history written for a restored community, reminding returned exiles who they were. Its long lists and temple accounts can seem dry, but they carry a point: worship is the centre that holds a people together. In the King James Version, the book offers a priestly counterpart to the prophetic history of Kings.
8021-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Ecclesiastes, attributed to Qoheleth, the Preacher, is the Bible's most sceptical book. Vanity of vanities, it begins, and it tests every human project in turn: wealth, pleasure, work, wisdom, and fame, finding each unable to satisfy. Time and chance undo the wise and the foolish alike, and death waits for both. Yet the book does not end in despair: it counsels enjoying simple gifts, food, work, and companionship, and fearing God.

Its honest, searching voice has made Ecclesiastes a favourite of readers who distrust easy answers. Poets and philosophers have quoted its refrains on seasons, toil, and the limits of knowledge. In the King James Version, its rolling sentences give doubt itself a kind of music, and the book remains Scripture's permission to ask hard questions.
8059-the-bible-king-james-version-book-5:
James, servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, wrote to the twelve tribes scattered abroad, and his letter is the New Testament's most practical. Count it all joy when you fall into trials, he begins, since the testing of faith produces patience. The letter goes on to warn against favouring the rich, to insist that faith without works is dead. To tame the tongue, and to call the proud to humility and the sick to prayer.

James reads like wisdom literature in Christian dress, closer to Proverbs than to Paul's arguments. Its demand that belief show itself in action has challenged comfortable religion ever since. In the King James Version, its direct, proverb-like sentences make it one of the most quotable and most convicting books in the Bible.
8075-the-junior-classics-volume-8-animal:
William Patten selected and arranged this eighth volume of The Junior Classics, with an introduction by Charles W. Eliot and a reading guide by William Allan Neilson. Its animal and nature stories include Little Cyclone, the story of a grizzly cub by W. T. Hornaday, true stories of tigers, wolves, foxes, and bears by W. H. G. Kingston, animal friends in Africa by Bayard Taylor, and a fight with a catamount. An illustration of a water lily fronts the volume.

The collection was made for young readers, pairing adventure with natural history in stories meant to be read aloud or alone. Its selections come from writers who knew animals first-hand, whether as naturalists or travellers. For families and collectors, the volume preserves an early twentieth-century ideal: that children learn nature best through vivid, true stories.
8091-sketches-and-studies:
Nathaniel Hawthorne gathered these sketches and studies, including his Life of Franklin Pierce, Chiefly about War Matters, Alice Doane's Appeal, and The Ancestral Footstep. The Pierce memoir opens with Hawthorne confessing that he is scarcely a politician and would not voluntarily have written a campaign biography, a task remote from his usual writing. The other pieces range from Civil War reflections to tales of old houses and family curses.

The collection shows Hawthorne outside his novels, as biographer, essayist, and storyteller. The Pierce life, written for a friend running for president, is candid about its own awkwardness. For Hawthorne readers, the volume rounds out the picture, adding political friendship and wartime observation to the romance and allegory of his fiction.
8092-tremendous-trifles:
G. K. Chesterton gathered these fleeting sketches from the Daily News into a book he calls a sporadic diary, recording one day in twenty that happened to stick in his fancy. His preface notes that even that diary he could only keep by keeping it in public, for bread and cheese. The subjects are deliberately small: a bed-post or a lamp-post, a window blind or a wall, things the reader looks at every day without ever really seeing.

Chesterton's point is that the commonplace is full of wonder once attention is paid to it. Each sketch turns a trifle into a small essay on gratitude, orthodoxy, or the strangeness of ordinary life. The book is a joyful introduction to his style, and it rewards reading in short sittings, one trifle at a time.
8105-imaginations-and-reveries:
AE, the pen name of George William Russell, gathered articles and tales from twenty-five years into this volume at his publishers' request. His preface explains the book's double pull: his temperament drew him to art, while his conscience drew him to work with other Irishmen at reconstructing Irish life. Birth in Ireland gave him a bias toward nationalism, yet he held that the politics of eternity ought to be his only concern. And that all races are children of the Great King.

The pieces mix mysticism, Irish politics, and literary reflection, and they refuse a single theme. Russell, poet, painter, and co-operative organiser, writes as a seer as much as a citizen. The book is a rich introduction to the Irish literary revival from inside, by one of its most original voices.
8107-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt, preacher, collected the principal navigations, voyages, traffiques, and discoveries of the English nation, and this is volume six of Edmund Goldsmid's edition. Its subjects include Madeira and the Canaries, and voyages to the south and south-east parts of the world, to ancient Asia and Africa, within the compass of sixteen hundred years. The text keeps the spelling of Hakluyt's sixteenth-century original, with manuscript abbreviations silently expanded.

Hakluyt's collection is the great archive of English exploration, preserving sailors' journals, merchants' reports, and diplomatic letters. This volume opens the southern routes that shaped England's overseas ambitions. For historians of travel and empire, it is a primary source of the first rank, and its old spelling gives the voyages their period flavour.
8111-after-long-years-and-other-stories:
Sophie A. Miller and Agnes M. Dunne translated these ethical stories from the German for the Sunshine and Shadow series, aiming to build character in youthful readers. Their note explains the method: ethics in lecture form fails, so the writers present truths through stories that help young minds withstand trials and temptations. An illustration shows a count falling at the feet of a countess in a tale called Royal Palace to Lowly Hut.

The stories are moral tales in the older sense, teaching through example rather than precept. Their German originals give them a flavour distinct from Anglo-American Sunday-school books. For collectors of children's literature, the volume preserves a period ideal: that fiction should form character while it entertains.
8112-houses-and-house-life-of-the-americ:
Lewis H. Morgan's Houses and House-Life of the American Aborigines, volume four of Contributions to North American Ethnology. Began as the fifth part of his manuscript for Ancient Society, on the growth of the idea of house architecture. When the manuscript outgrew a single volume, the part was removed and much of it appeared in detached articles, with a summary in Johnson's Universal Cyclopedia. The chapter on Aztec houses shows the work's range.

Morgan studies how Native American peoples built and lived in communal houses, from longhouses to pueblos, and what those dwellings reveal about kinship and society. His work founded the anthropology of architecture, though later scholars have revised his theories. For readers of Native American history, it remains a pioneering and richly detailed survey.
8113-literary-love-letters-and-other-sto:
Robert Herrick wrote these stories around literary life and love, opening with Literary Love-Letters: A Modern Account. Its first letter finds Eastlake renewing an episode of his past life at a chance meeting, and continuing in writing. With carnations lying beyond the page as a memento of a house on Grant Street. The letters urge tenderness and frankness, recalling what was precious in the past before it escapes into darkness.

Herrick, a Chicago novelist of manners, uses letters and stories to examine how writers love and remember. The collection is urbane and reflective, concerned with feeling rather than plot. For readers of early twentieth-century American fiction, it offers a quiet, literate portrait of educated life and its second chances.
812-catalan-s-constant-to-1-500-000-plac:
An electronic text gives Catalan's constant to one million five hundred thousand digits, computed with an algorithm by Greg Fee presented at ISSAC '90. The file notes that the maker checked the work against an earlier value of just over one million digits, using integer arithmetic in the main loop and text comparison.

There is no essay here: the file is the number itself, laid out for reference and checking. Readers use such a file to test programs, to verify sums, or to study the constant itself. Its length is its point, far beyond any hand need, and it stands as an exact record for mathematicians and coders.
8130-glimpses-of-unfamiliar-japan-first-:
Lafcadio Hearn's first series of Glimpses of Unfamiliar Japan records his early years in the country. Dedicated to the friends whose kindness made his sojourn possible: Paymaster Mitchell McDonald and Basil Hall Chamberlain of Tokyo University. Its chapters follow his first day in the Orient, the writing of Kobodaishi, Jizo, a pilgrimage to Enoshima, the market of the dead. Bon-odori dances, and Kitzuki, the most ancient shrine in Japan, with notes on the cave of children's ghosts.

Hearn writes with wonder and sympathy, dwelling on shrines, festivals, and ghost lore that other travellers missed. His Japan is unfamiliar even to many Japanese, seen through temples and villages rather than treaty ports. The book remains a classic of travel writing, and the best introduction to Hearn's lifelong love of Japan.
8133-glimpses-of-unfamiliar-japan-second:
Lafcadio Hearn's second series of Glimpses of Unfamiliar Japan continues his exploration of the country he had made his home. Its chapters cover a Japanese garden, the household shrine, women's hair, the diary of an English teacher, two strange festivals. The Japanese sea, a dancing-girl, the journey from Hoki to Oki, souls, ghosts and goblins, the Japanese smile, and a farewell. The first chapter describes his small two-story house by the Ohashigawa, dainty as a bird-cage but too small for the hot season.

Hearn's eye for domestic detail and folk belief makes this volume even richer than the first. He writes about gardens, shrines, and smiles as keys to a culture, not as curiosities. For readers who loved the first series, this is an essential continuation, and for newcomers, a vivid introduction to Hearn's Japan.
8138-war-time-silhouettes:
Stephen Hudson's War-Time Silhouettes sketches wartime London in short stories: Mr Reiss's Final Grievance, In the True Interest of the Nation. War Work, Business Is Business, Bobby, A War Victim, and Dulce et Decorum. The first story finds Mr Adolf Reiss, merchant, alone on a gloomy December afternoon, gazing into the fire in an expensively furnished but tasteless room that completely lacks home atmosphere. His grievance against life sets the book's tone.

Hudson's silhouettes are portraits in outline, sharp and brief, of civilians, profiteers, and victims in the First World War. The stories avoid battlefields to show war's pressure on ordinary rooms. For readers of wartime fiction, the collection offers a quietly ironic view of London at war, and of the moral evasions it encouraged.
814-hunting-sketches:
Anthony Trollope wrote these sketches of the hunting field, sorting riders into types with a novelist's eye. The man who hunts and does not like it, the man who does, and the lady who rides to hounds each get a portrait. The hunting farmer, the hunting parson, and the master of hounds follow, with advice on how to ride to hounds.

Trollope, a keen rider himself, writes with humour and knowledge of horses, country, and social rank. He praises the sport while poking fun at its vanities and its dangers. The sketches delight readers who love the English countryside, even those who never rode, for their sharp human comedy.
8141-mr-hawkins-humorous-adventures:
Edgar Franklin published Mr Hawkins' Humorous Adventures in 1904, narrated by a man who decides to build a quiet summer home in the Berkshires. Only to find that the next villa belongs to Hawkins. Hawkins, the narrator explains, is part inventor and part idiot, with money that mitigates idiocy but also gives free rein to his inventive genius, which is a bad thing. The narrator wishes his country seat were in central Illinois or western Oregon instead.

The stories follow Hawkins's inventions and mishaps, and his neighbour's exasperated attempts to live beside them. Franklin writes light, farcical comedy in the American humour tradition. For readers who enjoy tales of inventors and long-suffering neighbours, the book is a brisk, funny period piece.
8164-my-man-jeeves:
P. G. Wodehouse published My Man Jeeves in 1919, collecting stories of Bertie Wooster and his extraordinary valet. The contents include Leave It to Jeeves, Jeeves and the Unbidden Guest, Jeeves and the Hard-Boiled Egg, Absent Treatment. Helping Freddie, Rallying Round Old George, Doing Clarence a Bit of Good, and The Aunt and the Sluggard. Bertie opens by declaring that Jeeves is really a most extraordinary chap, so capable that Bertie would not know what to do without him.

The stories establish the perfect comic partnership: Bertie's scrapes and Jeeves's solutions, delivered with deadpan brilliance. Wodehouse compares Jeeves to the all-knowing clerks at Pennsylvania Station's inquiry desk, always right about trains and everything else. For comedy lovers, this is the essential first Jeeves book, and the start of a legendary partnership.
8176-death-at-the-excelsior-and-other-st:
P. G. Wodehouse's early stories, assembled for Project Gutenberg with original publication dates, open with Death at the Excelsior from 1914. Its first scene is a typical boarding-house bedroom, furnished with severe simplicity: two beds, a pine chest of drawers. Faded carpet, and a wash basin, with something on the floor that sets the room apart. The collection adds Misunderstood, The Best Sauce, Jeeves and the Chump Cyril, Jeeves in the Springtime, Concealed Art, and The Test Case.

The stories show Wodehouse before his full fame, already comic, already precise, with Jeeves beginning to take shape. They mix farce, misunderstanding, and the English world of clubs and country houses. For Wodehouse fans, the volume is a delightful early harvest, and a chance to watch a master finding his voice.
8178-the-politeness-of-princes-and-other:
P. G. Wodehouse's school stories, assembled for Project Gutenberg with dates from 1905 to 1910, open with The Politeness of Princes and the painful case of G. Montgomery Chapple, bachelor, of Seymour's house at Wrykyn. The collection adds Shields and the Cricket Cup, An International Affair, The Guardian, A Corner in Lines, The Autograph Hunters, and Pillingshot, Detective. The narrator reflects that this is the age of the specialist, even at school.

These tales of cricket, houses, masters, and boys' honour show Wodehouse's school world before Jeeves took over his imagination. They are light, funny, and affectionate, with the slang and loyalties of Edwardian school life. For Wodehouse collectors, they preserve the author's beginnings, and for young readers, they remain entertaining school stories.
8190-a-wodehouse-miscellany-articles-sto:
P. G. Wodehouse's miscellany, assembled for Project Gutenberg, gathers early articles, poems, and stories with their original dates. The articles include Some Aspects of Game-Captaincy, The New Advertising, In Defense of Astigmatism, Photographers and Me. A Plea for Indoor Golf, The Alarming Spread of Poetry, and The Agonies of Writing a Musical Comedy. Poems and stories follow, including When Papa Swore in Hindustani from 1901 and Tom, Dick, and Harry from 1905.

The collection shows Wodehouse as journalist, humorist, and lyricist before his novels made him famous. His lightness of touch is already present, whether on cricket, golf, or the theatre. For fans, it is a treasure of early Wodehouse, and for new readers, a funny introduction to a writer who made comedy look effortless.
8234-the-world-english-bible-web-judges:
Judges, in the World English Bible, tells Israel's turbulent years between Joshua and the kings, in modern English lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward. After Joshua's death, Israel asks who shall go up first against the Canaanites, and Yahweh answers Judah, who with Simeon strikes ten thousand men at Bezek and captures Adoni-Bezek. The cycle that follows repeats through the book: apostasy, oppression, a cry for help, and a judge raised to deliver.

Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson lead in turn, each flawed and each used for deliverance. The modern rendering keeps the stories' rough energy while easing their older language. For readers new to the Old Testament histories, Judges in this version reads as a dark, gripping chronicle of freedom without a king.
8240-the-world-english-bible-web-1-chron:
First Chronicles, in the World English Bible, begins with the genealogy Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The lists continue through Japheth's and Ham's sons, to Cush, father of Nimrod, mighty on the earth, and Mizraim's sons. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book then turns to David, his wars, and his preparations for the temple.

The modern version presents the chronicler's family record in readable prose, so the names carry their claim: Israel belongs to a story from creation onward. For readers daunted by genealogies, this rendering helps, since its plain sentences keep the lines clear. First Chronicles here serves as both reference and narrative, leading to David's reign.
8241-the-world-english-bible-web-2-chron:
Solomon, son of David, stands at the center of 2 Chronicles, a history book of ancient Israel told in plain modern English. It opens with Solomon asking God for wisdom, then follows the building of the temple in Jerusalem and the reigns of the kings of Judah who came after him. Kings rise and fall in turn, and the fate of the nation hangs on whether each ruler stays faithful.

Readers meet temple worship, royal courts, wars with nearby peoples, and prophets who warn kings to turn back. The book ends in ruin, with Jerusalem taken and its people carried off, yet closes on a note of return under a Persian king. For readers of the Hebrew Bible, it is the companion history to the books of Kings, retold from Judah's side.
8248-the-world-english-bible-web-ecclesi:
Ecclesiastes, in the World English Bible, opens with the words of the Preacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem: vanity of vanities, all is vanity. What does man gain from all his labour under the sun? One generation goes and another comes, but the earth remains forever; the sun rises and sets. The wind turns continually, and all rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book tests every human project.

The modern prose keeps the Preacher's rolling, questioning rhythm, and his counsel to enjoy simple gifts stands out clearly. Readers who find the older version's vanity puzzling may find this version's plain words easier to weigh. Ecclesiastes here remains Scripture's honest book about limits, work, and the search for meaning.
8299-filipino-popular-tales:
Dean S. Fansler collected these Filipino folk tales between 1908 and 1914 and published them in 1921, with notes comparing each story to tales from other lands. The Philippines, he argues in his preface, sits where East meets West: close to China and Japan, linked to Malay and Indian cultures, and shaped by three centuries of Spanish rule. That mix shows in the stories themselves.

Readers meet clever animals, tricksters, ogres, spirits, and heroes who win by wit as often as by strength. Fansler printed the tales in the English in which they were gathered, and added comparative notes for students of folklore. The volume still serves both as fireside reading and as evidence of how stories travel across seas and empires.
831-four-arthurian-romances:
Chrétien de Troyes, court poet of twelfth-century France, wrote these four romances in Old French: Erec et Enide, Cligés, Yvain, and Lancelot. They tell of knights of Arthur's court who quest for love and honour, facing giants, lions, and enchanted castles. The tales set the pattern for Arthurian romance in Europe.

Each romance turns on a test of heart: Erec must prove his love, Yvain learns mercy from a lion, and Lancelot risks shame for Guinevere. Chrétien blends adventure with courtesy, wit, and moral thought. The volume is a cornerstone of medieval literature, and the source from which later Grail and Round Table tales flow.
834-the-memoirs-of-sherlock-holmes:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathered twelve Sherlock Holmes tales in this volume, from Silver Blaze to The Final Problem. Holmes and Watson tackle a missing racehorse, a cardboard box with a grim secret, a stockbroker's clerk, and the Musgrave Ritual, among other puzzles. The Greek Interpreter and the Naval Treaty test Holmes's art to the full.

The set ends with The Final Problem, in which Holmes meets Professor Moriarty at the Reichenbach Falls. Doyle writes with brisk logic and vivid London detail, and Watson's voice keeps the tales warm. The book is a core Holmes collection, and the one in which the great detective first seemed to die.
8378-selected-polish-tales:
Else C. M. Benecke and Marie Busch translated this selection of Polish tales for the World's Classics series, first published in 1921. The contents run from Boleslaw Prus's Outpost, about a peasant's stubborn stand, through Adam Szymanski's Siberian sketches. They end with stories by Stefan Zeromski and others writing under partition, when Poland itself had vanished from the map.

Peasants, exiles, soldiers, and small-town folk carry the tales, and the translators' notes place each author for English readers. The volume offers a doorway into a literature long overshadowed in English by French and Russian neighbors. Readers meet a nation telling its own story while its state did not exist.
8399-manners-and-social-usages:
Mrs. John Sherwood wrote this etiquette manual, in a new and enlarged edition revised by the author, for Americans unsure of fashionable society. It covers the modern dinner table, calls, invitations, balls, morning and evening parties, visiting, and street etiquette, with the epigraphs of Whately and Emerson framing manners as funded politeness.

The book likely grew from newspaper and magazine columns, and it reads as advice from a woman who knew New York society from inside. Rules for who calls first, how to write invitations, and what to wear mattered to a rising middle class eager not to blunder. For readers today, it is a guide to Gilded Age manners, and to the anxieties beneath them.
8400-selections-from-erasmus-principally:
P. S. Allen selected these writings of Erasmus, principally from his epistles, to show the great humanist in his own voice. Allen's preface notes that Latin was a living language to Erasmus, and his letters move easily from everyday events to serious argument. A straightforwardness that made him the most famous scholar of his age.

Readers meet Erasmus writing to friends, patrons, and fellow scholars across Europe, on books, religion, and the follies of his time. The selections suit readers who want the Renaissance humanist without tackling his whole correspondence. Allen's choice gives a portrait in letters: witty, learned, and often impatient with both monks and reformers.
8415-the-magician-s-show-box-and-other-s:
Lydia Maria Child, author of Rainbows for Children, gathers children's stories in this volume, headed by The Magician's Show Box. Contents include The Violet Flame, Floribel, The Lady Intelletta, Venus's Dove, The Gala-Day, and Earning One's Own Living. The title tale opens with Gaspar, a boy whose uncle voyages to China and brings home chessmen, queer toys, and porcelain.

Child, a famous reformer and children's writer, writes tales that teach while they entertain, with wonder and morals side by side. Readers of classic children's literature get a gentle, old-fashioned collection, where magic boxes and faraway gifts open into lessons. The book suits reading aloud, as Child intended.
848-the-black-arrow-a-tale-of-the-two-ro:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this tale of the Wars of the Roses, centred on young Richard Shelton. Richard serves Sir Daniel Brackley, a lord of doubtful honour, and he falls foul of the Black Arrow, a band of outlaws who shoot black shafts at their foes. Joanna Sedley, a maiden in peril, crosses his path.

Stevenson moves the tale from castle to forest to battle, with disguise, ambush, and a slow unravelling of treachery. Richard must learn whom to trust as the red rose and the white rose tear England apart. The novel is a brisk, stirring romance for young readers, and a fine example of Stevenson's gift for adventure.
8503-among-my-books-first-series:
James Russell Lowell gathers literary essays in Among My Books, First Series, opening with a poem to F. D. L. Contents include Dryden, Witchcraft, Shakespeare Once More, New England Two Centuries Ago, Lessing, and Rousseau, among others, each essay mixing criticism with history and personal judgment.

Lowell, poet, critic, and later diplomat, was America's leading man of letters. These essays show his range: a poet on Dryden and Shakespeare, a New Englander on witchcraft and his own region's past, and a reader of Lessing and Rousseau. Readers get Victorian American criticism at its best, learned, witty, and opinionated.
8506-in-exile-and-other-stories:
Mary Hallock Foote gathers stories of the West in In Exile and Other Stories. Contents including In Exile, Friend Barton's Concern, The Story of the Alcázar, A Cloud on the Mountain, The Rapture of Hetty, and The Watchman. In Exile opens with Nicky Dyer and a schoolmistress on a hill slope above an arid Californian valley, crossed by narrow footpaths.

Foote, an illustrator and writer who lived in western mining country, writes of exile as a condition: easterners, miners, and women making lives far from home. Her stories mix romance with close observation of California landscapes. Readers of western literature get a woman's view of the mining West, literary and unsentimental.
8509-among-my-books-second-series:
James Russell Lowell gathers a second series of Among My Books, dedicated to R. W. Emerson, with a note that a love and honor of more than thirty years have deepened. Lowell tells Emerson that such feelings, though priceless to him, are of little import to one capable of inspiring them, yet he cannot deny himself the pleasure of public acknowledgment.

The essays continue Lowell's project of criticism as conversation: poets and prose writers judged by a fellow writer who knew many of them. Readers get American literary criticism in its classic phase, learned and personal. The dedication to Emerson marks the book's place: a New England man of letters honoring his master.
8538-a-touch-of-sun-and-other-stories:
Mary Hallock Foote gathers stories in A Touch of Sun and Other Stories, with contents including A Touch of Sun, The Maid's Progress, Pilgrims to Mecca, and The Harshaw Bride. The title story opens with the five o'clock whistle droning through heat, belonging to the oldest and best paying member of the Asgard group, a famous mining property of northern California.

Foote writes of mining country and its people with an illustrator's eye, and her stories follow women and men making lives in a hard, bright landscape. Readers of western fiction get a literary voice, less famous than Wister or Harte, but closer to daily life in the mines. The collection rewards readers who like place as character.
8542-things-mother-used-to-make-a-collec:
Lydia Maria Gurney collected Things Mother Used to Make, old-time recipes, some nearly one hundred years old and never published before, in New York in 1914. Her foreword notes that good food depends as largely on the cook's judgment as on materials. Her recipes and household hints are written very plainly, for those who have not cooked before.

Gurney's book preserves a century of home cooking, from a time before packaged foods, with recipes handed down in families. Readers get both a usable cookbook and social history: what American mothers cooked, and how. The plain directions suit modern cooks who like old-fashioned food, and readers tracing culinary history.
8567-the-iroquois-book-of-rites:
Horatio Hale edited this record of the Iroquois condolence council, the ceremony used when a chief died and a successor took his place. The book prints the ritual speeches and chants kept by the Iroquois themselves, with Hale's notes on their meaning and history. Its preface claims the tradition reaches back before Columbus landed, linking the Iroquois to still older peoples of the region.

Readers find the formal words spoken at mourning and raising up a chief, set beside explanations of the League's founding and its laws. The volume matters because it preserves Native words and ceremony in Native order, rather than retelling them secondhand. It remains a first source for the political and spiritual life of the Haudenosaunee, as well as a landmark in early American Indian scholarship.
8570-the-philistines:
Arlo Bates sets this novel among people weighing marriage, taste, money, and social standing, with chapter titles that move from account books to love and reputation. The story follows its characters through drawing rooms and arguments about art and conduct, where a wrong step in manners can cost as much as a wrong step in morals. Bates writes with a novelist's ear for how clever people talk past one another.

Beneath the social comedy runs a harder question: whether people who live by convention can tell real feeling from mere performance. The title points at the Philistines, those who judge art and life by fashion rather than by thought. Readers who enjoy novels of manners will find a sharp, talk-driven portrait of a society guarding its gates, and of the few who push against them.
8571-wolfert-s-roost-and-miscellanies:
Washington Irving gathers pieces in Wolfert's Roost and Miscellanies. It opens with the Chronicle of Wolfert's Roost, then Sleepy Hollow, Birds of Spring, and Recollections of the Alhambra. Abencerrage, Enchanted Island, and Adelantado of the Seven Cities follow, with National Nomenclature, Desultory Thoughts on Criticism, Spanish Romance, and the Legend of Don Muio, among others.

Irving, America's first man of letters, writes here as essayist and storyteller, mixing Hudson Valley legend with Spanish romance and literary talk. Readers get Irving in miscellany: the Roost itself, his home, and the tales and thoughts gathered around it. The volume suits anyone who loves Irving's voice, genial, learned, and fond of old stories.
863-the-mysterious-affair-at-styles:
Agatha Christie wrote her first detective novel about the mysterious affair at Styles Court, where Emily Inglethorp dies of poison in the night. Hastings, a young officer on leave, narrates, and his old friend Hercule Poirot, a Belgian refugee, takes up the case. Strychnine, a disputed will, and a household of suspects follow.

Poirot's method, order, method, and his little grey cells, is on full show as he sorts lies from facts. Christie plants clues with a fair hand, and the solution turns on a point of pharmacy. The book launched both Poirot and Christie, and it remains the classic debut of the queen of crime.
8649-indian-tales:
Rudyard Kipling gathers here the stories of his Indian years. From The Finest Story in the World and Wee Willie Winkie to The Man Who Would Be King and The Strange Ride of Morrowbie Jukes. Soldiers, officers, engineers, and civilians move through cantonments, barracks, and bazaars, with tales of ghosts, floods, courts-martial, and the drums of the fore and aft. Dinah Shadd, Muhammad Din, and Mulvaney return as familiar company.

The collection shows Kipling's early mastery of the short story: tight plots, soldier slang, and an India seen from inside the British ranks. Its view of empire and of Indian people reflects its time and needs reading with that in mind. Still, few books capture barrack-room India so vividly, and the best stories here, especially the title's famous king-makers, remain among Kipling's most anthologized work.
8652-crowded-out-and-other-sketches:
Seranus, a Canadian writer, offers these sketches of colonial life with proper fear and humility, hoping Canadian readers will recognize the scenes. Some are true, the preface admits, and others are shaped by fancy, which finds and heightens what fact leaves plain. Titles promise variety: Monsieur, Madame, and a pea-green parrot; the Bishop of Saskabasquia; a Christmas sketch; an island idyll. The story of Delle Josephine Boulanger; and how the Mr Foxleys came, stayed, and never went away.

French-Canadian settlers, priests, prisoners, and island folk populate the pages, with humour and sympathy for a young country's mixed society. The sketches are short, vivid, and unpretentious, closer to magazine pieces than to a plotted novel. They give modern readers a lively, ground-level view of Canada in the making, told by a writer who knew its parlours, parishes, and backwoods firsthand.
8663-tales-of-two-countries:
Alexander Kielland, the Norwegian writer from Stavanger, offers ten stories in William Archer's English translation, introduced by H. H. Boyesen. The tales range from a parsonage and a peat moor to a fair, two friends, a good conscience, and the Battle of Waterloo. Boyesen's introduction recalls Kielland as a young graduate of 1867, already poised and sure of himself, who went on to become one of Norway's leading realists.

Kielland's eye is ironic and unsparing: respectable people are shown protecting their comfort, while poorer folk pay the price. Romance and reality, withered leaves, and hope clad in April green all test how far fine words stretch. Readers new to Scandinavian fiction get a compact, readable entry point, and a writer whose satire of church, school, and small-town power still bites.
867-mrs-korner-sins-her-mercies:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this comic story about Mrs. Korner, who declares she likes a man to be a man. Her bosom friend points out that she would hardly like her own husband, Christopher Korner, to be that sort of man very often. Mrs. Korner admits she would like to feel he could be, even if he rarely is.

Jerome spins the paradox into a light comedy of marriage, where ideals and daily life pull in opposite ways. His dialogue is brisk, and his sympathy lies with both husband and wife. The story charms readers who enjoy Jerome's domestic humour, in which a small remark opens a whole view of married life.
8675-welsh-fairy-tales-and-other-stories:
P. H. Emerson collected these Welsh fairy tales while living in Anglesey during the winter of 1891-2, taking most of them down as they were told to him. He says he did little editing, preferring to give the stories as told, and his notes explain particulars about each narrative. One French story stands apart from the Welsh material, and an old book bought from a country bookseller, later identified as Williams's Observations on the Snowdon Mountains of 1802, supplied further background.

The tales carry the flavour of Welsh hearth storytelling: fairies, giants, clever poor folk, and the mountains themselves as a presence. Emerson's light hand keeps the tellers' voices close. Folklore readers will value a collection made in the field before such tales were smoothed into children's books, and anyone curious about Wales will enjoy stories rooted in Anglesey's villages and hills.
8682-the-naturalist-on-the-thames:
C. J. Cornish, a fellow of the Zoological Society, writes about the Thames as a living river, from Sinodun Hill down through Wittenham Wood. Chapters cover river shells, ancient river plants, insects, chub, butterflies at rest, crayfish and trout, fountains and springs, and bird migration down the valley. Sport, fox hunting, eel traps, osiers, watercress, and foggy dew ponds all find a place.

Cornish mixes close observation with local history, noting a February fox hunt, the relic at Ewelme, and the gains from wild-bird protection. His Thames is worked and fished, not merely picturesque. Readers interested in English natural history will enjoy a book that teaches the river's creatures in their seasons, and reminds us how much wildlife lived, and still lives, within reach of London.
8695-the-poetical-works-of-beattie-blair:
George Gilfillan edits the poetical works of James Beattie, Robert Blair, and William Falconer, with lives, critical essays, and explanatory notes. Beattie's section opens with his life and poetry, then The Minstrel, or the Progress of Genius. Followed by odes to hope and peace, an ode on Lord Hay's birthday, The Judgment of Paris, and The Triumph of Melancholy. Elegies, Retirement, The Hermit, fables of hares, wolves, and shepherds, and a battle of pigmies and cranes show his range.

Blair's Grave and Falconer's Shipwreck, the other poets' famous works, anchor their sections, with Gilfillan's Victorian criticism framing all three. The volume preserves eighteenth-century Scottish poetry in a form students once used. Modern readers gain three distinct voices: Beattie's gentle moralizing, Blair's meditation on death, and Falconer's sea narrative, all in one handy, annotated book.
871-the-golden-sayings-of-epictetus-with:
Hastings Crossley translated and arranged these golden sayings of Epictetus, the Stoic philosopher who taught that men should master what lies within their power and accept what does not. The sayings run in short, numbered passages, each a rule for life: on freedom, on desire, on anger, and on death.

Crossley adds the Hymn of Cleanthes, an early Stoic prayer to Zeus, praising the order of the world. The volume is brief, plain, and practical, meant to be read a little at a time. It remains a fine doorway into Stoic thought, for readers who want wisdom in short, memorable lines rather than in long treatises.
8715-gallantry-dizain-des-fetes-galantes:
James Branch Cabell gathers ten gallant tales in this volume, subtitled Dizain des Fetes Galantes, with an introduction by Louis Untermeyer. Untermeyer's image sets the tone: persons half in masquerade, playing the drawing-room or garden comedy of life, bathed in a light no real scene quite holds. Cabell dedicates the book to James Robinson Branch, praised as an exponent of gallantry's highest meaning in life and death.

The stories move through courts, gardens, and love affairs, where wit, honour, and desire play elegant games with serious stakes. Cabell's prose is ornate and ironic, treating romance as both artifice and truth. Readers who enjoy literary fantasy and the comedy of manners will find a distinctive, mannered voice. Those new to Cabell get a compact showcase of the Virginian fantasist at his most polished.
872-reprinted-pieces:
Charles Dickens gathered these sketches and short pieces, reprinted from Household Words and other journals. The Long Voyage, The Begging-Letter Writer, A Child's Dream of a Star, and portraits of English and French watering-places head the set. Bill-sticking, Lying Awake, and The Ghost of Art follow.

Dickens writes as Boz the observer, quick to catch a street scene, a lodging-house keeper, or a night thought. The pieces are slight beside his novels, but they show his eye and ear at their sharpest. The volume is a pleasant miscellany for Dickens lovers, full of London and of the age's small human comedy.
8720-tales-and-novels-volume-02-popular-:
Maria Edgeworth's second volume of Tales and Novels, dated 1857, gathers her Popular Tales, with a preface that defends the need for one. A good book needs no apology, some author says, Edgeworth notes, but a preface is like a bill of fare for readers who are epicures rather than gluttons in literature. She offers it to monthly critics too, as a fair statement of what she claims and how she treats it.

The tales themselves teach through story rather than sermon, following ordinary people through choices about money, work, pride, and kindness. Edgeworth, an Anglo-Irish writer famed for moral fiction, writes clearly and practically, with a sharp eye for class and character. Readers interested in the early novel will find here the didactic tale at its most readable, and a writer who believed fiction should improve its readers while entertaining them.
8727-the-last-galley-impressions-and-tal:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathers historical impressions and tales in The Last Galley, in two parts. Part one opens with the title story, set on a spring morning one hundred and forty-six years before Christ. On the North African coast with its golden sand and green belt of palm trees. Continues with the contest through the veil, an iconoclast, Giant Maximin, the coming of the Huns. The last of the legions, the first cargo, the home-coming, and the red star.

Part two turns to later and stranger matter: the silver mirror, the blighting of Sharkey. The marriage of the brigadier, the lord of Falconbridge, out of the running, De Profundis, the great Brown-Pericord motor. The terror of Blue John Gap. Doyle's range, from ancient Rome to modern mystery, shows a storyteller at ease in any century.
8778-the-water-of-the-wondrous-isles:
William Morris published The Water of the Wondrous Isles in 1897 with Longmans, Green, and Company, a late prose romance in his rich, archaic manner. The first part, Of the House of Captivity, opens with a catch at Utterhay, a house by the waterside, skin-changing, and the waxing of a stolen child. Birdalone grows into maidenhood, learns her raiment, adventures in the wood, meets the witch-wife, swims, hears new tidings, and bears guilt and chastisement.

Birdalone's escape by water carries her to wondrous isles, strange peoples, and a long quest for freedom and love. Morris's invented medieval diction slows some readers, but it creates a dreamlike world unlike any other fantasy of its time. The romance influenced later writers of quest fantasy, and it remains the fullest example of Morris's prose art, best read patiently, chapter by chapter, as a tale told by firelight.
878-yankee-gypsies:
John Greenleaf Whittier wrote this sketch of Yankee gypsies, the wandering folk who travelled New England with packs and budgets. He confesses himself keenly sensitive to skyey influences, and no stranger to the whims of the clerk of the weather, as he watches the wandering train pass through town and field.

Whittier writes with a poet's eye for roadside life, mixing observation with reflection on freedom and rootlessness. The sketch is brief and lyrical, a piece of local colour from old New England. It charms readers who enjoy Whittier's gentler prose, where a passing band becomes a prompt for thought.
8826-tales-and-novels-volume-01-moral-ta:
Maria Edgeworth opens her Tales and Novels with Moral Tales, and a preface that owns the difficulty of her task. Johnson said merely inventing a story is no small effort, Edgeworth notes. How much harder to build stories for youth that fit modern society's complicated relations, display virtue without initiating young readers into vice. Speak in a style level to their capacity, without tedious detail or vulgar idiom. She asks indulgence for errors that escaped her vigilance.

The tales that follow practise what the preface promises: short, clear stories in which honesty, industry, and kindness are tested in ordinary life. Edgeworth, writing for a former work's aim of innocent amusement and early instruction, became the leading moral tale writer of her generation. Readers interested in children's literature and the early novel will find the form at its most accomplished, and still readable for its wit and sense.
8847-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
James, bondservant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, addresses the twelve tribes scattered over the world with all good wishes, in Weymouth's plain version. Count it nothing but joy, he tells them, whenever trials hedge them in. Testing of faith leads to power of endurance, and endurance, given perfect results, makes a person complete, deficient in nothing. Anyone lacking wisdom should ask God, who gives with open hand and without reproach.

The letter that follows is the New Testament's most practical: control of the tongue. Care for orphans and widows, warning to the rich, patience for farmers awaiting rain, and prayer for the sick. Weymouth's modern speech suits James's proverb-like directness. Readers who want faith shown in action, rather than argued in theology, will find this short letter bracing. Its famous call to be doers, not hearers only, still sharp.
8871-a-desperate-character-and-other-sto:
Ivan Turgenev's A Desperate Character and Other Stories, translated by Constance Garnett in 1899, forms volume fourteen of his complete novels in fifteen volumes. The series runs from Rudin, A House of Gentlefolk, On the Eve, Fathers and Children. Smoke, through Virgin Soil and A Sportsman's Sketches, to Dream Tales, Torrents of Spring, A Lear of the Steppes, Diary of a Superfluous Man, and The Jew. Garnett dedicates the volume to Joseph Conrad, whose art, she says, often recalls Turgenev's in essence.

The stories include A Strange Story of 1869, Punin and Baburin. The title tale of desperate character, all showing Turgenev's mature art: restrained narration, vivid minor figures, and endings that refuse easy comfort. Readers who know the great novels will find the same humanity in shorter form. The collection is a fine entry to Turgenev's short fiction, and to Garnett's translations that first brought him fully to English readers.
888-the-lazy-tour-of-two-idle-apprentice:
Charles Dickens, with Wilkie Collins, wrote this tale of two idle apprentices on a lazy tour of the north of England. The pair drift from town to town, shirking work, meeting odd folk, and falling into scrapes that test their friendship and their wits. Illustrations by Harry Furniss add to the fun.
