Men have long argued the date of that church. Traces of Romanesque work survive in its walls. In the main it is Gothic, from the first half of the 1200s. Slender turrets mass round its western towers. An eight-sided central tower forms a lantern within. Rose windows with stained glass of the 1300s light the nave and choir. Two more churches earn a note. Saint Pierre mixes Renaissance work with Gothic, and Saint Nicolas dates from the 1500s and 1600s.
britannica-1911-couthon-georges:
Georges Couthon (1755–1794) was a French revolutionary born at Orcet, a village near Clermont in Auvergne. He studied law and became an advocate at Clermont in 1785. In that period men noted his honesty, kind heart and charity. His health was frail, and both his legs were paralysed. In 1787 he sat in the provincial assembly of Auvergne.

At the outbreak of the Revolution he served on the town council of Clermont-Ferrand. A pamphlet, L'Aristocrate converti, showed him as a liberal and a friend of constitutional monarchy. Fame came fast. In 1791 he led the town tribunal and entered the Legislative Assembly. The king's flight to Varennes soured his views in the meantime. Hostility to the crown marked him from then on. A health trip to Flanders drew him close to Dumouriez. In September 1792 he won a seat in the Convention.
britannica-1911-coverdale-miles:
Miles Coverdale (about 1488–1569) was an English translator of the Bible and bishop of Exeter. He was born of Yorkshire parents and studied philosophy and theology at Cambridge. In 1514 he was ordained priest at Norwich. He then entered the convent of Austin friars at Cambridge. There the prior, Robert Barnes, swayed his thought for good.

At Cambridge he met Sir Thomas More and Thomas Cromwell. Deep study of the Scriptures began in those years. He joined the men who met at the White Horse tavern to debate points of faith. When Barnes faced a heresy charge, Coverdale went to London to help frame his defence. Soon after, he left the convent and preached against confession and the worship of images. From 1528 to 1534 he spent most of his time abroad, with care. In 1534 a first book from his hand came into print. The entry then traces his Bible work.
britannica-1911-cowes:
Cowes is a seaport and watering-place in the Isle of Wight, 12 miles south-east of Southampton. West Cowes and East Cowes face each other across the mouth of the river Medina. West Cowes held 8,652 people in 1901 and East Cowes 3,196. The port between them is the chief port of the island. It is the headquarters of the Royal Yacht Squadron, founded in 1812.

Steamships link the towns to Southampton and Portsmouth on set runs. A steam ferry and a floating bridge cross the Medina, 600 yards broad at that point. Houses rise in fine order on gentle wooded slopes behind the harbour. Villas dot the lanes round about. Two forts of Henry VIII gave the towns their start. He built them in 1540, one on each side of the river mouth, to guard the coast. The east fort has gone. The west fort stands and serves as the yacht club's house.
britannica-1911-critius-and-nesiotes:
Critius and Nesiotes were two Greek sculptors of uncertain school who worked in the time of the Persian Wars. When Xerxes carried off to Persia the statues of Harmodius and Aristogiton made by Antenor, the pair were commissioned to replace them. Coins and reliefs have let scholars match their work. Two statues at Naples, long restored wrongly as gladiators, are known as copies of their tyrannicides.

Lucian praised the pair's figures as closely knit, sinewy, hard, and severe in outline. Those words, the entry says, fit the Naples copies well. Critius also made a statue of the armed runner Epicharinus. Replacing a stolen civic monument is the act that fixed both names in the record. Their school stays unknown, and no other works are listed for Nesiotes.
britannica-1911-croft-sir-james:
Sir James Croft, who died in 1590, was an English soldier and official from an old Herefordshire family. He sat for his county in parliament in 1541 and governed Haddington in 1549. In 1551 he became lord deputy of Ireland, where he gained a name for a conciliatory temper but achieved little. The entry calls him a double-dealer all his life. Mary jailed him in the Tower for treason, and Elizabeth freed and favoured him.

Croft governed Berwick, where John Knox visited him in 1559, and worked for the Scottish Protestants. Suspected of secret dealings with Mary of Guise, he spent ten years out of office. Elizabeth made him a privy councillor in 1570 and later sent him to treat for peace with the duke of Parma. Private dealings with Parma on that mission sent him to the Tower again. Freed before the end of 1589, he died on 4 September 1590.
britannica-1911-croll-james:
James Croll (1821–1890), a Scottish man of science, was born to a peasant family at Little Whitefield in Perthshire on 2 January 1821. Ill health barred him from manual work after a wheelwright's apprenticeship, and he turned to shop-keeping and insurance. Largely self-taught, he became keeper of the Andersonian Museum in Glasgow in 1859. That post led him into physical science, and he soon wrote for leading journals.

Croll's essay of 1864 on the physical cause of climate change in geological epochs won him a post on the Scottish Geological Survey. His book Climate and Time of 1875 argued that earth's revolutions owe much to cosmic causes, and it stirred warm controversy. Later works treated stellar evolution and the basis of evolution itself. The entry notes that his ice-age theory was later abandoned, yet calls his work under hardship heroic. He died on 15 December 1890.
britannica-1911-cujas-jacques:
Jacques Cujas (1520–1590) was a French jurisconsult born at Toulouse, the son of a fuller. He taught himself Latin and Greek, then studied law under Arnoul Ferrier. His lectures on Justinian won fame, and in 1554 he became professor of law at Cahors. Called to Bourges, he was driven out by a rival's stirring of the students. Valence took him in, and there his name spread across Europe.

Students such as Joseph Scaliger and de Thou gathered to Cujas at Valence. Posts, pensions, and offers from Charles IX, Henry III, and Pope Gregory XIII failed to move him for long. He ended his days at Bourges in 1590, refusing all part in the religious wars. His merit, the entry says, was to turn from weak commentators to Roman law itself. He collected over 500 manuscripts. His usual answer on the wars was that they had nothing to do with the praetor's edict.
britannica-1911-culdees:
The Culdees were an ancient monastic order with settlements in Ireland and Scotland. Older writers, above all Presbyterians, fondly pictured them as keepers of a pure early Christianity free of Rome. Hector Boece made them heirs of the Irish and Iona monks of earlier centuries. The entry states that Bishop William Reeves disproved both views. Their Irish name, Céle Dé, means God's comrade or sworn ally.

In the 800s Culdee communities appear at nine Irish places, Armagh and Clonmacnoise among them, as annexes to regular monasteries. They cared for the poor and the sick and took part in the music of worship. From Ireland they crossed to Scotland late in that century, filling gaps left at Iona. Their life there matched that of secular canons more than of cloistered monks. In Ireland the Culdees of Armagh lasted until the dissolution of 1541.
britannica-1911-damocles:
Damocles was one of the courtiers of the elder Dionysius of Syracuse. He spoke in outsized terms of the happiness of his master. Dionysius, the story says, answered with an invitation to a rich banquet. Damocles took his seat in state at the feast. Above him hung a naked sword, held by a single hair. The tale ends at that seat, with the sword over his head.

Cicero in the Tusculans, Horace in the Odes, and Persius all carry the story, and the entry cites those three sources. Nothing more is told of Damocles himself, his birth, rank, or later life. The whole entry is the one scene and its telling in three Roman authors. A courtier's flattery, a tyrant's lesson, and a sword on a hair make up the record. The name lives by that single image alone.
britannica-1911-danton-george-jacques:
George Jacques Danton (1759–1794) was a leading actor in the French Revolution, born at Arcis-sur-Aube on 26 October 1759. His family, of respectable rank and modest means, gave him a good schooling. He built a sound practice as an advocate at the Paris bar. When revolution came he led the Cordeliers club of his district, the centre of the popular cause pushed to its extreme. His robust, impetuous temper made him its natural chief.

Danton took no traced part in the great risings of 1789, the Bastille or the march on Versailles. In 1790 he defended Marat from arrest and took command of his district's national guard battalion. Posts in the government of Paris followed in 1791. Only in 1792, the entry stresses, did he rise to the height of a great revolutionary chief. The long life that follows traces that rise and his fall.
britannica-1911-de-loutherbourg-philip-j:
Philip James de Loutherbourg (1740–1812) was an English artist, born at Strassburg on 31 October 1740. His father, of a Polish family, painted miniatures there. The son spent most of his life in London and took British nationality. He shaped the scenery of the English stage and left a mark on the artists who came after him. He had been meant for the Lutheran ministry and was schooled at the university of Strassburg.

The call did not suit him, and he chose painting instead, studying under Vanloo in Paris. His skill grew fast, and he became known in high society. In 1767 he was elected to the French Academy below the age the rules required. He painted landscapes, sea storms, and battles, and his first show held twelve pictures, among them Storm at Sunset, Night, and Morning.
britannica-1911-demochares:
Demochares (about 355-275 B.C.), a nephew of Demosthenes, was an Athenian orator and statesman of the decline. He first appears in 322, speaking in vain against handing over Demosthenes and the other anti-Macedonian orators to Antipater. Banished in 303 for mocking a fulsome decree in honour of Demetrius Poliorcetes, he was recalled in 298 and spent four years fortifying Athens and stocking it with food and ammunition.

Fresh banishments and returns mark his later career, and in 280 he won a public monument for his uncle. His public services, recorded after his death, were cuts in spending, careful finance, and successful begging missions to Egypt and Macedonia. Cicero credits him with a history of his own times, written in an orator's rather than a historian's style.
britannica-1911-elmes-james:
Elmes, James (1782–1862), was a British architect, civil engineer, and writer on the arts, born in London on 15 October 1782. He was educated at Merchant Taylors' school and studied building under his father and architecture under George Gibson. As a student at the Royal Academy he gained the silver medal in 1804. He designed many buildings in London and served as surveyor to the port of London.

Elmes is best known as a writer on the arts. In 1809 he became vice-president of the Royal Architectural Society, but partial loss of sight forced him to resign that office and the port surveyorship in 1828. He died at Greenwich on 2 April 1862. His books include Sir Christopher Wren and his Times and Lectures on Architecture. He also wrote a General and Biographical Dictionary of the Fine Arts and a Treatise on Architectural Jurisprudence.
britannica-1911-empedocles:
Empedocles (about 490–430 B.C.) was a Greek philosopher and statesman born at Agrigentum in Sicily, of a noted family. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Empedocles article within it. Empedocles himself helped end an oligarchic rule at Agrigentum and was invited to become king, an honour he refused.

Of his poem on nature about 400 lines survive, in uneven fragments, out of an original 5000, and fewer than 100 verses of his hymns of purification remain. The entry shows him as at once statesman, prophet, physicist, physician, and reformer, a figure his age took for more than a mere man. Another has him leap into the crater of Etna, hoping to be thought a god, until the volcano cast up his brazen sandals and betrayed him.
britannica-1911-eperjes:
Eperjes is a town of Hungary, capital of the county of Sáros, 190 miles north-east of Budapest by rail, with a population of 13,098 in 1900. It stands on the left bank of the river Tarcza and was almost wholly rebuilt after a great fire in 1887. It is the seat of a Greek-Catholic bishop and holds a fine late Gothic cathedral of the 18th century.

The town makes cloth, table-linen, and earthenware, and trades in wine, linen, cattle, and grain. The entry also covers its county neighbours. Eperjes was founded about the mid 12th century by a German colony and made a royal free town in 1347. Its darkest fame is the “butchery of Eperjes” of 1687, when General Caraffa's tribunal condemned many citizens accused of Protestantism to death.
britannica-1911-epimenides:
Epimenides was a poet and prophet of Crete who lived in the 6th century B.C., though many fabulous stories are told of him and his very existence is doubted. While tending his father's sheep he is said to have fallen asleep in the Dictaean cave near Cnossus. From that sleep he did not wake for fifty-seven years, the story runs. When a pestilence struck Athens after the murder of Cylon, Solon called him in to purify the city.

The only reward Epimenides would take was a branch of the sacred olive and a promise of lasting friendship between Athens and Cnossus. He died in Crete at a great age; his countrymen, who later honoured him as a god, said he lived nearly three hundred years. The entry counts him, with Melampus and Onomacritus, among the founders of Orphism.
britannica-1911-eubulides:
Eubulides of Miletus was a Greek philosopher who succeeded Eucleides as head of the Megarian school. Nothing is known of the events of his life. Indirect signs make him a contemporary of Aristotle, whom he attacked with great bitterness. Tradition also counts Demosthenes among his pupils. His fame rests chiefly on a set of noted syllogisms tied to his name. The entry calls them false and captious, more verbal quibbling than logic.

Yet those puzzles still show real snags in language and in explaining sense impressions. Eubulides also wrote a treatise on Diogenes the Cynic. A number of comedies are credited to him as well. The entry is one of the briefest lives in this stretch of the volume. It points readers to the article on the Megarian school for the wider setting. No dates for his birth or death are offered.
britannica-1911-eucratides:
Eucratides was king of Bactria, about 175 to 129 B.C., who seized the throne by rebellion against the house of Euthydemus. Rival dynasts in Sogdiana, Aria and Drangiana challenged him, most known only from their coins. In the west Mithradates I of Parthia took two provinces from him. His great foe was Demetrius of India, who besieged him in a fortress with a huge army. Eucratides broke out and conquered much of western India.

Apollodorus credited him with rule over a thousand towns. His coins, struck with Greek and Indian legends, style him the great King Eucratides. They confirm his sway over Bactria, Sogdiana, Kabul and the western Punjab. He founded a Greek city, Eucratideia, in Bactria. Returning from India about 150 B.C., he was murdered by the son he had made co-regent. Under that son the kingdom lost its lands north of the Hindu Kush.
britannica-1911-explosives:
Explosives are substances which, under certain treatment, break down violently and generate force. They sort loosely into propellants and detonators, but the line will not hold sharp. The same substance may serve either role under changed conditions. A propellant burns fast and evenly, swelling a small volume into a large one of gas. Heat freed in the burning expands those gases further. A detonator wrecks a small area without throwing matter far.

Time, the article stresses, is the key factor in the difference. Plain burning can turn explosive when contact between fuel and oxygen supplier grows, as in gas and dust blasts. Heat alone does not make an explosion; aluminium and magnesium give great heat yet no blast without gas. True explosives are either mechanical mixtures or endothermic compounds. Endothermic bodies store energy taken in at their making, and release it as gas when they break down.
britannica-1911-fatimites:
Fatimites, or Fatimides, names a dynasty claiming descent from Fatima, daughter of the prophet Mahomet, and her husband the caliph Ali. It is also called Obaidi, after Obaidallah, its first sovereign, and Alawi, a title shared with other dynasties of the same claimed ancestry. Three rulers in north-western Africa came before the annexation of Egypt: al-Mahdi Obaidallah from 909, al-Qaim Mahommed from 934, and al-Mansur Ismail from 945.

The dynasty rose on widespread loyalty to the prophet's family, held by many to own the sovereignty by right. Its supporters backed the line of Ismail, son of Jafar al-Sadiq, though the claimed pedigree was later disputed at Bagdad. Rival accounts made the founder a heretic's scion or even a Jew. The long entry follows the caliphs' rule and closes by judging their practice close to orthodox Islam in most doctrine.
britannica-1911-fauriel-claude-charles:
Claude Charles Fauriel (1772-1844), French historian, philologist and critic, was born at St Etienne on 21 October 1772. Son of a poor joiner, he was well educated at Oratorian colleges. He served twice in the army, then in municipal office, and from 1797 to 1799 gave himself to hard study of Greek and Italian literature and history, ancient and modern. In Paris he became private secretary to Fouche, minister of police.

Fauriel resigned in 1802, in part because Napoleon, made consul for life, had broken strict republican principles. Articles on Madame de Stael's work on literature began a close friendship with her. Her circle and that of Madame de Condorcet shaped his life of love, friendship and learning. The entry follows his later scholarship and the posthumous papers, memoirs and correspondence by which his thought is known, including fragments on the close of the Consulate published in 1886.
britannica-1911-fearne-charles:
Charles Fearne (1742-1794), English jurist, was son of Charles Fearne, judge-advocate of the admiralty. He was born in London in 1742 and educated at Westminster school. He took up the law, and his talents fitted him to succeed as a barrister. Yet he neglected practice and spent his attention and inheritance on scientific experiments. He hoped for discoveries that would repay the cost. The hope failed, and he died in 1794 leaving his family in need.

Fearne's fame rests on one book, his Essay on the Learning of Contingent Remainders and Executory Devises. A decision of Lord Mansfield in Perrin v. Blake called it forth. The essay had the effect of reversing that decision. It passed through numerous editions as a legal authority. A volume of his posthumous works was published by subscription in 1797. That volume was issued for his widow's benefit.
britannica-1911-felix-popes:
Felix is the name borne by five popes, gathered here in one entry. Felix I held the see from January 269 until his death in January 274. Claimed as a martyr, he was probably confused with another bishop of the name. He appears in the Antioch dispute over Paul of Samosata. The emperor Aurelian gave the church building to the bishop recognized by Rome. Felix II, an antipope, was raised to the chair in 356 while Liberius was banished.

The entry follows each bearer of the name in turn. Felix III, from a powerful Roman family, died in 492. Felix IV, a native of Beneventum, is linked with the church of Saints Cosimo and Damiano. He died after a short reign. Felix V was the name taken by Amadeus, duke of Savoy, a rival pope. In the end he accepted a settlement, lands and a cardinal's rank.
britannica-1911-fleetwood-charles:
Charles Fleetwood, who died in 1692, was an English soldier and politician. He was third son of Sir Miles Fleetwood of Aldwinkle in Northamptonshire. Admitted to Gray's Inn in November 1638, he joined the earl of Essex's life-guard when the Great Rebellion began. He was wounded at the first battle of Newbury, gained a regiment in 1644 and fought at Naseby. By 1646 he sat in parliament for Marlborough.

In the quarrel between army and parliament Fleetwood played a chief part. He was said to be the main author of the plot to seize King Charles at Holmby, though he took no part in the king's trial. Made a governor of the Isle of Wight in 1649, he rode as lieutenant-general of horse in Cromwell's Scottish campaign and helped win Dunbar. Recalled to command the forces in England, he helped gain the final triumph at Worcester, as the entry follows his rise.
britannica-1911-foli-allan-james:
Allan James Foli (1837-1899), born Foley, was an Irish bass singer. He was born at Cahir in Tipperary on 7 August 1837. Trained first as a carpenter, he studied singing under Bisaccia at Naples. He made his first appearance at Catania in 1862. From opera in Paris he was engaged by Mapleson for the season of 1865. He appeared with much success in various parts, winning a wide public.

Foli sang Daland in the first performance of The Flying Dutchman in England in 1870. He also sang in the first performance of Gounod's Redemption in 1882. The entry praises his vigorous, straightforward singing. He was as distinguished in oratorio as in opera, and in great request at ballad concerts. He died on 20 October 1899.
britannica-1911-forbes:
Forbes is a municipal town of Ashburnham county, New South Wales, Australia. It stands 289 miles west by north from Sydney, on the Lachlan river, with a station on the Great Western railway. Its population in 1901 was 4,313. The town's weight as a trade centre comes from its position, handy between the northern and southern markets of the state. Steam-sawing and flour mills, breweries and wool-scouring works are its industries.

The country around Forbes yields good quantities of cereals, lucerne, wine and fruit. That is the whole of the short entry: a young Australian inland town fixed by its river, its railway and its place between two markets. Its mills, breweries and wool works, and the crops and vines of its district, stand as the signs of its Edwardian growth. No history or buildings are described in the hosted text beyond these plain facts.
britannica-1911-fourier-s-series:
Fourier's series, in mathematics, are series that proceed by sines and cosines of multiples of a variable. The multiples stand in the ratio of the natural numbers. Such series can stand for a function of the variable between set finite limits. Bernoulli, Lagrange and others had seen their value, above all in the theory of vibrations, and had debated their properties. Fourier was the first to grasp the arbitrary character of the functions the series can represent, and to try in earnest to prove the representation sound.

The long technical article follows that proof and its critics. It treats Dirichlet's conditions, the trouble at a point of discontinuity, and later work by Dircksen, Bessel and Lipschitz. Many later studies tried to free the function from Dirichlet's restrictions. No full set of needful and sufficient conditions had yet been won. It is a piece of higher analysis.
britannica-1911-fourmies:
Fourmies is a town of northern France, in the department of Nord. It stands on a tributary of the Sambre, 39 miles south-east of Valenciennes by rail. Its population in 1906 was 13,308. It is one of the chief centres in France for wool combing and spinning, and it produces a great variety of cloths. The glass-works of Fourmies date from 1599 and were the first set up in the north of France, giving the town an industrial past of three centuries.

Iron is worked nearby, and there are important forges and foundries, while enamel-ware is also made. In 1891 labour troubles at Fourmies brought military intervention and bloodshed, the dark event of the town's modern record. A board of trade arbitration and a school of commerce and industry stand among its public institutions. The short entry stands in a hosted file that opens with pages of the Fourier's Series article.
britannica-1911-fowler-charles:
Charles Fowler (1792-1867), English architect, was born at Cullompton in Devon on 17 May 1792. After five years of apprenticeship at Exeter he went to London in 1814 and joined the office of David Laing. He stayed there until he began practice for himself. His first important work was the court of bankruptcy in Basinghall Street, finished in 1821. The next year he won first premium for a design for the new London Bridge, though another man's design was built in the end.

Fowler designed a bridge across the Dart at Totnes and the markets of Covent Garden and Hungerford in London. He also built the new market at Gravesend, Exeter lower market, several churches, the Devon lunatic asylum of 1845, the London fever hospital of 1849 and the hall of the Wax Chandlers. The entry lists a practical career in iron, glass and stone, serving the markets, hospitals and asylums of the Victorian city.
britannica-1911-francis-i-of-the-two-sic:
Francis I (1777-1830), king of the Two Sicilies, was the son of Ferdinand IV and Maria Carolina of Austria. He married Clementina, daughter of the emperor Leopold II, in 1796, and after her death Isabella, daughter of Charles IV of Spain. When the Bourbons fled from Naples to Sicily in 1806, Francis was appointed regent in 1812. Lord William Bentinck had set up a constitution and stripped Ferdinand of power.

On Napoleon's fall his father returned to Naples, suppressed the Sicilian constitution, and joined his kingdoms into the Two Sicilies in 1816. Francis then took the revived title of duke of Calabria. As heir he professed liberal ideas. At the outbreak of the revolution of 1820 he accepted the regency in an apparently friendly spirit. But he was playing a double game, the entry says, and proved false to the constitution he had sworn to keep.
britannica-1911-francis-ii-of-the-two-si:
Francis II (1836-1894), king of the Two Sicilies, was the son of Ferdinand II and Maria Cristina of Savoy. He was the last of the Bourbon kings of Naples. His education had been much neglected, and he proved a man of weak character. His stepmother Maria Theresa of Austria, the priests and the Camarilla, the reactionary court set, influenced him greatly. He ascended the throne on his father's death, 22 May 1859, with Italy already alight after the Franco-Piedmontese victories in Lombardy.

Francis at once made Carlo Filangieri prime minister, who advised him to accept the Piedmont alliance Cavour proposed. On 7 June 1859 part of the Swiss Guard mutinied. While the king soothed them with promises, General Nunziante surrounded the mutineers with other troops and shot them down. The whole Swiss Guard, the dynasty's strongest bulwark, was then disbanded.
britannica-1911-fraser-james:
James Fraser (1818-1885), English bishop, was born at Prestbury in Gloucestershire on 18 August 1818. He read at Shrewsbury and Lincoln College, Oxford, won an Oriel fellowship, and took orders in 1846. Parish work in Wiltshire and Berkshire followed, but his name was made by reports on schooling for the government.

His 1859 report on the schools of thirteen poor-law unions won high praise, and in 1865 he reported on education in the United States and Canada. He declined the bishopric of Calcutta, then accepted Manchester in January 1870. There he worked with great energy across a fast-growing diocese and earned a title as the bishop of all denominations for his broad sympathy. He died suddenly on 22 October 1885.
britannica-1911-fremont-john-charles:
John Charles Frémont (1813-1890), American explorer, soldier, and political leader, was born in Savannah, Georgia, on 21 January 1813. After leaving the college of Charleston he taught mathematics in the navy, then joined the Topographical Engineers in 1838 and helped Nicollet map the country between the upper Mississippi and Missouri. In 1841 he married Jessie Benton, daughter of Senator Thomas H. Benton.

In 1842 he surveyed South Pass and climbed the Wind River peak that bears his name. His next expedition crossed to the Columbia and mapped the Great Salt Lake, the Great Basin, and the Sierra Nevada, and his 1844 report stirred American interest in California. A third expedition put him in California as war with Mexico broke out, and the tangled fight over command there ended in his arrest for disobedience. Later he served in the Civil War, was named for the presidency by a radical faction in 1864, and governed Arizona territory from 1878 to 1881.
britannica-1911-froben-joannes:
Joannes Froben, or Frobenius (about 1460-1527), German printer and scholar, was born at Hammelburg in Bavaria. After university study at Basel he set up a printing house there about 1491, and it soon won a European name for accuracy and taste. In 1500 he married the bookseller Wolfgang Lachner daughter and took him into partnership.

Froben was a close friend of Erasmus, who had his own works printed by him and oversaw his editions of Jerome, Cyprian, Tertullian, Hilary, and Ambrose. The Greek New Testament of 1516 from this press was the text Luther used for his translation. Hans Holbein illuminated Froben texts, and his planned editions of the Greek Fathers were carried out by his son and son-in-law after his death in October 1527. His work made Basel the leading centre of the German book trade in the 16th century.
britannica-1911-fulcher-of-chartres:
Fulcher of Chartres (1058-about 1130), French chronicler, was a priest present at the council of Clermont in 1095. He marched on the first crusade in 1096 with Robert II, duke of Normandy. He fought on the road to the Holy Land. He then became chaplain to Baldwin, chosen king of Jerusalem in 1100, and lived with him at Edessa and Jerusalem.

His fame rests on the Historia Hierosolymitana, in three books, running from the council of Clermont to 1127. The entry calls it one of the most trustworthy sources for the first crusade. Fulcher details only events he himself had seen, and William of Tyre used the work. It was first printed, incomplete, by Bongars in 1611. Fulcher died after 1127, probably at Jerusalem, and is not to be confused with two men of the same name.
britannica-1911-fulgentius-fabius-planci:
Fabius Planciades Fulgentius was a Latin grammarian of Africa who flourished in the first half of the 6th century AD, or perhaps the late 5th. He is not the bishop of Ruspe of the same name, though probably a kinsman. Four works pass under his name, and the entry walks through each in turn.

The Mythologiarum, in three books for a Carthage presbyter named Catus, tells 75 myths briefly and then explains them in the mystical manner of Stoics and Neoplatonists, leaning on far-fetched word origins. The Expositio Vergilianae continentiae brings Virgil himself on stage to read the Aeneid as a picture of human life. A third work explains 63 rare old words, with some quotations from authors who never existed. The fourth, on the ages of the world and of man, drops one letter of the alphabet wholly from each book in turn. His style is judged bombastic and hard.
britannica-1911-funeral-rites:
Funeral rites are the ceremonies practised for disposing of the dead. The entry sorts the ideas behind them under eight heads. First comes the belief that a corpse is polluting and taboo, as in Jewish law, which bars contact with the dead. Next come mourning customs and the belief that the dead live on and need housing, equipment, food and an orientation in the grave. Other heads cover feasts in communion with the dead, sacrifice and expiation, and death laid to witchcraft.

The last heads are protection against ghouls and fear of the ghosts of the dead. Examples range over many peoples. The Parsee towers of silence, night burial at Rome and in Greece, lustral water after funerals, and the Navaho destruction of the dead man's hut all appear. The Solomon Islands supply cases from Codrington's reports. The authorities cited include Frazer's Golden Bough of 1900 and Tylor's Primitive Culture.
britannica-1911-futures: Futures are bargains in the produce markets for goods to be delivered and paid for at a later date. They stand opposed to cash or spot bargains, which are settled on the spot. The word belongs to market practice, and the entry sends the reader to the articles on markets and on the marketing of cotton for the fuller discussion of dealing in futures.
britannica-1911-gabes:
Gabes is a town of Tunisia at the head of the gulf of the same name, 70 miles by sea south-west of Sfax. It stands on the site of Tacape and joins a port and European quarter to Arab towns set in an oasis of date palms. The oasis, watered by the Wad Gabes, holds about 20,000 people, 1500 of them Europeans, and exports dates. The native houses are built of dressed stones and broken columns taken from the ruins of Tacape.

Gabes is the military headquarters for southern Tunisia. It is also bound up with Commandant Roudaire's scheme to flood the Tunisian shats, salt lakes below sea level, by a channel from the Mediterranean. The company formed for the work turned to farming and made an oasis of olives and palms by sinking artesian wells. The gulf, the Syrtis Minor of the ancients, abounds in fish and sponge.
britannica-1911-gadsden-james:
Gadsden, James (1788–1858), an American soldier and diplomat, was born at Charleston on the 15th of May 1788, grandson of Christopher Gadsden. He graduated at Yale in 1806 and served as an army engineer in the war of 1812. As Jackson's aide he campaigned against the Seminoles in 1818, and in 1823 he superintended the removal of the Seminoles to south Florida. His treaty of 1832 provided for their removal west within three years, but the Seminoles refused to move and war followed.

In 1853 President Pierce made Gadsden minister to Mexico, and on the 30th of December he signed the treaty that bears his name. By it the United States gained 45,535 square miles in what is now New Mexico and Arizona, paid Mexico ten million dollars, and won free transit across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. Ratifications were exchanged on the 30th of June 1854. He died at Charleston on the 25th of December 1858.
britannica-1911-gaudichaud-beaupre-charl:
Charles Gaudichaud-Beaupre (1789-1854) was a French botanist, born at Angouleme on 4 September 1789. The 1911 Britannica entry has him trained in pharmacy, then serving as a dispenser in the military marine from 1810. In 1817 he sailed as botanist on the corvette Uranie, on Freycinet's voyage round the world.

The Uranie was wrecked on the Falkland Isles late in 1819, costing him over half his plant collections. He voyaged again to Chile, Peru and Brazil in 1830-1833, and sailed round the world once more on La Bonite in 1836-1837. His later years were spent in dispute over his theory of plant growth by joined units he called phytons, opposed above all by Mirbel. The entry lists his voyage accounts and papers on plant structure. He died at Paris on 16 January 1854.
britannica-1911-gibbons-james:
James Gibbons (1834– ) was an American Roman Catholic cardinal and archbishop. He was born in Baltimore, Maryland, on 23 July 1834. He was schooled at St Charles College in Ellicott City and at St Mary's Seminary in Baltimore. He finished his training for the priesthood there and was ordained on 30 June 1861. After a short time on the missions of Baltimore, he became secretary to Archbishop Martin Spalding. He also served as a helper at the cathedral.

In 1866 the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore took up the growth of new church districts. Gibbons was chosen to set up the new district of North Carolina, and he was made a bishop in August 1868. In his four good years there he wrote The Faith of Our Fathers. That book set out the faith of his church in brief, aimed in part at Protestants.
britannica-1911-gipsies:
Gipsies, in the 1911 Britannica, is a very long article on a wandering folk found in every European land, western Asia, Siberia, Egypt, America and Australia. It opens with numbers, warning that official figures often clash. Hungary's count of 1893, 274,940, is called the only correct one, most of them settled.

Country by country the entry totals the folk: Rumania at up to 250,000, Turkey in Europe at 117,000, Spain at 40,000, Russia at 58,000, and small bands in Germany and France. From distribution it passes to the questions of origin and language, with India and the Romani tongue at the centre of the argument. Later parts treat history, customs and the settled and nomad ways of life across the many lands named. It is among the fullest ethnographic articles in the volume.
britannica-1911-glaisher-james:
James Glaisher (1809-1903) was an English meteorologist and aeronaut, born in London on 7 April 1809. The 1911 Britannica entry puts him first on the Ordnance Survey of Ireland, then at the Cambridge and Greenwich observatories. At Greenwich he ran the new department of meteorology and magnetism for thirty-four years.

His dew-point tables of 1845 went through many editions, and he founded the Meteorological Society in 1850. But his fame rests on balloon ascents made between 1862 and 1866, mostly with Henry Tracey Coxwell. They were scientific flights, measuring temperature and humidity at great heights. At Wolverhampton on 5 September 1862 they reached the greatest height then attained by a passenger balloon, estimated at about seven miles, Glaisher losing consciousness at the top. He died at Croydon on 7 February 1903.
britannica-1911-glasites:
Glasites, or Sandemanians, were a Christian sect founded in Scotland by John Glas. The 1911 Britannica entry, signed by Dugald Macfadyen, says the sect spread into England and America but is now practically extinct. Glas differed from the Westminster Confession only on the church's spiritual nature and the magistrate's place.

His son-in-law Robert Sandeman added the mark of the sect: faith as a bare assent to testimony about Christ. Practice aimed at the primitive pattern. Each church had several elders of equal rank, decisions needed unanimity, and the Lord's Supper was kept weekly, with a love feast every Sunday. Members abstained from things strangled and from blood, held wealth suspect, and would not eat with the excommunicated. Churches stood from Paisley to London, where Michael Faraday was long an elder. The entry blames exclusiveness and the doctrine's antinomian lean for the sect's dissolution.
britannica-1911-grafly-charles:
Charles Grafly (1862– ) was an American sculptor, born at Philadelphia on 3 December 1862. He was a pupil at the schools of the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. He also studied in Paris under Henri Chapu and Jean Dampt, and at the École des Beaux Arts. In 1891 his work Mauvais Présage won an honour note at the Paris Salon. That piece is now at the Detroit Museum of Fine Arts.

Grafly won a gold medal at the Paris show of 1900 and medals at Chicago, Atlanta, and Philadelphia. In 1892 he became a teacher of sculpture at the Pennsylvania Academy. He held the same chair at the Drexel Institute in Philadelphia. In 1905 he was made a full member of the National Academy of Design. His known works include General Reynolds in Fairmount Park and the Fountain of Man, made for the Pan-American show at Buffalo.
britannica-1911-grant-james:
James Grant (1822-1887) was a British writer of tales, born in Edinburgh on 1 August 1822. His father was a captain in the Gordon Highlanders who had served in the Peninsular War. James spent some years in Newfoundland with his father. In 1839 he came back to England and joined the 62nd Foot as an ensign. He gave up his post in 1843 to write.

Grant wrote first for magazines, then poured out tales in a flood. Most deal with army scenes and army men, told with life and pace. The Romance of War, his first book of 1845, is among his best. Bothwell, Frank Hilton, and The White Cockade are also named with praise. He wrote on British battles by land and sea as well. His three-volume work on old and new Edinburgh holds lasting worth.
britannica-1911-grenadines:
The Grenadines are a chain of islets in the Windward Islands of the West Indies. The 1911 Britannica entry stretches them for 60 miles between St Vincent and Grenada, running north-east to south-west. Some 600 islets and rocks make the chain. A few are square miles in extent; others are bare rocky cones rising from deep water.

Administration is split between St Vincent and Grenada. Bequia, chief island of the St Vincent group, is long and narrow, short of water and slightly cultivated, but rich in game, with a safe harbour at Admiralty Bay. Carriacou, Grenada's largest, runs seven miles long and holds good building stone and two west-coast harbours. Its people work small lots on the metayer system. Oysters, cotton and cattle are the noted products. The group's population in 1901 was 6,497, mostly on Carriacou.
britannica-1911-grevin-jacques:
Jacques Grevin (c. 1539-1570) was a French dramatist, born at Clermont about 1539. The 1911 Britannica entry has him studying medicine at the university of Paris. He became a disciple of Ronsard, and one of the band who sought to bring classical drama to France. Sainte-Beuve, it notes, saw his comedies' kinship with the older farces and soties.

His first play, La Maubertine, is lost; from it grew La Tresoriere, performed at the college of Beauvais in 1558. In 1560 came the tragedy Jules Cesar, imitated from Muret's Latin, and Les Ebahis, called his most important but most indecent work. He wrote medical books and poems that Ronsard praised, until religious differences parted the friends. From 1561 he was physician to Margaret of Savoy. He died at her court in Turin in 1570.
britannica-1911-grevy-francois-paul-jule:
Francois Paul Jules Grevy (1813-1891) was president of the French Republic, born at Mont-sous-Vaudrey in the Jura on 15 August 1813. The 1911 Britannica entry has him an advocate from 1837, holding republican principles under the Orleans monarchy. His department sent him to the Constituent Assembly of 1848.

Foreseeing Louis Bonaparte's election, Grevy proposed suppressing the presidency itself, vesting power in a council president removable by the Assembly. The coup d'etat made the proposal look wise, and it gave him a lasting name for sagacity. Back in public life in 1868, he presided over the Assembly from 1871 to 1876, then over the Chamber of Deputies. When Marshal MacMahon resigned, he stepped naturally into the presidency on 30 January 1879, elected without opposition. The article follows his presidency and its end in scandal.
britannica-1911-guanches:
The Guanches were the aboriginal inhabitants of the Canary Islands. Strictly, the name belonged to the people of Teneriffe. Spaniards later applied it to all the islands' native peoples. Their name means, in their own speech, man of Teneriffe. Skulls and bones link them to the Cro-Magnon type. Scholars treat them as an offshoot of the Berbers. That race held northern Africa from Egypt to the Atlantic.

The Guanches are now extinct as a distinct people. Many fell resisting the Spanish conquest. Many more were sold as slaves. Others took the Roman Catholic faith and married Spaniards. Their language survives only in fragments and old chiefs' names. Those remains connect it with Berber dialects. Rock inscriptions on several islands proved to be Numidic. Teneriffe and Gomera kept the Guanche type most purely. Their customs and governments varied from island to island.
britannica-1911-guthrie-sir-james:
Sir James Guthrie (1859– ) was a Scottish painter. He was born at Greenock. He led the so-called Glasgow school of painters. John Pettie influenced him in London in his youth. He later studied in Paris. Yet his style owes most to observing nature directly. Joseph Crawhall's example in Lincolnshire also shaped him. Grasp of character marks his work. So do breadth and spontaneity.

Early pictures like the Funeral Service in the Highlands used thick paint. Experience brought greater economy and reticence of colour. He then turned almost wholly to portraiture. His first successes came on the Continent. Scotland elected him associate of its Royal Academy in 1888. Full membership followed in 1892. He became its president in 1902 and was knighted in 1903. His Schoolmates hangs at the Ghent Gallery.
britannica-1911-halle-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Hallé (1819–1895) was a pianist and conductor. He was German by birth, born Karl Halle at Hagen. He studied under Rink at Darmstadt in 1835. Paris took him in 1836 for twelve years. Cherubini, Chopin and Liszt moved in his circle. Alfred de Musset and George Sand were friends too. His chamber concerts with Alard and Franchomme succeeded greatly. The revolution of 1848 drove him to London.

His piano recitals became a feature of London musical life. They spread real knowledge of Beethoven's sonatas in England. From 1853 he directed Manchester's Gentlemen's Concerts. In 1857 he started his own Manchester concert series. Its orchestra reached a perfection unknown in England then. He married the violinist Madame Norman Neruda in 1888. He was knighted in that same year, 1888. He toured Australia and elsewhere with his wife in 1890 and 1891. He died at Manchester in 1895.
britannica-1911-halyburton-james:
James Halyburton (1518–1589) was a Scottish reformer. He was educated at St Andrews and graduated in 1538. From 1553 to 1586 he served as provost of St Andrews. That long tenure made him a national figure. In 1557 he was chosen a lord of the congregation. In 1559 he commanded troops from Forfar and Fife. They marched against the queen regent.

He helped defend Edinburgh against the queen's party. He fought at Langside in 1568 and Restalrig in 1571. He had stoutly opposed Mary's marriage to Darnley. Captured after Restalrig, he narrowly escaped execution. He represented Morton at the conference of 1578. Twice he served as royal commissioner to the General Assembly. Those commissions came in 1582 and 1588. He died in February 1589. The entry is a compact record of a reformer's public career.
britannica-1911-hamilton-james:
James Hamilton (1769–1831) was an English educationist. He devised the Hamiltonian system of teaching languages. His early life went to mercantile pursuits at Hamburg. A French emigré, General d'Angelis, taught him German there. In twelve lessons Hamilton could read an easy German book. His master used no grammar at all. He translated short stories word for word instead.

War ruined Hamilton's Paris trade with England. He reached America in 1814 intending to farm. Instead he taught in New York with remarkable success. Baltimore, Washington, Boston and Canada followed. He returned to England in 1823. His two principles were simple. A language must reach the pupil as a living organism. Its laws must be learned by observation, not rules. Interlinear textbooks carried his method widely. Sydney Smith explained it in the Edinburgh Review in 1826.
britannica-1911-hanbury-williams-sir-cha:
Sir Charles Hanbury Williams (1708–1759) was an English diplomatist and author. He was a son of Major John Hanbury of Pontypool. His family ran Monmouthshire iron-works from 1565. A godfather's fortune brought the Coldbrook estate. Charles took the name Williams in 1729. Eton gave him Henry Fielding as a friend. He sat for Monmouthshire from 1734 to 1747.

London knew him as a gallant and a wit. Following Pope, he wrote much satirical light verse. Collections of his poems appeared in 1763. Diplomacy took him to Dresden in 1746. Berlin, Vienna and St Petersburg followed in turn. At St Petersburg he pushed an Anglo-Russian-Austrian alliance plan. The plan broke down, to his embarrassment. He returned to England a broken man. He took his own life on 2 November 1759. Westminster Abbey holds his grave.
britannica-1911-hannay-james:
James Hannay (1827–1873) was a Scottish critic, novelist and publicist. He was born at Dumfries on 17 February 1827. His family, the Hannays of Sorbie, was ancient in Galloway. He entered the navy in 1840 and served five years. Literature became his profession in 1845. He reported for the Morning Chronicle. Quarterly and monthly journals took his writing next. He edited the Edinburgh Courant from 1860 to 1864.

London received him in 1864. From 1868 he was British consul at Barcelona. His Pall Mall Gazette letters from Spain were highly appreciated. His best books are two naval novels. Singleton Fontenoy (1850) and Eustace Conyers (1855) lead them. Satire and Satirists (1854) sparkles with epigrams. Its estimates of Horace, Swift and Pope are admired. He also edited Poe's poems with a critical essay. He died at Barcelona in 1873.
britannica-1911-heinsius-nikolaes:
Nikolaes Heinsius (1620–1681) was a Dutch scholar, son of Daniel Heinsius. He was born at Leiden on 20 July 1620. A boyish Latin poem on Breda's capture was printed in 1637. It attracted much attention at the time. In 1642 he began wandering in search of classical manuscripts. England gave him little courtesy on that quest. Paris welcomed him with open arms instead.

He collated manuscripts across France, Italy and the Low Countries. Florence paused him to issue a new Ovid. Naples fled him during Masaniello's revolt in 1647. Queen Christina summoned him to Stockholm afterward. There he warred with Salmasius over Milton's facts. Italy claimed him again in 1651. His later life split between Upsala and Holland. His last labours edited Velleius Paterculus in 1678. His son wrote the century's single Dutch romance, Mirandor.
britannica-1911-henley-on-thames:
Henley-on-Thames is a market town in Oxfordshire, England. It stands on the Thames's left bank. A Great Western branch line terminates there. London lies 35 miles west by rail, 57 by river. Its population in 1901 was 5,984. A five-arch stone bridge crosses the river. That bridge was built in 1786. The parish church mixes Decorated and Perpendicular work.

The town is famous for the Henley Royal Regatta. That amateur rowing gathering began in 1839. It usually takes place in July each year. The grammar school was founded in 1605. The manor was granted to John de Molyns in 1337. His family held it about 250 years. Incorporation came in 1570–1571 under Henry VIII's titles. Glass, malt, corn and wool trades brought earlier prosperity. A Thursday market and Corpus Christi fair survive by charter. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Henley entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-henner-jean-jacques:
Jean Jacques Henner (1829–1905) was a French painter, born on the 5th of March 1829 at Dornach in Alsace. He studied under Drolling and Picot, entered the École des Beaux-Arts in 1848, and won the Prix de Rome in 1858 with Adam and Eve finding the Body of Abel. At Rome he worked under Flandrin and painted four pictures for the gallery at Colmar.

Henner first showed at the Salon in 1863 with a Bather Asleep, and sent work there for decades. The pictures named include Chaste Susanna, Byblis turned into a Spring, The Magdalene, Christ Entombed, Saint Jerome, Herodias and The Dream. The Levite of the Tribe of Ephraim, shown in 1898, won a first-class medal. He took a Grand Prix at the Paris International Exhibition of 1900, rose to Commander of the Legion of Honour in 1889, and that year succeeded Cabanel in the Institut de France.
britannica-1911-hervey-james:
James Hervey (1714–1758) was an English divine, born at Hardingstone, near Northampton, on the 26th of February 1714. Schooled at Northampton and at Lincoln College, Oxford, he came under Wesley and the Oxford methodists. In the end he took a firm Calvinistic creed and stayed in the Anglican Church. Ordained in 1737, he held several curacies, and in 1752 took the family livings of Weston Favell and Collingtree.

Never robust, Hervey was a good parish priest and a keen writer with a rare eye for natural beauty. His Meditations and Contemplations ran through fourteen editions in fourteen years. Theron and Aspasio (1755) sold as well but drew fire, even from Calvinists, for leanings toward antinomianism. Wesley attacked it in print, and the row helped spark the Sandemanian dispute over saving faith. Hervey died on the 25th of December 1758.
britannica-1911-hierocles:
Hierocles was proconsul of Bithynia and Alexandria in the reign of Diocletian (A.D. 284–305). He is said to have been the instigator of the fierce persecution of the Christians under Galerius in 303. He wrote a work in two books, now lost, whose title means words of a lover of truth addressed to the Christians.

In it he tried to persuade the Christians that their sacred books were full of contradictions. He also argued that in moral influence and in miraculous power Christ was inferior to Apollonius of Tyana. The work itself has not survived. What is known of it comes from Lactantius, in the fifth book of his Divine Institutes, and from Eusebius, who wrote a formal refutation of it. So the case of a leading pagan official against the new faith reaches us only through the Christian writers who answered him.
britannica-1911-higgins-matthew-james:
Matthew James Higgins (1810–1868) was a British writer born in County Meath, Ireland, on the 4th of December 1810. He wrote over the pen name Jacob Omnium, which was the title of his first magazine article. His letters in The Times did much to expose abuses of the day. He contributed often to the Cornhill magazine.

Higgins was a friend of Thackeray, who dedicated The Adventures of Philip to him. One of Thackeray's ballads, Jacob Omnium's Hoss, turns on an incident in Higgins's career. He died on the 14th of August 1868. Some of his articles were gathered after his death and published in 1875 as Essays on Social Subjects. The short life thus shows a journalist whose weapon was the letter to the editor, and whose name survives chiefly through his friend's dedication and the social essays he left behind.
britannica-1911-hodson-william-stephen-r:
William Stephen Raikes Hodson (1821–1858), known as Hodson of Hodson's Horse, was a British leader of light cavalry in the Indian Mutiny. Born near Gloucester in 1821, he was educated at Rugby and Cambridge and took a cadetship at twenty-three. He fought through the first Sikh War at Moodkee, Ferozeshah and Sobraon. His letters home called that campaign a tissue of blunders, and such bluntness made him enemies for life.

In 1847 Sir Henry Lawrence set him as adjutant of the corps of Guides, and in 1852 he commanded the Guides with civil charge of Yusafzai. In 1855 two charges were brought: that he had wrongfully jailed a Pathan chief, and that his regimental accounts screened fraud. A court of inquiry found his conduct to natives unjustifiable and oppressive, and Dalhousie removed him from his civil post. The long entry weighs his faults against his cavalry fame.
britannica-1911-hogg-james:
James Hogg (1770–1835) was a Scottish poet, known as the Ettrick Shepherd, baptized at Ettrick in Selkirkshire in 1770. His ancestors had been shepherds for centuries, and he got hardly any schooling. From 1790 to 1799 he herded for Mr Laidlaw of Blackhouse in Yarrow, who treated him kindly and opened a large library to him. His first printed piece appeared in the Scots Magazine in 1794, and his Scottish Pastorals in 1801.

In 1802 Hogg met Sir Walter Scott, then gathering his Border Minstrelsy. On Scott's word Constable published The Mountain Bard (1807); his books earned him about £300. He sank the money in farming in Dumfriesshire and was ruined in three years. In February 1810 he set off to push his fortune as a writer in Edinburgh. The Forest Minstrel, his song collection of that year, won him 100 guineas from the countess of Dalkeith. He then started a weekly paper, The Spy.
britannica-1911-holland-charles:
Charles Holland (1733–1769) was an English actor, born in Chiswick, the son of a baker. He first appeared on the stage in the title role of Oroonoko at Drury Lane in 1755. John Palmer, Richard Yates and Mrs Cibber were in the cast. He played under Garrick, and was the first Florizel in Garrick's version of Shakespeare's Winter's Tale.

Garrick thought highly of Holland and wrote a warm epitaph for his monument in Chiswick church. The short life closes with a family note: his nephew, also Charles Holland (1768–1849), was an actor too, and played with Mrs Siddons and Kean. Two generations of the one Chiswick family thus reached the London stage.
britannica-1911-holroyd-sir-charles:
Sir Charles Holroyd (1861– ) is a British artist, born in Leeds on the 9th of April 1861. He studied under Professor Legros at the Slade School, London, with distinction. After six months at Newlyn he won a travelling scholarship and spent two years in Italy, a stay that deeply shaped his art. Back in London he taught two years at the Slade under Legros, giving himself to painting and etching.

His pictures include The Death of Torrigiano (1886), The Satyr King (1889) and Pan and Peasants (1893), counted perhaps his best. For Aveley church in Essex he painted a triptych of the Adoration of the Shepherds and designed a Resurrection window. His chief fame, though, is as an etcher of rare strength and delicacy: the Monte Oliveto, Icarus, Monte Subasio and Eve series are the best known. His principal dry-point is The Bather. Sincerity and a fine sense of composition mark all his work.
britannica-1911-howell-james:
James Howell (c. 1594–1666) was a British author of an old Welsh family, born probably at Abernant in Carmarthenshire, where his father was rector. From the free grammar school at Hereford he went to Jesus College, Oxford, taking his B.A. in 1613. About 1616 he became steward in Sir Robert Mansell's glass-works in Broad Street, and was sent abroad to hire expert workmen.

Howell did not return until 1622, having seen Holland, France, Spain and Italy. The glass trade left behind, he sought a diplomatic post, failed, and tutored briefly. Late in 1622 he went on a special mission to Madrid over a seized English vessel, just as Prince Charles reached the Spanish court. His elaborate allegories are now forgotten, and his language work superseded. But his Letters, the Epistolae Ho-elianae, issued in four volumes between 1645 and 1655, are still models of their kind, though their dates are often made up.
britannica-1911-hurlstone-frederick-yeat:
Frederick Yeates Hurlstone (1800-1869) was an English painter born in London. His father owned a share of the Morning Chronicle. His grand-uncle Richard Hurlstone had been a known painter of portraits a generation before. The young Hurlstone studied under Beechey, Lawrence, and Haydon. In 1820 he entered the Royal Academy as a student and soon began to show work there.

In 1823 Hurlstone won the Academy gold medal for a work of history painting. In 1831 he was chosen for the Society of British Artists, and in 1835 he became its president. He sent most of his work to that body's shows, for he grew into a sharp critic of how the Academy was run. He died in London on 10 June 1869. His works of history and his portraits were very many. A Venetian Page and Prisoner of Chillon are named among them.
britannica-1911-inaudi-jacques:
Jacques Inaudi, born at Onorato in Piedmont on the 15th of October 1867, was an Italian calculating prodigy. While herding sheep at the age of seven or eight, he already showed a striking gift for mental arithmetic. Showmen took notice of the boy, and he began to give public exhibitions of his powers.

Leading French scientists, Charcot among them, examined him with care. They studied him from the points of view of the body, the mind, and mathematics. His gift seemed to rest on a remarkable memory, made stronger by constant practice. It also depended on hearing more than on sight. He reached better results when figures were read aloud to him than when they were written down.
britannica-1911-jumieges:
Jumièges is a village of northwest France, in the department of Seine Inférieure, 17 miles west of Rouen by road, on a peninsula formed by a bend of the Seine. Its population in 1906 was 244. The village is famous for the great ruins of its abbey, a great Benedictine house.

The chief remains are those of the abbey church, built from 1040 to 1067. They include the front with two towers, the walls of the nave, and part of the great central tower. A small museum holds the stone that once covered the grave of Agnes Sorel and two carved figures known as the Énervés. Legend ties them to two sons of Clovis II, set adrift on the Seine after their tendons were cut for revolt. The abbey was founded in the 7th century by St Philibert, destroyed by the Normans, and rebuilt in 928.
britannica-1911-karaiskakis-georges:
Georges Karaiskakis (1782–1827) was a leader in the War of Greek Independence, born at Agrapha in 1782. Yet he saw the need to give the country a government, and he stood steadily by Capo d'Istria.

His most honourable work came in the middle and later stages of the war. He helped raise the first siege of Missolonghi in 1823 and did his best to save the town in the second siege of 1826. That year he led the patriot forces in Rumelia and won some successes against the Turks, welcome amid the disasters of the time. He was shot in action on the 4th of May 1827. Finlay calls him a capable partisan chief with great sway over his men.
britannica-1911-keith-francis-edward-jam:
Francis Edward James Keith (1696–1758) was a Scottish soldier and Prussian field marshal. He was the second son of William, 9th earl marishal of Scotland, and was born on the 11th of June 1696 at Inverugie castle near Peterhead. Schooled with care for the law, at Edinburgh University among other places, he gained a taste for letters that won him the regard of learned men across Europe.

But his bent was for a soldier's life. The rising of 1715, in which he showed signs of his future quality, forced him to flee to the Continent. After two years in Paris he joined the Pretender's failed expedition to the Highlands in 1719. Years of obscurity and poverty in Paris and Madrid followed before he won a colonelcy abroad. The entry follows his climb from exile to the highest rank in Prussian service, a Scotch Jacobite turned marshal of Frederick's army.
britannica-1911-kempt-sir-james:
Sir James Kempt (1764–1854) was a British soldier. He was gazetted to the 101st Foot in India in 1783, but when the regiment was disbanded two years later he was put on half pay. He is said to have taken a clerkship with Greenwood's, the army agents. The Duke of York noticed him, and through the duke he gained a captaincy, and soon a majority, in the new 113th Foot.

That regiment soon met the old one's fate, but Kempt this time stayed on full pay in the recruiting service. In 1799 he went with Sir Ralph Abercromby to Holland, and later to Egypt as an aide. After Abercromby's death he stayed on the staff to the end of the Egyptian campaign. In 1803 he took a lieutenant colonelcy in the 81st Foot and sailed for the Mediterranean.
britannica-1911-kenites:
The Kenites, in the Bible, were a tribe or clan of the south of Palestine, closely tied to the Amalekites, whose enmity toward Israel they did not share. For that reason Saul spared them when he was bid to destroy Amalek. David, too, in his Judah days, seems to have been on friendly terms with them.

Moses himself married into a Kenite family, and the varied tradition hints that the Kenites were only a branch of the Midianites. Jael, the slayer of Sisera, was the wife of Heber the Kenite, who lived near Kadesh in Naphtali. One dark note stands against them: a hint of their destruction in an addition to the oracles of Balaam, perhaps tied to the curse of Cain.
britannica-1911-kenney-james:
James Kenney (1780–1849) was an English dramatist, son of James Kenney, one of the founders of Boodles' Club in London. His first play, a farce called Raising the Wind, came in 1803. It succeeded thanks to the popularity of its character Jeremy Diddler.

Kenney produced more than forty dramas and operas between 1803 and 1845. Many of his pieces enjoyed a fair vogue, and leading players of the day, Mrs Siddons, Madame Vestris, Foote, Lewis, and Liston among them, appeared in them from time to time. His most popular play was Sweethearts and Wives, staged at the Haymarket in 1823 and revived several times after. Other successes named are False Alarms, a comic opera of 1807 with music by Braham, Love, Law and Physic of 1812, and Spring and Autumn of 1827. His tragedy The Sicilian Vespers came in 1840. Charles Lamb was numbered among his friends.
britannica-1911-kermes:
Kermes is a crimson dye stuff, now displaced by cochineal. It is got from a scale insect that lives on oaks. The species used is common in Spain, Italy, the south of France, and round the Mediterranean generally, where it feeds on a small shrub oak. As with other scale insects, the males are fairly small and can fly, while the females are wingless.

The females of the genus are notable for their gall like form. So plant like do they look that their animal nature was not found out until 1714. In May, when full grown, the females are round, six to seven millimetres across, of a reddish brown colour, and covered with an ash coloured powder. They sit fast to the twigs or buds by a round base.
britannica-1911-knight-charles:
Charles Knight (1791–1873) was an English publisher and author, the son of a bookseller and printer at Windsor, where he was born on the 15th of March 1791. After time in journalism he helped start Knight's Quarterly Magazine in 1823, with Praed, Derwent Coleridge and Macaulay among its writers. In 1827 he became superintendent of the publications of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge and planned The British Almanack, begun in 1828.

Knight went on to found The Penny Magazine and The Penny Cyclopaedia in 1832 and 1833, both with large sales, though heavy excise duty made the Cyclopaedia costly to finish. He issued illustrated editions of standard works, among them The Pictorial Shakespeare in 1842, and the Weekly Volumes series. From 1853 he edited The English Cyclopaedia and wrote a Popular History of England (1856–1862). He retired from publishing in 1864 but kept writing almost to the end of his life.
britannica-1911-knucklebones:
Knucklebones, also called hucklebones, dibs, jackstones and five-stones, is a game of very early origin. It is played with five small objects, at first the knucklebones of a sheep, thrown up and caught in set ways. Modern pieces are metal, with six points rising from a common base. The winner is the player who first works through a fixed series of throws. Named forms include "riding the elephant," "peas in the pod" and "horses in the stable."

The game is tied to the origin of dice, of which it may be a first form. Greek tradition credited Palamedes with teaching it during the Trojan War. Both the Iliad and the Odyssey hint at like games. Other accounts differ: Herodotus gives the game to the Lydians in a time of famine under King Atys. Plato names the Egyptian god Theuth as its inventor.
britannica-1911-lacaita-sir-james:
Sir James Lacaita (1813–1895), Anglo-Italian politician and writer, was born at Manduria in southern Italy and practised law in Naples. A moderate Liberal who joined no secret society, he was arrested in 1851, after the Bourbon restoration, for supplying Gladstone with information on Bourbon misrule. The British and Russian ministers got him freed, but when Gladstone's letters to Lord Aberdeen appeared he had to leave Naples. He settled in Edinburgh, then London, and was professor of Italian at Queen's College from 1853 to 1856.

In 1857 he went to Italy with Lord Minto, met Cavour, and became private secretary to Lord Lansdowne until 1863. After serving Gladstone as secretary in the Ionian Islands he was made a K.C.M.G. in 1859. In 1860 Cavour sent him to London to persuade Lord John Russell to refuse British co-operation with a French squadron meant to stop Garibaldi crossing from Sicily to Calabria.
britannica-1911-laches:
Laches, from the Anglo-French lachesse, negligence, is a term for slackness or negligence. In law it means failing to do what one is bound to do, or letting an unreasonable time pass before asserting a right, seeking relief or claiming a privilege. Laches often bars a remedy that could have been had if it had been pursued in proper time.

Statutes of limitation fix the periods within which actions of each class may be brought. Apart from those statutes, courts of equity will often refuse relief to suitors who have let unreasonable time slip by. The governing principle is that the laws help the watchful, not those who sleep.
britannica-1911-lactones:
Lactones are the cyclic esters of hydroxy acids. They form when water is lost inside the molecule, between the hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, as happens when a hydroxy acid is freed from its salts by a mineral acid. The α- and β-hydroxy acids do not form lactones; the tendency first appears with the γ-hydroxy acids, so γ-hydroxybutyric acid yields γ-butyrolactone. Lactones can also be made by distilling γ-halogen fatty acids, by treating those acids with alkaline carbonates, or from unsaturated acids with hydrobromic or dilute sulphuric acid.

Most lactones are liquids, readily soluble in alcohol, ether and water. Boiling with water turns them partly back into the hydroxy acids, and caustic alkalis saponify them easily. γ-Butyrolactone boils at 206° C. and mixes with water in all proportions; γ-valerolactone boils at 207–208° C. δ-Lactones are also known and can be prepared by distilling the δ-chlor acids.
britannica-1911-laestrygones:
The Laestrygones were a mythical race of giants and cannibals. In the Odyssey they dwell in the farthest north, where the nights are so short that a shepherd driving out his flock meets another driving his in. That detail may carry a hint of the nightless Arctic summer, reaching the Greeks through merchants who fetched amber from the Baltic coasts. Odysseus reached their coast in his wanderings and escaped with one ship only; the giants sank the rest with masses of rock. Their chief city was Telepylus, founded by king Lamus, while Antiphates ruled when Odysseus came.

Later Greeks placed the Laestrygones in Sicily, south of Aetna near Leontini. Horace and other Latin writers put them in southern Latium, near Formiae, which was supposed to have been founded by Lamus.
britannica-1911-laffitte-jacques:
Jacques Laffitte (1767–1844), French banker and politician, was born at Bayonne on the 24th of October 1767. He became a clerk in Perregaux's Paris banking house, a partner in 1800, and head of the firm in 1804. The house became one of the greatest in Europe. Laffitte was regent of the Bank of France in 1809 and governor in 1814. He raised sums for the provisional government in 1814 and for Louis XVIII during the Hundred Days. Napoleon deposited five million francs with him before leaving France.

After Waterloo he paid two million francs from his own pocket for the imperial troops' arrears, rather than let the government take Bank money. Elected deputy for the Seine in 1816, he sat on the Left and spoke chiefly on finance. In 1818 he saved Paris from a financial crisis by buying stock heavily, but in 1819 his defence of the liberty of the press cost him the governorship of the Bank.
britannica-1911-laguerre-jean-henri-geor:
Jean Henri Georges Laguerre (1858– ), French lawyer and politician, was born in Paris on the 24th of June 1858. Called to the bar in 1879, he made his name by brilliant pleadings for socialist and anarchist leaders. He defended Prince Kropotkin at Lyons in 1883 and Louise Michel the same year. In 1886, with Millerand, he defended the Decazeville strike leaders Roche and Duc-Quercy. Libellous attacks on prosecutors brought him suspension from the bar in 1886 and again in 1890. From 1893 he pleaded only in the provinces, shut out of the Paris bar.

He entered the Chamber of Deputies for Apt in 1883 on the extreme revisionist programme and became a leader of the Boulangist agitation. He had written for Clemenceau's La Justice, then directed La Presse himself. In May 1891 he rallied to the republican party, and he was not re-elected in 1893. He was also a noted lecturer on the revolutionary period of French history.
britannica-1911-lambeth-conferences:
The Lambeth Conferences are the assemblies of the bishops of the Anglican Communion, meeting since 1867 at Lambeth Palace, the London home of the archbishop of Canterbury. The idea was first proposed by Bishop Hopkins of Vermont in a letter of 1851, but the impulse came from Canada. In 1865 the Canadian synod wrote to Archbishop Longley. Privy Council decisions had troubled Canadian church members, who feared drifting into the status of an independent branch of the Church.

Longley consulted the Convocation of Canterbury and convened the bishops of the Communion to meet at Lambeth in 1867. Many doubted the wisdom of the assembly: the archbishop of York and most of his bishops stayed away, and Dean Stanley refused Westminster Abbey for the closing service. At a later conference, American bishops helped replace a proposed "tribunal of reference" with a resolution favouring a body for counsel, and the letter carried sixty-three resolutions.
britannica-1911-lamoureux-charles:
Charles Lamoureux (1834-1899) was born at Bordeaux. He made his name in Paris as a conductor and violinist. German music was his cause. Trained at Pau, he played at the Opéra. He ran chamber concerts from 1864. In 1873 he led the first Paris performance of Handel's Messiah. A sacred music society he funded himself backed that night.

His own concert series began in 1881. Those concerts spread Wagner's music widely in Paris. In May 1887 he staged Lohengrin at the Eden Theatre. The opera was new to the French capital. Protest stopped a repeat. Posts at the Opéra Comique and the Opéra followed. He died in Paris in December 1899. Days before, he had led Tristan und Isolde there at last.
britannica-1911-leo-johannes:
Johannes Leo (about 1494-1552), known as Leo Africanus, wrote the Description of Africa. That book long ranked as the best guide to Muslim Africa. Born most likely at Granada of noble Moorish stock, he learned much at Fez. Travel began young across the Barbary states.

Journeys of 1513 to 1515 took him to Timbuktu and the Niger lands. Egypt and Constantinople followed. On the way home about 1520, pirates seized him near Gerba. He was given as a slave to Pope Leo X. The pope freed his mind with a pension and stood sponsor at his baptism. Leo taught Arabic at Rome and wrote in Latin and in Italian. His Africa book came out at Rome in March 1526.
britannica-1911-leochares:
Leochares was a Greek sculptor of the 300s B.C. He worked with Scopas on the Mausoleum about 350 B.C. For Philip of Macedon he made gold and ivory statues of the royal house. Philip set them in the Philippeum at Olympia. With Lysippus he made a bronze lion-hunt group at Delphi.

Other works named are statues of Zeus, Apollo, and Ares. A Vatican statuette of Ganymede borne off by an eagle matches a group Pliny ascribes to him. The copy is much restored and poor in craft. Still, its Attic traits back the link. Close likeness in head and pose ties the Apollo Belvidere to the same hand, some argue. A fine Alexander at Munich is also held a copy of his Olympia portrait.
britannica-1911-leotychides:
Leotychides was a Spartan king of the Eurypontid house. He took the throne in 491 B.C. His claim beat that of Demaratus, with help from Cleomenes. He joined the second raid on Aegina. Ten hostages were seized there and left with Athens for safe keeping.

In spring 479 he led the Greek fleet of 110 ships. The fleet lay first at Aegina, then at Delos. In August he struck the Persian post at Mycale. The land army was crushed and the beached fleet wiped out. In 476 he marched on Thessaly to punish the Aleuadae. A bribe bought his retreat. Trial at Sparta followed. He fled to a temple at Tegea and took exile. His house was razed and his grandson took the throne.
britannica-1911-leptines:
Leptines was an Athenian speaker known for one law. His rule barred grants that freed men from state festival costs. Citizens and resident aliens both fell under it. One line alone kept the grant: the heirs of Harmodius and Aristogeiton. Festival funds were the aim. The treasury and the citizens were both short of cash.

Demosthenes spoke against the law in 354 B.C. His speech backed a plan to test each grant case by case. It warned that scrapping grants would brand Athens as thankless and false. It also charged a fault in form. An older law that backed the grants still stood unrepealed. Solon's rules barred a new law till the clash was cleared. The law was most likely struck down. Nothing more of Leptines is known.
britannica-1911-lesches: Lesches is the reputed maker of the Little Iliad, one of the cyclic poems of Greece. Custom makes him a man of Pyrrha in Lesbos, set about 660 B.C. The poem took up the tale where the Iliad stops. It opened with Ajax and Odysseus in strife for the arms of Achilles. From there it ran to the fall of Troy. A summary in Proclus ends it with the wooden horse inside the walls.
britannica-1911-leslie-charles:
Charles Leslie (1650-1722) was an Irish churchman who would not swear to new rulers. Dublin was his birthplace in July 1650. His father had held two Irish sees. Enniskillen school and Trinity College formed him. Law came first, then orders in 1680. A chancellor's post at Connor came in 1687.

Public debate with the Catholic bishop of Clogher opened his long war of words. Loyal to the Stuarts, he lost his post rather than swear to William and Mary. Twenty years of pamphlets followed. Quakers, Jews, Socinians, Catholics, and Deists all drew his fire. A warrant in 1710 sent him to the Pretender at Bar-le-Duc. Italy held him till 1721. Home at last, he died at Glaslough on 13 April 1722. His church works filled two folio volumes in 1721.
britannica-1911-limoges:
Limoges is a town of west-central France. It heads the department of Haute-Vienne. Orleans lies 176 miles north by the road to Toulouse. Town count in 1906 was 75,906. The commune held 88,597. A hill on the right bank of the Vienne holds the town.

Two old parts split the ground. The Cité, low on the slope, keeps tight streets and old houses. The upper town holds the Rue de la Boucherie and its strong butchers' guild. Ring roads sit where walls once stood. The cathedral leads the Limousin in fame. Work began in 1273. Choir came in 1327 and transept by the mid-1500s. Nave work ran again from 1875 to 1890. A fine Renaissance screen stands inside. Four bridges and a rail viaduct cross the Vienne. Two bridges date to the 1200s.
britannica-1911-patarenes: Patarenes, or Paratelli, is a name first used in Milan about 1058. It named the strong foes of marriage among the clergy. The party took its name from the quarter of the city where its members met to plan their acts. That quarter was the Pataria, the ragmen's quarter, from a local word for a rag. In the 1200s the Cathari took the name for their own and said it came from a Latin word for to suffer.
britannica-1911-patrocles:
